speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We see the sharpening rivalry between the United States (US) and China, and the erosion of the rules-based order that has enabled Singapore to survive so far.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Increasingly, we face a divided world where aggression, coercion and the weaponisation of trade have become commonplace, while rapid technological change reshapes our societies at an unprecedented pace.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Against this backdrop, the President set out four key challenges.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: More importantly, he reminded us that our future depends on unity; nurturing a “we first” society built on trust, resilience and shared purpose.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is through this lens that I shape my speech today.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: As a Member of Parliament (MP) and through my professional experience, I have had conversations with residents of Pasir Ris-Changi, Singaporeans from all walks of life, foreign professionals, investors, businesses from multinational corporations (MNCs) and small and medium enterprises (SMEs) to local stallholders in our pasar.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In our communities, including the Malay/Muslim community, two anxieties stand out most clearly.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And secondly, on the cost of living and the cost of doing business: from rent to wages to dealing with tariffs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In conversations with fresh graduates, a common refrain is their struggle to land that first job.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Many tell me they have sent over a hundred curriculum vitae (CVs) without a single reply.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: They have tried LinkedIn, career coaches, networking events, peer-support groups; yet remain unemployed.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Parents too share their anxiety, contrasting today’s reality with the past when jobs came more quickly.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Graduates lament that companies demand experience, but without the opportunity, how can they ever gain it?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Silence from employers with CVs submitted leaves them questioning whether vacancies are real, whether they are being overlooked, or whether there are deeper structural issues in the job market.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: For private institution graduates, outcomes were worse, with fewer securing jobs and fewer securing full-time roles.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: However, this is not a simple Private Education Institution versus Autonomous University comparison.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The real issue is whether courses equip graduates with the skills the industry demands.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The trend is clear: our young graduates face a tougher, more uncertain path.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And we must work together to make things better for them.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: On the other hand, employers see the problem differently but no less seriously.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: MNCs, SMEs and local enterprises all share the same challenge: they cannot find enough Singaporeans to fill the roles.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Hiring managers struggle to find the right candidates.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The 2025 ManpowerGroup Employment Outlook Survey found that 43% of employers still intend to hire.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: On MyCareersFuture, more than 23,000 of the 68,000 listed jobs are for fresh graduates, executives, and senior executives, in roles such as engineers, marketers, data specialists and operational planners.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: So we face a paradox: graduates say they cannot find jobs, while businesses say they cannot find workers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The mismatch lies not in the numbers but in alignment – between skills taught and skills and experience demanded and between expectation and realities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) has framed this paradox through four gaps: the Expectation Gap, the Skills Gap, the Opportunity Gap, and the Experience Gap.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I would add a fifth: the Job Redesign Gap.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: On the Expectation Gap: technology has reshaped hiring.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: With one-click portals and AI-tailored CVs, jobseekers can now apply for dozens, if not hundreds, of roles daily.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Employers are swamped with CVs, making it unrealistic to expect replies to every applicant.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Jobseekers and their parents must adjust to this new reality.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: On the Job Redesign Gap: with AI, businesses are struggling to define entry-level roles fast enough.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Tasks once designed by fresh graduates such as research, doing slides, doing minutes, are now automated.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Companies need graduates who can apply AI but within a business context.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This requires rethinking roles so fresh graduates remain cost-effective contributors while still gaining the experience.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: So, how do we bridge these gaps then?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And I would like to offer four suggestions.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: GRiT supports graduates from universities, polytechnics, the Institutes of Technical Education (ITEs) and private institutions, giving them industry-relevant skills.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It provides an allowance- up to 70% funded by WSG, and 30% by host organisations.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We need more businesses to come forward to invest in our graduates to mentor them, to give them the business context and prepare them for future roles.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Unlike short, unstructured internships which has limited success, apprenticeships must provide both technical training, the business context and workplace readiness.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Within government, industries and education institutions must align their efforts and set standards.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Germany’s dual education system is instructive: combining classroom learning with real workplace training which produces industry-ready talent.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: By adapting some of the useful elements of such approaches, Singapore can fill critical skills gaps and uplift vocational careers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In Pasir Ris-Changi, one of our volunteers, Arshad, together with Al-Mawaddah Mosque and M³ at Pasir Ris-Changi, organised an overnight biking event ending with professionals sharing their work experience with youths.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Such grassroots efforts from peer-support groups can link professional networks to the jobseekers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: If Government, businesses, educators, unions and the community stand together in a “we first” spirit, we can close the gaps, redesign roles and prepare our people for the future.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In Singapore, pressures are compounded by our reliance on imports and tight labour markets.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: While we can manage volatility, we remain a price-taker.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The sustainable path forward is for wages to rise faster than costs, through productivity and through better jobs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Government support through Community Development Council (CDC) vouchers, U-Save, service and conservancy charges (S&CC) rebates, cash payouts and MediSave top-ups has provided some cushioning for families.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But the rising cost of doing business must not be overlooked.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Small shops such as food and beverage (F&B) outlets, retailers, minimarts, lifestyle stores, gyms and neighbourhood shops, are place-makers, the heartbeat of our communities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: They greet us daily, serve our families for years and give our areas character.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: They make our communities vibrant and provide comfort in the familiarity of everyday life.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Yet behind the counter, many face this deep anxiety.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: They pour their savings into renovations and equipment, only to find leases shorter than their recovery periods.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The looming fear of the next rent increase weighs heavily on their minds.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Many cannot simply pass the costs to customers without losing them, nor can they sustain wages for their staff if margins collapse.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This uncertainty forces them to worry about survival instead of focusing on growth.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We must give these small businesses greater assurance and I would like to offer a few suggestions.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I am not suggesting rent control in any way.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Instead, let us provide incentives, such as tax benefits or recognition for landlords who adopt these fair guidelines.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Transparent rental benchmarks, tied to indices like CPI plus a margin for rent escalations, can prevent unreasonable hikes while preserving fairness.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: By embracing a "we first" mindset, landlords, businesses and Government can lower costs, reduce uncertainty and give small shops some peace of mind.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This might also encourage entrepreneurship and support the startup culture.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: When our small businesses worry less about survival, they can focus on what matters: improving their services, raising productivity and developing their staff.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: That is how we keep our communities vibrant, our livelihoods secure and our society coming together.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is about securing good jobs for Singaporeans, ensuring rising incomes and improving the quality of life for our people.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In every strategy that we take, our end goal must always be clear: to create opportunities that uplift our workers, strengthen our families and build a society where every Singaporean can look to the future with confidence.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Change also brings renewal, new opportunities, new industries and new ways of living.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I am encouraged that the Government has formed the Singapore Economic Resilience Taskforce, to help us seize these opportunities and chart our path forward with unity and purpose.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In this spirit, I would like to offer a few suggestions on how we can turn this moment of change into one of renewal and growth.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Opportunities are opening in AI, advanced manufacturing, biotechnology, clean energy, and sustainability.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In its totality, AI is projected to unlock billions in productivity gains across sectors, while advanced manufacturing and robotics will drive high-value careers in precision engineering.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Biotechnology is transforming medicine, food, and materials science and clean energy from renewables to emerging technologies like small modular nuclear reactors will strengthen our energy security.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Beyond these, niche sectors, such as quantum technologies, space and satellite services, cybersecurity, and the blue economy, they all hold potential for new growth.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: These industries are not the ends in themselves.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: They are pathways to secure better jobs, higher incomes and long-term competitiveness for our Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We must refresh our Industry Transformation Maps and align them with the Jobs Transformation Maps, our Company Training Committees (CTCs), our National AI Strategy, our CTO-as-a-Service and all other alphabet soups of support schemes that we have.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Many businesses, especially SMEs, find the landscape a bit fragmented and a bit harder to navigate.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: A single agency or a unified user-oriented portal would help simplify the access, enabling firms to focus on transformation and focus on growth.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: By doing so, we strengthen our enterprises, preserve Singapore's position as a trusted global hub and ensure that the opportunities created at the national level translate into tangible gains for workers and families.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Thirdly, we must anchor Singapore's aspiration to remain a global aviation and aerospace hub.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And here, I would like to declare my interest as one of the workers in the aerospace industry.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Within less than 60 minutes of Pengerang, just 20 kilometres away and Batam, the Northeast Singapore is also strategically positioned to complement Pengerang's oil and gas sector at the Pengerang Integrated Complex and Batam's manufacturing base in addition to its central location and its global connectivity.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Together with the Johor-Singapore Strategic Economic Zone (SEZ), this ecosystem can secure good jobs for Singaporeans, boost supply chain resilience and anchor Singapore firmly within the global economy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: An inclusive society is one where every Singaporean has the chance to contribute and more importantly, flourish.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Technology can and must be used for good and there are ways to which we can use technology towards building a more inclusive society Firstly, through supporting the less able.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Assistive technologies, such as screen readers, navigation apps, sensors, provide independence.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: For example, AI-powered wayfinding tools integrated into Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) stations can help guide the visually impaired.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: One of my residents lost his sight in his 50s.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: He travels with his elderly mother in a wheelchair and his special needs sister who is also in her 50s.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Each contributes a different sense of touch, mobility, vision, or knowledge as they navigate through the town.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: He was excited by the pilot of wayfinding tools, such as CityGeni, to help his family move independently.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: More can be done for families like this.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And with a "we first" mindset, agencies and partners can make inclusive innovation a reality.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: While grants like the Home Caregiving Grant help financially, technology can lighten the load.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Smart eldercare sensors, telehealth, AI-enabled scheduling, and robotic aids can reduce strain.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Scaling these solutions into community care networks, while keeping them affordable, gives caregivers peace of mind and helps seniors live with dignity.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We must find ways to adopt them quicker and scale faster to move beyond pilot trials.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The Assistive Tech sector, CareTech and the Silver Economy are fast-growing industries.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: By investing here, Singapore can export solutions and become a trusted hub for inclusive technology.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We will build not only a competitive economy, but also a compassionate one where every citizen feel they matter and belong. :   In my speech earlier, I expressed our thanks to the President for providing a clear backdrop during the Opening of the 15th Parliament.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The President reminded us that the world we face today is volatile and he described it not as "transient headwinds" but as "fundamental shifts in the tides." Under such circumstances, two core emotions shape human responses.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Second, hope – for growth, opportunities and a brighter future.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is through these two lenses that I frame my speech today.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In Singapore, this situation is further complicated by our dependence on imports and our tight labour market.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The reality is that we remain as "price-takers".

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Therefore, upskilling and mastering new skills must become part of our lives.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In my dialogue with Malay union leaders such as Mr Abdul Samad Bin Abdul Wahab, they emphasised how Unions help workers upskill; by shifting mindsets from merely protecting jobs to protecting workers by providing a better future.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Our community must also leverage on national programmes such as SkillsFuture Credit, WSQ, Career Conversion, Career Transition, and the Tech Accelerator programme.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: As the Malay saying goes, loosely translated as "no pain, no gain." In Pasir Ris–Changi, we have worked with NTUC to bring these programmes closer to the residents.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: While changing tides bring a lot of anxiety, they also bring a lot of hope.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: New industries are emerging; such as advanced manufacturing, robotics, precision engineering, biotechnology, quantum technology, satellite services and many more.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: All these are new pathways to better jobs and higher incomes.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: To seize these opportunities, we must first raise awareness.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Through these networks, opportunities are made available to our community.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In fact, just last week, a resident shared that her husband got an engineering job through one of these networks.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I strongly encourage more in our community to join them.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Additionally, these professional networks also give back to the community.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Just last week in Pasir Ris-Changi, the M³ Engineering Professional Network, together with SUTD and Mendaki, organised Robot Wars, where students built AI-based robots, learnt coding, sensors and object recognition.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: For some participants, this was their first experience with robotics.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It was very moving to see their confidence increase and their eyes light up with these new skills.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Another source of hope is progress for our asatizah.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: With the implementation of phase three this year, more will be within the CSG guidelines.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Asatizah are the pillars of our community, and their work must be recognised and fairly compensated.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This college will produce asatizah and future leaders, not only for Singapore, but also for the global context.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Its adjacent location to SUSS is very meaningful.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It opens up cross-institutional opportunities; combining Islamic studies with fields such as social work, Islamic finance, business, and mental health.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This demonstrates our strength as a united community – a "we first society" as mentioned by the President.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: By leveraging on national programmes, strengthening professional networks, elevating the status of asatizah and realising SCIS, we can build a brighter future.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Let us work hand in hand to think far ahead, invest in our community, and build pathways with much hope.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This is how we transform anxiety into hope and ensure our community continues to progress in the years to come. : Mr Speaker, Sir, the challenges before us are real.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The worries of our jobseekers, the struggles of our families coping with costs and the worries of small businesses are real.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In new industries, in new inclusive innovation and in refreshed economic strategies that can bring about better jobs and better ways to care for our society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Let us, therefore, choose to be a "we first" society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This is how we can turn anxiety into hope.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This is how we renew our social compact.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This is how we can build a stronger, more united Singapore together.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While the Workers' Party (WP) is in opposition, we call on Singaporeans to heed the call to build a better Singapore for ourselves and our future generations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Today, I will highlight what the WP sees as the international and domestic pressures facing us.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: After that, I will focus on the President's call for a "we first" society, a term that Prime Minister Lawrence Wong also used at his National Day Rally last month.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I remember at the time, a newly-retired Minister shed tears at a press conference over what "globalisation had done to Singaporean workers." This year, US President Donald Trump has challenged globalisation more directly than ever before.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: His Liberation Day tariffs in April put the brakes on several decades of an economic era that Singapore had ridden successfully, albeit not without its discontents for some Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For the foreseeable future, nearshoring, friendshoring and protectionism are the order of the day.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We enter an uncertain and unpredictable post-SG60 world.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To use the parlance of the late US Secretary of Defense Donald Rumsfeld, the imposition of additional tariffs on Singapore exports to the US are more of a known unknown rather than an unknown unknown.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the Asia Pacific, we are in the throes of a geostrategic transition.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Recently, China showcased both its ambition as well as its alliances at a spectacular military parade commemorating 80 years since the end of World War II.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: China demonstrated that it is ready to take its place as a leading power in the world.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: China, a hugely successful economic power, is fast becoming a military juggernaut.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It can no longer bide its time nor hide its strength.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To many, this must mean a diminution of US influence in the Asia Pacific.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But China appears to have considered that it need not behave like a hegemon and displace Pax Americana.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: China seems intent on deepening friendships and collaboration, thereby representing itself as a force for stability and cooperation even as it stands up to America whenever it deems necessary.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As for the US, its current administration is recalibrating the norms and values that traditionally underpinned its pre-eminent position in the Asia Pacific and beyond.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, the US still retains significant goodwill from many Asia Pacific countries.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Its historical actions at the cost of American blood arrested the advance of Communism in the region.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It provided an effective security umbrella that allowed Southeast Asian nations, including Singapore, to grow and prosper.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There may well be enough space for the US and China to coexist in the region even as flashpoints, such as Taiwan, and possible nuclear weapons proliferation in East Asia remain known unknowns.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What is clear is that defence spending is rising all around.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We must brace for turbulence, even as we hope that the turbulence remains only that, while we look to secure our future in a new strategic environment.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A strong SAF, Home Team and a first-rate diplomatic corps give us the agency to think for ourselves and our own national interests.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The current strategic environment is yet another reminder of how critical the Singapore Armed Forces, the Home Team agencies and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs are.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It also reinforces the importance of National Service.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The security that our people in uniform provide is an important strength of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I repeat this call today in light of the President's address.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Domestically, SG60 comes at a unique inflection point for us.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fact, the first Ministerial Committee on Ageing was set up decades ago.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, living through a transition and being on the cusp of it hit differently.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In addition, more employers prefer to offer short-term contract jobs rather than permanent positions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: From the slow demise of traditional foods to the closing down of cinemas and the downsizing of bookstores, all these contribute to a sense of loss that weighs heavily on many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These emotions are not unexpected, because Singaporeans do not want to become a people who know the price of everything, but the value of nothing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We must try to preserve as much of the different strands of our cultural tapestry in our national interest instead of resigning ourselves to the inevitability of change.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Just as there is value in learning new things, there is value in remembering the past and the wisdom it endows.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At this critical junction in our nation's journey, how does the WP define its Parliamentary role?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Five years ago, at the Opening of Parliament then, I said that the WP will chart an independent path and fulfil its duty as a loyal opposition.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Our loyalty is the people and to the nation and, this term, fidelity to the three key functions of Parliament: to make laws, to check on the Government and to scrutinise the state's finances, will come into distinct focus.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With so much happening domestically and internationally, the opposition will primarily focus on the function that Parliament demands of us, checking the Government's policies and actions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Every question we ask is one that needs asking, especially since the opposition does not receive any special Government briefings, unlike the People's Action Party (PAP) MPs; and neither are there Parliamentary Select Committees to scrutinise the work of the various Ministries when Parliament is not in session.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, over the last three months, as we heard during Parliamentary Question Time today, there has been a spade of Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) breakdowns from July.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Like anything mechanical, breakdowns do occur and this in and of itself is not the issue.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some Singaporeans think that when we ask questions, we are trying to embarrass the Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The WP does not see it that way.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Checking the Government is a function of system design.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is something our early leaders understood and is an essential feature of the Westminster system we adopted from the British.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To borrow an old technological phrase, questioning the Government in Parliament is a feature, not a bug.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Embracing this feature will be an important priority for the WP in this term of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Where alternative proposals and improvements to existing policies need to be raised, we will raise them accordingly.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If our fellow Singaporean workers and professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs) wish to suggest matters for us to raise in this House, please contact us.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We welcome inputs which are backed by evidence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We also welcome organisations, including small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and corporates to engage with us with a view towards better policies for our economy and our people.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We believe that the prospect of the opposition raising issues in Parliament has a strong nudging effect in getting the issues recognised and addressed by the Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We thank all parties for their good faith and engagement, most recently over the issues faced by platform workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: All Singaporeans are collectively interested in the betterment of our people.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Engagement with the opposition and the WP, in particular, reflects a society that treasures, supports and makes effective use of a balanced political system.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A Singapore that understands that it is both government MPs and opposition MPs who contribute to make Singapore worth fighting for, puts Singapore on a stronger footing for the challenges to come.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The individual must feel a sense of belonging to Singapore and an affinity to the community around him or her.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This brings me to the President's call to put "we" before "me".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is a theme that continues from the Prime Minister's National Day Rally.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is a simple idea, but a timeless one too.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singapore has wrestled with the ambit of such communitarian concepts in the past, but one can understand the significance of reiterating this call in light of present times.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The White Paper on Shared Values was subject to intense debate over two days in this House.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Former Speaker Abdullah Tarmugi argued that two values, first, "Nation before community and society above self” and second, "Regard and community support for the individual", slanted too heavily towards society and community, with not enough premium placed on the individual.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: He said, and I quote, "People are afraid that these values would lead to a stifling of the individual.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While individualism, per se, is not a good value to promote, over-emphasis on the community could lead to a stifling of innovation and creativity and hence reduce our competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The line between the two has to be carefully drawn." Another PAP MP, Dr Ong Chit Chung, shared that the most problematic of all values appeared to be "Consensus instead of Contention", as there was a fear or suspicion that the Government would use this call for consensus to browbeat critics, stifle creativity and muzzle opponents.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Yet another PAP MP asserted that his conversations with students, grassroots leaders and business colleagues gave him, and I quote, "the distinct impression that many people scoff at the idea of a paper on Shared Values.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Most of these things are obvious, they say.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is it necessary for Government to try to push yet another load of sanctimony down our throats?" The public reaction and the qualified cynicism aside, the vision of the White Paper itself was not objectionable.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Despite references to Singapore as an Asian society, the White Paper acknowledged that not everything Asian was good and not everything Western was bad.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Senior Minister of State, Dr Tay Eng Soon, sought to clarify that the Government neither wanted, and I quote, "blind conformity and compliance in the name of nation or of consensus", which he alluded to as a disease that, I quote, is "not unknown in the East and that tyranny of the majority may be even worse than individualism".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: He argued that the shared values must never be an excuse to stamp out individual ideas and aspirations that can lead to new achievements.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: His view was that we must always encourage individual excellence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I believe there is a wisdom to them, because they foment and advance a unifying ethos.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And there is evidence that many of us care deeply about what it means to be Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That was a conversation series on Singapore's COVID-19 experience and Singaporeans' aspirations for a more resilient post-COVID-19 society.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, it is clear that the idea of "we" is important to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But I would assert that it certainly does not mean suppressing or minifying the importance and central role of the individual and his or her place in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would instead argue that "we" and "me" are perspectives that exist on a continuum.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A binary treatment is limiting, while an over-emphasis on one is not consistent with our lived experiences.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We should aim for excellence as individuals and venture forth with confidence as individuals and be respected by society as individuals, regardless of race, language, religion and backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At the same time, an awareness of "we" beyond our comfort zones opens opportunities for us not just to be better, but to be the best versions of ourselves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A sense of personal fulfilment and purpose are more likely to be achieved when we contribute to something larger than ourselves and aim beyond self-enrichment and personal outcomes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Perhaps the most important point to be made here is that Singaporeans are well and truly in the driver's seat of shaping the Singapore they wish to see.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While Singaporeans may struggle today to list the five shared values of 1991, as naturally as they say the pledge or national anthem, the importance of living harmoniously in a multiracial and multi-religious society is not lost on many.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Increasingly, however, there is a sense that being a member of a racial and religious group, on the one hand, and our identity as Singaporeans are both equally important.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For some, like myself and those of my generation, being Singaporean and a part of the country and something larger, edges in importance compared to one's cultural rootedness and sense of loyalty to our individual communities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For some younger people, the Singapore identity can be said to have even transcended race.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The former Chief of Government Communications was recently quoted in a podcast as saying that his younger colleagues did not make much of the fact that the squadron commander who led the flypast at this year's National Day Parade was Malay.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would suggest that this shows that, for a younger generation of Singaporeans, at least some Singaporeans, a democratic society based on justice and equality ought not to be declared just in words but must be manifested in deeds.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It may well be that the aspiration of the pledge has morphed, at least for some, into an expectation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We should acknowledge and even celebrate such expectations as the ultimate reflection of a more united people than ever before.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Hybrid conflicts are already a reality and we can see how misinformation and disinformation, especially online, have been employed by some to fuel narratives that divide communities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In speech, be it online or offline, it is easy to bully and intimidate others with rank, popularity and labels, and by punching down at those who may not have the full facts or see the world differently.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is much harder to take on someone your own size or bigger or engage an issue respectfully regardless the counterparty.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But we should all choose the more difficult path of empathy and mutual respect, even if we agree to disagree.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is even as we hold dear and celebrate our individual mother tongues, traditions, religions and cultures.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We do this in an English-speaking environment, one that goes a long way to create an accessible and welcoming global city for trade and investment, and an accessible and expansive public space for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If we succeed in building on this foundation, we will not just shine but survive and thrive well beyond SG60.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The WP will continue to play its part.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 4.24 pm until 4.45 pm.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Because of our collective efforts, many workers, including professionals, managers and executives (PMEs), have seen real improvements in wages, welfare and work prospects.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Amidst rising cost of living, we raised our lower wage workers' incomes.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Workplace Fairness has also been strengthened so that all workers – especially our mature PMEs – are assured of a level playing field.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We provided new support for our involuntarily unemployed workers and supported our caregivers' flexible work arrangement (FWA) requests.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Senior workers now have a longer runway, should they choose to do so, to work.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: But Mr Deputy Speaker, beyond policies and numbers, what mattered most really, is the impact on ordinary people and workers.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Amidst the rising cost of living, every wage increase, every new protection and every training scheme made a real difference.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Families and workers were able to be better provided for.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: This is why I am in the House today, to ensure that every Singaporean worker and family can face the future with confidence.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Trade wars, tech wars, hot wars are redefining the rules-based order that Singapore has long depended on.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: And technologies, like AI are reshaping how we live, learn and work – faster than many of us can keep up with.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Internally, the realities of becoming a superaged society will hit us.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: More of our workers will be older and more families will experience more strain from caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: During my block visits in Jalan Kayu and in many conversations with workers at union events and community gatherings, I have heard the anxieties of our people.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Young graduates worry if they will find good jobs; mid-career and older PMEs fear being displaced by AI and economic restructuring; families struggle with the pressures of caregiving – wondering how they can cope with the financial, physical and emotional strains.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: They are the daily worries of ordinary Singaporeans trying to secure a better future for themselves and their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Two, uplift our vulnerable lower-wage workers, platform workers and freelancers by ensuring fair earnings and dignified work.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Three, stronger support for our caregivers, so no Singaporean has to choose between caring for their loved ones and keeping their job.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: My fellow labour MPs and I will outline the priorities of the Labour Movement to advance these fronts.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: I will focus my address on two areas today, ensuring good jobs amidst AI disruption and better support for caregivers.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: It can boost productivity and help businesses stay competitive.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: On the flip side, I know many workers, including PMEs, see AI as a threat.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Big companies, such as Amazon and Microsoft, are cutting jobs.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Drivers worry about being displaced and replaced by autonomous vehicles.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: They do not know what AI will mean for them and their jobs.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: It can be daunting not knowing what to expect and perhaps worse, how to keep up.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: They say: "I know AI is here, but Sec-Gen, I don't know what I can do." This is why we must do more to equip our workers to meet AI disruption head on, bring the right tools and know-how to the businesses and our workers, so that they can take proactive steps to seize AI-driven opportunities.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: It will serve as a one-stop platform to integrate existing resources from Government and tripartite partners, so businesses and workers can be truly AI ready.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Through "AI-Ready SG", workers can access dedicated resources for upskilling and navigate career transitions.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Employers can tap into resources to embark on practical AI transformation.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: The "AI-Ready SG" initiative can ride on the CTC ecosystem to support AI transformation.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: And this goes in part in answering some colleagues' earlier speeches about converging business interest and marrying it to workers' interest.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Businesses get help to figure out what AI means to them, chart out their transformation roadmap and implement projects that deliver real productivity gains.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: At the same time, workers, including PMEs can better map out their AI skills upgrading pathways, boosting their job security and work prospects along with their companies' business transformation.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: In fact, NTUC and employers have started using the CTC model to catalyse AI transformation.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Take BSL Unify, a manufacturing services company, for example.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Through the CTC, they embarked on a company-wide digital transformation programme and implemented an AI-powered service portal.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Previously, customer service and operations staff relied on excel sheets to labouriously track inventory and manage enquiries manually.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: This is just one example of how "AI-Ready SG" can help companies move up the value chain and bring workers, including PMEs, along.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: For workers, including PMEs, AI upskilling must mean better jobs, better wages and better work prospects.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: If we can do these, we will be able exploit AI to transform our economy and better Singaporean lives.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Yet, many workers still struggle with the day-to-day reality of caregiving.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Balancing a job while tending to the needs of a sick elderly parent, a child or an adult with special needs, can be exhausting.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: It is not just about managing the time.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: It is about the stress, the sleepless nights and the emotional weight that caregivers carry every single day.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: I recently met Mr Goh, a 45-year-old freelancer and beneficiary of NTUC's U-Care Fund.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: He and his wife are both working and they have four children – two of whom have special needs.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: He shared, and he is grateful that while subsidies help, he worries about medical expenses chipping away at their family's savings.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: What troubles him most is not just about today's struggles, but the future.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Will his children be able to cope when he and his wife can no longer take care of them?

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Will they be able to retire with dignity?

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: More than anything, he hopes that families like his would not be left to carry the heavy load of caregiving alone.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: During my house visits in Jalan Kayu, caregivers shared with me some of the same worries – how to juggle work and caregiving, and the stress and mental toll it takes on them.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We must do more to support caregivers to take care of themselves and their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We must do more to strengthen caregivers' support in these areas.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Having a job is essential for long-term financial resilience.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We must expand FWAs and enshrine caregiving leave, making them more widespread, accessible and most importantly, stigma-free.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Second, help caregivers who have left work, return to work.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We must redouble our efforts on "Back to Work" programmes to ease their transition – especially for those who have stepped off for long periods of time.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We must better design and enhance our existing schemes, to bridge skills gaps, find suitable job opportunities, provide mentorship and give employer incentives to hire returning caregivers.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We must make bold moves to ensure that care support for elderly and disabled loved ones is available, affordable and accessible.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: And importantly, strengthening care coordination so families do not have to struggle to navigate the generous but multiple schemes across different agencies, not knowing what to do.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Let us take bold steps to ensure that Singaporeans have the support they need to care for their loved ones, while staying resilient at work and at home.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: (In Mandarin):   In the coming years, our workers will face greater challenges.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: On the one hand, there is the impact brought about by the rapid development of AI.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: On the other hand, they have responsibilities caring for families.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: For businesses, AI could bring better development potential for workers, especially PMETs.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: AI can bring higher quality employment opportunities, higher wages and better career development prospects.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: As Singapore moves into a super aged society, more workers and families need to strike a balance between work and caring for loved ones, which is truly not easy.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We must strengthen support for caregivers to ensure that no one is forced to make difficult choices between career and family due to caring for loved ones.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: First, we must help caregivers remain in the workforce.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We recommend expanding the scope of flexible work arrangements and establishing a comprehensive caregiver leave system.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Second, we must help caregivers return to the workforce.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We can launch a national return to work programme to reduce difficulties they face in returning to work, especially for those workers who have been away from their position for extended periods due to caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Third, we must take decisive actions to build a stronger caregiving ecosystem, particularly to provide support for elderly, sick and disabled loved ones.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We should boldly promote reforms in caregiving services to ensure that relevant resources are accessible, affordable and convenient for those in need.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, let me conclude.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This has in turn created good jobs, lifted real wages and raised the standard of living for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Our success has been built on solid fundamentals – sustained investments in infrastructure, extensive global connectivity, a skilled workforce and a pro-business environment.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Just as importantly, being a small and open economy, we have benefited from an open, rules-based, multilateral trading system.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This has enabled companies here to participate in global supply chains, benefit from global economic growth as well as established Singapore as a hub for goods, services, capital and talent.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: But we are now facing three fundamental challenges.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In many parts of the world, countries are turning inward, erecting barriers to trade and investment and prioritising economic security and national interest.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The rapid acceleration of technological advancements such as AI will disrupt industries and jobs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Last but not least, our resource constraints, such as land, carbon and manpower, will become increasingly binding.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: However, amidst these challenges and difficulties, there are opportunities and new possibilities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Companies around the world are looking to diversify their production bases and supply chains in response to the evolving global economic landscape.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This will create new opportunities for us to capture new investments and enter new markets.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It has a young population, a rising middle class and good physical and digital connectivity, and it is poised to be one of the fastest growing regions in the world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Technology, while it may disrupt industries and jobs, can also open up new frontiers for research and innovation and drive the creation of new products and services and even new industries.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Similarly, the low-carbon transition will catalyse the growth of the green economy such as green manufacturing, clean energy, carbon services and trading, and sustainable finance.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: While there is now greater certainty, greater clarity over the tariff rates that the US has imposed on many of its key trading partners, significant uncertainties remain.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Negotiations with several countries, including China and India, are still ongoing.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Details on how the deals will be implemented remain unclear.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In fact, we have already seen a number of conflicting interpretations emerge.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: But I should say that even at 7%, they are significant.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The full effects of these tariffs will take time to flow through in the months and years ahead.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Singapore Economic Resilience Taskforce will continue to monitor the developments and assess the impact of the tariffs on our businesses and workers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We are prepared to do more for our companies and our workers if necessary.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The global developments we have seen over the past few months are not a passing storm.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Instead, they point towards a changed world – a new norm that is more fragmented, with sharper competition for investments and a shift towards economic security and national interest.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These call for a new economic blueprint to steer Singapore forward in this changed world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: That is why we embarked on the Economic Strategy Review.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Economic Strategy Review is consulting and engaging stakeholders and will submit its recommendations next year.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I will not want to preempt their conclusions at this point.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: But let me just talk broadly about our approach.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: First, we must strengthen our positioning in existing growth sectors and establish a strong foothold in new areas of growth, as pointed out by Mr Sharael Taha.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Over the decades, we have established Singapore as a global node in key sectors such as semiconductors, healthcare, specialty chemicals and aerospace.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I attended the opening of ST Engineering's new engine MRO facility last week.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In addition to ST Engineering, we are also a key aerospace manufacturing and MRO site for leading firms such as SIA Engineering, GE Aerospace, Rolls Royce and Collins Aerospace.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These moves will strengthen Singapore's positioning as Asia's leading aerospace hub and a critical node in global supply chains.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have also established our position as a leading services hub, such as in commodity trading, digital industries, tourism, financial services and professional services.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will build on this foundation to further reinforce Singapore's status as a services hub for the region, especially with the fast-growing digital economy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We must also position ourselves well to establish a strong, early foothold in new growth sectors.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Our strengths as a leading biomedical sciences hub put us in a good position to capture opportunities in the research, development and commercialisation of life science tools, diagnostic testing and therapeutics in this rapidly growing sector.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In addition to precision medicine, we are also exploring other potential growth areas such as AI and deep tech, green economy, autonomous vehicles and space.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Second, we will make Singapore a home for leading firms.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will reinforce the presence of today's industry leaders and nurture companies with the potential to become future industry leaders.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have established a strong base of industry leaders in key sectors.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will work with them to further grow their businesses and anchor new high value-added activities here in Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Seven out of the 10 top life science tools companies have significant R&D and manufacturing activities in Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This has enabled us to be among the top global manufacturing sites for high-value manufacturing instruments and consumables.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will partner with these industry leaders to establish best-in-class manufacturing facilities and R&D activities, develop new capabilities such as AI and expand their product range.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Many Singapore enterprises are also industry leaders in their respective sectors.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will support them to deepen their capabilities and help them to expand overseas.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is an example of how our Singapore companies are tapping into growth opportunities overseas.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: By growing in overseas markets, these companies will become bigger and stronger to support the value creation, innovation and headquarters functions here in Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This will also reinforce our status as a hub for globally competitive firms.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: There are companies which may be small today but have the potential to become future industry leaders.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will seek them out and anchor them in Singapore, so that they may be new engines of growth for our economy in time to come.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Ambiq manufactures ultra-low power processors that consume one-tenth of the power compared to their competitors.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Their technology can be found in smart watches and was used to power up the TraceTogether token during COVID-19.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Ambiq established their presence in Singapore in 2021 and has since grown and successfully listed.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: To support their international growth, the company has established their regional headquarters and R&D activities here in Singapore and we hope to further anchor their presence in Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: At the same time, we will study how we can better support our local startups and entrepreneurs from initial stages to scale-up and grow.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This could include access to growth capital, space and infrastructure needs, and partnerships in overseas markets.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Aliena is a space-tech startup that develops electric propulsion systems which enable small satellites to fly closer to Earth for higher quality data collection.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Third, we will strengthen our fundamentals to stay competitive.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: One, our capacity to deploy and diffuse new technologies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Each new wave of technology, from computerisation, the Internet and now to AI, has shown that it is not just the technological breakthroughs themselves, but the ability and speed at which we can deploy and diffuse them effectively across the economy that determines whether we can sustain our competitiveness.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We must, therefore, be a nation of both innovators and fast adopters.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have made good progress in accelerating AI-driven innovation through the establishment of AI Centres of Excellence.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: At the same time, we must complement this by broadening and deepening AI adoption across the broad base of enterprises, including SMEs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will develop AI playbooks and toolkits to guide companies in adopting AI-driven solutions, as well as raise the AI fluency among both technical professionals and non-technical professionals.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The quality of our human capital has been a key competitive advantage for Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As we transform our economy towards higher value-added activities, we must also ensure that our upskilling and reskilling efforts keep pace.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We must empower workers with new skills for the future, including being AI-fluent, so as to remain relevant.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Similarly, we want our workers to gain overseas work experience and exposure.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This will position them well to take on regional and global leadership roles in future.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We must also stay open to global talent, so that we may tap on their strengths to complement our resident workforce.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is critical to ensure that our industries and firms stay globally competitive.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Our years of investments in our port and airport infrastructure have been critical to Singapore’s excellent connectivity today, which underpins our role as a regional hub.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Similarly, we must plan for the energy transition and help our businesses transition to a sustainable future.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is why we are pursuing multiple pathways to decarbonise our energy mix.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We are ramping up our domestic solar deployment, facilitating low-carbon electricity imports and building capabilities in emerging low-carbon alternatives, such as hydrogen and nuclear energy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will calibrate the pace of the transition carefully.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Even as we decarbonise, we must ensure that Singapore stays cost-competitive and our energy security is safeguarded.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Even as we secure our long-term growth, we have not lost sight of the challenges that some of our SMEs are facing, including those in the retail and F&B sectors, as well as our heartland enterprises.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is because of a variety of factors, including more intense competition from e-commerce players, shifts in consumer preferences and rising costs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have rolled out several initiatives to support such businesses.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For example, those in F&B can tap on Enterprise Singapore’s FoodX programme and heartland enterprises can tap on the Enhanced Visual Merchandising Programme and the Heartland Enterprise Placemaking Grant to revamp their storefront to drive more business.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Our CDC and SG60 vouchers will also encourage consumers to spend at the heartland enterprises.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will help these SMEs raise their productivity, restructure their operations and rejuvenate their businesses.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is comparable to many other small, advanced economies, such as New Zealand, Switzerland and Sweden.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: But we should not take that as a given.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is already challenging, judging by the historical experience of economies with similar size and level of development.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: There will also be times when the global economy will slow down and our growth will also slow down consequently.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: And, therefore, that will bring us to between 2%-3% per annum.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: However, we see opportunities to get a larger productivity lift from technology, such as AI, robotics as well as automation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will also grow other higher value-added industries as I have outlined before.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I spoke earlier about how Singapore’s success has been closely intertwined with an open, rules-based, multilateral trading system.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Singapore pursues an active trade strategy through our Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) and other platforms.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These FTAs have opened doors for our companies to access new markets, diversify supply chains and build deeper economic partnerships around the world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Our network of FTAs also makes us an attractive destination for foreign investments and has enabled us to build a resilient economy that provides good jobs for our people.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We must double down on our efforts to preserve and expand our international economic space.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Bilaterally, we will deepen our cooperation and integration with our key economic partners.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Both the US and China remain our key economic partners.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The US is our largest foreign investor and China is our largest goods trading partner.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: While competition between the US and China has intensified, we must continue to work with both US and China in areas of mutual interest and mutual benefit.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: India is another economy that is poised to grow strongly in the years ahead.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Beyond India, we are deepening our economic cooperation with other key economies, such as Australia, the European Union (EU), Japan, Korea, New Zealand, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates and the list goes on.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Closer to home, we are also deepening our economic cooperation with our immediate neighbours, including in Johor through the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone and in Batam-Bintan-Karimun (BBK).

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We are further exploring how the three of us can work together for even stronger synergies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These examples illustrate how Singapore will continue to broaden its network of economic partnerships, including in areas, like digital economy and green economy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: And by doing so, we will open up more opportunities for our businesses, diversify our markets and strengthen our resilience in an increasingly fragmented world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These efforts will also strengthen the rules-based trading system.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The World Trade Organisation (WTO) is not perfect, but it remains an important foundation on which to build a better global, rules-based trade architecture.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: With limited land, manpower and natural resources, we have to work harder and plan longer, further ahead and move faster than others.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We can take heart at the success we have achieved over the past six decades, but we cannot afford to be complacent.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We must also continue to expand our international economic space, by strengthening our network of trade and investment, reinforcing a rules-based global trading system and positioning Singapore as a trusted hub in a more uncertain and turbulent world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Our circumstances may be challenging, but our foundations are strong.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Together with determination and imagination, we can continue to grow our economy, create good opportunities for our people and build a better and brighter future for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We were carried through ups and downs, in no small part due to those who stood by us and who were our rocks as we were tossed around by turbulence.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Through this, our team of volunteers showed up every day, week after week, all doing their part to make sure that we were able to carry on our work within the community for our residents in Sengkang and for that, we are deeply grateful.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These five years have crystallised how being an elected MP is an incredible privilege and responsibility afforded to us here in this House.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We saw joy and pride in the eyes of parents sharing pictures of how much their children have grown visiting our meet-the-people's sessions (MPS) to show us with excitement their children's EduSave awards.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We also sat with residents grieving loved ones and other losses.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We look forward to working alongside you to deepen and continue the relationship to work together to make Sengkang and Singapore a better place for all.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A theme that has played in my mind on results night and ever since, is the power of us and not just the strength of us but also the full spectrum of who we are as a people, our resilience, our skills and our values, but also our limitations, mistakes and flaws.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And instead of viewing these as opposite sides of the coin, I have come to see these as part of the richness of the tapestry that comprises our towns, our society and our people.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Compared with five years ago, the world has undergone many changes, even as memories fade, of the pains and coming together in the face of COVID-19, we see living pressures continue to mount.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Global conflicts and the straining of the previously accepted world order, add to concerns about climate change and it is no wonder that there is so much talk about climate anxiety, a mental health crisis.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We are also faced with ongoing challenges to our own food security in Singapore and how to forge forward to balance where our country sits in a world where sustainability challenges seem insurmountable.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, when financial pressures grow, community often takes the back seat.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Individuals, families and social relationships are put under strain: physical and mental health declines, civic engagement drops and people withdraw from social activities to save money or because they feel ashamed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In communities, social capital may be weakened, diminishing community resilience, risking a downward spiral where vulnerable groups end up even more disproportionately affected by weak economic winds.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Ask ourselves, compared with five years ago, are we a stronger, kinder, more inclusive society?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In my maiden speech in 2020, I talked about how I felt that the perception of a lack of social mobility and the presence of elitism, regardless of data, is a real and often overlooked danger.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: How are we faring in terms of the perception that our people have of our much cherished system of meritocracy?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: How often, too, have we over the last five years had fellow Singaporeans give us a shrug and say, what to do?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Not because we have given up, but because we feel pressured up against forces that are just so strong.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: So, what have we done to prevent this feeling of helplessness in the face of global uncertainty and challenge from taking root?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I believe that the answer to this is in the power of community, of a people-centred community.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Human beings are essentially social in nature, relying on one another for our well-being.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This deepening of the networks of our community in Sengkang and beyond is something we deeply appreciate.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These are some examples of groups that have reached out to us.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
