speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Recently, Nanyang has seen more of such birds, and I believe many other parts of Singapore face the same issue.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: When I noticed people feeding birds, which technically counts as littering, I referred the matter to the National Environment Authority (NEA).

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But NEA explained that they only handle high-rise littering, such as when food is thrown from windows to feed the birds.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: On the issue of bird control, they told me it is not under their purview and referred me to the National Parks Board (NParks).

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: When I approached NParks, I was told that they mainly manage pigeons.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: For crows, they would request the Town Council to remove nests from trees.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: As for birds scavenging for food waste, responsibility depends on location.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: When the birds eat on the food waste in hawker centres, NEA steps in.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If it happens at coffee shops, the Housing and Development Board (HDB) takes charge.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If it happens at food courts in industrial estates, then JTC Corp is responsible – and the list goes on.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Surely, we should not need to escalate this, the fight against bird nuisance to our Defence Minister, who is also the Coordinating Minister for Public Services, to lead the war against bird nuisance.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But, of course, ChatGPT or generative AI cannot chase away the birds for us.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But it remains an important tool to help us tackle everyday challenges.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: During my recent trip to China, I once again saw first-hand how technology is transforming daily life, from sophisticated self-driving functions in mass-market electric cars to simple voice commands that can open curtains or switch off lights in a modest three-star hotel, technology has touched everyone's lives.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: What I witnessed shows us the true potential of AI.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It can amplify human creativity, solve problems once thought impossible, and unlock entirely new levels of productivity.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: More than that, AI adoption creates new kinds of jobs, just like the rise of social media created opportunities for content creators and influencers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Yet, we must also acknowledge the very real concern that AI may displace jobs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: As tasks become streamlined, some roles will inevitably be lost and this is where our greatest challenge and our deepest responsibility lie.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We must embrace technology but also ensure no one is left behind.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We must not see displaced workers as collateral damage.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Workers must feel empowered, not fearful, when faced with new technology.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Instead of asking, "Will AI take my job?", we should encourage them to ask, "How can I use AI to do my job better?" Secondly, let us look into community-based learning hubs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This makes reskilling accessible at the heart of every neighbourhood.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: A displaced worker does not mean a discarded worker.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Each career transition is not an end, but a new beginning.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: With unity and courage, we can turn every challenge into opportunity, protect every worker and ensure every Singaporean has a place in the future.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We often label ourselves as a small country with limited resources, no hinterland of our own, but, perhaps, in this century, physical size and natural resources have become secondary.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Singapore's population exceeds most of the top 10 GDP per capita countries and many of which do not enjoy abundant natural resources.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Africa's struggles with the resource curse reminds us that natural endowments are no guarantee of prosperity.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I am sure everyone knows of Nvidia, now the world's most valuable company at more than US$4 trillion or roughly $5.5 trillion, yet it employs merely 36,000 workers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Consider instead, one of the largest palm oil plantation companies listed on the Singapore Stock Exchange, which employs over 100,000 workers and yet creates far less value with a market capital of about $4 billion.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Human capital and financial resources now loom larger than natural endowments or physical space.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And why is the cost of living the top voter concern, according to the Institute of Policy Studies' (IPS') post-election survey, when we are supposedly one of the richest countries in the world?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In our day-to-day interactions, we witness residents anxious about their financial security and seeking help through MPS.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Though ranked the world's third happiest city by the Institute for the Quality of Life in 2025, one cannot help but feel a healthy dose of scepticism as to whether this reflects the lived reality of most Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Numerous surveys in recent years point to widespread workplace burnout.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: One in four primary school students experience bullying.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And we see all these manifestations of anxieties and stress around us, from growing neighbour disputes and noise complaints, to road rage and superiors lashing out against junior employees.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Economic growth, growing the pie has always been the Government's fundamental goal and the Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong recently affirmed that we should grow as much as we can, aiming for rates faster than the eventual 2% to 3% long-term target.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But we must now ask, is it more important to grow the pie or to grow most Singaporeans' share of the pie?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: President Tharman reminds us, "The old playbook is no longer sufficient." Yet, in the short term, much remains largely unchanged.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On the capital front, the focus remains on attracting foreign direct investments (FDIs) to anchor multinational companies (MNCs) here.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Singapore is still keen to continue incentivising MNCs, in spite of Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) 2.0 and the global minimum tax.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And with regulatory certainty and the rule of law in place in Singapore, as opposed to what we are seeing in other countries, including the US right now, I am sure there will be companies keen to locate themselves here.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On the labour front, again in this fractured world, there will be many who will want to call Singapore home.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, there are limits to growth by boosting capital and labour.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The world's largest economy, the US, increasingly ties trade agreements to domestic investment for tariff reductions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: How will global supply chains shift and will Singapore's economic relevance continue to endure in this new world order?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Meanwhile, Singapore's population has touched six million, raising questions: how much further can we drive economic growth through workforce expansion in one of most densely populated cities in the world?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, Mr Speaker, I fully agree with our President that we need to urgently rethink our playbook.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I acknowledge that we have been attempting to refresh our economic strategies and Singapore has never lacked taskforces or committees: the Economic Strategies Committee launched in 2009; the Committee on the Future Economy in 2016; which was followed by the Future Economy Council; Future Economy Advisory Panel; Industry Transformation Maps; then the Emerging Stronger Taskforce in 2020; and most recently, the Economic Strategy Review and Singapore Economic Resilience Taskforce this year.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, if you take stock of where we are today, our economy remains very much driven by attracting global MNCs and capital.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is a model that has prevailed since Albert Winsemius advised Singapore in the 1960s.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Looking at the share of value-add to the indigenous workforce and citizen-owned companies, this has declined from roughly 70% in the late 1980s, to 50% to 60% in the decade prior to 2015.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Yearbook of Statistics 2012 noted eloquently that Singapore's economic development depends heavily on foreign capital, foreign technology and foreign workers, with a large share of employee compensation and operating surplus accruing to foreigners and foreign enterprises.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Per capital GNI, as conventionally defined on the residential basis, may not, therefore, reflect correctly the income accrued to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: How many homegrown Singapore firms have become global giants?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: AI is the buzzword of the day, prompting reflection.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: You do not need huge physical space or underground natural resources.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Mira Murati's Thinking Machines Lab is valued at US$12 billion, with just around 50 employees.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Why do we not have our own open AI equivalent, despite Singaporean students having one of the best math and science scores in the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), for decades?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: When local entrepreneurs succeed, many still choose overseas listings and foreign bases to access supportive ecosystems.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This despite our financial hub status and acclaimed business friendliness.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Prime Minister Wong's Addendum to the President's Address highlights investing in productive capacity, ensuring stable tax, customs, regulatory environment and infrastructure investment.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To me, these are necessary, but insufficient conditions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Because, as what President Tharman has said, "Above all, we must foster an outgoing and experimental spirit among our enterprises and people." In the near term, it is crucial to prevent a lost generation by securing jobs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: AI-driven seniority-biased technological change may disproportionately impact juniors and entry-level positions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Grades is a good start, but full-time entry-level role creation must also be incentivised.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For example, reintroducing the jobs growth incentive for fresh graduates.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If GRaduate Industry Traineeships @ Gov (GRIT@Gov) mimic full-timer duties, then the Government should take the lead in levelling pay and benefits.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Long term, re-invigorating our workforce demands that our education system fosters critical thinking and independent learning, not rote memorisation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As Alvin Toffler wrote back in 1970, the illiterate of the future are not those who cannot read or write, but those who cannot learn, unlearn and re-learn.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Looking at our population pyramid, one might be forgiven for thinking we do not have an ageing population, thanks largely to immigration.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We recently debated the Families Motion and without repeating myself, our low TFR remains an existential threat to Singapore and our identity.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: President Tharman pledged, "in this term, we will do more to help parents better manage their work and family commitments and work with stakeholders, such as employers and community partners to build a culture that celebrates and values families".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Minister Indranee has said earlier that our marriage and parenthood policies are not incremental.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But, perhaps, the most urgent task force we need now is one to tackle the critical challenge of our record-low TFR.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Do we show the same resolve in tackling population as we do economic challenges?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Because without enough Singaporeans, there will be no Singapore economy to speak of.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Ultimately, our greatest challenge, in my view, is how to refrain from rent-seeking or rent-maximisation behaviour as a society.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To develop an entrepreneurial culture and let the thousand flowers bloom, we must encourage open-mindedness and diversity of ideas.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: More entrepreneurs mean more risk takers, but this also requires robust safety nets so Singaporeans can pursue entrepreneurial or vocational change without risking destitution.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Individuals buying investment properties, prompting Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty measures; companies prioritising property over their core business; even Government that focuses on maximising rents and nothing less than market value for land, lest it be seen as raiding the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But such behaviour permeates every corner of the economy, raising costs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We must set the right tone at the top.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Policy should not inevitably reward the highest bidder at the expense of wider societal outcomes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: (In Mandarin):   The 15th Parliament convenes at a critical juncture and we have a long road ahead.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The nation faces severe challenges: geopolitics, the rivalry between the US and China, trade wars, and the revolutionary changes brought by AI will all test the collective wisdom and resilience of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The President spoke passionately, emphasising unity, trust, a “we first” society .

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I believe that the spirit of unity and “we first” Singapore does not mean everyone speaking with one voice, but rather, that we can address issues by exchanging different opinions with a rational and open attitude.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Workers' Party (WP) Members of Parliament (MPs) have always been a minority in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, I believe that the presence of WP MPs can demonstrate the value of diverse voices and better embody the “we first” Singapore spirit mentioned by the President and Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Especially in the coming five years, the variables in the international situation and the transformation of the global economy will become increasingly rapid.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: How to pool collective wisdom to respond to drastic changes is homework we must do.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Therefore, I hope the Government can listen to different views from Singaporeans with an objective, rational and open attitude.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: From a policy-making perspective, some core issues are interconnected, for example, the various problems brought by AI and economic transformation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To ensure that no one is left behind, we must strengthen employment stabilisation policies in the short term and encourage the public sector and private enterprises to increase employment opportunities.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Most crucially, in the age of AI, education should not just be for examinations but should prepare people for life.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We need to align education with economic needs and help students develop important soft skills.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: These human qualities cannot be replaced by AI and are essential for future social and economic development.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In summary, Mr Speaker, a “we first” society also requires us to uphold the principle that collective interests take precedence over individual interests.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: When the nation achieves success but many citizens still feel forgotten, trust becomes difficult to maintain.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We need not just economic growth but also inclusive growth that ensures every Singaporean can share in the nation's future.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am heartened by how our people and the Government have been working hand in hand to overcome the numerous waves of challenges pounding our shores.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They emanate from continents far from our island – economic upheavals, armed conflicts, technology changes – yet, they have significant impact on our everyday lives.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On the one hand, I am confident of our ability to catch some of these waves to survive and thrive.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On the other hand, let us never forget the need to protect the vulnerable amongst us and prevent these powerful waves from sweeping them under.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am cognisant of the immense responsibility that my residents and fellow Singaporeans have entrusted me with.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I applaud the great progress that we have made so far together to address some of the issues faced by our vulnerable groups.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But our work is far from done and that is why I continue to champion change that will benefit Singaporeans and my residents and keep our country going in this new reality.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: MPs play an important role to help the Government to continue to review the effectiveness of our policies on the ground.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Where necessary, we must be willing to recalibrate and make improvements to narrow the gaps and plug any loophole.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Let us never forget that spirit of sensible policy-making and pragmatic government administration that has been a hallmark of Singapore's success.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Sometimes, the solutions can be deceptively simple and I would like to call upon us all, the people, private and public sectors, to be daring to raise practical and smart solutions, and our policy-makers to listen to good ideas from our people.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is how we stay united as a nation, by caring and looking out for one another.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is worth reminding ourselves that we are only as strong as our weakest link and the tides of change must not leave anyone behind.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am assured and heartened by the commitments made by the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) in its Addendum to the President's address.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our social and healthcare workers play an essential and critical role in ensuring that appropriate help and care is provided in a timely manner.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This was best demonstrated during the COVID-19 pandemic, but now that we have moved on from that crisis, it does not mean that we forget their roles and contributions.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our social care workers are professionals and they must be treated as such.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They need to be equipped with more support and resources in order to achieve better outcomes for their clients.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Much research worldwide over the last two decades have resulted in new findings in this field and we can tap on these to provide constant professional upgrading so that they can be even more effective.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition, we should elevate and accord better recognition of and compensation for their work.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Due to the nature of their jobs, burnout and attrition rates are high.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have to do more to better retain our existing talent pool of social workers, while attracting new blood to boost our ability to care for our people.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Foreign workers do help to fill many of the gaps, but let us not end up as a country that relies too heavily on others to take care of our very own.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We must accelerate efforts to strengthen community-based eldercare, expanding Active Ageing Centres, daycare facilities and home-based support services.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These not only enable our seniors to age-in-place, with dignity and autonomy, but also reduce pressure on families.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Caregiving, often performed by middle-aged adults juggling work and family, must also be better supported.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Caregivers want to be able to care for their families, but they also have their own dreams and aspirations.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: All too often, I have met residents who have had to sacrifice their careers to look after their loved ones.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Indeed, they have chosen to do so out of love, and we need to celebrate that and provide them with better support.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our seniors are not a burden; they are a blessing.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Let us honour their contributions not just in words but through concrete policies that uphold their well-being as well as that of their loved ones.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have to double down on our efforts to support families holistically, so that they can remain strong and resilient in the face of change.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For families under duress, our social care workers need to be empowered to coordinate with partners, such as mental and physical healthcare professionals, financial counsellors, schools, eldercare centres and so on.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Families living in rental flats, often headed by single parents or elderly caregivers, face daily struggles.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For children in these households, we must do more to ensure their well-being and that they can access healthcare, nutritious food and be able to focus on their education.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Empower them with good parenting skills, stable employment, access to mentoring and even overcoming addictions, such as to vaping, alcohol and even drugs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There are heightened tensions between established resident communities and new arrivals, and distrust between the rich and the poor, manifesting in rallies, riots and violence.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Almost daily, we see alarming images of looting, burning vehicles and buildings, and people attacking each other on television and social media.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is the result of careful stewardship, addressing root causes of problems as soon as they surface, building mutual respect and reaching the national consensus to agree to engage in difficult conversations, even over sensitive topics.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Yet in today's digital age, we face new threats, from misinformation, polarisation and imported ideologies that can erode trust and amplify division.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many of our youths that I met have good questions and think about such issues very seriously.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Let us support engagements for deeper, ongoing conversations about faith, tradition and coexistence, especially among our youths.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We must move beyond mere tolerance, to deepen our mutual understanding, appreciation and respect.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Strong communities are not built by governments alone.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They exist when neighbours look out for one another, when residents take ownership of shared spaces and when there is deep trust among people, in our institutions and in our leadership.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We must also support faith and community leaders who work quietly to build bridges.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our bridge-builders must be seen, supported and safeguarded against threats.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our Community Development Councils (CDCs), Social Service Offices (SSOs) and grassroots organisations must continue to be strongly supported to work closely with ground-up groups and volunteers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Policies must enable not only professional help, but also "kampung"-style initiatives and mutual aid.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For years, residents have been putting up with the disamenities of noisy and inconsiderate visitors who litter, smoke, urinate and cause disturbances even in the wee hours.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Volunteers, despite feeling burnout, continue with patrols, even as we continue to engage with HDB, the Town Council, Residents' Committees, NEA, the Police and other Government agencies.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Unfortunately, the disamenities continued and we sought to present alternative solutions which have been proven effective in other sky gardens, such as the Pinnacle @ Duxton.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When problems remain unsolved and proposals are not accepted, it is not surprising for my residents to feel disappointed.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I will not hesitate to speak up for my residents if I feel that more can be done.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Securing Singapore's future lies not in grand slogans, but as our President put it, in everyday deeds and action, like little acts of kindness; helping an elderly neighbour with groceries; guiding a child in need; and lending a hand in crisis.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These are the encounters that strengthen our social compact and build a "we first" society.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In closing, allow me to reiterate our first principles.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To build a united and resilient Singapore, we have to be inclusive and caring, respectful of differences in diversity and united in core values.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Every child who falls through the cracks, every elderly person who dies alone, every caregiver who burns out is a reminder of work yet to be done.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Similarly, every neighbour who helps another, every volunteer who steps forward, every employer who provides a second chance, is a sign of the better Singapore that we are building together.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, securing Singapore's future lies not in grand slogans, but as our President puts it, in everyday deeds and actions, like little acts of kindness: helping an elderly neighbour with groceries; guiding a child in need; and lending a hand in crisis.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These are encounters that strengthen our social compact and build a "we first" society.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In closing, allow me to reiterate our first principles.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To build a united and resilient Singapore, we have to be inclusive and caring, respectful of differences in diversity and be united in core values.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Every child who falls through the cracks, every elderly person who dies alone, every caregiver who burns out, is a reminder of work that is yet to be done.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Similarly, every neighbour who helps another, every volunteer who steps forward, every employer who provides a second chance, is a sign of the better Singapore that we are building together.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is a new world fraught with peril, but awash with opportunity, one that needs a new strategy to not just survive the challenges ahead, but to thrive despite them, a strategy built on security, investment and trust in our people.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Two great forces define our current moment: the great re-ordering of global power and the AI revolution transforming how we work.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Together, they represent a convergence of challenges that invite a rethinking of how we approach governance and policy.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is a near-term reality already reshaping our economy.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But this AI wave is fundamentally different from previous technological revolutions.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Where past disruptions primarily hit the factory floor, this one targets the boardroom, the artists' studio, the claims desk.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: From administrative assistants to software developers, from graphic designers to even chief executives, AI capabilities can now match many tasks performed by these workers.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In Singapore, this threat is amplified by our unique economic structure.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some of us call this the knowledge economy.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But for Singapore, given our economic make-up, this figure is probably higher still.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Half of these jobs could benefit from AI integration, boosting productivity and wages.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But the IMF thinks that the other half face automation, creating downward pressure on wages and hiring in these sectors.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore's success to-date comes from world-class execution of a sound playbook.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But as we chart the course for tomorrow, we must question if yesterday's maps are still adequate for these new waters.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I agree with the diagnosis, but temporary reliefs are insufficient for the systemic challenges ahead.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In an era of AI-driven disruption, we should acknowledge that our existing social safety nets are ill-equipped for the scale of the change ahead.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A stronger, permanent foundation of security is required, and this is not charity, but is the cornerstone of national competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The impact of this AI revolution can already be felt.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Recent surveys of US employers showed 25% of AI users expected to hire fewer workers in the next six months, versus just 10% who intended to hire more.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can already see the same early warnings here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Younger workers, lacking the tacit knowledge that accumulates with experience, are particularly vulnerable to task replacement from AI.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To put that in perspective, for a median income earner, that is just over $5 a month, and only half of that is paid for by the worker.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This creates a true safety net that catches everyone, one that gives workers the confidence to explore new opportunities rather than clinging desperately to dying industries.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This represents a profound shift in how we should think about support for the unemployed.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the AI age, career transitions will become the new normal, not the exception.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Workers need the security to retrain, to upskill, to reinvent themselves without the spectre of destitution haunting their choices.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Housing security must also evolve to acknowledge changing aspirations and economic realities.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Build-To-Order (BTO) prices should be pegged to a house price-to-income ratio of three for first-time applicants.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should offer 70-year lease options at lower prices for those who prefer affordability over asset appreciation.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The BTO access age for singles should be lowered to 28 and grants should be equalised for single parents who face unique challenges in building stable homes.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is dignity, stability and the foundation upon which families build their futures.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As someone who has navigated this journey myself recently, I know the anxieties many young Singaporeans face.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When we cannot settle into our first homes until our 30s, we are denied the chance to put down roots, to plan for families and to contribute fully to society's fabric.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Just as a home provides foundational stability for the family, our economy also requires its own form of security.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Platform work has emerged as the primary economic buffer for this era, offering a crucial bridge for those transitioning between traditional jobs.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Platform Workers Act is a commendable first step to shore up this vital buffer.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But it stops short of addressing algorithmic management, the digital boss that controls every aspect of the platform worker's existence.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Concerns about a "digital boss" are not new, but the AI revolution brings renewed urgency.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These black-box algorithms determine job allocation, pricing, performance evaluation and even disciplinary action.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Recent advances mean that they could become supercharged, rendering them even more powerful and even more inscrutable than before.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We cannot allow the digital economy to become a digital dystopia where human dignity is sacrificed on the altar of algorithmic efficiency.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The freedom to explore and chase one's dreams should not be the exclusive playground of the bold or the privileged.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By strengthening our foundation of security, every Singaporean will have the licence to try new things because should you fail, you will not have too far to fall.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But Mr Speaker, a strong foundation of security is only the first step.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To truly thrive, we must build upon it.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This brings me to the second pillar of our strategy: investment in our people.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But for all the good intentions, there remains a persistent disconnect, a "last mile disconnect" between training and employment.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many workers still see SkillsFuture as a supermarket of courses, a system that provides plenty of choice but sometimes lacks clear pathways to career advancement.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We hear from those who have diligently completed courses, only to find their new certificates hold little currency with employers who still prioritise degrees, certificates and linear work experiences.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is the paradox of our current system.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have built a comprehensive architecture for upskilling, but we have not yet solved the problem of market recognition.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The challenge, therefore, is one of pace and integration.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Last year, the former Minister for Education articulated a vision for stackable micro-credentials and cross-recognition between our IHLs.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Backed up by the collective reputations of our renowned institutions, this would go a long way to bridging the disconnect between adult learners and employers.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This acknowledges the busy, unpredictable reality of adult life and provides a flexible pathway for all Singaporeans to stay relevant.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We possess world-class universities, but we hear of a persistent concern from both employers and graduates themselves, a gap between academic excellence on the one hand and the practical skills that are needed in a modern workplace.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our polytechnics and the Singapore Institute of Technology have proven the value of structured work-integrated learning as a core part of the tertiary curriculum.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A targeted grant to help our local small and medium enterprises (SMEs) offset the costs of providing such placements could be a powerful catalyst.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But crucially, payouts should be structured to incentivise retention and discourage exploitation.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This ensures our graduates enter the workforce with the practical, real-world skills that the AI age demands.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: SMEs should continue to receive assistance to adopt AI tools and AI literacy should be woven into our school curriculum.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Students should be encouraged to command it as a creative and analytical tool.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: SkillsFuture credits should also be allowed to cover subscriptions to AI assistants and tools, ensuring that all Singaporean workers, regardless of their means, are able to utilise the latest and best tools to enhance their own productivity.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But above all, we must continue to be vigilant to ensure AI serves our workers, not replaces them.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In an age of AI, our people's ability to learn, adapt and apply knowledge quickly is our single greatest competitive advantage.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The right investments in our people will ensure that AI's promise translates into better wages and better jobs, not just higher profits for shareholders.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yet, even the best-laid plans for security and the most ambitious investments in our people will fall short if they are not built on a foundation of mutual respect and this requires the final and perhaps, most crucial pillar of our strategy: trust.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To truly thrive, trust in Singapore must become a two-way street.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have long been asked to trust the Government's judgement, wisdom and intentions.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this new era, the Government must also learn to trust its people with information, with genuine dialogue and with the fundamental dignity of participation.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When the Government holds data that could inform public debate, it should be shared.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When policies are formulated based on evidence, that evidence should be accessible to scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Trust is also demonstrated through genuine dialogue rather than managed consultation.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Defending robust debate shows we trust the wisdom of our people to engage with complex issues and reach sound judgments.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But the deepest trust of all is demonstrated through permissive discourse.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is a call we can all get behind.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These three pillars – security, investment and trust – form the foundation of a strategy for a thriving people.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A compass for our next chapter and a promise about the society we can become.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: As one of the younger new political office holders in this House, allow me first to share my thanks, for what my generation has received.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Then, Mr Speaker, amid the many challenges that Singapore faces, I would like to speak about our children and their childhood, and offer some suggestions on how we can help our next generation thrive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: I grew up in the 1980s and 1990s in a simple HDB flat in Bedok.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Studying was important, but my fondest memories were from playing football during recess, going to the nearby playground and wandering around Bedok Town Centre shops and the library.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: A simple childhood, a heartland experience, like most Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: And I am grateful for what I had, for it shaped me into who I am today.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Proud that our small country was able to punch above her weight as one of the four "Asian Tigers", proud that we stayed principled and resisted external pressures, proud that we were bold and planned long term.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: We owe gratitude to our grandparents and our parents whose hard work and strong values enabled them to overcome tough cycles of retrenchment, global conflicts and the severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) epidemic, so that we all can have a much better life than they ever did.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Now, it is our turn to take on the mantle, to navigate through the dark clouds, to support and take care of our seniors and to raise our children well to become future leaders of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: And if I may add, on a more personal note, it is precisely my heartland upbringing and my pride in Singapore that has kept me committed to serving in the SAF for many years as well as in the community as a grassroots leader through the past two decades; and now, to do even more, as I take this step into politics.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Just as our Pioneers had their challenges, my generation, our generation, will have ours to confront as well.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: As a nation we have no lack of issues to think about in our next lap.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: In a world of rapid change, geopolitical situations, climate change, intense economic competition, the opportunities and challenges that AI brings, the dominance of tech and mobile devices, the explosion of choices that face us all will be even more daunting for young minds.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: It is, therefore, our responsibility to help them thrive and we have to do as well as we possibly can.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Singapore is already one of the best places for our children to grow up in, with a high-quality of life, safe and secure environment, excellent healthcare and schools.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: But with new uncertainties ahead of us, we need to ensure our next generation is ready to brave it and resilient enough to stay ahead.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: We must help our young people develop in the right way, to shift from “what to think and do”, to “how to think and do”.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: So that they have the confidence and curiosity to navigate those winds of change.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: So that they develop the critical thinking for them to discern what’s right and what is wrong for them to possess the grit and perseverance to keep pushing when the going gets tough and to have the resilience to get up when they fall.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: To do so, we, as a nation, need to change the way we raise our children and that begins with changing our mindsets.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Amongst all the shifts that we need to make, sometimes changing mindsets is the hardest.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: But just like how our grandfathers and fathers have prepared us well for today’s challenges, it is now for us, our generation to prepare our children for their future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: We all want our children to get the best possible start in life and the good thing is, many parents today already send their children to preschool, although starting ages differ.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Children develop better and learn better, with preschool.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: So, I strongly encourage all parents to start your children in preschool early.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Of course, parents need to be able to identify and secure a good preschool, especially if both parents are at work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: As a parent myself, I care deeply about my children’s education.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Eight years ago, when choosing a preschool for my first-born, there was no vacancy in any of the nearby Government-supported preschools.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: This leaves options for some Singaporeans to pursue private centres.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Furthermore, our early childhood educators, our teachers, are well qualified and committed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: I had a chat recently with a young couple.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Marine Parade is a mature estate, but we do have our fair share of young parents.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: They grew up in the East, like myself.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: They are happy, living and starting a family in Marine Parade.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Even though they did start the conversation by telling me that they were disappointed they did not get to vote in the recent General Election.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: But it was a good reminder to me to never take our residents’ trust for granted.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Growing up, I recall friends around me being drilled in abacus classes to help with their math and there are many more examples like that.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Our children must develop and must have good numeracy and literacy skills, because it is important in life to go on.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: But I think Singapore as a country, we are already doing well in these areas.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: The way to give our children the best start in life, is to build them up well, to make sure they have a proper childhood.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: A childhood rich with opportunities to develop important values that will help them to become inventive, resilient and flexible.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: A childhood where they truly learn to be a good person, as opposed to just being academically clever.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: When you are a young child, the most powerful lessons, the most powerful learning, comes not from books, not from tuition centres, but from experiences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Our children need a childhood where they can enjoy the freedom to explore and learn from their own experiences because that is how they learn best.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: I learnt about a butterfly’s life cycle from keeping a caterpillar.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: I was pretty good at playing marbles and that helped me quickly understand Newton’s Laws on Action and Reaction, many years later.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: It was my own experimentation and playful experience that taught me these powerful lessons and more.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Our children need such experiences to grow their curiosity for a lifetime of learning.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Bring them out to our parks and playgrounds, they need to learn through doing and experiencing for themselves.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: But child development is not just about intentional learning experiences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: There is much to learn through play, unstructured play.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: There are important lessons from play that every child deserves.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: From playing five stones and zero-point, my generation honed our hand-eye, leg-eye coordination and learnt how to focus and persevere.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: From falling from a swing, we learnt about resilience.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: It is not how we fall, but how we get up and swing faster and higher.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: From the pain of blisters that came from playing football barefoot, we learnt about consequences and how to keep ourselves safe in the future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Yet in our effort to want to keep our children safe, we sometimes deprive them of these lessons.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: While we ironically overprotect, in the real world; we may have under-protected, in the virtual world, allowing our children to indulge in their devices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: After MOH’s advice on screen time for young children, parents are anxious.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Parents say it is not easy to pull back on those devices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: My own child will also argue with me that digital play is also a form of play.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: We can do more to support our families to dial back on screen use.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: For a start, one simple change is to devote more time and energy to interacting with our children face-to-face and listening to them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Rebalance away from tuition centres, away from devices and cater more time for play.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Yes, it might mean sacrificing some peace and rest for us caregivers, but nothing beats spending quality family time together.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: And for those of us who need to work long hours to make ends meet, our communities and our schools can do more to engage our children meaningfully.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Growing up, I recall playing many variations of catching, at the playground, in the void decks, what the catcher can and cannot do.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: We made up our own rules and played by them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: We learnt to convince, to negotiate, to compromise.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: We can be playing football and basketball on opposite ends of the same court.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Through it all, more importantly, we found ourselves friends, best friends, friends that we can reliably call upon later in life.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: An article I read on World Suicide Prevention Day a couple of weeks ago, emphasised how important friends are in helping us navigate the stresses and storms of life.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Through supporting one another, our children can learn about care, about compassion, about empathy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: These are important in building a "we first" society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: So, let us help families rebalance – more real time, less screen time; more play, less pressure; more emotional intelligence, not just artificial intelligence and give space for our children to learn how to learn, because when learning is fun, it becomes its own destination, rather than a means to live up to an adult's expectations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: As parents, our children look to us and what we emphasise and define as success influences them too.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Is a child successful only because of straight "As" and a delightful co-curricular activities (CCA) record?

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: As adults, how do we measure our own success?

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Is it only about our job titles and salaries?

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Is it about what vacations we take and what car we drive, if we drive?

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Comparison is the thief of joy and in this age of social media, it is easy to feel that we pale, in comparison, to others.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: But social media is not an accurate reflection of most people's lives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Many of us will curate and share only the best and the most positive aspects of our life, while filtering out the mundane or the natural realities of everyday.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: So, I want to encourage Singaporeans with this.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Let us define our own success, our own sense of meaning, of purpose and this is how we can pursue our own dreams and our passions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Perhaps, the "kiasu" spirit is ingrained in all of us.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Perhaps, this sense of exceptionalism is what got us this far in the first place.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: But let us channel this competitiveness more positively, away from rigid definitions of success, towards self-improvement, not for the purpose of outdoing others, but to become better versions of ourselves.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: It is my hope that we become better known as "mommy bears" instead.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: I use "moms" and "mommy" carefully because that is how these phrases are coined, but it includes all the fathers, myself included.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Mommy bears are nurturing and warm, and very cuddly too.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Mommy bears raise their cubs to be independent, to be able to survive, to hunt and to be able to explore on their own.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Mommy bears allow their cubs to stumble, because that is how they learn and become more resilient.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: If we do this, then our next generation will not only be able to face the future but also shape it with confidence, resilience and heart.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, hon MPs, good afternoon.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: It is my great honour to speak here today and I am deeply aware of the weight of this responsibility.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: As a member of the younger generation, I want to thank our parents and grandparents for their hard work and dedication.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: They have weathered economic fluctuations, regional instability and the trials of the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Through their relentless efforts and perseverance, they have given us a better life.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Here, I would like to say “thank you”!

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: The responsibility of building and safeguarding Singapore has fallen upon our shoulders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: We must learn from the good examples set by the previous generation, and prepare for the future, planning ahead for the next generation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: The future is full of uncertainties: geopolitical situations, climate change, artificial intelligence and the impact of the digital world will all bring new challenges.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Singapore is one of the best places in the world for children to grow up but we cannot become complacent because of this.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: We must help our children build confidence and curiosity – learn to think and make judgements – whilst cultivating resilience and tenacity, so that they can face future storms with composure.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: This requires us as parents to change our mindset.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: What is truly crucial is giving children a proper and meaningful childhood.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Children should have the freedom to explore and play, to learn creativity and resilience through trying and falling.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: At the same time, we must pay attention to the influence of the digital world.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Many parents worry about their children becoming addicted to screens.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: I myself am often "persuaded" by my children to treat online gaming as a form of play.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Children also need to interact with their peers, learning empathy and care through communication, collaboration, and sharing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: These values cannot be replaced by textbooks and tuition classes, but they are key to building a “we first” society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Parents have a profound influence on their children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: We need to rethink the definition of "success".

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: We should guide our children to pursue growth, not merely materialistic achievements.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Bears are warm and caring, they protect their cubs, but they also let the little bears explore independently, learning to stand up on their own after falling.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Only in this way can children become truly resilient.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, and Social and Family Development (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Let us work together to cultivate the next generation's character of confidence, resilience and compassion, so that they can not only respond to the future, but also shape it. : Mr Speaker, Sir, I support the Motion.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I rise to support the Motion of Thanks for President Tharman's address.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: My topic today is moving our society from fear to hope.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But first, let us acknowledge the fears of our time.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: At work, many of us worry: will technology especially AI threaten our jobs?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Will it displace more jobs than it creates?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Will we be qualified for the new "good" jobs?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What happens to those who cannot catch up – some of the elderly, the disabled and those who are less skilled?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: As a small nation, our survival depends on global stability and open trade – the rule of law.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: As we live longer, will our savings last?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For households already stretched, how will they endure the next disruption?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What if my child does not do well in the Primary School Leaving Examination (PSLE)?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Will our children have the same, or better, opportunities?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Parents of children with disabilities ask: who will care and provide for them when we are gone?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They are signs that we care deeply for our future and the home we have built.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They mean we are invested and not ready to quit.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We can let these fears turn us inwards, making us suspicious of change and leading to paralysis or blame, or we can choose a different path.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We can choose, as spiritual thinker Henri Nouwen urged, to move from fear to hope.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We must not let the world set our agenda.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Our shared destiny surely must be built on our shared values.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How do we turn collective anxiety into collective agency and how do we build the bridge from fear to hope?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: First, to ensure AI serves humanity and not the other way around.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is no denying the breathtaking opportunities it presents.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Yet, we must also confront the risks with equal honesty.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I know this because I am always looking for jobs for some of our disabled and elderly.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Today, this exclusion is starkly visible in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We see it as Neighbourhood Police Posts are shuttered and replaced with digital kiosks.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For many, this is not convenience; it is a barrier.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In our economy, this fracture manifests in the rapid automation of routine jobs, leaving behind seniors and persons with disabilities who struggle to navigate a world increasingly alien to them.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The Government can and must lead this mission with compassion and foresight.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is a constant of human progress, in every generation.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But every such revolution risks marginalising a segment of the population.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They are a vital lifeline of inclusion, especially in essential services like healthcare, security, transport, legal and so forth.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And two, we should mandate inclusive design, require that every public-sector AI system complies with the highest accessibility standards.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I saw the Government Technology Agency (GovTech) doing that as there was an exhibition at the hall, in Parliament last year.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We can adopt universal design at the start and not as an afterthought.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I have raised questions in this House on the ways Government agencies what measures they have for those who are not digitally-savvy.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But closing this gap is not the duty of the Government alone.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: To businesses, I say, adopt inclusive design, universal design at the start.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Create solutions that blend technology with the human touch.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For example, banks that still provide personal counter services for seniors should not be rare exceptions.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These should be the industry standard until there is no need for it.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Can some businesses deliberately choose not to automate every routine job, but instead preserve some roles for older workers and persons with disabilities?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These are ways by which they can continue to contribute meaningfully, earn a livelihood and even engage socially outside their homes.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: L'Oréal, a renowned cosmetic powerhouse company, once operated a special packaging and assembly facility in Taiwan dedicated to employing people with disabilities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: That primary mission was social, not purely commercial and industrial.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is to provide meaningful, stable and supportive employment for people with various physical and developmental disabilities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It was a counter-intuitive move for business, I know.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But L'Oreal set its own agenda and did it their own way.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: That programme was later successfully merged into a larger facility to expand its impact and also promote greater inclusivity.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And to the community, I say this: volunteer your expertise, advocate for accessibility.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: People like Mr Peter Ng, an IT specialist in Kreta Ayer-Kim Seng, for instance, have for years, coached seniors like his mother and her neighbours on using smartphones and the common apps that they should know.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: That sustainable, community-driven help is the model that we should commend and need.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, the is not if AI will advance, but what kind of society we will become.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Let us ensure AI is a lifeline for all, and a landmine for none.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Second, on updating our safety net for this new age.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These have served us well in an economy where jobs were relatively stable, careers linear and disruption more gradual.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: AI has not only automated tasks, it will reconfigure entire industries.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This is an economy and age where work is fragmented, transitions frequent and inequality risks are sharper.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
