text: The task before us is not to abandon the pillars of CPF, MediSave, SkillsFuture and all the good things, but to adapt them for an economy such as this.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Their contribution to the new economy must be matched with a commitment to their security.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For the larger population, accelerate the move towards portable benefits, like healthcare and insurance.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They are tied to the individual and not the employer, providing a foundation of security in a world of fluid work.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The CPF LIFE system, which I think is brilliant, provides a secure retirement for members with substantial savings.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: However, a segment of the population, particularly those with irregular employment histories, remains financially vulnerable in their old age.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We should develop targeted measures to augment the CPF savings of individuals who are not on track to meet their retirement needs, not just those who qualify for Silver Support.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We should conduct a comprehensive review of the Silver Support scheme, too, to ensure its parameters align with the original objective of providing a safety net.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This review must account for contemporary economic pressures, such as inflation and longer life expectancy, to guarantee that that the payouts remain sufficient.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And third, to install an affordability assurance body.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Move from reacting after the fact to at least guarantee or ensuring affordability upfront.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And lastly, on supercharging our culture of lifelong learning.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But now in its 10th year, we must propel it beyond a Government programme into a lifelong habit embraced by every Singaporean.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This vision resonates with the direction outlined by Minister Desmond Lee at MOE's Work Plan seminar recently, where the Minister spoke not only about AI in schools, but also about creating a lifelong learning ecosystem, fostering a broader definition of success and meeting the needs of learners who are different.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Visionary Chinese education thinker, Prof Zhu Yongxing argues that the school of the future will, in fact, evolve from what is the traditional classroom into a network of open, flexible student-centred learning centres, breaking down the barriers of time, space, age and institutional structures.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I will talk about that hopefully in a speech next year.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: That vision of the school for the future is important.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But there are now, a few ways that we can do to reach the lifelong learning ecosystem that is fit-for-purpose for the future.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: A broader definition of success means valuing skills and competence as much as, if not more than academic qualifications.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We need to review the current playbook in this space.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: As long as academic qualifications or certificates remain the default currency for school entry and hiring, Singaporeans, parents will rationally contribute or continue to chase them; to chase these paper qualifications and the pressures will cascade down into high-stakes exams.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How many times do you have the experience that I have, when I ask a parent, "How old is your child?" And the parent says, "PSLE year." I have spoken long about through-train, 10-year through-train and whether PSLE is still relevant or not, many times in this house, but again, that is for another occasion.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And that includes recognising the value of jobs, what they call blue-collar jobs, such as our plumbers, our technicians, our rail technicians and our MRT technicians, our repair technicians and other blue-collared workers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: AI can now make personalised learning possible at scale, providing rich and timely feedback.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Special education has long used individualised education plans (IEPs) to tailor learning to each child.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I have seen this approach work brilliantly also for non-special needs kids in home-based education systems.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And third, ensure equal access to lifelong learning.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We have the school-to-work programmes, but they are transitional steps that last only a few years – a good, sincere attempt by SG Enable will need more visioning and resources.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But let us be clear, we are not passive bystanders in this era of change.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The future does not simply happen to us.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is shaped by the agenda and the choices that we make as the people of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We have done this before and we will do it again, and together we will move from a society of fear to a nation of hope.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: They sunk their roots here, threw in their lot with Singapore and made this island their home.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Our Pioneers, led by Malay leaders like Yusof Ishak, Othman Wok and Ahmad Ibrahim, strived hard to meet the social, economic and religious needs of our community.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: They were also crucial members of our Pioneer leadership team, united in the common vision of a Singapore for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The courage, dedication and tireless work of our Pioneers laid strong foundations for our community to make progress generation after generation.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Last month, I joined many Singaporeans in celebrating our nation's birthday, and like many in our community, my heart swelled with pride as Lieutenant Colonel Firdaus Ghazali led the National Day Parade; and as Lieutenant Colonel Muhammad Iskandar led the F-15 bomb burst salute.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This is just one of the many examples of how members of the Malay/Muslim community have excelled in their respective fields and continue to contribute to the Singapore story.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: As we celebrate SG60, it is timely to reflect on our progress as a society and as a Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Over the last 30 years, I had the privilege of journeying with our community, through my community work and across six Ministries.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I have seen first-hand what we can achieve when Government and the community strive with common purpose.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Indeed, our community has grown in strength, in confidence and in our ability to rally and contribute to Singapore's shared future.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The M3 agencies and Malay/Muslim organisations (MMOs), which include the Indian Muslim organisations (IMOs), have worked together with Government agencies to better serve the needs of the Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: However, the world is undergoing significant shifts: technological advancements, trade wars, climate change and geopolitical volatility are just a few examples.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The Malay/Muslim community must similarly confront these uncertainties.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I am encouraged by the renewed vigour from many community stakeholders, such as our MMOs, to find new and better ways to engage, collaborate and synergise efforts to take us forward.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: As the Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs, I hope to build on the good work of my predecessors and fellow community leaders.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I will deepen collaborations among the M3 agencies, MMOs, IMOs and the Government, to chart a stronger future for our Malay/Muslim community while contributing to our multiracial and multi-religious society.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Since taking office, I have been engaging widely and listening actively.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I have engaged our youth groups, mosque committees, working professionals, grassroots volunteers, MMOs and IMOs, arts and cultural groups and many more.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I have also engaged the community at various settings, including coffee shops, markets and food centres and formal dialogues.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I am touched by their stories of resilience and contribution, feel their concerns and inspired by their hopes and aspirations for community and the nation.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: To achieve these, we must tap on our collective energies and abilities as well as imagination.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Every member of our community should have the chance to be the best version of themselves at different stages of their lives.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Let us share in the joy of each other's success and rally around those who stumble so that they can find their feet again.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: For instance, Mr Muhammad Feroz Haron is the founder of Action in Motion (AIM) Society, which recently celebrated its sixth anniversary last month.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Sharing his past experiences, Feroz founded AIM with three other ex-offenders to provide social and emotional support for others on the drug rehabilitation journey.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: His wife, Madam Salmah Johari, also founded Women in Support to Develop Outstanding Men (WISDOM), a support group for spouses and partners of ex-offenders.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Or the story of Dr Norham Erlyani, who inspires us through her pursuit of excellence.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: She holds a PhD in stem cell and developmental biology from the National University of Singapore Graduate School and currently serves as Head of Strategy and Public Relations at Hilleman Laboratories.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Beyond her professional portfolio, she contributes actively to the community as the lead for Life Sciences under the MENDAKI Professional Networks and as a member of the Majlis Ugama Islam Singapura (MUIS) Council.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I am committed to supporting people like Mr Feroz and Dr Norham Erlyani, who have taken diverse paths at different stages of their lives, so that they can do better for themselves, and give back to those around them.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: They create stable and loving environments for us to pass shared values from one generation to the next, and for our children to realise their potential.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Strong marriages are the first step to flourishing families.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Over the years, we have seen good progress from our investments to support strong marriages.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We will continue to do more in this area, led by incoming Minister of State Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: With strong families as a foundation, we will invest more in the development of our children and youths.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Education is key to provide our children with a good start in life.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: As a community, we can do more to encourage the enrolment of our young into preschool, and to sustain their attendance.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We must also better support the learning of our students in primary and secondary schools, including after school hours.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: For instance, under Project Jalan Kukoh, MENDAKI, Majlis Ugama Islam Singapura (MUIS), the People’s Association Malay Activity Executive Committees Council (PA MESRA), 4PM, and other Government agencies reach out to youths in the Jalan Kukoh precinct.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Outside of school, we will equip our youths to deal with the challenges of the future.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Beyond the academics, we will also support them with career guidance, personal development opportunities and exposure to new experiences.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I hope that these efforts will position our youths to seize new opportunities in our fast-evolving economic landscape.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The workforce in the years to come will look very different from today and our workers must be prepared to ride the waves of growth in the future economy.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This will require a culture of lifelong learning, underpinned by the partnerships between the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC), MENDAKI and other MMOs.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Senior Minister of State Zaqy Mohamed and labour MP Dr Wan Rizal will helm this area to develop community platforms to complement national-level programmes to support our workers.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In particular, I hope that more of our workers can tap on opportunities in growth sectors like advanced manufacturing, technology and professional services like finance.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: As we progress, we cannot forget our seniors, particularly those in the Pioneer and Merdeka generations.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Prime Minister Lawrence Wong outlined Singapore’s plans to improve long-term care options through the Age Well Neighbourhoods for our seniors and their caregivers at the National Day Rally.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This initiative builds upon national programmes like HealthierSG and Age Well SG.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I similarly hope to mobilise our community, so that we can better meet the healthcare, social and emotional needs of our seniors.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I look forward to the support by Members.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: For instance, how can we tap on the experience of our seniors to benefit the community, as they transit into retirement?

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Or how can we better support caregivers through active ageing services and caregiving networks?

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: To this end, the Santunan Emas programme by Masjid Al-Muttaqin, in collaboration with Ma:een and Muhammadiyah Active Ageing Centre, is a commendable effort.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The programme provides holistic support for our elderly – from spiritual guidance through lectures by former Mufti, Ustaz Dr Mohamed Fatris Bakaram, to physical and social activities led by volunteers from Muhammadiyah for their overall well-being.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Let us continue to explore new ways to collaborate with various partners in support of our seniors.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I have spoken about improved social and economic outcomes.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Our faith is central to our character as a Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: It guides our values and how we engage one another, whether family members, neighbours or fellow citizens.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Our faith also guides us to live harmoniously with others in a multicultural and multi-religious society.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Since taking on this role, I have visited different mosques each week.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: These visits gave me the opportunity to meet congregants from all walks of life and speak with them on religious life in Singapore, among others.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We are also exploring how interim prayer spaces can be provided while mosque upgrading and development works are underway.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Our mosques and prayer spaces are fully funded by the community.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: So, we must be prudent in designing them and maximise our existing spaces by conducting second sessions for Friday prayers.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Two, beyond physical spaces, we must groom the next generation of religious leaders.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Our asatizah play a critical role in guiding our community and should be recognised and fairly compensated for their work, as Mr Sharael Taha mentioned earlier.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: As we navigate a more complex world, they must be keenly attuned to global changes while appreciating our local context.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I also agree with Mr Sharael Taha that SCIS’ partnership with the Singapore University of Social Sciences will be important in exposing our future asatizah to diverse academic experiences and develop them not just as capable religious teachers, but also compassionate community leaders who can help the community navigate contemporary social challenges.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Three, our religious institutions must develop new capabilities to guide the community in contemporary issues.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: These rulings exemplify how our Fatwa Committee and asatizah can provide guidance that is both religiously sound and practically relevant.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We will continue to empower our asatizah to guide the community in these complex issues and in so doing, deepen trust in our religious institutions.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Importantly, the ability to maintain confidence in our religious life depends on the trust in our religious institutions and the partnerships with the broader network of Muslim organisations.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We will strengthen these networks of trust and partnerships to address the religious needs of our community.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Together, I am confident that we will engender a fulfilling life for our Singapore Muslims who actively contribute to their community and society.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I have spoken about improved social and economic outcomes, and about practising our faith in a multicultural society.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This is an integral part of Singapore’s cultural diversity and national identity.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Pak Zubir Said's composition of our national anthem, "Majulah Singapura", is a prime example of how Malay artistic expression has shaped our national identity.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Contemporary Malay artists like Madam Som Said are instrumental in championing Malay dance in Singapore, while writers like Djamal Tukimin have become cornerstones of Singapore’s Malay literary scene.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We also have practitioners dedicated to preserving our living heritage and craft, such as Yaziz Hassan who is passing down the knowledge of crafting and repairing traditional Malay drums to future generations.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In my engagements, many in the community have told me that they hope we can hold fast to what has nourished our hearts and souls over generations, even as we pursue economic growth and prosperity.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: My team and I hope to galvanise the community to celebrate and develop our arts, culture, and heritage sector, showcase the vibrancy of our unique Singaporean Malay culture and preserve our cultural traditions for future generations.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: It will provide a new platform to celebrate the stories of the Malay community and recognise how their contributions have shaped Singapore's development and national identity.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The refreshed centre will enhance representation of Malay ethnic sub-groups, showcasing the diversity that exists within our community, with increased focus on women's contributions to education, literature and the arts.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The centre will also see newly commissioned works by both emerging and established Malay artists in support of contemporary cultural expression.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The National Heritage Board is also partnering with community and precinct stakeholders in Kampong Gelam to strengthen its distinctive cultural identity and heritage value.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Our culture should be celebrated and enjoyed by all.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We will continue to support the People's Association Malay Activity Executive Committees Council (PA MESRA) and the Malay Activity Executive Committees (MAECs) in various events to preserve the Malay culture, whether through performances during festive seasons, or through cultural festivals and activities.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This is borne out of the courage, dedication and resilience of our pioneers, such as Yusof Ishak, Othman Wok and Ahmad Ibrahim, to make this country home – a place where we belong.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: They worked alongside fellow Singaporeans to build a strong foundation for the nation and enabled us to progress as a community and society.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I hope to build on the good work of our past leaders, together with our community.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Since taking office as the Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs, I have engaged widely with various segments of our community, from youth groups, arts and heritage groups, mosque committees, professionals, grassroots volunteers, Malay/Muslim organisations and many more.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I am deeply grateful for the feedback and feel inspired by their ideas to strengthen our bonds, uplift lives and realise our potential.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: My fellow People's Action Party (PAP) Malay/Muslim MPs and I are committed to continue supporting the Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We will focus on three key areas in the years ahead.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We also want to equip our workers so that they are able to seize opportunities in emerging sectors, and support our elderly to age gracefully and with dignity.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Three, we will preserve our Malay arts, culture, and heritage which have nourished our hearts and souls over generations.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: However, we will constantly refine it through continuous engagement with more members of our community.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We must consider how our actions and choices contribute to the well-being of the larger society.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: By looking out for each other, we can go far together.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: It is not just for the Malay/Muslim community but the whole of Singapore.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Therefore, I call upon every member of our community, regardless of age, profession or background, to contribute to our shared success.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Our pioneers and the past generations played a pivotal role in writing the Singapore Story.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: They chose to build a multiracial and multicultural society regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Now, it is our turn to expand the Singapore Story and write the next chapter that charts the journey and progress of the Malay community, in particular, and the wider society.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: It encompasses our efforts to celebrate strength in diversity, forging close ties between communities to strengthen our solidarity and work alongside fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This solidarity is key in helping Singapore navigate uncertainties ahead and build an endearing home for all.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Let us embark on this journey together, guided by lessons learnt and wisdom gained from past endeavours, as well as with the hopes and dreams of our community to contribute to the happiness, prosperity and progress for our nation.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: When we speak of social mobility or inequality, we often talk about wages, jobs, housing, even cars.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But we talk less about how socioeconomic background also shapes health, education and opportunity – across a lifetime.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Residents in rental flats are hospitalised and re-admitted more often, even after adjusting for their conditions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And preventive care – the very thing that could break the cycle – is patchier, with fewer screenings, fewer follow-ups, fewer regular doctors.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Like my Woodlands resident, Mr K, a lift technician and father of two who came to my Meet the People session to appeal some parking fines.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: His wife had walked out on the family.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: He works nights, so he brings his children along.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They wait in the car in the unloading bay, hence the parking tickets, while he does his work.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: His children lose sleep, lose focus in school and sometimes, they skip school.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: He himself suffers from depression but cannot afford treatment.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Or Ms S, living with chronic mental illness and hypertension.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: She wants to work, but her workplace makes no accommodations.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Each day she cannot bring herself to go in to work, she slips further away from the stability she craves.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: When the dialysis centre in Woodlands was closed for renovations and her dialysis treatments were transferred to Ghim Moh, their transport subsidy lapsed.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In despair, he asked me, "Should I just stop taking her and let her die?" Mr Speaker, when poor income, poor health and poor education reinforce each other, the cycle of disadvantage is brutal.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And breaking this cycle must be a most urgent duty.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: KidSTART supports parents and children from the earliest years.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Uplifting Pupils in Life and Inspiring Families Task force (UPLIFT) narrows achievement gaps, improves attendance and well-being.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Grow Well SG and Healthier SG help families build healthier habits and access preventive care, Age Well SG keeps our seniors active and ComLink+ brings in family coaches and Progress packages.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Families face many schemes, many officers, many forms that strain their already strained mental bandwidth.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There is a lot of coordination and referrals, fewer active interventions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Too much is left to chance – whether a child or senior shows up for vaccination, whether a family completes a form correctly.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What we need are not more and more piecemeal programmes, but joined-up longitudinal pathways that follow a family through an extended period of time – structured where necessary, empowering where possible, that provides support, while building personal agency.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Pathways that ensure no child, no parent, no senior falls through the cracks.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I propose three pathways: an education pathway, a health pathway and a career pathway, all linked together with ComLink+.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We know early childhood education is one of the strongest levers of social mobility.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It must continue though primary and secondary school, not only after school and tuition, but also enrichment in arts, sports and coding, because talent is not the exclusive domain of the wealthy and must not be capped by income.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Integration between KidSTART, UPLIFT and ComLink+ must be seamless – no six-month gaps, no missed transitions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A child's progress should be tracked, with early interventions when they fall behind – whether in literacy, attendance or well-being.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The goal is not just to graduate more students, but to graduate them resilient and ready to seize the opportunity.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: From KidSTART to Grow Well SG, to Healthier SG, to Age Well SG, a continuum of care, one longitudinal journey.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Family coaches, or dedicated health coaches must go beyond health coordination and referrals.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If a child misses a vaccination, reschedule it.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If medication is not taken, find out why.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If meals are not nutritious, connect the family to food support.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And for working adults, let us pilot Health Secure Jobs – workplaces where chronic illnesses or caregiving duties do not mean job losses.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Instead MOH and MOM partner with employers to keep workers employed in jobs, while managing conditions like diabetes or depression, because health must not mean unemployment.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The ComLink+ Employment Package is a step forward – with coaching, training, retention incentives and wraparound support.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They must provide progression, skills and dignity and build confidence.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Here we can learn from the US programme "Year Up" , which offers six months of intensive training, tuition free, in skills that today's employers need followed by six months of corporate internships – coupled with mentorship, coaching, professional development and the possibility of college credit for coursework, along with stipends and other support services and essential resources, such as, housing, food, transportation and childcare to remove any barriers to participants' success.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We could roll this our in Singapore, where a young person from a disadvantaged family who once felt locked out of opportunity, gains not only skills and networks, but also confidence, dignity and hope.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The three pathways: education, healthcare and career cannot stand alone.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They must be linked and linked by ComLink+.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If a child struggles in school, it should trigger a check on nutrition or sleep.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If health appointments are missed, it should prompt a check on school or work attendance, because no one lives life in silos, and neither should our policies.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Policy must empower our offices to act holistically and not within narrow silos.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If we can link the pathways effectively, we should end up achieving more by doing less.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Without linking them, each silo can feel like it is pushing on a string – much effort, little outcomes – and gets pressured to invest even more in its own silo.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Underpinning all of this is our care workforce: family coaches, social workers, healthcare teams.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They are the ones who journey alongside families on each pathway, not for weeks, but for years.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Studies have shown how having that one mentoring figure, whom you have a genuine connection with, a genuine relationship, can make all the difference in changing the life of a low-income person.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We must invest in their training, understand their workload and reward them fairly.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We must select and empower them to be not just case workers, but life-changers.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: He paints meritocracy as corrosive, an ideological belief to justify and explain away inequality and the lot of those left behind.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The danger is not in practicing meritocracy but in abandoning it, because success would depend not on effort or talent, but on connections and privilege.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And that is why we are here, to refine it, to strengthen it, to make sure that meritocracy in Singapore remains fair and real, not just in principle but in practice.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The truth is meritocracy in Singapore has never stood still.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We have broadened and deepened the definition of meritocracy precisely to address the risks Mr Fadli Fawzi raised.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: First, merit is no longer exclusively seen through your exam scores and the schools you go to.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Today, we have multiple pathways – university, polytechnics, the Institute of Technical Education (ITE), SkillsFuture, we have subject-based banding.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I have talked about KidSTART, UPLIFT, Comlink+ earlier.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Yes, we can push further, but all are designed to level the playing field.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Third, we now explicitly recognise unequal starting points.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This has been mentioned by both our Prime Minister and our President.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Fourth, we also now recognise that merit is not just about individual effort, but as something shaped by community, family and society.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Many initiatives bring together Government, volunteers, employers to uplift families together.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And among the most visible are in our Malay community, where under the auspices of M³@Towns, our "gotong royong" spirit shines through, whether it is in Kelas MateMatika (KMM), Mendaki Tuition Scheme (MTS) or youth mentoring.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And lastly, we celebrate values and character, not just grades or how much money you make.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: At every Edusave awards, we give the Edusave Award for Achievement, Good Leadership and Service (EAGLES) award and the Edusave Character Award (ECHA) award.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Resilience, service and contribution to society are part of how we define merit.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What I have just described cannot possibly be seen as an elitist meritocracy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Ours is a progressive and compassionate meritocracy, one which recognizes effort and ability, while also investing heavily in those with fewer advantages and we keep improving.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Framing meritocracy as an ideology risks dismissing these hard-won efforts.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I do not discount that there are many families, including many in our Malay community who are really struggling.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I see them at my Meet the People session.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But there are many issues at play, that weigh families down regardless of effort or merit.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And while we must keep improving our system, I humbly remember both Member Fadli Fawzi and I are, ourselves, beneficiaries of Singapore’s meritocracy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is this system that enabled us, children from ordinary families, to study, to work and now to serve in this House.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, there is no need to disparage or dismiss the system that has uplifted and continues to uplift so many.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And certainly, there is no need to mischaracterise it to our community as promoting the belief that "those who succeed are entitled to their success because they have worked hard, while those who are left behind deserve to be left behind because they have not worked hard enough".

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But secondly, words like this do not help families who are struggling.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What helps them is when we, as leaders, acknowledge the gaps honestly and work together on solutions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This includes lingering experiences of prejudice and discrimination, perceived or otherwise.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This is not an abstract goal to me.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: My own journey, I know that of many in this Chamber and many, many more outside this Chamber, and it is proof of what Singapore has made possible.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But 60 years after Independence, our society has changed.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Minister of Health who is also now the Coordinating Minister for Social Policy happens to be my anchor Minister in Sembawang group representation constituency (GRC) and I seek his understanding that no matter how good a job the Government is doing on this topic, I will always press us to do more, do better.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Because social mobility is not just a policy goal.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I look forward to working with Members of this House to heed the President’s call.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 3.38 pm until 4.00 pm.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I will speak on how our foreign policy is adapting to geopolitical shifts and the growing presence of foreign interference, and how Singapore can remain vigilant against it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: As noted by previous speakers, the global economic and strategic order is indeed shifting.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: As a small, open and trade-dependent country, Singapore is especially sensitised to these shifts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Asia Pacific region has become a primary arena of their contestation which spans trade, security, ideology and technology.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The South China Sea is an example of how tensions between major powers could have direct implications for peace and prosperity in our neighbourhood.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Second, geopolitical conflicts weigh heavily on the international system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Some wars continue unresolved and are difficult to end, while others have been rekindled in recent times.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: They have resulted in immense humanitarian suffering and generated strong emotional resonance in many countries, including ours.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Such conflicts have also delayed or impaired decision-making at regional or international groupings, making cooperation more difficult.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Countries are taking a narrower and more transactional view of their national interests.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Declining strategic trust between countries has also led to increased contestation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We are seeing the fragmentation of global trade and technology ecosystems, export controls on sensitive technologies and competing standards in areas, like AI.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Consequently, multilateralism and rules-based international trade are under considerable strain.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: These trends are keenly felt by Singapore, an open economy and global business hub, whose security and prosperity have been boosted in the post-war era by favourable conditions, such as an extended period of relative peace in Southeast Asia, a rules-based international order largely shaped by US leadership and China's success in reform and opening up.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We now face greater risks, narrowed room for manoeuvre and sharpened trade-offs in our foreign policy decisions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We took pains to develop a diversified diplomatic strategy, just we have built a diversified economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) has invested as much effort and energy into advancing Singapore's contributions at multilateral fora and regional groupings, as we have in maintaining bilateral accounts with our partner countries, which together, constitute a broad geographical spread.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We have also remained consistent in being a trusted friend and honest broker to our partners, adding value wherever we can, but also accepting the limitations of being a small country.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: While there will be some adjustments to our diplomacy, these will not be abrupt shifts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: At the core of this effort is ensuring that our relationships with our closest neighbours – Malaysia, Indonesia and Brunei – remain strong, wide-ranging and forward-looking.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We have embarked on long-term projects to enhance connectivity and strengthen economic and people-to-people ties, such as the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (SEZ) and the Rapid Transit System (RTS) Link.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We will also expand our partnership into emerging areas like renewable energy and human capital development.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: ASEAN remains a cornerstone of our foreign policy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Deeper economic integration within ASEAN remains vital to unlocking the vast potential of our region.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We will work towards this by upgrading and fully implementing our trade agreements, deepening cross-border digital frameworks, developing the ASEAN Power Grid and advancing green economy standards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We will also expand ASEAN's network of partnerships, ensure key international players have a stake in our region's success and maintain an open, inclusive and ASEAN-centred regional architecture.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We have built strong relations with major powers over the years and will continue to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The US is our top trading partner in services and our largest foreign investor.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We are also the US' only Major Security Cooperation Partner.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: China is our top trading partner in goods and we are China's largest foreign investor.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Our bilateral interactions with China are multi-tiered, led by the Joint Council for Bilateral Coorperation at the Deputy Prime Minister level, and comprising three government-to-government projects and eight province-level economic councils.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We must remain clear-eyed and have the resolve to make decisions that are in Singapore's long-term national interest.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We have also been deepening strategic relationships with other partners, such as Japan, the Republic of Korea (ROK), India, the European Union (EU), Australia and New Zealand.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: With the EU, our Free Trade Agreement and latest Digital Trade Agreement have given Singapore businesses preferential access to one of the world's largest markets, while our cooperation in sustainability and green transition opens up new areas of growth.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: As we embark on the next round of our Comprehensive Strategic Partnership with Australia, we are exploring initiatives with a regional focus, as well as collaborations in frontier areas, like critical technologies and space.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: With New Zealand, we are upgrading our Enhanced Partnership to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership with significant initiatives across the defence, trade and economic, and supply chain and connectivity pillars.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: By anchoring trusted partnerships across different regions, we will reduce our exposure to volatility, such as supply chain disruptions, and strengthen our national resilience in key domains, such as defence, energy and technology, and continue to serve as a "safe deposit box", not just for capital but also technology and innovation, and be a trusted and secure node in the global network, where ideas, data and partnerships are protected, nurtured and scaled.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In addition, through our Development Partnerships Directorate, MFA will enhance the Singapore Cooperation Programme to share Singapore's experience and best practices in areas where we have relevant strengths.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This is part of our diplomatic toolkit to deepen relationships with partners.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: And when humanitarian crises strike, we will contribute where we can and seek to deliver practical assistance to alleviate the immense civilian suffering and displacement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We have done so when a magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck central Myanmar in March 2025 and are providing ongoing aid to the civilians in Gaza, something that we discussed in this House yesterday.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The rules-based international order may be under strain, but many countries still believe that there is more to be gained from cooperation than contestation and that like-minded partners can continue to cooperate on initiatives like digital economy agreements, green economy partnerships and global governance initiatives, albeit on a smaller scale, and we are among them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This is why we will do our utmost to support multi-lateral institutions, enhance international law, contribute to global governance discussions and promote peaceful dispute resolution.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We contribute actively to the development of global norms, by leading groupings like the Forum of Small States and the Global Governance Group, to discuss issues affecting small states and to champion practical cooperation on issues, such as respect for international law, climate change adaptation and digital transformation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Agreement on Marine Biodiversity in Areas Beyond National Jurisdiction agreement, successfully concluded under the leadership of Ambassador Rena Lee as President of the Intergovernmental Conference, has just crossed the threshold of 60 state ratifications and will soon enter into force.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Singapore has also made contributions to the world Intellectual Property Office (WIPO) Treaty on Intellectual Property, Genetic Resources and Associated Traditional Knowledge, and the Paris Agreement on Climate Change, particularly, the development of carbon markets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Singapore will also continue taking up leadership roles in international bodies where we have significant expertise.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: For example, at the International Civil Aviation Organization, the International Maritime Organization, the Commission on Narcotic Drugs and WIPO, as mentioned earlier.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: To be sure, countries have long interfered in other countries' domestic politics, overtly or covertly, to advance their own interests.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: What is new is the landscape in which foreign actors conduct these operations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The ubiquitous digital environment and development of advanced digital tools have supercharged their ability to mount hostile information campaigns (HICs) to advance their interests.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: By exploiting the internet, digital and social media, foreign actors can mount HICs at scale, speed and precision.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Colleagues may have heard of the "sprinter" network, a complex web of fake accounts that spread disinformation on the war in Ukraine, manipulated public opinion and amplified politically-charged content.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In 2023, the Guardian uncovered a team of contractors that conduct disinformation operations for private companies, intelligence agencies and political campaigns.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: With a diverse population that is highly digitally connected, Singapore is an attractive and vulnerable target.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The network could have been used to mount other HICs against Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: At the same time, traditional methods of interference continue apace, through local and influential proxies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In 2024, the US arrested and charged a former CIA analyst for allegedly acting as an agent for a foreign country, while an Australian court convicted a businessman for secretly attempting to improperly influence an Australian federal minister through donations, in order to advance the aims of a foreign power.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Singapore is not immune to these examples of interference.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Transparency requirements and reporting are imposed on these individuals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Foreign interference tactics will evolve and grow in sophistication.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: They touch on our everyday lives – through what we see, hear and read in an increasingly permeable infospace.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It could also aim to influence the targeted country’s policies, including its foreign policy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Vigilance against foreign interference is therefore a shared concern of Governments and foreign policy circles throughout the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: But this does not mean that we discourage the public from learning about and discussing foreign policy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: On the contrary, we would like Singaporeans to continue being interested in and knowledgeable about global affairs, because it affects our security and prosperity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Even as we consume and exchange views on foreign policy, let us remain alert to the possibility of external attempts to influence our foreign policy by shaping our people’s perception of, and support for it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Through manipulating public sentiments, including through local opinion leaders, in addition to spreading misinformation and fake news.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We encourage Singaporeans to be discerning about the news and messages we are constantly receiving, including on social media, from a wide variety of sources.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Always question what you see, hear or read – ask where the information came from; is it true and what is the intent?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Inflamed sentiments can hamper judgement and create rifts between groups of Singaporeans that are hard to repair, especially if race and religion are involved.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Let us maintain calm and mutual respect when discussing current affairs, including global developments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Second, where discussions centre around which countries Singapore should be closer to, or which countries’ lead Singapore should be following.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Such chatter, though not uncommon, does not reflect how Singapore conducts foreign policy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Those who find themselves in such conversations could gently remind their friends and associates that Singapore bases our foreign policy on our national interests.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Third, where leaders of local institutions and groupings or those with a following, find themselves commenting publicly on international developments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In such instances, it would be useful to consider the content carefully beforehand, and check if it can be construed to mean anything other than the view of a Singaporean who is well-versed in our national interests.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Through more of such engagements, I hope that youths and community leaders can spread the word in their own circles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Singapore’s relevance to the world depends on our ability to create value.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We can be reliable and trusted by other countries only if we remain principled and consistent.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We can only achieve this if we speak with one united voice and this stems from domestic stability as well as public trust in the Government.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: If our social fabric frays, our international credibility will weaken.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Malignant actors may seek to exploit our divisions for their own interests.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Support for our foreign policy does not mean unconditional agreement with all decisions, but a shared commitment among Singaporeans to safeguarding Singapore’s sovereignty and long-term national interests.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: National unity and domestic support allow our leaders to stand firm under external pressure, to say no when it matters most and to negotiate confidently on behalf of all Singaporeans to protect and advance our interests.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Government will continue to do its part through legislation, broadening education and regular engagements with different segments of society to raise awareness and understanding of our foreign policy considerations and Singapore’s global contributions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: But more crucially, we must, as a nation and as a people, be alive to attempts by foreign actors to interfere in our politics, policies and way of life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Legislative levers can only do so much, and they are often brought into play only ex-post.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The ultimate line of defence against foreign interference is an aware and discerning people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Deputy Speaker, the international order is being weakened day-by-day, the world is also not very peaceful.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Under such circumstances, we need to guard against foreign interference and hybrid threats.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: There are many objectives for conducting foreign interference.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Foreign interference aims to weaken the targeted country, for instance by sowing division and internal strife.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It could also aim to influence the targeted country’s policies, including its foreign policy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Vigilance against foreign interference is therefore a shared concern of governments and foreign policy circles throughout the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: But this does not mean that we discourage Singaporeans from learning about international developments and discussing foreign policy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Even as Singaporeans consume and exchange views on foreign policy, we need to remain alert to the possibility of external attempts to influence our people’s understanding of international developments and change their perception of, and support for Singapore’s foreign policy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This could be done through manipulating public sentiments, including through local opinion leaders, as well as spreading misinformation and fake news.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We encourage Singaporeans to be discerning about the news and messages we are constantly receiving, including on social media, from a wide variety of sources.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: There are a few scenarios where it would be particularly useful for Singaporeans to exercise more vigilance and remind others around them to do so too.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: First, where discussions grow emotional, inflamed sentiments can hamper judgement and create rifts between groups of Singaporeans that are hard to repair, especially when sensitive topics such as race and religion are involved.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Let us maintain calm and mutual respect when discussing current affairs, including global developments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Second, where discussions centre around which countries Singapore should be closer to, or which countries’ lead Singapore should follow.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Such chatter, though not uncommon, does not reflect how Singapore conducts foreign policy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Those who find themselves in such conversations could gently remind the speakers that Singapore bases our foreign policy on our national interests.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Third, where leaders of local social and business institutions comment publicly on international developments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In such instances, it would be useful to consider the content carefully beforehand and check if it can be construed to mean anything other than the views of a Singaporean well-versed in Singapore’s national interests.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We can only achieve this if we speak with one united voice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This stems from domestic stability as well as public trust in the Government.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: If our social fabric frays, our international credibility will weaken.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Malignant actors may seek to exploit our divisions for their own interests.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We have succeeded by staying united at home, relevant abroad and nimble in adapting to change.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I believe that with the trust and support of our people, we can continue to secure a better global future for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Fadli Fawzi, you have a clarification of a speech given by a Member in this debate, do you?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi
text: And I believe even in her speech, she gave a lot of examples of the people who are falling through the cracks of the system.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi
text: And I think, ultimately, these are the people who both are advocating for.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Ms Mariam Jaafar, would you like to respond to that?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: I think the Member now says that his point was if meritocracy is taken to the extreme.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: But that is precisely the problem of his argument.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: I meet them every day and I try my best to help them every day.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Fadli Fawzi, do you have a clarification of that?

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I will try my best to keep it within 40 minutes.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At each Opening of Parliament after a General Election (GE), it is customary for the PAP Government to reflect on our continuing political journey, what the people have told us with their votes during the GE.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We then take stock of where we are, and what we need to do from here.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: GE2025 was held against a global backdrop of war and uncertainty.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It was also the first GE since the leadership transition.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The stakes were therefore very high, as the outcome would shape how Singapore responds to the challenges ahead and would set the tone for our politics over the next five years.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the end, Singaporeans made a decisive choice.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are witnessing first-hand this outcome reflected in the Chamber today.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The PAP, with a decisive majority, and in a position to act fast and adapt to changes in our environment, for the benefit of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And at the same time, the WP is now the only opposition party in Parliament, with a sizeable presence to provide a check on the ruling party.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Voters have clear expectations of the role they want each party to play: the PAP, as the Government they want; and the WP, as the opposition they want.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Each party now has the important task of fulfilling the roles the electorate expects of us.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: How we perform our respective roles will influence our nation's political development.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is just as critical as our economic or social development.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Because having the right politics that preserves our values, and maintains trust in the system of governance, is essential.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It helps keep our social order intact and allows individuals and communities to flourish.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Without the right politics, our society will be broken, and no amount of economic growth or Government programmes will be able to put things right.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And how, should we, as elected representatives, do right by Singapore and Singaporeans?

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As we reflect on GE2025, these are my key takeaways and there are four.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, GE2025 showed that Singaporeans value a stable and effective Government that will safeguard our well-being.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The uncertain global and economic environment was undoubtedly on Singaporeans' minds when we went to the polls.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Voters therefore leaned towards stability, choosing a government with a proven track record of steering the country through crises.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We did so after "September 11", the Global Financial Crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic.
