speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Given the global circumstances, I believe Singaporeans also want a government that not just takes care of domestic concerns, but also defends Singapore's interests on the global stage, ensuring that Singapore stands tall among the community of nations.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We, on this side of the House, therefore cannot be complacent.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will continue to step up our efforts to engage Singaporeans, understand the people's concerns and address them.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will uphold the PAP's ethos, always think and plan long-term, to serve the current and future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The second lesson is that our political system is still evolving.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The GE2025 results show that Singaporeans want the PAP to remain in Government and to act decisively for Singapore.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At the same time, the people also want an opposition in Parliament, as an alternative voice, and to provide a check on the Government.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Not long after GE, I went to a coffeeshop, queuing up for "tze char".

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: After I ordered, I chatted with fellow patrons, a middle-aged couple.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They said opposite their house, Bukit Canberra, there were a wonderful swimming pool, a polyclinic and a hawker centre.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And finally, when they got their food, they were leaving, they said, "Minister, I want to tell you.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I did not vote for you because we have to give the opposition a chance".

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But this is the reality the PAP is facing.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We may work hard, we deliver for residents, who may even say they like us.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Yet, they vote for the opposition, while expecting that the PAP will still return to government.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Voters like this couple did not form the majority in Sembawang during GE2025.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If their numbers had been bigger, I might not be standing here today, neither will Ms Mariam Jaafar.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The PAP understands and accepts our voters' desires for an opposition.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is why after GE2020, then-Prime Minister Lee formalised the position of the Leader of the Opposition.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In GE2025, even before the campaign began, we said that the chances of an opposition wipeout were zero and we were right.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The election outcome suggests that Singaporeans are judiciously balancing between having PAP as government and an opposition presence as a check and balance.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The WP, in fact, deliberately chose to contest fewer than one-third of the seats.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I do not think this was solely for lack of suitable candidates.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It was a considered, strategic decision, reading the mood of the electorate.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I infer that voters must have felt that it worked well for Singapore in the previous term of Government.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: After all, with a decisive majority, the PAP attended to important matters of the state and could guide Singapore through a devastating pandemic crisis.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: On issues such as cost of living, the opposition amplified ground concerns in Parliament.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Through GE2025, I believe voters are saying to us, "Make this composition work for Singapore once again".

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Any future shift from this current composition will, no doubt, be carefully weighed by Singaporeans.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Voters' judgement will depend on many factors, such as the quality of the candidates on both sides, the performance of the PAP as the ruling party in leading the country, our sensitivity and response to ground concerns, the performance of the WP as a responsible opposition voice, as they characterise themselves and the standards of honesty and integrity displayed by both parties.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is quite possible other opposition parties besides the WP will come in the next time.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They certainly are working hard to remain players.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The third lesson is that Singaporeans continue to be moderate and pragmatic in our political philosophy.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Voters expect our politics and politicians to reflect that.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To be clear, every politician hopes to be popular.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But to be a populist and practise populism, that is entirely a different thing.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Populists tend to employ an "us versus them" framing, which pits one group against another.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They gain support by presenting themselves as champions of "the people", standing up fighting against elites, the institutions, or outsiders.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Further, populists offer simplistic solutions to complex problems and appeal mostly to emotions.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Upon closer scrutiny, people will realise these simplistic solutions do not work.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But when people are disillusioned and they are disgruntled, they hope for a silver bullet and they may give these simplistic solutions a chance.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Across the world, we have seen the rise of populism.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It can be on the extreme left; it can be on the extreme right.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, left-wing populism has a long history in Argentina – heavy taxes on the rich and on businesses to fund social spending, and a fight for labour rights.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There is nothing inherently wrong with those positions and those policies.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But when pushed to the extreme, businesses in Argentina prefer to go elsewhere.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Jobs are destroyed, confidence evaporates, the currency collapses, and the economy goes into a tailspin.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the end, the workers and the ordinary people are the ones who suffer.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This has happened to Argentina many times over the decades, but the populist movement persists in the country.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: More common now is right-wing, far-right populism, often attributed to higher levels of immigration.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We see it in the US, in Europe, in United Kingdom (UK), even in Australia and Japan.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When the population starts to feel uncomfortable with the size of the inflow of immigrants, far-right politicians seize the opportunity to stoke nativist and anti-immigrant sentiments.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Populism takes societies on the road to ruin, creating irreconcilable rifts between communities, and fuelling xenophobia and racism.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: With no consideration for the long-term consequences or broader impact on society, eventually, either their fiscal system goes broke, or the society breaks apart.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have witnessed populism in this Chamber too.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is for the benefit of new Members.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Soon after GE2020, there were allegations by the Progress Singapore Party (PSP) that our Free Trade Agreement (FTA) with India, the Comprehensive Economic Cooperation Agreement (CECA), allowed professionals from India "a free hand" to come work in Singapore, and that was the cause of the employment challenges faced by Singaporean professionals.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It was a seductive and simplistic argument, which took on an ugly racial tone.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: CECA-themed websites sprouted, filled with disturbing xenophobic views.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Minister Shanmugam called out the behaviour in Parliament.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I knew that the allegations were false, and I volunteered to deliver a Ministerial Statement on how FTA works, to debate the PSP and to clear the air.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Then Minister Tan See Leng explained what the Government was doing to address the challenges faced by Singaporean professionals, which were not caused by the FTAs.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: More constructive engagement helps build up our defences against populism.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But the best defence against populism is for the people to reject it.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But we must understand this: populism does not appear out of nowhere or out of thin air.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It arises from genuine, understandable concerns among the people, over the inequality they see in society, or excessive competition for jobs and space from foreigners.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Hence, the seeds of populism exist in every society.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The question is whether these seeds are allowed to take root and grow.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Anyone who peddles soft, partial truths, easy but incomplete solutions, waters these seeds; anyone who refuses the hard cognitive work of formulating rational policies provides fertile ground for the seeds.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Prime Minister himself had to call this out in the middle of the campaign.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If things had played out differently, there would have been dire and lasting implications for the unity, harmony and very fabric of Singaporean society.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will have more to say about this later in this debate.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The final lesson from this GE is that Singaporeans are holding political parties to higher standards.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This includes demanding more substantive information and arguments during an election.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It has led to a torrent of memes and attention-grabbing short videos popping up online, especially during the campaign.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many offer nothing more than a moment of entertainment or an emotional outlet.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some amount of such froth and frivolity is unavoidable during election season.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But I do not think that the average voter has therefore become frivolous as a result.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: On the contrary, Singaporeans are becoming more discerning, demanding quality information on policies put forth by various parties.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The fact that Singaporeans take their duty as voters seriously was particularly apparent during GE2025, when voters attended rallies, if they missed these, they watched them online, some watched a second time Many turned to long-form podcasts, invested time to listen to candidates’ motivations and opinions; they left thoughtful comments and suggestions for candidates to think about.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Voters showed us that they are not easily persuaded by slogans or catchy phrases alone.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They carefully weighed in-depth opinions and substantive explanations of policy proposals; while populist and simplistic proposals were treated with suspicion.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This willingness to take the time and trouble over political issues that we saw emerge during GE2025 may well be the defining characteristic of the Singaporean voter, but we cannot take it for granted.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Shortly after the hustings, the Leader of the Opposition appeared on a podcast with Keluar Sekejap in Malaysia and said that the PAP avoided engaging on difficult issues during the campaign.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I have a different view from Mr Pritam Singh.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In fact, I think there was substantive discourse during the GE2025 campaign.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ministers spoke at rallies and went on podcasts to further explain our policy positions.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The fact that the subject of GST did not catch fire during the campaign does not mean there was no discourse.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It means that the PAP’s explanations went at least some way to soothe people’s natural unhappiness over a tax increase.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Hence, more importantly, political discourse should not just happen during election campaigns.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A hallmark of good governance is sustaining it throughout the term.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And we have been engaging Singaporeans in this House, in and outside this House, on issues such as housing, cost of living and immigration.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The WP themselves participated actively when we have debates in this Chamber.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As politics in Singapore mature, this is what Singaporeans expect.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They want to hear different perspectives, and see a contest of good ideas, so that the best ones can be used to take Singapore forward.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is why alternative visions and pathways matter.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The PAP has its set of governing principles and policies to take Singapore forward.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Opposition parties can play an important role by setting out their long-term ideas, presenting clear alternative visions for governance, and outlining the pathways and policies to get there.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For alternatives to be meaningful, they must go beyond tweaking at the margins of Government proposals, or simply jumping on the bandwagon every time an issue goes viral.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Singaporeans want to see clear, well-considered visions that allow them to weigh real choices about our nation’s future.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We see this dynamic institutionalised in other mature democracies.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the UK for example, the Tories were in favour of Brexit; while Labour was pro-EU.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In Germany, the Christian Democratic Union is more conservative; the Social Democratic Party leans towards social spending; the Greens champion environmental sustainability.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the US, the Republicans traditionally favour low taxes and a small government; the Democrats, the opposite.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These distinct futures entail very different sets of policies.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Such as how government taxes and spends, how it grows the economy and creates jobs, tackles inequality, brings about greater social mobility, or protects the environment.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Different political parties ought to make clear these differences in their pitch to voters.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The WP has perhaps done this from time to time.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In a maturing democracy, voters deserve and want more than positions that agree with the PAP’s policies in general but suggest "let’s do a bit more", or offer something that appears to be more generous, more compassionate, and yet requires fewer hard choices.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This falls short of being a real alternative.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A real alternative promises gains with accompanying trade-offs, so that voters can make informed decisions and not be lulled into comforting illusions.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In a mature democracy, these are the kinds of issues that should form the substance of political debate.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It should be a design feature, not a bug.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That way, a vote for the PAP is not just a vote for a government that is decisive and nimble, but also an endorsement of the PAP’s principles and tried and tested methods of governance.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And if voters vote wisely, this is how we can continue to strengthen trust, accountability and good governance in Singapore.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: On one of them, the host asked me, in all seriousness: "Why can’t the political parties just get along?

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Someone come with a good idea, you say 'That is a good idea, lets work on it together.' Why can't you do that?" My response to him was along the following lines, but today I am elaborating a little bit.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Humans are the only living things capable of living in large and complex societies, where different groups with diverse, sometimes diametrically opposed interests, aspirations and affiliations can co-exist peacefully.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One might hope that such harmony be a perpetual state of affairs.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In fact, in the earlier civilisations, humans formed tribes and kingdoms to compete against and kill one another.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Tragically, this is still happening in some societies today.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our ability to co-exist in complex societies rests primarily on good governance.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In societies with the right preconditions, democracy plays a big part.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Various groups find their representation in political parties which then contest elections.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The winners secure a mandate to govern in line with the vision and plans that they campaigned on.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Not everyone will be happy with the outcome, but in a mature democracy, the minority will accept what the majority have chosen.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The majority may also make compromises so that the minority can better accept the outcomes.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As for the parties that lost, they will bide their time, and hope to topple the winner in the next electoral cycle.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: What would have been brutal wars and bloodshed amongst competing factions is now replaced by political debate and a democratic contest between political parties.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Contest, debate, compromises and political parties trying to outdo each other are therefore inherent to our society and system of governance.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It was a serious response to a serious question on the podcast.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: My hosts made light of it, but I think they were disappointed, even worried.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have seen, elsewhere, how political contestation has hardened into divisive politics often tied to identity and driven deep wedges between communities.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Voters and politicians alike take increasingly polarised positions.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The result is entrenched division and lasting discord.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But this need not be the inevitable outcome of political contest.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To do this, society must get its politics right.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: All of us in this Parliament have a role to play, by conducting ourselves in a manner worthy of the trust Singaporeans have placed in us.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I have gone through my takeaways from GE2025 to remind us of what these roles are.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To my fellow Singaporeans, I say: continue to be discerning, demanding of information, insights and alternative visions and pathways for the nation, so that collectively, we can decide the kind of future we want, and who best to lead us there.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To my fellow MPs, I say: address the needs of our residents at the local level; discharge our roles as legislators in this Chamber; and most importantly, perform our duties with integrity and with honour.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We must uphold the principles of governance that brought us here.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We must recognise the trade-offs in every policy move and carefully balance the various considerations and then explain to the people our decision.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Above all, we must always think long term for Singapore.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And as for the WP, I hope you are, as you have described yourself, a loyal and responsible opposition, deserving of your significant presence in Parliament.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That means remaining loyal to Singapore, to our people and to the national values that have brought us peace, stability and progress over the last 60 years.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: An alternative path and vision are the essence of democratic discourse, and also what a more discerning and informed populace expects to see.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And there are some cardinal rules that all political parties must abide by, whether in or out of Parliament.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Whether it is the Prime Minister or the Leader of the Opposition, the same standards must be upheld, both by the persons themselves and by the public.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Unfortunately, from time to time, we will have members that commit acts that are unethical, even illegal.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Human nature being what it is, no political party is immune to that.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But when that happens, how we respond as a political party matters.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We need to acknowledge the shortcomings, take decisive actions, take responsibility, reflect and do what is necessary to prevent future occurrences.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have an overriding duty to preserve the integrity of our institutions and of the political system as a whole.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The President also spoke about needing to prioritise our unity and resisting any politics that seeks to divide Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Never pit one group against another, nor sacrifice the common good for narrow interests or short-term political gains.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I hope everyone in this Chamber will agree with what I just outlined.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is my sincere wish that both sides of this House will come together in this long-term endeavour to forge a strong system of governance for Singapore and all Singaporeans, regardless of race, language, religion, or political affiliation.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Only then, can politics truly serve the greater good of our country.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Only then, will we continue to draw strength from our diversity, as we always have so far.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is, and must remain, our unique Singapore advantage.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That way, Singapore will be better governed than most.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will remain proud to be Singaporeans – who sing the same national anthem, recite the same pledge, and call this little red dot home.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And we will know, deep in our hearts, that we are unbreakable as one people.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Leader of the Opposition, you have a clarification of the speech by the Minister?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I must say I never expected a report card of the PAP performance and GE2025, so I will respond as how the Minister delivered his speech in that order as far as I can.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Taking that as my preamble, the first point I would like to make is about a point I know the PAP harps on a lot, which is a demand for alternative policies, ideas and so forth.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Minister spoke about mature democracies, he used the example of political systems in the UK, in Germany, real choices.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We have to look at both these societies as what they are and how deep the political systems are compared to ours.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We have had a one-party dominant system since Independence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: These two societies are very different, so it is inevitable that alternatives would be a key function of what each of these parties – be it democratic socialists, christian socialists, labour, conservatives – what they bring to the voter in their societies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In that time the opposition, specifically the WP, we have got to organise the individuals we have, the members we have, and persuade them to stand for the GE.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It is a short period of time, and in that period of time, you also have to deal with the reality of new single member constituencies (SMCs), sometimes new GRCs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Unlike the Government, we do not have the capacity to conduct survey after survey to understand where the population is on certain issues.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But in spite of that, I take the Minister's point that Singaporeans want an alternative and since they want an alternative, we do our best to present it to them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In the circumstances that the PAP is in, and the opposition are in in Singapore, given the tremendous resources that are available to the PAP to reach out on a day-to-day level in the constituency, through the Peoples Association (PA), for example, it is chalk and cheese.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Singh, if I could invite you to kindly progress to your clarifications, rather than preamble it with a long speech?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I have listened very carefully, and I am trying to thread through what you are saying based on what Minister Ong Ye Kung has said.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I think you can get to your clarifications in a little bit more efficient manner.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: So, I invite you to go to your clarifications, Mr Singh.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, my clarification really has been already shared in terms of the Minister's view of whether there was a deliberate decision made to contest fewer seats.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Like I said, we are not clairvoyant, we put the best people we can find forward and present what we can in the circumstances, to represent an alternative for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The last clarification that I would like to put forth is with regard to what was shared with the Minister in the podcast, where I think the words were "why can't everyone work together?" The Minister used a very interesting analogy, which I probably would not. "Jaw-jaw and war-war" if I remember, was used by Churchill in a very aggressive way.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I would say the question that we face as a society now is a little simpler.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We are at a very interesting juncture, an important transition in our history as a country.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Is the Government prepared to allow opposition MPs to be present and to welcome these new citizens as part of our society?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Because that would reflect a certain maturity that I believe is where Singapore has arrived at, and if I can be so bold, it may well be something that Singaporeans demand of the PAP.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, as much as the PAP wants us to consider alternatives, which I think you are entitled to, I think the PAP should also consider from the WP's perspective, how we can be more united as a people.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Singh, if I could kindly request you to summarise your last point?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: You have gone a little bit further than what the content of Minister Ong's speech was.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Please summarise your last clarification in order for Minister Ong then to reply if he so wishes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, I would suggest that as much as there is scope for alternatives from the opposition, there is scope for the PAP also to play a part in building a more united Singapore with the opposition in mind.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Minister Ong Ye Kung, would you like to respond to those clarifications?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It should not quite be presented as clarifications, so I will try to respond in general.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The people demand many things of us, both as ruling party as well as opposition.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think the people will increasingly demand coherent alternatives from WP, put together principles, philosophies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And to your credit from time to time you have mentioned some of them but the people will demand coherent set of consistent policies and principles.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And they will demand likewise PAP to do better and for all their demands, we will have to reflect, "What can we do better for the people?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Leader of Opposition mentioned a couple of his pet peeves, one is boundaries coming out a month and a half before the election.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I should say this: most PAP MPs in this House, when the boundaries reports come out, everyone scrambles, we were equally scrambling.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Whenever the boundaries come out, suddenly you have an SMC, suddenly you have to form another division, re-deploy your volunteers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We may have an advantage because we are present in every constituency, so maybe there is an advantage there.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we are also scrambling every time the boundaries reports come out.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The population changes, new developments, a group of civil servants look at the data and they propose new boundaries.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have to let them do their job and adapt to it.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That we decided to set up a Statutory Board, gather as many volunteers as we can, and gauge the ground, bring communities together, help the children grow up well, help parents cope with parenting, help the seniors stay healthy, promote exercise – none of this is in the law or Constitution.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we do that to help our constituencies and our residents.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I do not know of any country where you become a new citizen, the grassroots hold an event and talk to you about being Singaporean, what it means and then sing the national anthem and gather together.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, these are all part of the PAP policies to engage the ground.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Leader of Opposition talks about no chance of a wipeout.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In the hearts of Singaporeans, they know that there is no chance of a wipeout.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And reading the ground, we know there is no chance of a wipeout.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The desire for a check on the PAP is very strong, precisely because we have a good majority.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And that desire is so strong we see cases all the time, like what I mentioned, the couple at the tze char stall, friendly to us, like what we are doing, "want you to be Government", want me to continue as Health Minister, but "I am not voting for him, I need to support the opposition".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There is no equilibrium, it is a dynamic balance.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: From term to term, people will have a different balance in their mind, but we must accept that people now want the PAP government; for now, they want the PAP government, but they also want an opposition presence.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Pritam Singh talked about our circumstances being different from the UK or US.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In 1963, this was a much smaller Chamber with 13 Barisan Sosialis Members, minority, small minority.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But they stood for a different vision, with different sets of policies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They disagreed with the PAP on big issues of the day – merger with Malaysia, teaching of language, particularly Chinese, National Service.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: After 1965, of course, it then became PAP-dominant.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But over the years, we saw WP come some way – from one to two single seats, they now have two GRCs, plus a couple of single seats and two NCMPs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Pritam Singh is now the Leader of the Opposition.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Next election, no doubt, it will be even more tough.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And when you have come this far, I do believe the people will demand and Singapore will need WP to come up with alternate policies, as in the past, Barisan Sosialis did with a small number of seats.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I say all these not that I wish it will come true.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But should WP really rise to the occasion and do this and be able to stand and contest the ruling party as the democrats and republicans do each other in the US, or Tories and Labour do each other in UK, actually, life will be harder for PAP.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: People will be so much more discerning with who they choose.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But it is the right political direction for Singapore; focus our energy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I take the Member's point about "jaw-jaw" and "war-war".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are not really fighting, but we are arguing.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are arguing the merits and trade-offs of those directions, and those visions when Singaporeans choose.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If we focus our energy on such discourse, I think it is the right direction for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As the President reminded us, we are living in "a more unsettled and chaotic world".

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But what we can control is how we strengthen our social compact at home.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That is how we ensure peace, security and prosperity for our people.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singapore has long held meritocracy as a core value, that effort and ability should determine success, not birth or background.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While aggregate inequality measures have not worsened materially in recent years, the lived experience tells a different story.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Basic costs, housing and education opportunities still weigh more heavily on some households, and perceptions of unfairness remain real.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is what academics call the gap between macro trends and lived realities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If left unaddressed, it can weaken trust in our social compact.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Equality, like fairness, is never absolute but our duty is to keep narrowing the gaps so that opportunities and security are shared across society.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I will focus on three areas: protecting livelihoods, ensuring retirement adequacy and empowering every Singaporean, young and old, to co-pilot our shared future.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Nevertheless, families still feel the pressure at the market, at clinics and when paying utility bills.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Prices today are much higher compared to three years ago.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, Government measures, such as the Assurance Package and CDC vouchers, have helped significantly.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But as the Prime Minister reminded us, these are not long-term solutions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While inflation affects everyone, its impact is most keenly felt by low-income families.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Meritocracy only works when basic needs are met and opportunities are distributed fairly.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With smart monitoring using artificial intelligence, this relief can be delivered accurately in a timely, targeted and predictable manner.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To make this proposal more practical, I recommend three key features.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, essential basket trigger based on inflation in food, utilities, transport and healthcare.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When inflation exceeds 3% to 4% on an annual average, assistance is adjusted in the next cycle.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: More assistance is given to those who are less fortunate, with limits to ensure fiscal sustainability.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the US, social security benefits are automatically adjusted according to inflation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Canada and many European countries also adjust pensions and social welfare annually.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Even Japan links pensions to the Consumer Price Index (CPI), despite experiencing periods of low inflation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This shows that COLA mechanisms are not excessive promises, but prudent measures to protect dignity and stability.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But what matters more is our people’s actual experience when food or utility prices increase much faster than the average CPI.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For families living on tight budgets, even moderate inflation feels very burdensome.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is why a targeted COLA mechanism can provide assurance where it is most needed.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I also acknowledge concerns that such a mechanism might be seen as fiscally unsustainable, seemingly creating unlimited liability when inflation spikes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singapore's version must be targeted, capped and reviewed annually.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It would only apply to certain basic schemes, activated only when clear thresholds are exceeded, and assistance provided according to need.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In this way, we balance compassion with fiscal discipline, building a safety net for the most vulnerable, while maintaining Singapore's traditional prudence.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Such a scheme could provide CPF contributions or direct financial support, so that caregivers do not have to sacrifice their long-term security while caring for family.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I heard all these during the M3 post-National Day Rally dialogue last year, where I received appeals from caregivers requesting improvements, for instance, on the issues of caregiver leave and financial assistance for them. : Mr Deputy Speaker, I will now continue in English.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Beyond helping families manage today's cost pressures, we must also think long-term, about retirement adequacy and how Singaporeans can age with dignity.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The President reminded us that fairness is a work never finished.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One of the key tests of fairness is how we care for seniors after a lifetime of work.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We should be prepared for more elderly couples living on their own, as more and more young Singaporeans aspire to live independently sooner.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Ensuring the retirement adequacy of each and every Singaporean is, therefore, critical in our goal for our seniors to age actively with dignity and purpose.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our CPF system is rightly regarded as one of the most sustainable in the world.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Having previously been involved in the earlier round of CPF changes as a member of the CPF advisory panel, there is broad consensus that our CPF system works, even as we try to figure how we can tweak it to make it better.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In contrast, rising life expectancies, inflationary pressures and changing work patterns have caused many pension systems abroad to falter because benefits have not kept pace with inflation, or because public finances are overstretched.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must act early to guard against these risks.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This way, families can plan ahead with confidence and each increment will hopefully be less politicised or face less sceptical questioning of its motives.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We should further strengthen CPF top-ups and matching schemes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We could, perhaps, expand it to include part-time workers, caregivers re-entering the workforce and even selected groups of younger workers in their 30s and 40s, so that interest compounding works in their favour earlier in life.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Currently, CPF LIFE only offers lifelong monthly payouts on the decreasing Basic plan, the constant Standard plan or the increasing Escalating plan.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Under my proposal, the base payouts may start slightly lower, but they will rise in tandem with the CPI.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A modest increase, or alternatively, on a tiered floor for the first $60,000, would especially benefit lower-income seniors who have smaller CPF balances.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Simplify the Lease Buyback Scheme and create a family buyback option, letting children co-purchase part of the lease to provide parents retirement cashflow, for example.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Enhance re-employment incentives, longer contracts and phased-down roles for seniors, while keeping CPF contributions meaningful.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And finally, seventh, Mr Deputy Speaker, healthcare assurance.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This would reduce anxiety for seniors, who often fear that a single hospital bill, a single hospital bill, could wipe out their retirement savings.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This can be implemented with an opt-out mechanism for seniors who are adequately secured by hospitalisation or accident insurance.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They will give assurance that no Singaporean, after a lifetime of work, will be left to face old age amidst insecurity.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They must be co-pilots of our journey and not passengers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Youth unemployment is higher than national average and many worry about employability in an age of AI.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, first, evolve SkillsFuture into a family credit system: more credits when more family members upskill together.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, the suggestion will be to expand the SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme to Singaporeans below 40, so that younger workers can also upgrade and pivot.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Let us celebrate entrepreneurship, trades, the arts and sports, not just traditional jobs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For the arts, perhaps, the expanded National Arts Council scholarships could also explore a "dual career" pathway, similar to what spexEducation provides for our Team Singapore athletes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This would reassure talented artists that they can pursue their craft with confidence, while also having academic and career options to fall back on.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It would make a career in the arts not just inspiring, but also sustainable.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With one in three youths facing severe stress or anxiety, we must normalise seeking help, expanding counselling access and create safe spaces.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must broaden our pathways if equality of opportunity is to remain real.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At the same time, vices like vaping pose risks.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, we must guide youths back through positive communities – in gaming, arts, social causes or professional networks.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our youths are our future and our promise for the next 60 years.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As the President reminded us, fairness is never finished.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And if fairness is never finished, then equality and meritocracy are also work never finished.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is not enough to reward effort – we must also level the playing field, so that every Singaporean, regardless of birth or background, has a true chance to rise.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singapore’s story has never been written by Government alone.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It has always been co-authored by our people – families, workers, entrepreneurs, communities alike.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If we hold fast to this spirit of partnership – recognising that putting “we first” does not mean neglecting “me first” – that our personal success is strengthened when our community succeeds.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We can forge a new compact: one where growth is inclusive, every Singaporean has a stake and our youths are inspired to lead the future.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The President called on us to build a "we first" society, where growth uplifts everyone, and trust remains the foundation of our nation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This message resonates deeply in the Labour Movement.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For me, as a representative of workers and their families, this means ensuring that every worker matters, no family is left unsupported and no individual is left to struggle alone.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Today, I will speak on three areas: supporting our lower-wage workers, strengthening employability in the Malay/Muslim community and finally, addressing an issue very close to my heart – mental health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They are the quiet hands and steady feet that keep Singapore moving each day.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Over the past decade, we have made substantial progress.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The wage gap between lower-wage workers and the median worker has narrowed.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This is progress we can take pride in.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It shows that when we walk together, Government, employers and unions, we can shift the escalator of social mobility upwards.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: First, enhance funding for PWM and the Progressive Wage Credit Scheme (PWCS).

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The PWCS has been instrumental in helping employers support wage increases.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Second, let us address how wage increases can lead to a loss of social assistance.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They fear they will lose eligibility for Workfare or ComCare.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I call for a comprehensive review of our wage support and social assistance schemes, so that no one is forced to choose between a higher salary and essential aid.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Third, future-proof upskilling of our lower-wage workers, including training in Artificial Intelligence.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I call for AI training to be extended to PWM workers, such as, administrators who can leverage AI to optimise workflows.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: NTUC LearningHub already offers an AI learning ecosystem, covering skills across different proficiency levels.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, let us make this accessible to all workers, including our lower-wage workers, so that they, too, can benefit from the AI economy.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Starting from ITE, she pursued a Work-Study Diploma while working, overcoming challenges in a male-dominated industry.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Today, she leads a team maintaining 600 lifts across Sengkang and Punggol.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The Progressive Wage Model has transformed her career.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Before PWM, lift maintenance was low-paying, but today, she earns a stable income that supports her family and future.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: That is how we build an inclusive growth.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Through Focus Area 4 (FA4) under M3, we pay special attention towards enhancing the marketability of Malay/Muslim workers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: With close collaboration between NTUC and MENDAKI, we will build a robust support ecosystem to help workers adapt to the increasingly changing job market.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We will continue to strengthen support, especially for mature PMEs, as well as our youth who will inherit the challenges and opportunities of the future economy.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For mature PMEs, support will focus on empowering them with new skills, including digital and leadership skills, so that they can remain relevant and trusted by industry.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We also need to further expand the network of career advisors to help them adapt to market changes and pave the way towards a meaningful second career.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For our youth, we need to provide more diverse pathways.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This includes apprenticeship programmes, work-study schemes as well as development opportunities in new fields, such as green technology, artificial intelligence and the care economy.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Next month, we will organise the Youth Skills and Career Fair @ SCAPE on 6 and 7 October.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This event will be a great opportunity for youth to explore career pathways, receive expert advice and build the skills needed to succeed in an increasingly challenging job market.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Additionally, e2i together with the Happiness Initiative, will launch a special workshop for youth and young professionals aged 18 to 35 years.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The focus of this workshop is to build mental resilience, by equipping participants with skills to manage stress, and building confidence when seeking employment or starting a new career.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When every community can progress together, Singapore as a whole will become stronger and more resilient. : Mr Speaker, I now turn to an issue that I have been championing throughout my stint in Parliament.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: An issue that cuts across workers, families and communities.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The President reminded us that our responsibility is to give Singaporeans assurance at every stage of life.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Nearly 47% of workers in Singapore report feeling exhausted after work.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The prevalence of poor mental health remains at 15% in 2023, higher than the pre-pandemic levels.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Behind each statistic is a worker, a family and community.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Their struggles with stress and burnout remind us that productivity cannot come at the expense of health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As the co-chairman of the PAP mental health group, I have continually engaged stakeholders from the healthcare professionals, community partners, to employers and workers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And together, with my colleagues, we tabled a Motion of mental health in the last term to place this firmly on the national agenda.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In this new term, we intend to move forward further, ensuring that mental health remains a sustained national priority.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In my Malay speech earlier, I had spoken about employability initiatives for our youths and young professionals under the FA4 initiative.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Employability must go hand in hand with resilience.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Resilience will help them to keep it, grow in it and strive in the long run.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We must build emotional resilience in all schools and IHLs alongside academics skills.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our youths should not only survive the pressures of school and work, but thrive with confidence and work.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I continue to call for mental health and well-being literacy to be embedded within the curriculum, so that everyone is equipped with the skill.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And as we progress as a nation, everyone can play their part better.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: NTUC hears their concerns about long hours and blurred work-life boundaries.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But beyond that, we must call for stronger workplace mental well-being initiatives, so that employers build cultures where mental wellness is part of daily practice, not an afterthought.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For our seniors, dignity is not only about medical care, but also about connection, purpose and being seen.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As seniors age, they may face loneliness and other mental health concerns, but it can also be a stage of renewed contribution if the right support is given.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We must continue to expand community facilities, so that help is never too far away.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Workers need adequate rest between shifts and more explicit guidance on after-hours communication.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Otherwise, exhaustion will erode both well-being and long-term safety.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Leaders must be equipped, not only to deliver results, but also to recognise early signs of stress, to intervene with empathy and to create psychologically safe workplaces.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So often the perception is that innovation is seen as a way to squeeze more output from the same worker.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Instead, we must harness innovation to ease the pressures of long hours to streamline repetitive tasks and to allow workers to focus on higher value and more meaningful work.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When we do this, productivity gains will be matched by healthier, more motivated teams and by workplaces, where people feel proud to contribute and confident about their future.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Returning to work after a period of illness, injury, or a mental health challenge is never easy.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Many workers tell us they feel anxious, worried that their colleagues may see them as less capable, or that their employers may judge them for needing more time to recover.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: That is why the return-to-work journey must not add to their stress.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Instead, it should be a bridge of support, where adjustments are made to help them regain confidence at their own pace.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When a worker is supported in this way, they are more likely to bounce back stronger, to contribute meaningfully and to inspire others.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And when we care for our workers in their most vulnerable moments, we strengthen not just productivity, but the bonds of trust in our workplaces.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Trust between people and the Government, between employers and workers, with the unions at the centre of everything and among, of course, citizens themselves.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As we turn the page after SG60, let us reaffirm the trust by standing with our workers, uplifting every community and safeguarding the mental health and well-being of every Singaporean.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Let us show that in Singapore, progress is not for the few, but for all.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And this is how we will build not only a stronger economy, but also a stronger society.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: One where every worker has dignity, every family has assurance and every community has hope.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Before I begin, I declare my interest as Deputy Group Managing Director of Commonwealth Capital Group.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: We are a Singaporean global enterprise operating businesses across the food value chain – from cold-chain logistics to food manufacturing and to food services.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Collectively, our businesses steward more than 1,000 livelihoods and we provide nourishment to thousands of Singaporeans daily.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Dr Wan Rizal and Ms Denise Phua spoke earlier.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I was introduced only in April this year, just one month before the GE.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I am grateful for their trust in me.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I will do my best to do our residents of Jalan Besar GRC and Whampoa proud and give them a voice in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I have been a civil servant for more than a decade and I have had the pleasure to be involved in previous speeches by the President at the Parliament’s Opening.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Invariably, the speeches cover the following themes: one, the world is a dark and dangerous place; two, the economy is the solution to many of our problems; three, we need to address the challenges of an ageing population; four, we need to build an inclusive society; and five, we need to keep Singapore united.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: But if you thought these themes were from the 2023, 2020, 2018, 2016, 2014 or 2011 speeches, you would also be right!

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: That is not to say the President’s speech was boring nor is it an indictment of the speechwriters.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Rather, it demonstrates that our challenges are enduring.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: However, I submit that below the surface of these high-level challenges, there are emerging trends within each theme that require us to rethink and reimagine our policies in this term of Government.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I will spend the rest of my speech to share some thoughts about these trends and, importantly, their implications.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: First, the international economic order has changed, permanently.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Our earlier economic growth strategy was premised on foreign MNC investments riding the wave of globalisation, which enabled firms to headquarter in Singapore, while the bulk of markets and operations would be outside the country.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: But now, foreign MNCs, even if they want to invest in Singapore, may find themselves torn between other geopolitical considerations.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Manufacturing investments are being onshored in other countries.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Yes, we can press on with anchoring investments from foreign MNCs.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: My former colleagues at the Economic Development Board (EDB) do a valiant job.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I, myself, spent a couple of years at the EDB looking at how to grow our Singaporean MNCs.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: And now, I lead a local company that aspires to be an MNC one day.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: These are some issues that I hope to explore as part of my role on the GPC for Trade and Industry.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: AI, which many Members have spoken about, represents a stepped increase in technological advancement.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Some have likened this to the discovery of the steam engine that catalysed the industrial revolution and disrupted many jobs.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: But even before AI, the pace of job creation and destruction felt like it was already accelerating.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Make no mistake, this means that skills will become obsolete faster.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Today, we can no longer rely on what we learnt in full-time education to carry us on to retirement.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Perhaps there may even come a point in time where what we learn in the first year of tertiary education will become irrelevant by the time we graduate.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: We see this manifest in greater anxieties amongst our new graduates and our older PMETs.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I have spoken to many in Jalan Besar and Whampoa.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: What does this imply for the direction of Government policy?

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Many Members have actually spoken up about this.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Mr Andre Low gave the suggestion of the redundancy insurance scheme.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I agree with the intent that it is about reducing the anxieties that many of our workers feel.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: However, I respectfully disagree in the implementation of the idea for two reasons.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: The first is that we have just implemented a Jobseekers Support Scheme.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower has spoken about this earlier.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: It is still early days, but our residents are already benefiting.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: The scheme provides the support required for our workers to get the assurance they need if they fall into redundancy, for a targeted group.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: The second reason is because I am not sure whether the numbers add up.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I looked at the suggestion in quite some detail.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: The Member suggested that if you contribute 0.1% of your monthly wage, you would have enough in the insurance pool to cover the redundancy payouts.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: However, I am not sure whether that is enough because in the Jobs Support Scheme, the MOM budget was already $200 million and this was for a targeted group of unemployed individuals.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: So, a national unemployment or national redundancy insurance scheme should cost more, and not less.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Do more to help employers give workers jobs and then train them on the job.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: The best place to pick up relevant skills is in the workplace, working for best-in-class companies, hopefully local companies, that are closest to the market and closest to the frontier of innovation.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Businesses can be incentivised to hire Singaporeans and then train and re-train them in those jobs.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: And Singaporeans will benefit because they have the assurance of a job first, before they commit to training.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: The GRIT programme is a step in that direction.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: If I had it my way, I would call it the Graduate Employment Assistance through Training programme, or the GREAT programme.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I am glad to be able to look into this further in my role on the GPC for Manpower.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Third, extreme longevity will raise new questions for town planning and policymaking.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: For the first time in our history, there are now two generations in retirement at the same time.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: In Whampoa, I encountered someone above 90 years old at almost every block visit.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: And quite regularly, someone above the age of 95.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I think it is the same for many Members of this House.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I see the future complexion of Singapore in Jalan Besar and Whampoa.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Our town planning assumptions will have to change.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Looking ahead, we will need to design our towns for the extreme user – the 90-year-old, not just the 70-year-old.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: A 10-minute walk means very different things for these two individuals.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: At Whampoa, our ramps on our overhead bridges are increasingly useless.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: My elderly residents tell me that it is too tiring to walk up the ramps.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: And if we do not plan ahead to build lifts and other infrastructure early enough, we will end up isolating many of our oldest seniors and this will be a growing problem with senior frailty.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: It also means that the provision of senior care and other social support services may need to be more distributed in the neighbourhood, even if it means a less efficient model.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Beyond planning, our policies will also have to be updated.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
