text: We cannot make policies assuming that all those above 65 are a single monolithic block with the same needs.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Mainly because, after a certain age, perhaps 85, they would all have lived beyond what they expected to live when they first retired.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: None of them would be automatically included in CPF LIFE.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: But almost all of them would be anxious about the cost of living and they would not be able to benefit directly from the higher wages that a strong economy may bring.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Fourth, the work to build a more inclusive society is far from complete.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: The new challenge of this generation is to address wealth inequality.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: It is no longer just about income inequality or the inequalities of starting points in life.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Earlier terms of Government focused on equalising opportunities for our young and improving wages of our lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: This is no doubt important and I strongly support it.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: But an important assumption here was that incomes and education would continue to be the best way to close the gaps in life outcomes.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: What if this assumption turns out to be only partially true?

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: We are already seeing early signs that wealth inequality is becoming worse.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: And if we do not address this fast enough, it will threaten to divide society.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: We would be broken into a million pieces, and we cannot go back.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: At my weekly meet-the-people sessions, some residents struggle with affording a basic HDB rental flat.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I regularly appeal to lower the rent of these rental flats.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: At the same time, my constituency set the record for the most expensive Design, Build and Sell Scheme flat transaction, at more than $1.5 million.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: That is more than 100 years of rent for the HDB rental flat, just think about that.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: And I do not even have landed properties in my area, where many have complained about higher property taxes.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: With smaller family sizes, wealth will get passed down to fewer children and could become increasingly concentrated.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I worry when I hear people say that the only way to be rich in Singapore is to be born rich.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: If the greatest predictor of wealth is who your parents are, then I think we have a big problem.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: How can we ensure that the returns to labour and effort, exceed the returns to other assets, such as real estate investments?

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: How can our asset tax system, including property tax, be even more progressive?

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: And how can we build a more effective form of wealth redistribution?

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: It makes me very optimistic about our future because it shows that Singaporeans, especially the next generation, cares not just about themselves, but about others in the community.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: These are the first fruits of a "we first" society.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: And I hope that as the Government makes policies at the national level, we would also do more to encourage the building of these local community bonds at the local level.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: This is not something that I came up with myself.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: This is something that my wife who coincidentally celebrates her birthday today, always reminds me about.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: And when our communities are strong and united, our country will likewise be strong and united.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: With that, Mr Speaker, I support the Motion and wish the Government and all civil servants the very best in delivering on the policy agenda.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I am a brand-new Member of the House.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, I seek your guidance and the indulgence of other Members of the House as I begin my parliamentary journey.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Today, we are a first world nation with an advanced economy.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: These numbers put us in the leaders' pack globally.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: They are a reflection of decades of good governance, careful planning, and investment in the future.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: But these are not numbers just to feel good.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: More importantly, they are indicators that we have built a just and inclusive society, where opportunities and prosperity are not limited and concentrated in a few, but broadly shared.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It is a validation of our social compact and the promises of our founding fathers made good.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Yet, we must never forget the fundamental and unchanging hard truths of our nation.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We are highly connected, and therefore highly exposed, to the rest of the world.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Changes to the winds and currents of the outside world will affect us deeply.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We must always remain clear eyed and unflinching in the face of challenges.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: As the President has noted, we are sailing into choppy waters.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Shifting global economic currents, a changing new world order, and AI-driven disruptions in the workplace make for some powerful headwinds.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Each alone has the potential to reshape our society in profound and lasting ways.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It is in this context that I would like to speak on some of the challenges ahead and share thoughts on how we can approach them.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The most immediate challenge before us today is, of course, jobs, jobs and jobs.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It is also an accelerant and amplifies the effects of all other challenges that we face.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: There are three aspects of the AI disruption that we should take note of.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The rate of technological disruption today is unprecedented.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Previous waves of tech disruptions, from personal computing to the Internet, unfolded over decades.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Societies had the relative luxury of time to absorb and adapt.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Entire sectors, and entire industries, could be reshaped in a flash.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The AI disruption will touch every sector of our economy.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It will strike further up the value chain, at knowledge intensive and cognitive tasks, tasks which are the very heart of PMET roles.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It is also impacting tasks once thought to be uniquely human, such as creative and artistic endeavours.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: What is not displaced, will be reshaped and redesigned.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Consider the tech sector, which gave us the very tools of this disruption.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Today, one can create, debug and deploy a website or an app without writing a single line of code.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The work of junior developers, routine programmers and similar roles is rapidly becoming obsolete.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Those who can harness and adapt to the disruption will surge ahead.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We will see high skill, high pay jobs created, even as many entry- and mid-level PMET roles are hollowed out or displaced.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Those who climb up the value chain will advance rapidly, while others risk being pushed into lower value work.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: This will not just be a disruption in the workplace.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It is a potential widening of social disparities.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Our advanced economy is also knowledge and services heavy, exactly the sectors where AI disruption will move fastest and hit the hardest.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Entry and mid-level white collar roles are the most vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Without timely upskilling and adaptation, many may find themselves displaced.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Entry and mid-level job opportunities may shrink in the near future.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: New graduates may face tough prospects, a trend we are already beginning to see.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Conventional assumptions about career progressions and success may no longer be taken for granted.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Many jobs will be reshaped; hard earned skillsets may be rendered obsolete in short order.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The narrowing of opportunities also risks trapping more on the lower rungs of the socio-economic ladder.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: All of this presents a comprehensive challenge for our Government, for it will impact not only the economy, but also the very fabric of our society.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The pace of change and breadth of disruption means there is far less time for the Government and our citizens, to react.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It is also not only a distant problem.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Recent news of hiring freezes and layoffs among big tech companies in the US and other advanced economies, highlight the tangible, near-term impact of the AI disruption.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The first waves are already hitting our shores.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Among my Mountbatten constituents, I am seeing fresh graduates struggling to find full-time jobs, and mid-career PMETs trying to pivot after losing theirs.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The mid-career PMETs, with much heavier obligations, are having a hard time.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: But I would be remiss if I do not highlight that this challenge, while daunting, carries with it enormous promise.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The Chinese term for "crisis" – "危机" – combines the characters for danger and opportunity.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It will be disruptive, and perhaps painful in the short term, but it also holds immense potential for Singapore to advance, to innovate, and to capture new growths.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: While some jobs may become obsolete and displaced, entire new industries will emerge.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Work that we cannot yet imagine will become part of the economy of tomorrow.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Singapore is uniquely positioned to ride this wave.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: And also, our high proportion of PMETs, in particular, can be our strategic advantage.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: With the right choices, together, we can transform this disruption into an era of renewed opportunity and prosperity.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Conventional wisdom in economics holds that growth slows down in advanced, mature economies like ours.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: AI may just be one of the key enablers that allows us to break that mould.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: This could be the greatest opportunity of our generation.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The choices before us are clear and stark.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: In truth, it is not even a choice.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We can either learn to ride it and thrive or be left behind.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: This is a challenge for our society and for every Singaporean.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I am glad to note the Government has already moved decisively to position Singapore ahead.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I actually encourage everyone to read the latest 2.0 version.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The work of the Economic Strategy Review Committees will be critical in shaping the policies and initiatives that ensure Singapore is ready to confront the challenges and embrace the opportunities ahead.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It is not enough to look only at jobs and the economy.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: To ride this wave successfully, we must pay attention to the social impacts.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: In particular, we must guard against the inequality of outcomes.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: These stresses will be felt across society, but not equally.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The PMETs also form the core of our middle class.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Together, they constitute the broad middle ground of our society.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: A healthy society always has some degree of social mobility.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: As long as we ensure that the pathway up is equally accessible to everyone, that is natural.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: But we must guard against too many sliding down.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We must especially guard against the hollowing out of the middle because when that happens, it erodes the very centre that holds us together and shakes confidence in the whole.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Not only are they the bedrock of our economy and drive our progress but they also embody the success and promise of the Singapore Story.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We are successful, only because they are successful.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Most crucially, this is because the broad middle is the one that anchors our social compact.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: A thriving middle class is therefore essential to our social stability and cohesion.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: If our middle-class shifts or gets squeezed, the ground beneath all of us becomes less steady.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The pressures come from many fronts: job insecurity, a tightening labour market, inflation, rising cost of living and household debt.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Many also shoulder the burdens of the sandwich class, supporting children on one side and caring for elderly parents on another.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: My ward, Mountbatten, has the full range of the socio-economic demographics, from rental flats to standalone bungalows.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: In my conversations with constituents, it is from the middle-class residents that I sense most anxiety and frustration.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Our focus has always been to uplift those on the lowest rungs of the economic ladder and rightly so.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: They must get the most help, and they do.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The wealthy, by large, can weather the storms.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: They are better insulated from the pressures that buffet the rest of society.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: But it is our middle-class that often bears the heaviest burdens.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: In the challenges ahead, it is this group that stands most exposed.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: And it is this group that has the most to lose.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: They have been carrying the rest of us.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Beyond preparing them to seize new opportunities, and guiding and supporting those who may face setbacks, I hope we can do more to lift some weight off their shoulders.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I intend to speak up more for our PMETs and middle-class in this house.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It is trust that underpins the partnership between Government and citizens, and it is this partnership that has allowed us to navigate many past crises together.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The same will be true for the challenges that we now face.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Performance legitimacy is formed in people's minds not from numbers and words, but from their lived experience, from what citizens actually see and feel in their daily lives, from how policies and initiatives land on the ground.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It cannot be assumed, nor can it be taken for granted.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It can be eroded and must be earned and re-earned every single day.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: After all, while we welcome foreign talent as a necessity, we should never be disadvantaged in our own country.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Yet, the consistent feedback that we see online paints a rather different picture.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Many reported very low call-back rates and few positive outcomes.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: To me, this is a missed opportunity and a great pity, not because the intentions were unclear, but precisely the opposite.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Our people are truly at the heart of everything that this Government does.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I spent years with the grassroots before entering this House and I have witnessed this first-hand.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Yet, I know good intentions and good policies alone are never enough.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We must always be mindful of the fragile and finite nature of this trust.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: That is the only reason we are still here.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We do live in an imperfect world and no government is perfect.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: But this Government is the Government of the day.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The awesome responsibility of governing Singapore and the trust of our fellow citizens rests with this party.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We can and we must aim to do ever better.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: But our children, and our children's children, will be.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We now stand on the cusp of a brave new world.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Andre Low you have a clarification to make?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
text: My clarification is to the hon Member for Jalan Besar GRC.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
text: The way this scheme can work is for the premium reserves to be built-up in times of relative stability, like today.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
text: So, we would say that this would have to be implemented as soon as possible so that over time these reserves can be built up and then they can be drawn down from in times of disruption.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: I actually wanted to clarify my own speech, so I will make two clarifications.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: One, my own speech; and then, two, in response.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: In my own speech when I mentioned the numbers for the Jobseekers Support Scheme, as well as my back-of-the-envelope calculations for the premium collections, I may have misspoken.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: I take the Member's point that he wants to build up premium reserves over time.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: If that is the case, then we will not be able to build up the reserves over time if the estimate is only $160 million from this year.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: But the broader point is that we probably want to look at the numbers a bit closer to see what is the appropriate premium collection amount that could reflect that proposal more accurately.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: So, for example, if it is a targeted scheme which the Member has also acknowledged that cost $200 million this year, then a national insurance scheme should collect more premiums this year even though it is to build up its reserves over time.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I rise in support of the Motion of thanks for the President's Address.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: First, I wish to take this opportunity to thank the residents of Potong Pasir for their warm welcome to my team and me.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Potong Pasir SMC is almost as old as Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Formed in 1968, it has grown in population size by 2.6 times.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: The transformation that it has undergone is a fair reflection of a cross-section of our Singapore society.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: On the one side of Upper Serangoon Road, the mature estate of Potong Pasir with its landmark sloping roofs, rich heritage and a high number of seniors; and on the other side, the young vibrant families of the Bidadari Estate.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: As I spent these last few months getting to know my residents and understanding their concerns and aspirations, I find myself reflecting on the notion of well-being.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: According to the Oxford English Dictionary, well-being is defined as, "With reference to a person or community, the state of being healthy, happy, or prosperous; physical, psychological, or moral welfare." Today, I would like to speak a little about being healthy and happy.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: When I speak with retired seniors in the community, they often tell me that they hope to be physically and mentally healthy.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Having led active lives in their younger years, they worry that their silver years could become mentally meaningless, physically debilitating or financially a burden to their families.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: For our seniors, staying healthy with affordable healthcare is about living with dignity and peace of mind.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In a "we first" society, how do we ensure this?

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Dignity is about the quality of life in a senior's silver years.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Conditions, such as cognitive impairment or the loss of any of the Activities of Daily Living, reduce their quality of life significantly, and in the eyes of a senior, his or her dignity.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Ideally, our lifespan and our health-span should be closer.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: The concern that we live long but not well, is real.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: The increasing number of seniors who reached out to me over the last nine years, first in Paya Lebar and now in Potong Pasir to certify their Lasting Power of Attorney (LPAs) on a pro bono basis, is both heartening and concerning at the same time.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: While on one hand, seniors are making conscious choices with awareness on what is a very difficult and life-changing issue; on the other hand, it is clear to me, that more seniors are anxious, worried and unsettled about what could happen to them as they age.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Preventive healthcare for our seniors can reduce years of bad health while increasing their quality of life.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Many seniors in Paya Lebar benefited from the Programme.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: We focused on Brain and Bone Health because these are common and potentially debilitating conditions that our seniors increasingly face.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: They showed that an overwhelming number of seniors were unaware that they suffered from mild to severe cognitive impairment and/or poor bone health.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: When Healthier SG was announced in 2023 with its focus on preventive healthcare, including various screenings and fully subsidised flu and pneumococcal vaccinations, it gave me cause to cheer quietly to myself as it meant that we had been on the right track.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Unfortunately, Healthier SG has yet to cover screenings and support for conditions, such as pre-dementia and osteoporosis.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Dementia is debilitating and scary for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Poor bone health on the other hand, leads to deteriorating mobility for our seniors, particularly after a fall.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Both conditions take a tremendous toll on caregivers in the family.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: If this can be created in a familiar environment within the estates that they live in, all the better.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I therefore read with great interest, Minister Ong's remarks last month about Age Well Neighbourhoods.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I believe that if we succeed in the four areas of expanding our Active Ageing Centres, introducing the Community Health Posts, Home Personal Care and upgrading the physical environment of such estates to suit the needs of seniors, we can create an environment where seniors can live and socialise in surroundings that they are familiar with, stay active with friends and care for their health through easily accessible preventive healthcare programmes.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I understand that Toa Payoh has been selected to pilot the Age Well Neighbourhoods.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Since Minister Ong is not in the Chamber, but perhaps, I could very humbly, on behalf of the seniors in Potong Pasir, make a pitch for our estate to be next.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: As set out in the 1993 White Paper on Affordable Healthcare, the framework is premised on providing a sustainable healthcare system, based on the objectives of personal responsibility, avoiding over-reliance on state welfare and providing good and affordable medical services to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: To qualify for Government subsidies, means testing applies.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: First, the per capita household income (PCHI) is assessed.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: If the household does not have PCHI, then the annual value of the residence is considered.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: By and large, it has been a progressive and fair assessment regime aimed at providing targeted assistance to Singaporeans who need it the most and many have benefited over the years.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I wonder, however, if it is time for us to review the framework, particularly the assessment of our seniors' eligibility for Government subsidies, given the changing demography of Singapore and their evolving needs and circumstance.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: As shared widely by other Members in this House, this number is set to become about one in four by 2030.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: At the same, time, an increasing number of seniors above the age of 65 either lives alone or alone with their spouses.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Many Singaporeans above the age of 65 years are retired, or nearing retirement, often with a significantly reduced income.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: One can argue that in the 1990s, around the time the White Paper was released, we were a younger nation, with a vibrant workforce underpinned by a strong growing economy.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: The general healthcare needs of a smaller pool of seniors could be supported by a larger, younger workforce.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: We have many more seniors with smaller families.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Using the Annual Value (AV) of a senior's residence as part of the means test may not reflect a senior's means or financial ability.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Even where seniors live with their families, financial circumstances can be challenging.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I got to know Jeffrey in the middle of 2024.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Jeffrey and his wife were in their 60s and, at that time, lived in a larger HDB flat.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Jeffrey's father was in his 90s and was previously living in a smaller HDB home in Toa Payoh where Jeffrey grew up.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: As an only child, Jeffrey had arranged for his parents to move in with him.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: As a result of this, however, when Jeffrey’s father grew older and had more healthcare needs, Jeffrey realised that his father's entitlement to Government subsidies was significantly lower due to the AV of Jeffrey's home.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Given that the household had no income, the added cost caused the family financial challenges.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: To his credit, in all my conversations with him, Jeffrey did not advocate for universal healthcare nor complain about the financial burden.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: He however shared that others like him, who had no income but had to care for their aged parents, face similar financial challenges when the ability to afford and the assessment of the level of subsidies was based on the AV of the home that they lived in.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: He wondered if his decision to be a responsible child, even though he himself was in his 60s and retired, had effectively penalised him and his father, financially.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: As Minister Ong shared during the Committee of Supply debates earlier this year, the Government takes a practical approach, balancing the trade-offs in achieving the three objectives of affordability, availability and quality in our healthcare policies.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: It is, without a doubt, a delicate balance.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In fact, the Government had recently revised the thresholds for both per capita household income and the AV criteria to include more Singaporeans within the threshold.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: This is an acknowledgment that public policy is contextual with time and when there are opportunities to refine, address gaps and/or respond to fundamental shifts.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: We must, as we always have, continue to do so.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: We have a duty to try to give them the best opportunity to live a life of quality with dignity and peace of mind in their silver years.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: At the recent Emmy Awards, the Netflix show Adolescence swept up awards for eight categories.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Its grim, yet compelling portrayal of children, smartphones and social media resonated globally because it reflected a reality many of us recognise.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: As a father of two Gen Alpha children, I wish for them, as all parents do, to enjoy an ideal childhood, like a gentle spring season: fresh, full of promise, and unburdened by the storms of life, a time for imagination, exploration, and forming lifelong bonds with family and friends.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Where once parents told children to beware of strangers outside the home, today, we must also guard against the "strangers" and dangers lurking within – in the digital world.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Technology offers promise, but it has also dramatically altered childhood experiences, self-worth and social relationships over the past decade.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I believe, Mr Speaker, that we are at an inflexion point as a society.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Aside from online safety, the data and literature on the harm caused to the overall well-being of children and youths, growing up in a digital environment is well-researched and publicised.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Many Members of this House would be, for example, well-versed with Jonathan Haidt's book, "The Anxious Generation".

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: We have also all read reports that indicate that while our children are well-connected in the digital world, they remain lonely and disconnected in real life.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Younger respondents also report higher levels of social isolation and loneliness.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I recall watching The Emoji Movie with my children.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I am not sure if Members have watched this movie.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: But imagine all the emojis come together, through animation, in a story about young people expressing their inner thoughts through emojis to interact with each other.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: To me, the movie was an excellent depiction of how our young are growing up socially in a digital world.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: To be fair, adults also regularly and, as a matter, of course, express emotions through emojis.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: However, most adults of today grew up in a less digitally enabled time and therefore are more likely to be equipped with strong relationships and real-life experiences with family and friends in the "physical world".

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I for one am glad that the Government is keeping a close watch on this trend and is prepared to take steps to intervene by introducing the appropriate legislative safeguards to protect our young.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: But will this be enough to shape behaviours especially when the digital space is all pervasive?

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Even if we manage to somehow reduce or limit access to the digital world for our young, it is likely to leave a gaping void that needs to be filled.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: We have done this successfully for our seniors with our Active Ageing Centres.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In fact, we could consider co-locating centres for our children and youth with our Active Ageing Centres.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I believe both our seniors, children and youths will benefit from being close to each other with opportunities to interact.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I am confident that we will have the support of many parents for such centres.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In the Bidadari Estate, I have been approached by parents of young children who are prepared to put in the time to set up and run such community spaces to keep our youths engaged.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: They recently shared their proposal with me and I would like to share their vision statement with this House.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I quote, "To create a space where parents and children can connect, learn and grow, strengthening their bonds and building resilience together.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: By fostering a culture of well-being, we aim to nurture a new generation of healthy, confident children and resilient, supported parents.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: We believe that when families flourish, communities do too", unquote.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: We are only as strong as our weakest link.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: We have a duty to support our seniors and for the future of the nation, ensure that our young grow up healthy, happy and safe both in the digital and the physical realms.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Together with the foundations of resilience, unity and fighting spirit as a people, I am confident that we can overcome our challenges and shape a future in which we will continue to not just survive but thrive.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, I would like to declare my interest as an entrepreneur within the circular economy space, specifically running a food circularity business.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I also serve as an Exco member of the Restaurant Association of Singapore and as an advisor to the Singapore Association of Ship Suppliers and Services, the National Instructors and Coaches Association, and the Visual, Audio and Creative Content Professionals Association (VICPA).

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I echo the President's call to refresh Singapore's economic strategies, and to build a future that is both resilient and inclusive.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Global markets, once seen as stable, are now weighed down by war, protectionist tariffs, and domestic upheavals.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Multinational corporations are recalibrating supply chains and rethinking strategies, while trade itself is increasingly weaponised.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In this climate, countries are competing fiercely with subsidies and incentives to win investments.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore cannot and should not compete on size or subsidy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must compete on relevance, on the strength of our ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They provide the embedded networks and value that anchor investors here, and they give Singapore its relevance.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In uncertain times, agility often trumps scale and agility is where our SMEs shine.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They are adaptable, deeply rooted in our communities and reflect the entrepreneurial spirit that built modern Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Strengthening them is an economic imperative and also a social one.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They enrich livelihoods, sustain communities and make Singapore a more cohesive nation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To unlock this potential, we need a mindset shift, to see SMEs as co-creators of our national transformation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To unlock the potential of our SMEs, I put forward eight recommendations.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These recommendations fall under three themes, providing targeted relief with accountability, fostering collaboration that scales, and driving structural reforms that reward both economic performance and social impact.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Crucially, a Restart grant ensures that entrepreneurs with deep experience and networks are empowered to restart so that the jobs they create, the communities they anchor, and the know-how they carry are not lost, but preserved as economic and social value for our nation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It must be tied to forward-looking transformation plans, such as digitalisation, process redesign, internationalisation and workforce upskilling.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The aim is not to prop up outdated business models, but to catalyse renewal and innovation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Support should be structured with clear milestones, co-funding ratios and sunset clauses.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Firms that meet their transformation goals could tap into productivity credits and other grants.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Those who do not should exit the support framework to safeguard public value.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In short, Mr Speaker, we must help experience restart, not expire.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These measures should be calibrated with risk-based pricing and require recipients to commit to basic financial reporting and cashflow transparency.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In my maiden speech, I called for repayment schemes to go beyond rent arrears.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Today, I reiterate that we should extend them to a wider range of obligations – personal guarantees, insurance bonds, trade financing and term loans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Just as the COVID-19 framework gave many businesses a lifeline, such calibrated extensions can give SMEs the time and confidence to press on with transformation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At the same time, we cannot rely on traditional banks alone.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Alternative financing models must be expanded – revenue-based financing and venture debt designed for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These instruments are especially crucial for high-growth sectors, like agri-tech, clean energy, health tech and the digital economy, where upfront investment is heavy but long-term returns can be transformative for Singapore’s future.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In short, we must give SMEs not just capital, but also time, because time is the oxygen they need to grow, adapt and thrive.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Forming consortiums allows SMEs to pool talent, share resources and punch above their weight for larger contracts.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To facilitate this, agencies can provide higher grant quantums for firms that collaborate in enterprise around projects, seeking greater collaborative ventures.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Beyond this, the Government should enhance grant support and offer favourable financing terms for consortiums, including joint training programmes, shared intellectual property frameworks and common procurement platforms.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Trade associations and chambers of commerce should act as neutral convenors and custodians, ensuring accountability and fair distribution of benefits, while giving SMEs the confidence to collaborate at scale.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In short, by encouraging collaboration, we multiply the impact of our SMEs, turning small firms into a connected ecosystem that strengthens Singapore’s competitiveness and resilience.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Fourth, we must improve payment terms to ease cash flow for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Delayed payments from large corporates or Government-linked entities can cripple small businesses.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In addition, I propose introducing automatic late-payment interest clauses to encourage discipline and predictability.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This should also include the timely disbursement of grants once project milestones are met.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Fifth, I call for a more efficient regulatory system.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And to make this stick, we should institutionalise a scorecard that tracks timeliness of approvals across public agencies.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My sixth proposal addresses the issue of rising manpower costs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While the PWM is a critical and necessary step toward uplifting lower-wage workers and affirming the dignity of labour, we must also acknowledge the strain it is placing on our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many are struggling to keep pace with mandated wage increases, especially when productivity gains take time to realise and passing on costs to consumers risks pricing them out of the market.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This pressure is further compounded by the rising total cost of foreign manpower, fuelled by higher dormitory costs, steeper qualifying salaries and persistent foreign worker levies.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Let us recall that these levies were originally intended to guard against wage suppression.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But in sectors already governed by PWM, where wage ladders are clearly structured and enforced, such levies are increasingly redundant, even counterproductive.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My seventh proposal addresses rent, a structural issue that continues to weigh heavily on our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For years, SMEs have called for greater rent data transparency.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It ensures fairer negotiations and it allows businesses to make informed decisions.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the residential property market, URA already publishes rent and property sale values, giving tenants and buyers clarity.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In addition to transparency, as the largest landowner in Singapore, the Government has the opportunity and also the responsibility to shape how market systems evolve.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I propose that public tenancy evaluations scale and expand the Price Quality Method.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Crucially, "quality" component should reflect not just financial bids, but also social and environmental value.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This can be aligned with the Corporate Purpose framework under the Company of Good by the National Voluntary and Philanthropy Centre, where firms are assessed not only on profits, but on their contributions to people, society, governance, environment and the economy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Firms recognised with one to three hearts, or as Champions of Good, could then be awarded proportionate scoring in tenancy evaluations.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because, Mr Speaker, our enterprises are not just economic agents, they are also social change agents and a rent model that rewards placemaking, inclusivity and sustainability will strengthen businesses and enrich Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Lastly, we must acknowledge that automation requires space, both physical and financial.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, an automated production line may require space for conveyance systems, robotic arms, storage buffers, or automated sorting and quality control stations.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These spatial needs can significantly increase upfront costs and logistics complexity, particularly for SMEs operating in compact facilities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For such businesses, I propose that the Government offer property tax relief, accelerated capital allowances, longer lease tenures, calibrated foreign worker levy reductions, provided these are tagged to productivity gains and worker upskilling outcomes.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such support would lower the barriers to automation adoption, while ensuring that public resources lead to real, measurable improvements in efficiency, skills development and competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That alone shows how vital they are and how much more we can unlock if we support them better and support them now.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It may be tempting to focus on larger enterprises for quick wins in GDP and jobs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But SMEs are not just smaller versions of multinational enterprises (MNEs).

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They provide the networks, the know-how and the connections that make Singapore attractive to global investors.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And when MNEs bring in technology and market access, SMEs gain, scale-up and innovate.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Stronger SMEs mean better jobs: progressive, higher-value, future-ready jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They anchor communities, build skills and nurture innovation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By growing our SME sector, we create a pipeline of local global champions.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And we ensure Singapore remains relevant, wherever and whatever the future economic order may be.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Strong SMEs, better jobs, a resilient and inclusive Singapore.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I seek your guidance as I embark on my journey as a Parliamentarian.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: As the youngest elected Member, I carry two duties today: to honour the foundations we inherited and to help build the next bound for my generation so that the Singapore story continues.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In my view, the biggest task Singapore faces today is what I call the "Singapore Puzzle": how do we compete in this changing world, without losing ourselves?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: To hold together what seems to pull apart – racing fast while moving as one, reaching for the stars while catching those who fall.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The global tide is shifting, currents are turning fast.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: As we chart our course through stormy seas, we need an anchor.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The President and the Prime Minister have called for a "we first" society.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It will decide whether we succeed in solving this Puzzle.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: And first, we must first know who “we” are.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: At its heart lies the family – the puzzle piece that anchors us with its web of relationships and gives us a sense of identity.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If this piece weakens, so too will every other piece.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Our local workforce will decline, our national security will weaken, our communities will thin without intergenerational bonds, and our sense of “home” and national identity will erode.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: A "we first" Society cannot endure unless we first know who “we” are.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Young parents today are stretched – striving to build their careers, but strained by caregiving responsibilities, costs and the unpredictability of early childhood.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But so too is our ability to ease it.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This is perhaps the best time in Singapore to start and raise a family – because this Government is listening, learning and determined to act.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I will play my part to speak on policies that strengthen families, so that the Family Puzzle piece can maintain its place in the heart of the Singapore Puzzle.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Over the years, the Family Puzzle piece has changed its shape.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Technology has rewritten the playbook on raising children.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Our seniors seek connections in this fast-changing world.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If the pieces do not align, the picture will reveal its fault lines.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But the other corners of this puzzle piece are no less important.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Many in my generation are young parents or parents-to-be.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We grew up in a Singapore that was prosperous and stable.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We have been given opportunities our parents could only dream of.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We take pride that Singapore consistently punches above its weight internationally.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The world is racing ahead, and so must we.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We must move quickly to find our niche in a contested and fragmented global market and adapt our people for new technologies, like artificial intelligence (AI).

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But at home, we are stretched – caring for young children, ageing parents and coping with rising costs of living.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But the reality of raising a child in today’s Singapore weighs heavily on young parents.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Young parents today want to be present for their child.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Many prefer not to rely on a domestic helper or on the help of grandparents.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Others do not have the benefit of these options.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This means that young parents are often saddled with heavy caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The problem is exacerbated by the increase in dual income families.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Juggling careers with the unpredictability of childcare and childhood illnesses, the unspoken shame of pumping at work or leaving office in the evening for school pick-ups, the unseen second shift of housework and childcare after work.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: There are expectations at work, if parents want to be seen as equal next to their non-parent colleagues.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Especially in a competitive job market like ours.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Especially in a time of economic change where, as the President noted in his address, workers need to adapt and evolve to stay relevant.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Especially in a generation like ours today, where the number of non-parent employees is increasing and parents start to feel more like outsiders, pushed into the periphery.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Do our working mothers feel the need to expedite their return to the workplace, or suffer the consequences?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Another example which is a common experience for most parents: hand, foot and mouth disease (HFMD) outbreaks happen frequently in preschools.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Add to this preschool closures and other childhood illnesses, coupled with the pressures and insecurities of work and rising costs, and it is easy to see how the early years can become overwhelming.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: There is also the omnipresent pressure to live up to society’s ideal of a “good” parent – pouring immense time, energy and resources into securing a child’s future.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: With technology, AI and rising expectations, that pressure has only grown.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: And unlike past generations, ours has more choices.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Parenthood is no longer the default – there are other options, some of which feel more urgent and important, others feel more comfortable.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Do we perceive family as an ideal that looks good on paper, but not a realistic goal or an attractive experience?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I am concerned that these sentiments are spreading.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The desire to marry is slowly falling across the years.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But perhaps most critically, it will affect our identity as a nation.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: What can we do to arrest this trend?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We can further strengthen the bridge between work and caregiving.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Singaporeans have consistently told us that career and raising a family are equally important to them.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Let us not make them choose between work and family.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Let us empower them to thrive in both.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We have made tremendous progress in this area, especially in the last few years.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: These policy changes will need time to make an impact, and in the meantime, we must continue the progress.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But before I do so, I want to acknowledge that these suggestions cost money and can exacerbate manpower challenges.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Our employers are still adjusting to the new parental leave regime and face an uncertain global market.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We do not want to introduce these suggestions at the expense of our businesses.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We need mindset shifts from both employers and employees to make the following suggestions work in a mutually beneficial way, and in a way that will last in the long term, and in a way that will not be abused.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: And there is something in it for employers too.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In today’s competition for talent, family-friendly human resources (HR) policies build trust, retain top talent, and save employers the hidden cost of good people walking away.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Dual income families are contributing to our economy, and I believe our young working parents want to be able to do right by their children and by their employers.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We can strengthen workplace culture and HR practices so that young parents are supported to thrive both at work and at home.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: And we can reshape how society and workplaces see parenthood and families – by bringing to light not just its challenges, but the deep joys and meaning it brings.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Bridging the care gap will take a whole-of-Government and whole-of-society approach, all of us rowing in the same direction.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Second, let us do more to equip parents with raising a child in this brave new digital world.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Technology is pervasive in all areas of our lives and, by extension, our children's lives.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: As far as child-raising goes, with grandparents stepping back, Google, TikTok, ChatGPT, YouTube and Instagram have stepped in.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But the Internet is no wise elder and viral content often outruns accurate advice.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We must help young parents with what they need to make the best decisions for their children – from food choices to schooling, healthy sleeping practices and well-being.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In this way, we not only ease their burdens, but give every child the strongest start in life.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: With the right support, parents can spend less time firefighting and more time strengthening the bonds that matter, with their children and with their own parents.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: That brings me to my third point, connecting with seniors.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The number has doubled in the last 10 years.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Where do seniors belong in our Singapore Puzzle amidst all these fast-paced economic and social changes?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We must not only provide for our seniors physically.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We must not forget to connect with them emotionally.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Empowering seniors to find their second lease of life will also ease the load on their children as they balance work and caregiving.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We can bring together Active Ageing Centres and schools – seniors reading to children, youths teaching digital skills to seniors, youths inventing interactive games to train seniors' agility and memory, and seniors passing on life lessons that cannot be found in textbooks, lessons especially important in this age of AI.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We can also create opportunities for inter-generational sports.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: What the Singapore Puzzle will look like at SG100 depends most of all on today's young parents and those deciding whether or not to be parents.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The suggestions raised will come at a cost.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We must decide whether it is worth the cost.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We, as a society, must ask ourselves: do we want to have children?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: What does it take for us to build families and have children?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: They shape the strength of our workforce, the resilience of our national defence, the cohesion of our communities and the depth of our national identity.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If we want Singapore at SG100 to remain cohesive and stay ours, we must start now to secure the foundation.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Let Singapore be a place where our children grow up with roots to ground them and wings to let them soar.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We must solve the Singapore Puzzle together and shape the next bound of Singapore not as bystanders, but as builders of our common future.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, in my view, the greatest challenge Singapore faces today is what I call the "Singapore Puzzle".

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: How do we compete in this changing world whilst walking hand in hand with our people; how to reach for the stars and chase dreams without forgetting to help the vulnerable?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: To solve this puzzle, we must first secure the puzzle piece that is the "family".

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Once the family puzzle piece loosens, all other pieces will inevitably shift out of place.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The "we first" that the President and Prime Minister speak of, has family at its core.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: New parents today face tremendous pressure, having to care for both young and old at home whilst striving to keep up with the increasingly competitive workplace.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: They harbour big dreams yet often find themselves exhausted.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Marriage and parenthood are no longer seen as necessary or default.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: All the more so when we look at friends who have become parents – exhausted, constantly on the run, barely catching a breath.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Some begin to think it is better to enjoy some peace and quiet.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Seeing such pressures, many family and friends advise: one child is enough, or even no children is okay!

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Gradually, more people choose to have fewer children, or none at all.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I hope we can work together to lighten the burden for young parents.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I will champion policies to strengthen families so that families find their right place in the "Singapore Puzzle".

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But most importantly, we must engage young Singaporeans to work with the Government, to put our heads and hearts together, work hard side by side and piece together a Singapore Puzzle that belongs to us.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We must confront this reality and seriously ask ourselves: what kind of Singapore society do we hope to see at SG100?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Will it be one with smaller families, fewer people, and shrinking workforce; where elders and younger generations grow distant and the sense of “home" and national identity slowly fades away?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Or will it be one where home endures, people remain, where young parents can work with peace of mind and raise their children with joy, where the bonds and responsibilities of family are firmly held and passed on, allowing our familiar Singapore culture and stories to be carried forward, generation after generation, continuing the legacy left to us by our forefathers?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The ones who understand this situation best are our younger generation – those who face these pressures every day.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I hope that our young Singaporeans will take part in completing this Singapore Puzzle together.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If the younger generation remain un-involved, allowing society to drift away from their ideals and aspirations, then, amid the many alluring choices before us, I cannot be sure that our people will still choose to call Singapore their home.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I sincerely invite our youths to join me in shaping our nation's future, to share your hopes and constructive ideas for Singapore, and to make this choice together: to choose Singapore.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I am honoured for this opportunity to deliver my maiden speech in Parliament in our national language.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Today, I will touch on the issue of mental health and the steps we can take as a society to play our part in caring for and helping one another.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In our efforts to care for the mental health of the Malay/Muslim community in Singapore, we need to acknowledge traditional beliefs, integrate modern practices and create inclusive discussions so that every individual receives support without going against their religious and cultural values.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: However, the issue of stigma and misconceptions about mental illness still exists despite various efforts that have been undertaken to change public mindset.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: One important step to reduce this stigma is encouraging open conversations and providing integrated mental health services that are easily accessible.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: When we discuss with open minds, support one another and respect religious and cultural backgrounds, we will certainly be able to strengthen the mental health of our entire community.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I will elaborate further on how we can work together as a society to improve mental health in my English speech later. : Mr Speaker, in Tamil, please.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: (In Tamil): Those shall long live who have mastered the five senses and who stand true to righteousness.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This is the sixth couplet of the Thirukkural.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The meaning of this verse is, it is important to lead a righteous life through the abstinence of harmful desires that the body, the mouth, the eyes, the nose and the ears seeks.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Those who do so will lead a long life, proclaimed Thiruvalluvar.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In order for humans to control these five bodily senses, it is not only important to have physical strength; it is essential for one to have good mental health too.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Hence, to live a long and fulfilling life, mental health is of utmost importance.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Today, mental health is of equal importance to physical health.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: However, in our Indian community, some are shy in talking about mental health and mental illnesses.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: At times, it is considered a stigma too.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In time to come, this may lead to a difficult situation.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Depression, anxiety, loneliness – these are silent ailments.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: As mental illness is hidden from the outside and the intensity of it increases day after day, it could even take away one's life.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Therefore, as a united community, what we have to do is very clear.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: First, we have to come to a realisation that this is a real problem that we have in our society and take it face to face.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Next, is to look after one another; our families and friends, and support them.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Third, if need be, one should not hesitate to approach doctors, counsellors or seek social resources.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This is a burden that we could all come together and carry as a society. : Mr Speaker, Sir, I rise in support of the Motion and do so with gratitude to the residents of the West Coast-Jurong West group representation constituency (GRC), especially those in Jurong Spring and Gek Poh, who have given me the honour of serving them and to my colleagues and mentors who have guided me on this journey.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The President in his address has urged us to make Singapore a place where every citizen can have a joyful and fulfilling life as they age.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Joy, however, is not simply the ticking off of years on a calendar.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Joy to someone could be seeing their grandchild take their first steps to a parent whose joy is seeing their children smiling and reading.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The joy could be within the community when volunteers see someone get up from a fallen position.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Without mental well-being, colours fade and the world's beauty becomes harder to see, even for the most positive of people.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: How long we live really depends on how well our mind can function.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In this country, we are in the midst of re-working how health is understood and delivered.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Mental health also has rightly received attention in recent years.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Yet, while our frameworks for physical illness are clear, mental health often presents hidden challenges.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Through Healthier SG, we screen widely for hypertension, high cholesterol and diabetes.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: A simple blood pressure machine, you slap on a cuff, you see a reading above 150, you know that is a trigger for action, right?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: You would see a doctor to assess it further.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Even if it is white-coat hypertension, it is just a sort of guide, you get anxious when you seek medical attention.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Similarly, you prick your finger and you see a glucose reading that is more than 15, you panic, and you see a doctor.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But mental health, Members of the House, this is different.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: A person with early anxiety, with early depression or, perhaps, with a hoarding disorder, may not even realise that they have a problem.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Not long ago, a resident noticed a food parcel hanging outside her neighbour's door for three days untouched, so she reached out to me, deeply worried for her neighbour.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: So, with community partners and our agencies, we entered the unit and found not just an empty flat, but one filled wall-to-wall with decades of hoarded items, leaving only a narrow strip of path for me and my volunteers to walk.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This story illustrates why mental health is different.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It is not just the individual that suffers.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Symptoms often are subtle, often noticed by family, friends or neighbours, and sometimes too late.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Families are left helpless, not knowing where to turn.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Volunteers, grassroots leaders and social workers often become the first responders, and they too carry an emotional weight when doing so.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: So, Members of this House, unlike hypertension or diabetes or high cholesterol, where objective markers drive treatment, mental health conditions lack such clear triggers for action.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Just as we screen for hypertension after we are 40, we can use simple, validated point-of-fact questionnaires to pick up early depression or anxiety.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In fact, today, Members and I, we could go Healthhub.sg and just answer nine simple questions from the Patient Health Questionnaire to see whether we have early depression or anxiety.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We could go to mindline.sg, interact with the chatbot to see how our mental well-being is like.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But some in our community need that additional nudge.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: They need some for barriers to be removed before they can take action.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Often, mental health issues are multi-faceted and require multi-agency coordination and intervention.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We already today have Community Outreach Teams (CREST), social service agencies and volunteer networks doing great work.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
