text: A coordinated platform in our community would ensure that anyone knocking on the door will receive timely help and guidance.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Third, we should nurture safe community spaces where residents and neighbours can share concerns and know that timely help will be available for those showing signs of distress.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Just as hypertension, high cholesterol and diabetes can debilitate, we must understand that so too can mental health conditions and often more insidiously.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: All of us want to remain healthy in our homes, not end up in hospitals.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: A life lost because of a missed diagnosis or untreated mental health disorder is one life too many.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Our aim should be not just to prevent illness, but to preserve dignity and to restore hope.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Like the wind, we may not see it – but we feel its effect in the homes, in the blocks and the communities that we serve in.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Now, before we know it, a gentle breeze may become a storm.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We need to own this problem before the problem owns us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is among the highest in the world and greater than most advanced industrialised economies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That we were able to attain the standard of living in the relatively brief span of 60 years since our Independence is a testament to just how far we have come in terms of income and wealth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet in spite of these undeniably impressive achievements, many Singaporeans still express a sense of frustration at their lot, hold perceptions that their world-beating incomes remain inadequate and argue that they are struggling to make ends meet.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We can choose to believe that Singaporeans are simply too sheltered, too pampered, too ungrateful to recognise the good thing that they have going on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But as policy-makers, we must surely take such feedback in good faith and seek to understand why so many households feel this way but somehow have been unable to adequately express why.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In the speech, I will expound on why I think many Singaporeans indeed feel this way.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My explanation has to do with different notions of what it means to live, survive and thrive in a society where policy-making is still largely made on the basis of efficiency.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This stands in contrast to other notions of justice that many hold dear, such as whether something is equitable or if it is fair.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Imagine, if you will, that if you had to cut the cake, if it helps, you can think of my daughter's favourite, like forest cake.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For those of us that are unfamiliar with this make, it has parts that are composed of chocolate, cream and cherries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Say, I am interested in splitting the cake between my daughter, who loves chocolate, but would not typically touch cherries or cream; and my wife, who prefers cherries and cream more, you could say that an efficient splitting of this cake involves carving out the chocolate bits for my kid and leaving the parts with cherries and cream for my better half.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is efficient because we gave each one what they value more, and as wisdom tells us, "happy wife, happy life".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, both my wife and daughter are happier than they would otherwise be were you to propose a swap.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If we were deciding public policy along these lines, one could make a compelling argument that this is a very fair division.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, if I was splitting the cake between my daughter and myself, things would be rather different.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, even if you gave me more cherries and cream, I would still find the split unfair.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For me, then, it would be better to cut the cake exactly in half, say, so that we will have equal shares of chocolate that we both like.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This equitable distribution would, perhaps, be another sound principle for public policy, but it would not strike my daughter as very fair.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Setting aside how in reality I will probably end up giving my share of the cake to my daughter anyway.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This simple thought experiment illustrates how we cannot simply think about public policy in terms of just one idealised principle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Government may value efficiency, for instance, but society may actually prefer one that is more equitable or perhaps one that they may perceive as fairer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am an educator, so let me begin with schools.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Excluding appropriations for certain specialised programmes, such as the Independent Schools Programme, the Special Assistance Plan or Special Education Schools Programme, these are typically distributed according to the general principle of equality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Each school receives resources proportional to their needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, this does not mean that schools receive exactly equal budgets.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If a school enrols more students or requires or offers additional programmes, such as language elective programmes, it will naturally receive funding that exceeds the baseline.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Still, the approach is to slice the educational pie in a manner that treats every student essentially as equal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Allocating a proportional amount to each school fails to account for how, in reality, students in different schools have access to different amounts of resources.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Our so-called neighbourhood schools are predominantly comprised of students from their nearby housing estates and are mostly middle-class.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In contrast, many who attend a so-called brand name school hail from the wealthiest tier of households.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, schools in the latter category, by dint of their longer history and more successful alumni base, can easily raise additional funds through donation drives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The de facto resources that each student in Raffles or Anglo-Chinse School or Saint Nicholas is clearly more than that available to students in Compassvale or Outram or North Vista.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Here, what is equal does not seem fair.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This could be simply by sending relatively more funding their way or reducing what top schools receive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Or we could ensure that the best graduates in each teaching cohort spend significant time in such schools and tie their career advancement to how well they have raised the standards there.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I have spoken more about this in the Adjournment Motion, but for now I will return to my arguments on whether the principles behind the system are fair.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: COE, like most options, purports to be neutral.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, rather than inferring whether one household or another might deserve a car, quarter auctions ask those interested in owning a car to bid for the right to own one.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The COE system takes this a step further by seeking efficiency in this outcome for both buyers and sellers, while ensuring that it raises a comparable amount of revenue for the Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What is absent from this scenario, however, is whether this efficient allocation is fair in the sense that those who own cars are also those who need it the most.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is tempting to say that there is no way to know for sure who are the ones that are most in need of private transportation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, bidding allows market prices to determine who these might be.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, those who need a car more are likely to reveal themselves by bidding more.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This implicitly assumes that those who bid less do so because their needs are lesser.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Simple introspection will reveal that this is a flawed understanding of human behaviour.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, we will only bid as much as we can afford.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Bidding less does not mean that we value something less or need something less.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It just means that we do not have enough money.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We may well bid more if budget were not a constraint.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: By abrogating the allocation decision to the market, we therefore are not truly neutral.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Rather, we are implicitly accepting how allocations based on market prices, efficient though they may be, are also fair.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Again, a little introspection will reveal how incomplete this claim is.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Not only does this resonate more with our Asian values, they are also groups that already explicitly receive support in various Government policy programmes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Most of us can easily, therefore, buy the argument that the needs of these groups for a car are, all else equal, larger than that of a wealthy household purchasing a third car to use on weekends.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A fairer system would make private transportation more affordable to them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: When it comes to the economy, the most common pair of trade-offs, something I teach my students in their "first principles of economics" class is that, often, one needs to balance efficiency with equity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The common refrain we hear in response to calls for us to raise our taxation on companies is that this will discourage investment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Increasing the corporate tax rate would not only be inefficient, since higher investments would typically lead to higher growth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But it may even be counter-productive, since the diminished profit may mean that companies choose to relocate elsewhere, where taxes are lower.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Let us set aside the claim that investment need materially be affected by the prevailing tax rate, a matter on which I had spoken about before and concluded that the evidence suggests not much.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is still a separate issue of whether the tax burden on companies versus households is even equitable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is not possible to perfectly compare the two.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In contrast, personal income taxes are imposed at the margin and progressively increased according to one's tax bracket.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even allowing for errors in these estimates, the tax rate faced by businesses and households are evidently not equal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Admittedly, increases in the corporate tax rate could result in a loss of economic efficiency and performance, but it will be much more equitable since we are evening out the burden that capital bears relative to labour.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Second, let us look at our Goods and Services Tax (GST).

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Government has sought to make it more progressive by rebating part of the tax in the form of GST vouchers (GSTV).

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Despite this concession, the GST is likely to remain somewhat regressive, albeit less so than in the absence of vouchers altogether; and especially, if poorer households have a greater propensity to spend out of their incomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But let us say we believe that even greater progressivity is preferred, relative to the GST cum GSTV arrangement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Then, we may choose to rely, instead, on changes to the marginal tax rate on higher income brackets, because this would be yet more progressive and fairer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Or perhaps, we believe that every individual, rich or poor, should have an equal right to essentials, such as rice, oil and water.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In this case, exemptions from a list of such staples becomes justifiable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Thus, when seen from solely the lens of efficiency, a GST may seem like the only credible form of taxes on consumers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But once we can see the values like equality and fairness are just as important, other more inefficient forms of household taxes suddenly become palatable too.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But as anyone who has taken even an introductory class in economics would be aware, this is only the case if we disregard additional costs external to these private actors, but whose consequences are born by everyone else due to climate change.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For true equity, such externalities must be accounted for by those who generate carbon, which is why we have a carbon tax.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Climate change also brings to bear whether we are doing enough to ensure inter-generational equity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That is because our children and their descendants cannot yet choose the sort of policies that will result in the world that they will eventually inherit, again with a situation where what is efficient is not automatically equitable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Some may argue that there are more efficient ways to have countries bear the cost of their carbon footprint, through a quota system accompanied by a tradeable emissions permit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In theory, this is likely to be more efficient than even a carbon tax, since it will allow those who are best able to mitigate emissions to absorb the cost of doing so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But in practice, this means that richer countries will likely be able to purchase permits from poorer countries to allow them to emit more.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It suggests that it is right for rich countries to effectively dump their pollution into poor ones, in the name of efficiency.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As this example show, what is efficient, what is equal, what is fair, differ not just in principle, but also in reality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I could offer further instances of what is perceived as fair and just continues to elude many in Singapore, ranging from residual discrimination in the workplace due to age or sexual orientation to how our system of fines and penalties is felt more acutely by the lower-income than higher-income households; or to how the rich are able to access healthcare services more quickly than the poor.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But why should we concern ourselves with such distinctions?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The hard truth is that if we want public policy that society can embrace as fair, efficiency alone simply will not do.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We also need to assure our citizens that everyone has an equal chance to succeed in life and that no one is left behind.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Most will regard fair equality of opportunity as more appealing and attainable than the single-minded focus on equality of outcomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, redistribution must still play a role.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Redistribution is also needed as a counterweight to blood luck, since success owes as much to good fortune as it does to pure merit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Parents, outcomes, after all, are their children's opportunities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Equality of opportunity should be a means to advance our goals of social justice rather than an end per se.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, if it is not already amply clear, ensuring equal opportunities is not solely about pushing for equal outcomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is not only because of the impossibility of sustaining blunt equality of this nature or the corrosive effect that such crude redistribution has on individual incentives to work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is also because redistribution alone does not address the concentration of power in the economy or offer individuals agency, dignity, meaning and recognition that comes through work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, even with equal opportunities, we also need to remember that we are only as good as the least among us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This means that terms like shared prosperity must be anchored in a very concrete way: that we cannot be satisfied with our economic success, our vaunted world-beating incomes, until the least advantage among us have a fair shot at living a life of dignity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This means that we should be horrified that there are uncles and aunties in our midst, approaching the ninth decade in their lives, who still feel compelled to work just to make ends meet.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In my speech, I have explained why, despite our material success, many still feel that the Government policies remain unfair, still view their opportunities as inequitable and still search for justice for the most vulnerable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In this term of Parliament, I hope that we will continue to make progress in helping every Singaporean live dignified lives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is what so many of the voters in Sengkang, whose confidence, indeed, returned us to this House, yearn for; and one that we, as their elected voices, will continue to fight for.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: I think when we had the Adjournment Motion debate, I do not remember us characterising the system as neutral.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: In fact, I said that the COE system should be seen as part of our overall transport system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I should emphasise that when I mentioned the term "neutral", I did not mean fiscally neutral.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I should also stress – and this was something I raised in my Adjournment Motion as well – that I did not downplay the importance of public transportation.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, I support and thank the President for his address.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Today is my first time speaking in Parliament and it reminds me of how I felt in 1985 when, as a national gymnast, I represented Singapore for the first time at the Southeast Asian Games.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Although 40 years have passed, my feelings then and now remain the same.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I have always linked my personal beliefs, sense of mission and the interests of the nation together.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Singapore has been a nation for 60 years and has experienced many difficulties and challenges.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Our economic direction has been adjusted multiple times, yet our gross domestic product (GDP) has steadily grown year by year.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This is mainly due to our stable and efficient government, sound systems, and the unity and hard work of our people.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Singapore is a country that relies heavily on foreign trade.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In a complex international environment, it naturally faces many uncertain risks.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But we know that Singapore's development is not only for economic growth, but also for social stability, the well-being of our people and the future of our next generation.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Only by working hard together, supporting and encouraging one another amid uncertainty, can Singapore remain resilient.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Although our country is small, with a land area of about 735.7 square kilometers, we have made rapid progress in finance, technology, industry and manufacturing.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Limited land has not hindered our goals but, instead, driven us to build a high-efficiency, high-value and balanced industrial structure.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It is precisely because of this solid foundation that Singapore can remain a strong haven amid storms, giving us protection and confidence.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But the question we must ask is this: while the nation shelters us, can our communities and families also be shelters for each other?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Can they offer warmth to everyone, regardless of age or background, so that all may feel, "Someone cares about me.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Someone is willing to listen to me?" Singapore is known as a "bright little red dot" not just because of its strong economy or good infrastructure, but also because of the unity and compassion of its people.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Many Singaporeans volunteer, donate and help those in need through various groups and organisations.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This also reminds me of a psychological theory – the hierarchy of needs.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It suggests that after meeting physiological and safety needs, people seek higher levels of social connection, esteem and self-actualization.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In today's rapidly developing era of AI, technology is not only changing business models but also affecting relationships between people.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We must ask ourselves: how can we build a loving society in a fast-paced, efficiency-driven environment?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They do not just create jobs they preserve our culture and spirit.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In recent years, more young people have chosen to give up stable jobs in order to preserve their families' food culture.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Take Lin Huiyi, 27 years old, who was once a bodyguard to both our former and current Presidents.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Not wanting the flavours of her hometown to be lost, she now runs a Cantonese porridge stall with her parents.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: She not only preserves traditional tastes but also uses social media to attract younger people, introduces new management styles, and builds a team culture.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Despite challenges, her passion and perseverance are admirable.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: She reminds us that when dreams are rooted in culture and community, they deserve our support, recognition and attention.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Enterprises like hers are not just part of our economy they are continuations of our heritage.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Behind the seemingly cold data is a group of hardworking entrepreneurs who support countless families.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We must value and protect their efforts so they can continue contributing to the nation and preserving this culture and spirit.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Therefore, when we formulate policies, we must not only listen to their voices but also provide concrete assistance.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This support is not only for economic growth, but also a social investment.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Recently, I have used my spare time to engage with entrepreneurs to discuss the trends of AI, as well as the challenges and opportunities it brings.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I encourage them to participate in AI-related events, learn new skills and prepare for the future.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: These entrepreneurs come from different generations and run all kinds of SMEs.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In our conversations, they not only learn from one another, but all agree that AI will become increasingly important.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They also hope for more community platforms like this to continue learning, practicing and progressing together.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Family is the core of society and the first place where children learn empathy, responsibility, and values.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: To build a resilient society, we must first support every family.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In our communities, we often hear from parents, they work hard while taking care of their children, all in hopes of providing a better life for their families.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: What we are promoting is not just community activities or family policies, but more importantly, a culture of mutual care and concern.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: A truly strong country is not one without problems, but one where people are willing to help each other and solve problems together in times of difficulty.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Therefore, we must place emphasis on building "heartware", not just hardware.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: What we need to strengthen is trust, empathy and a spirit of community care.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This includes mental health and also whether our seniors feel secure, whether our young people are confident about the future, whether our families are supported, and whether our workers, including platform workers, are respected and able to work with dignity.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Every day, they work hard delivering food and transporting our loved ones.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Their jobs may seem ordinary, but they support the daily lives of many.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Platform work also reflects the nature of today's economy: fast-paced, diverse and flexible.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: True progress depends on whether we can build bridges of trust and understanding between generations, between communities, and between people's dreams and opportunities.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: National harmony and progress are not to be taken for granted.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In these 60 years, I will not say we started entirely from zero, but we have gone through many processes from nothing to something.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Our pioneers laid every brick and built step by step to establish a stable, prosperous and respected country.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This would not have been possible without the hard work of our people.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Our nation, our businesses, our families and our people are closely connected.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As the saying goes, "When the lips are gone, the teeth feel the cold." This means that if one falls, the others will be affected too.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: When the nation is stable, businesses thrive; when businesses thrive, families are stable; when families are stable, people can live and work in peace and contribute to the nation.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: These four elements are the most important pillars of our society.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We are building not just a functioning country, but a home where everyone can live in peace, with mutual trust.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The nation is our shelter; we must also make our communities shelters for everyone, and make every family its own shelter.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Only then can we be more confident, knowing that no matter what happens, we will always have a safe, orderly, warm, and caring community and family to rely on.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Tomorrow's Singapore should also be warm, joyful and fulfilling.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Challenges will continue to exist, but as long as we trust and support each other, Singapore will remain a ship that sails steadily even through stormy seas.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   The President noted how each generation has built on the legacy of those before, embracing change and persevering through crises.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He spoke of the need for unity as we navigate turbulent waters.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would add that true unity does not mean uniformity.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It means recognising and embracing that diverse viewpoints strengthen rather than weaken governance.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The complex challenges that Singapore faces in an uncertain world do not come with easy solutions.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When we welcome different perspectives in policy discussions, when we create space for constructive debate, when we listen to voices that may challenge conventional wisdom, we make better decisions for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The President spoke about how families are stretched in caring for both young and old, and the Government will strengthen support for caregivers.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I agree that we can and should do more to support our caregivers.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yet our policies do not always fully reflect this understanding.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should value unpaid care work as much as paid employment.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Families should get equal support regardless of their choice of care arrangements.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is how we truly cultivate a "we first" society. : Mr Speaker, please allow me to continue in English.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The President noted how each generation has built on the legacy of those before, embracing change and persevering through crisis.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He spoke of the need for unity as we navigate turbulent waters.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would add that true unity does not mean uniformity.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It means recognising and embracing that diverse viewpoints strengthen rather than weaken governance.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The complex challenges that Singapore faces in an uncertain world do not come with easy solutions.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When we welcome different perspectives in policy discussions, when we create space for constructive debate, when we listen to voices that may challenge conventional wisdom, we make better decisions for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yet, even as economic indicators tell us about our productivity and competitiveness, they say little about our well-being, relationships, sense of purpose and belonging.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can and should go further – towards a society where prosperity encompasses not just economic well-being, but also emotional, social and spiritual flourishing.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The President spoke about preparing our youth for a future that will be different, helping them secure good jobs and giving them a stronger voice in shaping Singapore.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Indeed, our children are growing up in a world that is changing at unprecedented speed.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How can they be ready to take on jobs that do not exist, overcome challenges that we cannot imagine and seize opportunities that we have not conceived?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe many Members in this House who had spoken about how quickly AI is transforming the workplace, especially for entry level positions, will agree that these questions have become all the more urgent.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Preparing our youth for the above requires more than just enhancing curricula or revising the Primary School Leaving Examination (PSLE) scoring system.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It demands an educational environment that celebrates different forms of intelligence, have many definitions of success, and which values collaboration alongside competition.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And perhaps most importantly, in today's world, it demands an emphasis on the cultivation of uniquely human traits and values that enable meaningful work where machines are limited.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yes, we now speak often about the importance of soft skills.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The reality is that success in all of our milestone exams – the PSLE, the "N" and "O" level exams in their current and future form, the "A" levels – remain overwhelmingly defined by individual academic performance measured largely through written papers.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We value adaptability in uncertain times, yet our assessment ecosystem mostly rewards those who can perform consistently within familiar formats and timeframes.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We value resilience, yet we rarely assess our students for their perseverance through failure.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This holistic approach to education becomes even more critical when we consider the well-being challenges that our children already face today.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This discrepancy suggests that we may not be seeing the full picture of what our children are experiencing in schools today.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I commend MOE for embarking on a Comprehensive Action Review on Bullying, but addressing this challenge requires us to go beyond strengthening protocols and safeguards.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We must get to the roots of why children hurt other children, both online and offline.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Studies show that bullying has a lasting negative impact on mental health and behavioural development, effects that can persist well into adulthood for both those who are bullied and those who bully.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They also reveal that children who bully are often children with poor well-being, those who feel unseen or unheard.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: All of these tell us something about the profound transformation that our education system needs.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How do we nurture resilience in our young so they can better deal with stress, adversity and setbacks in an uncertain world?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How do we help more parents recognise signs of distress before they manifest as harmful behaviour?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How do we create cultures of empathy and support in and outside of schools, so our children are prepared for meaningful lives as contributing members of society?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The emphasis on recognising the value in every job resonates strongly with a challenge that I hope we can address more directly.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The undervaluation of unpaid care work that forms the backbone of society.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This recognition is all the more vital as Singapore becomes a super aged society next year.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many more Singaporeans will find themselves in a sandwich generation of caring for ageing parents while raising children and/or setting aside their careers.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can and should do more to support caregivers.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When a parent stays home to care for a child, when an adult child takes leave to care for an ageing parent, when grandparents provide childcare, these are work.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Work that creates immense value for families and society, even though it is not typically captured by economic indicators.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yet our policies do not always fully reflect this understanding.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even as we endeavour to give every Singaporean child the best start in life by enabling access to quality preschool education, subsidies for infant and childcare remain tied to maternal employment status.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Every child deserves the best start in life, and every family deserves support in accessing it, whether the mother works in an office or runs a household, while providing care for other family members.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Paid caregiving leave would be another meaningful step forward.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But many Singaporeans who work and care for elderly parents or have older children with additional needs must tap on their annual leave when urgent caregiving needs arise, leave meant for their own rest and recuperation.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am encouraged that Members on both sides of this House share this concern.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Caregivers should not have to choose between caring for their loved ones and taking care of themselves.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When we force such choices, we undermine both the caregivers' well-being and the quality of care they can provide.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To truly become a "we before me" society, we must do more to recognise and support those who dedicate their lives to caring for others, whether temporarily or permanently.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should value unpaid care work as much as paid employment.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Families should get equal support regardless of their choice of care arrangements.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But more importantly, we should aspire to be a country where every citizen ages successfully with dignity. 2024 MOM figures show that more seniors are staying in the workforce compared to a decade ago.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many of our elderly work in our coffee shops, hawker centres and shopping malls as cleaners, servers, security guards, and in other physical roles.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Work can indeed be a source of dignity, purpose and social connection, and we should absolutely support those who choose to.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, we must also honestly examine the full spectrum of motivations behind why many of our seniors continue to work well into their seventies.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For others, it may be primarily driven by economic necessity.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are not mutually exclusive, but we must ask, do all our working seniors have genuine choice?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As we celebrate increased lifespans, we must acknowledge that living longer costs more.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many seniors, including those that I meet in Tampines, face not just the rising cost of living, but also the recurring costs of managing chronic conditions, paying for mobility aids and specialised care.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For some, these costs may not be fully covered by their retirement savings or the various subsidies available.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As families and households get smaller, more of our seniors also have the additional challenge of navigating ageing without the social support networks that past generations have had.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Ageing with dignity means having genuine choices about if and how much to work, and meaningful options for social connection and purpose.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It means ensuring that those who do work do so because work contributes to their well-being, and not because it is essential for their survival.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As Singapore ages, I hope we will have deeper conversations about what adequate retirement really means, because beyond the economics of ageing lies a fundamental human need for connection, purpose and community.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some may view the above suggestions as costly in an era where we must be physically prudent.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I respectfully suggest that these are not costs, but investments.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When we support families, we invest in our demographic future.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When we prioritise our children's well-being and nurture their resilience over test scores, we invest in a generation that is capable of thriving in uncertainty.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One that is guided by trust, firm in resolve yet open to change, confident yet humble, diverse yet united.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is the Singapore I want to help build.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yet this chapter can only materialise if there is trust.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Trust cannot be taken for granted, nor can it be held and maintained by the Government alone.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It must be cultivated at every level of society, within families, between neighbours and across generations.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Building trust means having difficult conversations about the gaps between our dreams and aspirations.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Trust grows when we engage each other constructively and in good faith.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Success follows when we trust each other and work together towards a shared goal, a shared goal of building a Singapore that embraces different definitions of success.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A Singapore that understands that true national strength comes from both economic competitiveness and social resilience.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A Singapore that is not just a successful nation but a society worth living in.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is how we will successfully navigate an uncertain future and build a better Singapore, not just for ourselves, but for generations to come.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I look forward to working with all Members of this House to make our shared aspirations a reality.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: It is an honour for me, as a new Member to participate in this debate.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: When my son was a toddler, he walked up to the television and he scrolled across the screen as though it were a giant iPad.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: That simple moment captures the paradox of progress.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: As technology propels us forward, it also reshapes our psychology, our families and our society.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: The question before us is not whether we progress, but how we progress without losing our values and humanity.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Our children today are born into a world of touchscreens and instant connectivity.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: They are growing up with Google Gemini, ChatGPT, generative AI and technologies not yet imagined.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: But, the ease of technology, however useful, always comes with trade-offs – especially for families.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: In Tampines East, many young parents tell me they struggle with these trade-offs.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: With long days spent juggling work, children and ageing parents, they are exhausted.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: On the surface, we see children pacified with screens.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: But in truth, parents are simply trying to survive the day.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: And it is here that we must confront the deeper paradoxes of technology.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: We saw the rise of the "Me Generation" with the arrival of Facebook in 2004.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: It amplified our natural tendencies for social comparison.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Trolling, cyberbullying and toxic exchanges fuel stress, anxiety and depression among our youths.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Worse still, harmful behaviours are not only displayed, but rewarded.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: When such conduct gains likes, shares and attention, it creates a dangerous kind of social proof, signaling to our young that bad behaviour is normal behaviour.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: We also see instant gratification becoming the norm.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Short-form videos and reels serve up endless distraction, curated by algorithms that create echo chambers.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: We are seeing shorter attention spans, weaker critical thinking and reduced emotion regulation.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: This in turn erodes social cohesion, resilience and grit – all qualities that have defined Singapore's success.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: And then there is the third paradox of convenience.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Technology promises to save us time – groceries at a tap, emails answered on the go.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Yet, these same devices have also become relentless sources of stress.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Because we can work from anywhere, we end up working everywhere.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: The flood of emails, WhatsApp messages and notifications deplete our mental reserves.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: And it mirrors daily life: the more we let technology think for us, the weaker our focus, the weaker our resilience and the weaker our grit.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: The lesson is clear, even as we adopt new tools, we must remember that these technologies are fundamentally just tools and we must closely guard our human strengths: judgement, intuition and compassion.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Prime Minister has spoken about the "we" generation.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: President Tharman has called for a "we first" mindset – one that places the collective good above self interest.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: I believe this is the mindset Singapore needs as we enter our next phase of progress.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: A mindset is a lens through which we see the world.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: It shapes how we interpret events and how we respond to them.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: And mindsets are not born, they are shaped, by what families emphasise, what schools teach and what society chooses to reward.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: So, how do we nurture such a "we first" mindset?

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: But it is the foundation of empathy, resilience and perspective-taking; the very soft skills our young will need to survive in the AI era.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: And kindness must be lived in every sphere of life – at home, in school, in the community and in the workplace.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: In schools, this means teaching empathy alongside knowledge and equipping our young with stress and emotion management skills that must be practised continuously throughout their school years to be truly honed.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Experiential learning – whether through community service projects or outdoor challenges, give children first-hand experience of responsibility and interdependence, and works best when reinforced with encouragement.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: These approaches should be built systematically into our school curriculum at every level, so that empathy and emotional resilience are not left to chance.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: And to make them work, we must strengthen support with more counsellors and psychologists to guide programmes and walk alongside our young as they navigate mental and emotional challenges.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: In families, it means modelling kindness at home, not only to strangers, but to one another.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Too often, we forget to be kind to those closest to us.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Children may not always listen to what we say, but they notice what we do, including our unkind behaviours and the way we use devices.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: But kindness does not stop at home; it must extend into our communities.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: And in communities, it means designing systems that make care second nature.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: In Tampines East, I have seen residents care for one another in many ways.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Youths teaching seniors digital skills, volunteers delivering meals to neighbours and families looking out for elderly folks living alone.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: These small acts of care may seem ordinary, but together they sustain the kampung spirit that defines Singapore.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: At the national level, we must also renew the Singapore Kindness Movement.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Campaigns are useful, but lived experiences matter more.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Kindness must reach into digital spaces – from gaming platforms that reward cooperation, to workplace tools that encourage us to appreciate a colleague.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: And by celebrating small, everyday acts of care, we show that it is not distant or heroic, but something each of us can practise daily.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Businesses, too, can be a force for good.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Corporate social responsibility has grown and companies today are rightly held accountable by consumers.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Yet business pressures can sometimes relegate kindness to the background.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: We should instead support organisations that embed kindness into their DNA, whether through inclusive hiring, supporting employees who show empathy, or giving staff time and resources to serve the community.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: In many parts of the world, divisions of race, religion and class are hardening.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Singapore has been fortunate to avoid this, but we cannot be complacent.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Yet numbers alone do not capture the lived experience of inequality.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: A worker may be diligent and talented, but if hiring unconsciously favours those who "look the part", it is not merit that decides, but stereotype.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: And when such institutional barriers combine with self-doubt or prejudice, they can quietly block opportunity.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: A student who keeps hearing "people like you cannot make it" may begin to believe it.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: A society where opportunities are not predetermined by background, but created through ability, effort and fair chance.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Because only then can progress feel meaningful, not just for the successful few, but for every Singaporean who works hard and contributes.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: It is about ensuring that even as we advance, we do not lose sight of who we are.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: As we mark SG60 and look ahead to SG100 and beyond, let us remember the lessons of history.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Civilisations that endured were not only those that adapted to change, but those that did so while holding fast to their values.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: (In Mandarin):   In this fast-changing world, we must not forget the most fundamental values of being human.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: To be Singaporean is to share the spirit of being in the same boat, moving forward shoulder to shoulder.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: We all know how hard it is to bridge race, religion and class, and to strive together as one.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: But our forefathers did it and our generation will surely do it too.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: As long as we support one another and hold firm to our resolve, the marathon ahead is ours to win. : It is our unity, our resilience and our spirit of looking out for one another that will carry us forward.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: As we race to the top, let us make sure we do not leave anyone behind.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Because the true test of progress is not how high we climb, but how many we bring along with us.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is a Special Assistance Plan (SAP) school.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I did have one Malay classmate in Primary 1, his name was Hamzah.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I remember him to be rather cheeky, but other than that, I saw him as one of us classmates and did not think much more then.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many years later, I went to Cardiff University in the United Kingdom (UK) and I was the only non-British student in my programme.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It was not easy for me in the beginning.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, several classmates started conversations with me, they took an interest in who I was, where I came from and invited me for gatherings, and over time, we became good friends.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In fact, three of them flew to Singapore for my wedding.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Two of them were part of my "brothers" gang and they braved the gatecrashing with me, undergoing "酸甜苦辣", or joys and sorrows.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And I would have actually flown to Cardiff for one of their weddings earlier this month, but it coincided with the official Opening of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But I think Dewi and Sophie will appreciate this quick mention in my speech.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Having gone through my experience in Cardiff, there are times when I think back to Hamzah.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How had he felt being a minority in school?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We may have treated him as one of us, but had we embraced him for who he was?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It requires a lot of effort and heart to understand and then to embrace our differences, so that everyone feels appreciated being who we are – "same same but different".

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We do not want our people to let external developments affect our social cohesion.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But it is hard not to have strong emotions when we see grave atrocities.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There are other areas, the political contestation between the United States (US) and China, the cultural wars between the conservatives and the liberals.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These all evoke emotions amongst segments within our population and they often come with an inclination to choose sides.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And then, I worry whenever I scroll Instagram.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The algorithm will keep on feeding us videos which confirm, double confirm, triple confirm our own worldview, and then it whips us into a frenzy with this strong sense of injustice against every other worldview that appears to lay siege against ours.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is, frankly, the most influential echo chamber ever invented.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And I worry when I meet residents who do not know their neighbours are or have not spoken to them in several years.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And I ask, how effective is the Ethnic Integration Policy (EIP) if neighbours are not speaking to one another, much less building relationships?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I worry when our youths tell me that they seldom hang out in public spaces like the community centres and basketball courts now, unlike maybe for my generation.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How effective are these spaces as well, if they do not foster engagement?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Yet, amidst the storm, these are also the best of times where our multiculturalism can shine as Singapore's superpower, because bridge-builders can bring light to a fragmented and dark world.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: All of us who grow up in a multicultural environment and can build connections across cultures are strongly positioned to seize and grow opportunities in this global future.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But we will need to re-evaluate our levers and be bold to make changes so that they can be more effective.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And let me share a few quick suggestions.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, instead of focusing only on our common values, which certainly continues to be important, we need to make much more effort to understand our differences.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The more we are inundated with views similar to our own, the more we must seek out alternative, even opposing viewpoints, resolve ourselves to hearing them out and understand where they come from.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Because with deeper understanding of each other, we can eventually still agree to disagree, but we will do so holding hands and not coming to blows.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, let us take a hard look at our policies that seek to foster multiculturalism and consider if they are achieving their objectives.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Now I know that this will require further studies, but my larger point, really, is that it cannot just be the numbers that we seek.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It must be the quality of the relationships forged, that we aspire towards.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Third, we need to reimagine our public spaces.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These spaces must be the heart of our communities – where we come together to partake in common interests, but also where we come to embrace our differences.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We do not have to be limited to conventional spaces, such as the community centres or the basketball courts, if that is not what interests our youths.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We can invite ground-up proposals for other state buildings or land that aim to strengthen our multicultural community, facilitate these with funding support.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We can also open up a much wider drawing canvas for our residents to design their neighbourhoods.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope these initiatives will excite our youths to come forward and have a larger stake in community building.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And I aim to do so in Tanjong Pagar-Tiong Bahru.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, Sir, in the five months since I entered politics, my happiest times have been participating in community activities with my Tiong Bahru residents from Tanjong Pagar.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Through singing, exercising and dancing, I have been able to better understand my residents, especially the elderly.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They even sing "The Moon Represents My Heart" (月亮代表我的心) and "Ai Piah Cia Eh Yia" (爱拼才会赢), or "Fight to Win".

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I constantly remind our Chinese residents one thing, when non-Chinese residents participate so enthusiastically in community activities despite not knowing Chinese, it demonstrates their commitment and contribution to our multicultural and multiracial society.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is a good example for all of us.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Therefore, at these occasions, I make it a point to speak in English as well.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When singing, I would also encourage them to sing English and Malay songs.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that our activities will be welcomed by all our citizens.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: After all, Singapore is founded on a multicultural society.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Therefore, our goal is to bring everyone together through implementing policies and making good use of our public facilities and community activities, so that we can deepen the understanding between and feelings for each other. : Sir, let me return to where I started.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Singapore I want to build is one where every little child grows up, knowing and feeling that they can be who they are, in every setting and season of life.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Singapore I want to build is an orchestra of different musical instruments: we look different, we sound different, we have different ranges, but when we work together in harmony, we create the most magical and timeless symphonies.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: This is the first speech in this Chamber, and it means everything to me, not just because it marks the start of my Parliamentary journey, but also because it reflects the trust that Singaporeans, in particular, my Canberra constituents, to speak honestly, with heart and with purpose.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: The President, in his address, reminded us that Singapore can only stand tall if we act as one people, by putting "we" before "me".

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: This unity, built not despite our diversity but through it, has always been our strength.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Our future depends on nurturing a society where we look out for one another, where success is measured not just by what we achieve, but by what we do together for the common good.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Personally, it is not enough to look at where someone starts.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: What matters just as much is the courage they show when life knocks them down and how we support them in getting back up.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Today, I want to speak about something deeply personal: second chances.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: I want to talk about what it means to fall behind and how we, as a society, can help people stand tall again.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: I also want to touch on two things we often avoid discussing: financial literacy and planning for death – wills and Lasting Powers of Attorney (LPAs).

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: I am talking about any Singaporean who has made a wrong turn: bad financial decisions, toxic relationships, addictions, even just giving up on themselves too early.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: I have been championing for second chances since 2011 and have seen first-hand the repercussions to the families of those incarcerated, with addictions, and who made wrong financial decisions.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: It often takes years for the families to recover if they recover at all.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: One wrong choice can lead to a lifetime of despair.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: We have made good progress in some areas, for example, our prison’s recidivism rate has been steadily dropping.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: But second chances are not only about statistics or systems.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: They are also about whether people feel life itself is worth holding onto.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: I met a young resident not long ago at my meet-the-people session (MPS).

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: She came with her mother, and I noticed the scars of self-harm still healing on her arms.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Her bank account had been misused by someone else, and the bank froze it.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: She was caught in a spiral – unable to access her own money, losing hope.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: We worked with the local police post and even wrote to the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) to try to resolve it.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Last month, her father wrote to me and shared that his daughter was admitted into Institute of Mental Health (IMH).

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: This is what it looks like when someone feels there is no way back.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: It is not just about mental health in the clinical sense.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: It is about society giving people reasons to believe tomorrow can still be better.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: The national suicide rate stood at 5.91 per 100,000 residents.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: In recent years, it has been heartening to see communities coming together, various organisations that champion different causes coming together to help those in need.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: But we must first acknowledge that more can be done and more must be done.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: That we must teach a person to fish and not just provide them fish.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Second chances only work if someone is willing to give a first “yes”– the landlord who does not judge your past, the human resources (HR) officer who looks at your potential, the auntie at the void deck who asks, “You okay or not?” instead of crossing the road in avoidance.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: That means relooking into our hiring culture, our housing rules and our public communications.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Can we move from a society that punishes mistakes endlessly to one that corrects, supports and uplifts?

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: I have met too many Singaporeans, especially in their 40s and 50s, who have fallen into debt because they did not understand the system.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: But because no one ever taught them how credit works, what “compounding” means, or what it means or what to ask before signing a loan.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: That is not financial play; that is pressure.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Earlier this year, I met a resident during a house visit and he explained that his sister had taken multiple loans with both licensed and unlicensed moneylenders.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: This led to his family being harassed, afraid and needing help.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: It eroded their relationship leading to a breakup of the family.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: That is nearly 2,300 people in a single year needing help, each a signal that money struggles are growing, not shrinking.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Back in 2019, CCS handled about 3,250 new cases.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: That number dropped during COVID but is now climbing back again.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: The trend is clear: financial health is not just a private matter; it is a public concern.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: We need to stop thinking of financial literacy as a “good-to-have.” It is a life skill as essential as reading or writing.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: We should be teaching this in primary schools, in National Service (NS), in SkillsFuture classes.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Not just budgeting but how to read contracts, avoid scams, manage risks.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: And for those already in debt, we must offer a real way out.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: You cannot rebuild a life when you are buried under guilt.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: But financial resilience is not only about individuals.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: It is also about whether our businesses and workers can adapt in a changing economy.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Across Singapore, I have met business owners and workers who share similar worries: rising costs, digitalisation and the challenge of keeping up with rapid change.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Transformation cannot just be about large firms or multinationals.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: It must also include our kopitiam stalls, our SMEs, our local family-run businesses that anchor the communities.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, transformation must go hand-in-hand with protecting and uplifting our local workers.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: When industries change, it is workers who feel the disruption most keenly.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Older workers especially fear being replaced or left behind.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: We must strengthen retraining pathways, wage support and on-the-job learning opportunities, so that transformation is not something done to workers, but with them.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: If we can help our local businesses thrive and ensure our workers grow alongside them, then transformation will not divide us – it will uplift us together.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: The next taboo I want to talk about is death.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: I know, Mr Speaker, these are not exciting topics.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: That is despite a campaign pushing for 240,000 by end-2025.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Yet, more than one in 10 Singaporeans do not know what an LPA is and nearly 20% are not aware of advance care planning.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: I was at an MPS where I saw this resident whose husband had just passed away a year ago and as there was no will and no LPA before he lost mental capacity, it led to complex legal challenges and emotional distress.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: But many still do not know what an LPA is.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Some think it is only for the old, others worry it is about “giving up power.” But it is the opposite.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: An LPA protects your voice when you can no longer speak for yourself.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: And wills, especially for lower-income families, are equally crucial.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: For some lower-income families, a partially paid or older HDB flat may be their life’s only tangible asset.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: If that transfer is contested or mishandled, it could break a family apart.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Canberra Community Club (CC) has had a series of will and LPA workshops, and I know more can be done to raise awareness.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: And dignity means giving people agency over their story.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: In Singapore, we are trained from young to fear failure.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: We are embarrassed to reach out for help.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: But I believe we must make space for the comeback.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
