text: That means companies hiring not just based on clean records but also on character growth.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: It means schools giving students time to catch up.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: It means neighbourhoods, where asking for help is not seen as weakness.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: I have been blessed to know of company owners who do not look at overcomers as cheap labour, or just another recruitment channel, or to exploit them, but to invest in them, to give them opportunities to grow, to groom them, to help them develop and equip them to overcome challenges that lie ahead.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: That is the culture I want to see more of.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Because sometimes, it just takes one "yes" to save someone from a lifetime of "no." Mr Speaker, in conclusion, the President spoke about the importance of putting "we" before "me" – of building a "we first" society where our success is measured not only by what we achieve alone, but by what we do together for the common good.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: But I think this is not just about bouncing back when times are hard.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: It is about building a country where people help each other rise again.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: I want Singapore to be known not just for its discipline, but its compassion.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Not just for its efficiency, but for its empathy.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Let us be a society where someone who messed up once is not forever defined by it.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Where dignity is not earned only by success but granted simply because you are human.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Let us be the kind of country where every Singaporean knows this: even if you fall, you are not forgotten.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Even if you are lost, there is a way home.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: And I thank the House and Singaporeans for giving me the chance to speak and to serve.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: I am grateful, but also a little anxious.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Anxious – not in a way that paralyses, but in a way that reminds me of the gravity of this moment and the privilege that I have to serve Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: So, I will try my best, in this speech, to turn my anxious energy into something useful – words that carry hope and assurance, and words that do not put you to sleep.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: The Prime Minister and Senior Minister Lee asked me earlier this year if I read books.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: And they said I should read more widely.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: I read parts of the book "A Different Kind of Power" by Jacinda Ardern, the former Prime Minister of New Zealand.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: She is known for her conviction about fairness, opportunity and empathy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: She spoke openly about how her anxiety reminded her of the weight of leadership.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: She also said that she knew her maiden speech might one day "haunt" her, because words in politics and parliament linger; they are remembered, they are scrutinised and they are tested against our actions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Standing here today, I know, that what I say in the next 20 minutes – yes, do not worry, not more than that – will not simply vanish when I sit down.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: They will be mentioned in debates years from now.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: And they may come back to haunt me.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: And perhaps, that is what gives weight to this moment – to know, that we are accountable not only for the commitments we make, but also for the spirit and the values in which we make them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: As someone entrusted with responsibilities for both education and digital development, I had no excuse not to read it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: But is it only one generation that is anxious?

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Every generation of Singaporeans has been anxious, though in different ways and through different seasons.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Our Pioneer Generation felt existential anxiety: would Singapore survive?

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: The Merdeka Generation – my parents’ generation – carried another form of anxiety: how to build stable families, how to create industries from scratch.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: And they worried through recessions and restructuring: could they keep their jobs, would their children have better lives than them?

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: And then there is my generation, parents of young children today.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: We live in one of the safest, most successful nations in the world and yet, we worry endlessly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Can they thrive in a world that changes faster than the one we grew up in?

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: And what if we get it all wrong?

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Our young people, too, carry their own burdens of anxiety.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: The irony is that they live in a world and a time of endless opportunities and yet, they carry the weight of immense expectations, from society, from their families and often from themselves.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: This anxiety is real and it is not a weakness.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: It is a signal that they care deeply that they are searching for meaning and that they need assurance and safe spaces to turn their restlessness into purpose.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Anxiety, then, is not the condition of one generation, but an inescapable part of being a human.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: The real question is not whether we feel it, but what we do with it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Now, a little something for the Science students.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Brownian motion describes particles that move around randomly with no clear path; plenty of movement, but no direction.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: When my netball teammates and I were younger, when we had energy and stamina, we often ran around the court like headless chickens.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Our coach, Prof Yap from the National University Hospital (NUH), who actually just returned from Egypt, she would say to us, “Brownian motion is useless.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: This way, we can channel the anxieties of Singaporeans into purposeful action.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: (In Mandarin):   We Chinese have an idiom, "be prepared for danger in times of peace", which means that even in good times, we must think about future challenges.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: It reminds us that we care about the future, our families and our nation's prospects.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: They worried whether Singapore could survive, whether it could provide enough food and water for the next generation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: They worried about economic recession, their children's employment and future prospects.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Although Singapore is already a safe and prosperous country, we still worry: are our children resilient?

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Can they grow up in this complex world?

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Anxiety is not a weakness, but a driving force.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: The key is not whether we have anxiety, but how we face it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: We can let anxiety behave like Brownian motion – vibrating randomly and aimlessly; or we can transform it into a driving force for action, making us to be more resilient, creative and confident.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Only in this way can we transform worry into strength, transform unease into hope and lay a more solid foundation for Singapore's tomorrow. : I will now share my thoughts on my two portfolios: Education first, followed by Digital Development and Information.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: As a mother of two preschoolers, my days are filled with joy and worry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Each morning, Papa and I hold our little boys' hands, and we walk them into their schools.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: We kiss them goodbye and we watch them take their small steps into the world, a world that feels faster, harsher and more complex than the one I grew up in.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: And at night, after they are asleep, I often find myself asking, "Am I doing enough for them?

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Am I present enough as a working parent, and am I patient enough as an exhausted parent?

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Will they be bullied, or will they bully others?" These questions are not unique to me.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: They are questions every parent would ask themselves in quiet moments.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: And I want to say here, as a parent and as a policy-maker, I see you.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: I hear you and I carry the same questions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Education, at its heart, is not simply about grades.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: The best way to defeat bullying is to make kindness our norm.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: The real revolution is not against bullying but for kindness.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Let us not just tell our children to be kind to each other.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Let us, as adults, be kind and respectful to each other, so that our children in Singapore, watch, learn and mimic the kindest generations of adults.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: I will work with parents, youths, educators and community groups to reframe the way we approach our challenges.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Our work will not be just about preventing bullying but making kindness our norm and finding meaning in caring for others.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Our work will not be just about helping children pass our mother tongue subjects but reconnecting them with our cultures and strengthening their ability to communicate with the world.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: And our work will not be just about avoiding screen time but helping children, and parents, rediscover the life lessons from play and nature, and strengthening parent-child relationships.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: My other portfolio, Digital Development, brings me face to face with a different kind of anxiety.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: We worry about children glued to screens, exposed to online harms, workers displaced by AI and seniors left behind in a fast-changing society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Yet, just as with anxiety, technology can either paralyse us or propel us.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Our youths wonder if AI will take away the jobs that they aspire towards or if they will be able to keep up with machines that learn faster than humans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Yet, when I meet students at hackathons, I also see their excitement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: They want to experiment, they want to create and they want to shape how AI can be used for good.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: So, I believe, that if we guide them well, our youths will not just adapt to AI, but they will help define the future with it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: As we embrace technology and prepare our young for an AI-driven future, we must remember never to lose our humanity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Machines can process faster than us, but they cannot feel for one another.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: They cannot comfort a friend in pain, forgive a mistake or show compassion to a stranger.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: These are deeply human capacities – empathy, kindness, moral judgement – that no algorithm can replace.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: So, as we advance, let us hold firmly to the values that make us human because it is these values that will guide how we use technology and ensure it serves people, not the other way around.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: These values of empathy and kindness also guide me, as I fulfil my duties as the Minister-in-charge of GovTech.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Our public service must continue to be best-in-class, setting the tone for how technology can serve and strengthen people, not the other way round.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Our pioneers built homes while anxious about survival.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Our parents built industries while anxious about recessions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: As leaders, our role is not to erase anxiety because that is impossible.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Our role is to steady the anxious hearts and to channel the restless energy into constructive action.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Years from now, people may ask, “Jasmin, did you live up to these words?

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Did you carry through on what you promised?” I hope that when that day comes, I can say, “I gave it all I have got.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Yes, I was anxious but I took action.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Yes, I spoke of assurance, and I worked every day to provide a little bit more of it.” Every evening, I see the real reason for my work – my children, sleeping soundly, full of unspoken trust that tomorrow will be okay, that the world will be kind.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: In their faces, I am reminded of why I stand here – to help build a Singapore where every child can grow up confident, kind and courageous.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: To serve with both head and heart, to walk alongside Singaporeans in their anxieties, and to help transform those anxieties into action for a kinder, more resilient, more compassionate and confident Singapore.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.50 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 3.31 pm until 4.40 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: First, I would like to apologise to all Members.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: President Tharman has set out the challenges ahead and the key priorities for this term of Government.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Members have raised many issues in this Debate and also shared useful ideas and suggestions.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Government will study all of your feedback.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Today, I want to take a step back and speak about the larger mission before us.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As we move beyond SG60 and as the world around us undergoes profound changes, we must ask ourselves: what kind of Singapore are we building?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: How do we ensure better lives for our children and grandchildren?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The past 60 years have been a miracle.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: When our founding leaders embarked on the journey of an independent Singapore, it felt like the most unpromising of startups.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They would have been astonished at what Singapore has become today.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: From third world to first, we have lifted the lives of Singaporeans beyond the wildest dreams of our pioneer generation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We created opportunities for all and improved living standards across the board.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We enjoyed decades of peace and progress, of stability, harmony and unity.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The external environment is more contested, more unpredictable and more challenging for small states like Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our economy is maturing and our population is ageing, so growth will inevitably slow.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Many young people worry that they may not do better than their parents.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In the past, when education levels were lower, securing paper qualifications was seen as a sure ticket to success.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Now almost all have tertiary education, and half the cohort have university degrees.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Young people sometimes feel like they are trapped in a relentless rat race – from classroom to the workplace.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They also worry that society is becoming more stratified.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That the rich and wealthy are pulling ahead, while others struggle to keep up.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Social media amplifies these anxieties, triggering constant comparisons and envy.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Across the world, younger people are reporting higher levels of anxiety, and responding in different ways.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In China, there is the phenomenon of tang ping or lying flat.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In Japan, they talk about hikikomori, not leaving the house.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In Europe and America, there is “quiet quitting”, “downshifting”, or the “great resignation”, and so on.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Here in Singapore, we must do everything we can to defy this global trend.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: My team and I make this pledge to our youths, and to the generations that follow.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will build Singapore with you in mind.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will strive to create more fulfilling lives for you.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And not just for a few among you, but for all of you.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have new ideas and plans to achieve this.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Through Forward Singapore, we have set out our shared goals.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: To keep social mobility alive, so the escalator keeps moving, and everyone has the opportunity to rise over time.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: To strengthen our safety nets, so that no one falls through the cracks.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: To deepen our sense of solidarity, so we bridge differences and remain one united people.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: First, we will do more to keep the escalator moving and help every Singaporean realise their full potential.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have seen how other societies have become more stratified, increasingly, with privilege becoming more entrenched.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In extreme cases, your caste and your social class determine who you are, what you can do and what you can become.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Even in meritocratic societies, we see admissions to universities or top jobs in public and private sectors dominated by those from privileged backgrounds.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, I read recently in the UK, the government announced that civil service internships will be reserved for students from “lower socio-economic backgrounds” – defined as what jobs their parents did when they were 14.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, if you come from a working class family, you get the civil service internship.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But they often fail to work as intended.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have to tilt the balance continually and keep opportunities open at every stage of life.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will invest more in the early years.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Because as several Members have highlighted in this debate, opportunity gaps are opening up earlier – due to the advantage that better off parents confer on their children.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And if we do not close these gaps quickly, they will only widen.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will expand KidStart and enhance ComLink+ – so that more families get help earlier, and more children gain a stronger footing in life.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will deepen support for children from disadvantaged backgrounds.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But attendance is less regular among the children from lower-income families.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will redouble our efforts and work closely with parents, preschool operators and social service agencies to ensure these children get the consistent support they need to thrive.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will not only do more, but we will also take actions across agencies with a more integrated family-centric approach – which several Members also spoke about.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In schools, we will continue to press ahead with reforms.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have changed how the PSLE is graded.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is no longer graded on a curve, as Members know.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is about your own achievement, not about how well you did relative to your peers.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They take subjects at different levels, according to their abilities.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But I know for many parents, education still feels like an arms race.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We all know of friends who are taking leave from work to help their children prepare for their PSLE.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: When you speak to each parent, they often tell you the same thing: they wish they could cut back on the endless tuition and give their children more space to grow up and play.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Because deep down, they worry: what if my child loses out?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I feel strongly about this as a result of my own personal experience.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: My friends and I in school did not grow up with family advantages or a head-start in life.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It gave us opportunities that we would not otherwise have had, the courage to dream and the chance to pursue our aspirations.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I want every parent and every child to feel the same – that education is not a burden, but a springboard.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: A place where our children can learn, grow, discover their strengths and reach for better opportunities.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But education reforms alone are not enough to accomplish the transformation we seek.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Because if employers still cling to narrow academic criteria to judge ability, then the arms race will simply shift from schools to workplaces.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Parents will continue to feel that grades are the only ticket to success.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I remember when we had the “Our Singapore Conversation” some years back, someone told us: “I am glad you are trying to make every school a good school, but you cannot succeed unless every job is a good job”.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We must change how we hire and promote.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is not at all an easy task, but we have already started.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It means recognising that people have different gifts and strengths.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Some may excel in mathematics but not in languages, or vice versa.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Others may struggle in written exams, but thrive in practical problem-solving.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If we only use general academic results to sort out talent, we will undervalue many capable Singaporeans.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will miss out the many other competencies and intelligences that exist amongst us and that are just as important.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Academic results are no longer the be-all and end-all.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They are just one part of the overall assessment.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In some roles, we have stopped looking at grades altogether.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, GovTech engineers are recruited through coding and problem-solving tests and interviews – because what matters is not your paper qualifications, but whether you can do the work.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Once you enter the Public Service, how well you do does not depend on your grades or school.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It depends on your qualities, your contributions and your performance on the job.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: One CEO shared with me: he used to insist on top academic credentials, focusing on school, universities, ticking all the right boxes.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But he soon realised that academic credentials did not predict subsequent success in the company.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: What was more important was the individual’s attitude and mindset – their ability to learn, adapt, and work with others.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So these changes are happening, but clearly there is still a long way for us to go.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Nevertheless, step by step we will move more towards skills-based hiring and progression, because what matters most is not where you started from, but what you can do and how far you are willing to go.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Valuing every job also means narrowing the gaps in how different professions are recognised and rewarded.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This too is not easy, but we have been working on this for some time, and we too, have been making progress.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will continue to professionalise other skilled trades, including those that are considered “blue-collar” work.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Together with the Labour Movement, industry, and Institutes of Higher Learning, we will create more structured career and learning pathways so that tradespeople and essential workers can advance, grow their skills and be recognised for their contributions.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Pay matters, but ultimately this is not just about pay.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is also about mindset, a whole-of-society mindset.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Much depends on how society as a whole views the different pathways that people choose.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In the past, parents resisted when their children wanted to pursue careers in fields like sports and culinary arts.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Many young people would take a more conventional path first to please their parents, then only chased their passion later.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I know of many friends who did that.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Today, more parents embrace such choices, because society now celebrates our athletes, our chefs, and our artists.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We take pride when their achievements put Singapore on the world map.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Yet we all know that there remain vocations where pay is not the main issue.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Rather, it is societal recognition and respect that continue to lag behind.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Step which we have been making already over the years, but we must continue to move more in this direction.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: A broader and more inclusive meritocracy that encourages excellence in every field, that values a diversity of abilities and talents, that accords dignity and respect to all forms of work, and to the people who carry them out.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is how we keep social mobility alive, so every Singaporean can rise on the strength of their contributions and will be respected.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The shift towards more pathways to success must be underpinned by a strong and dynamic economy.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: To be clear, economic growth is not about chasing GDP.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is about uplifting lives and creating a wide range of good jobs and opportunities for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will redouble our efforts to keep our economy competitive and vibrant.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For the last 60 years, multi-national enterprises have been a key driver of our economy.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They remain critical anchors in sectors like electronics, pharmaceutical and finance.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have to keep attracting new investments from leading global companies, so that Singapore can stay plugged into the frontiers of innovation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At the same time, we must work harder to energise our enterprise eco-system.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We want to make Singapore a more attractive place for startups and emerging companies, be it here or overseas.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These can be home-grown firms looking to venture abroad, or overseas growth companies seeking a base in Asia.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These are the companies that will shape our future success.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And to do this well, we will need a different approach.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: When they do, there will inevitably be calls for the Government to step in – I am sure from both sides of the House – from the Workers' Party (WP) and the PAP asking the Government to do more.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And perhaps from time to time, we will.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But if we try too hard to shield every company, we risk ending up with more "zombie firms" – propped up artificially, stifling renewal and enterprise dynamism.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And that is not the path we want to take.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we must be prepared for more churn.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And we should not only celebrate success stories but also learn to embrace failures and setbacks.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Because it is only through constant experimentation that more innovative companies can emerge.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But it is necessary to create new value, and ultimately to create new and better jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, let me be clear: our focus must always be on the worker, not the job.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But every worker matters, every citizen matters; and no one will be left behind.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In this fast-changing world with greater churn, we also need to offer Singaporeans sufficient assurances so they can deal with the disruptions with a greater sense of confidence and security.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And that means making sure that their essential needs are taken care of – quality education, healthcare and housing, for example, must remain accessible and affordable.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Housing was one of the biggest concerns in the last term.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Because COVID-19 disrupted construction and the supply of new homes.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But since then, we have ramped up supply.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Today, there is a healthy pipeline of new BTO flats as well as land for new private properties.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At the same time, we must update our system to reflect demographic changes, especially increased lifespans.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I spoke about healthcare at the National Day Rally.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And we will have lots to do in this area through Healthier SG, Age Well SG, and Age Well Neighbourhoods.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are studying what further moves we can make.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In particular, we want to help Singaporeans save more during their working lives, so that they have enough to meet their basic retirement needs for life, for a longer life.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And for those who despite their best efforts cannot build up a sufficient nest egg, we will provide additional support so that every Singaporean can retire with dignity.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will also continue to strengthen our safety nets for those who need more help.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For children with special needs, we will provide more support in their education and help make their transition to adulthood and work smoother.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For people with disabilities, we will give them more opportunities to pursue their aspirations and lead fulfilling lives.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It has just started, but we will make this a far better scheme than the unemployment insurance found elsewhere.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: All of these measures are helping to bring down income inequality in Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Previously, the Gini was measured only on income from work.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Department of Statistics has since updated the measure to include income from all other sources, like rental and investments.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We had expected this but what matters more is the trend.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And we are determined to keep it that way.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have ways to mitigate wealth inequality in Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, taken together, our measures are helping to narrow both income and wealth inequality and we will press on, and continue to innovate in our social policies.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, that at every stage of life, Singaporeans feel assured, supported and confident about the future.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So that opportunities and progress will always be fairly shared across our society.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As we work towards a fairer society, we must also accept a basic truth: not every journey will reach the same destination.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Even if we succeed in levelling the starting point for everyone, some skills and talents will always be more in demand than others.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And that is why those who do better must never forget this: no one succeeds alone.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Opportunities do not come from individual effort alone.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They come from the broader system – from the teachers who nurtured you, the workers who keep our city running, and the safe and stable environment that society as a whole provides.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, every successful and fortunate person in Singapore owes a debt to the community.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Those who are more successful should therefore contribute more, not just in taxes, but also in compassion and care.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Because no taxation system, however progressive, can legislate the spirit of solidarity.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That must come from within each of us, it must come from the heart and it must be nurtured by a culture that puts "we" before "me".

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is why I spoke about a "we first" society.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is one that strives for the collective good, not just self-interest; it is one that values solidarity even as we recognise our individual differences.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: To be clear "we first" doesn’t mean surpressing the "me".

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It means the "me" can only thrive when the "we" is strong.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we need to embrace our individuality and help everyone be the best possible versions of themselves.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At the same time, we have to look out for one another and lift each other up.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Only then can we be greater than the sum of our parts.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This "“we first" spirit of solidarity is not new.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is how our forefathers of different origins, languages and religions came together to forge One Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And over the decades, through painstaking and patient effort, we have built up this social capital.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And today the bonds among Singaporeans are stronger than ever.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That more than half said that most of their friends were from the same socio-economic group or race as them.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We worry about these trends: because if we know less of one another, if we have less in common, then we risk seeing each other not as fellow citizens, but as competitors, as people from different tribes.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And competition can easily turn into envy, resentment and division.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we must work harder to create more spaces and opportunities to mix and interact – be it at school, in the workplace, or in our neighbourhoods.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It will take the concerted effort of everyone, generation after generation, to make sure that our diversity adds and does not subtract.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Sometimes we overdo it, and the efforts become contrived.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The older Members of this House will remember when People's Assocation (PA) started the Community Games back in 2012, it required teams to include members of different races.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That was the rule to take part in a community game.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But some groups signed up "phantom players" just to meet the quota.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The intent was good, but the outcome fell short.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And it is easy to look back and laugh at what happened then.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But we all know that fostering more of such interactions is very hard to do and at the same time, it cannot be left to chance.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Since then, we have learnt better how to do this.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Today, PA organises more sports and activities that more naturally bring residents together, regardless of age, race, or background.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have merged Residents’ and Neighbourhood Committees into Residents’ Networks, so that people from public housing and private property can interact more freely.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And as a Government, we will continue to work hard to build up our social capital, to bind communities together, to connect us each to each, regardless of race, language or religion – and I might add also, regardless of socio-economic background.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At the same time the whole society must make an effort.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Singaporeans need to step out of our comfort zone, learn from more other cultures and interact with people from different backgrounds.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But over time, they help to strengthen our social fabric.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Because trust grows from these everyday encounters – eating together, celebrating one another’s festivals, or simply knowing your neighbour.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There is no doubt that our shared Singaporean identity has grown stronger these last 60 years.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In his speech, the Leader of the Opposition Mr Pritam Singh said that being a member of a racial and religious group and our identity as Singaporeans are both "equally important".

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Indeed, we all have multiple identities and we celebrate these.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But we should be clear-eyed about our present realities.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is why race and religion, if exploited, can easily arouse passions and tear apart the very fabric of our society.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We see this happening in so many other countries and Singapore is not immune to these powerful forces.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In one instance, they attacked the credibility of certain candidates because these candidates allegedly failed to advocate the rights of a particular religious community.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In another instance, they praised a candidate for arguing against the separation of religion and politics.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At home, we also had Singaporeans who exhorted certain groups to vote along racial and religious lines.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They said, "Vote for this candidate because he or she is a better representative of your race or religion".

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Or they compared candidates and said, "Vote for this person because he or she has been a more vocal champion for your race or religion".

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Thankfully, many Singaporeans rejected the calls to vote along racial and religious lines.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They voted for the candidate that they felt was best for Singapore, regardless of race or religion.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Had the election outcomes rewarded those who had pushed people to vote for racial and religious reasons, it would have caused a serious fissure in Singapore society.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Other racial and religious groups would have mobilised to protect their own interests in the future elections.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This would have jeopardised the harmonious, multi-racial and multi-religious society that took us 60 years to build.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is the reason why Singapore became Independent.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our unity and the trust we have in one another also depends on how we conduct our politics.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The way we debate, disagree and decide as a country.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is what constructive politics in Singapore is about.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our society is maturing and our politics will evolve, too.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And so, I welcome the opposition presence in Parliament.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In this GE, Singaporeans have chosen to send both PAP and WP Members of Parliament (MPs) here, and both sides have a duty to serve Singaporeans faithfully.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For the PAP, we do not assume we are automatically entitled to govern, just because we have done so since self-government.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our right to lead must be earned, by working hard and delivering results that improve the lives of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Doing well in one election does not guarantee success in the next.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Every election is a new test and we must take nothing for granted.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In this term of government, I fully expect WP to keep us on our toes – raising questions, scrutinising our policies and holding us accountable.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is their role as the opposition, and I am sure they will play it vigorously.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The WP will try to build up its ranks and grow its presence in Parliament over time, as any political party would.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: One day, it will want to take over from the PAP as the ruling party, even if it may not say so openly now.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But in the end, be it the PAP, WP or any other political party, we are all servants of the people.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They will decide which parties deserve their trust, both in Government and in opposition.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If any party falls short of the public's high expectation and standards, there will surely be consequences.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Privilege given today can easily be taken tomorrow.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, let us all conduct our politics with seriousness, with integrity and with a deep sense of responsibility for the longer-term interests of our nation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And that is how I hope our politics will evolve and our democracy can strengthen over time.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Besides welcoming diverse views in Parliament, the Government will do more to engage and involve Singaporeans outside of this House.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As I said in the National Day Rally last month, we do not just want to do things for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We also want to do things with Singaporeans.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, I invite all Singaporeans to join us, to connect, collaborate and shape our future together.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We already have many channels for public consultations.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will open up new opportunities for Singaporeans to have deeper conversations and engagements.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: To shape the character of our neighbourhoods and estates, for example.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In particular, we want to involve our young people.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They have energy, ideas and a strong sense of purpose.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we will give them more platforms to step forward, contribute and make their voices count.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, to all young Singaporeans, I say, "We will not let you down.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are building Singapore for you and with you."   And you, too, have a part to play.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Work with us to secure a brighter future for yourself and your fellow citizens.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is something you create, and we need you, our young Singaporeans, to be the authors of this next chapter; to write what must become your Singapore Story.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, be bold in chasing your dreams, seize the opportunities before you.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There will be setbacks along the way, but you will never face them alone.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Embrace the failures as well as the successes.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For it is often at the edge of our comfort zones that we learn, grow and become the best versions of ourselves.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Most important of all, remember this: success is not just about what we achieve alone, but what we build together.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: True fulfilment comes from creating a society where every Singaporean can stand tall and we all move forward as one people.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is what has defined us for the last 60 years, a Singapore Spirit rooted in trust, solidarity and resilience.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And it is this same spirit that will carry us into the future.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I hope every Singaporean can get behind this shared endeavour.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Together, let us build a Singapore that remains a land of endless possibilities.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: A home where every generation does better than the one before and a nation that continues to shine brightly for the next 60 years and for the generations beyond.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: I stand here for the first time because of the people of Sembawang and the generations who came before me, including my own parents, who worked hard so I could have the chance to carry the hopes and dreams of many Singaporeans, especially parents and grandparents, who are quietly wondering, "How will my children cope with the challenges and complexities of tomorrow?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Can they have a better life than ours?" These questions matter because Singapore has never had natural resources to fall back on.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: And what we have achieved in the last 60 years is nothing short of remarkable.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: And more importantly, our people are known not just for being smart, but for being honest, hardworking and resilient.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: It came from sacrifice, from seniors and parents who gave up their dreams so their children could have one.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: This is the Story of Singapore, where we know that we need to invest in our people, where we know that human capital is our only competitive advantage and where we know this is the only way towards a brighter future.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Today, our children are growing up in a very different world.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: In my conversations with parents on the ground, I have heard real concerns, "My child is doing okay in school, but is that enough?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: How do I raise them to be strong, kind and happy?" As a young father myself, I feel these worries too.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: That is why as a youth volunteer, I had focused my community work on supporting the young – from launching Healthy Plate programmes with a local social service agency, to guiding a group of youth leaders to launching an anti-vape campaign.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Because every child matters and we all have a part to play.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Even as we worry, we must remember: our young people are also full of hope.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: They dream not just of stable jobs, but also of meaningful lives.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: They talk about AI, sustainability, creativity, not just because these terms sound cool, but because they truly want to make a difference and do something meaningful with their lives.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: I saw this passion come alive when I met a group of young entrepreneurs.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Yilina and Jay, both business students, are two of the co-founders of Fossa Chocolate.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Matthew, a lawyer by training, and Trevor, an accountant, are the owner and manager of All Would Envy.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: These youths were not confined by their degrees but set out to pursue their passion and built something of their own.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: When their businesses do well, they will go on to inspire their children and future generations.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Proving that in Singapore, if we believe, we can achieve.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: They are building blocks of trust between the state and our people.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Raising a child and helping our youths to maximise their potential is still a community effort.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: As a grassroots adviser, I continue to have a soft spot for youth-related topics.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: In my engagements with our youths, I hear anxieties and insecurities from our students in higher learning and fresh graduates about their job prospects and career options.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: So, my Parliamentary colleague, Ms Poh Li San and I are leading a new community initiative to address this issue.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Together with the advisers in Sembawang GRC and Sembawang West single member constituency (SMC), we have pulled together our own networks of companies to organise company visits and fireside chats with executives.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: I am excited to work with you to secure our future for our nation, for our people and for our future generations.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: In my term as a Member of this House, I will work together with you to support the young and to build not just a place, but a home where our people and local businesses can sustainably grow and thrive.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: These are real areas where we can do better and I intend to raise them here.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: As we celebrate SG60, let us remember, it was not just deliberate planning or a stroke of good luck that brought us here.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: And like in a garden, if we want strong trees in the future, we must care for the young shoots today.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: That means giving our young the right mix of guidance, trust and room to grow.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In his address, Mr President highlighted fundamental shifts in the tides, leading to a far less predictable world.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Just in the last month, we have seen protests in Indonesia, UK, USA and leadership upheavals in countries from Japan, Thailand to Nepal and France.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Leaders raced to uphold promises, undo the work of their predecessors and bring forth change within a political term, often, an impossible task.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The global and economic order is in transition and people are clamouring to be heard.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Compounding this are ongoing conflicts felt not just as remote death tolls beyond our shores but real atrocities which citizen reporters, humanitarian workers and everyday residents stream online.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we travel to work and feed our children at night, these dominate our feeds and we feel the suffering from half a world ago, a stereo split screen like watching two worlds exist at once.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While real-time information promotes compassion, it also magnifies anxiety in our hyperconnected world and there is dissonance within so difficult to reconcile.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: All these, amidst the slow yet inevitable backdrop of climate change, no longer a distant march but here in the form of hottest years on record, flash floods, droughts, rising sea levels.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Extreme weather destabilises food sources and supply chains, causing scarcity and rising costs.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our youth faces anxieties about the future they will inherit.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Working adults feel sandwiched as they shoulder pressures at work and at home.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Every child is precious in an ageing society and they are the future of our nation.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But they carry a heavy load in the face of turbulent around us and this can manifest in mental health conditions, bullying and self-harm.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With increased digital exposure, our children are subjected to the mercy of algorithms designed to sustain their attention, often with sensational or emotional posts.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What our children see today may not be the same tomorrow.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Social media also forces our children to grow up too fast.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Primary school children dance to mildly risque dance moves ala K-Pop Demon Hunters, chasing likes before they have the maturity to process their own actions.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Coupled with deepfakes and false content, this results in a disorientation of body image and a disjoint in their perception between what is portrayed online and the real world.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Despite their willingness to take action, some feel wary to create change as an individual, questioning the impact which they can make as one person in the face of bigger nations and corporations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This Government is taking serious steps to fortify our food supply chains, tackle rising sea levels and develop innovative cooling systems towards heat resilience.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Climate change is a wicked problem of the generation.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is important to deepen their knowledge as part of school curriculum and involve them as co-creators to climate solutions and a voice at the table.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, I was very grateful to hear the Prime Minister's speech earlier.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Building accurate understanding and active participation will help move helplessness to agency and foster a shared mission, like Captain Planet.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With a volatile economy and reports of company layoffs, many working adults feel greater stress that is coupled with cost-of-living worries.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For some, the need to earn and provide, pretend that everything is okay, results in them pushing past the point of burnout, requiring more intensive and longer treatments.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some are concerned about gaps in their curriculum vitae and stigma by employers, leading to potential unemployment should they take that much-needed step to seek treatment.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To be self-aware and recognise one's need to rest is courage.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Worries about the cost of treatments remain a key barrier.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Under the National Mental Health and Well-being Strategy, the "Parenting for Wellness" toolbox for parents was released.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How can we work with parents to understand and put this into practice in a bite-sized and practical way, like how I consult Instagram Reels at night to find out whether I have gentle-parented my son hard enough, or could I actually have fed what I fed him at 10 months old.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can workshops be made more accessible in our neighbourhoods to improve mental health literacy and equip parents to have hard conversations with their children?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We often speak about youths transitioning to the workforce, facing uncertainty, but less is spoken about older adults, who stop work and are confronted with a loss of identity, companions or health, becoming empty nesters or taking on a caregiving role to a spouse.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Sometimes, these stressors compound, resulting in harmful or suicidal thoughts among older adults.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One of the most difficult parts of being our people's representatives is sitting in wakes or on the living room floor the morning after or waiting for the ambulance next to a cold canvas in the immediate aftermath.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our seniors have given so much of themselves to see Singapore become what she is today.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Seniors do not have the same vocabulary to search symptoms online like our youth.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to think about local neighbourhoods as a community of first responders and equip primary care as a critical touchpoint for prevention, as these conditions first materialise as somatic concerns, such as pains or insomnia sometime.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond the good work of the Silver Generation Office, Active Ageing Centres and the community centres, can we leverage technology and have automated messages regularly reminding seniors of health and well-being support, similar to messages which new parents, such as myself, receive when our babies hurt certain months in age.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A text or push notification could remind them that they are not alone.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: An elderly who would often come to my meet-the-people sessions week after week with a different challenge, once stopped short and said, "I just want someone to know that I am still alive." More often than not, out of good intentions, we tend to share with our seniors, "It is dangerous, you should not do that, be careful." This deficit approach diminishes their confidence.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we reshape the ageing narrative, I hope we take a strengths-based approach to emphasise to our seniors what they can do.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Where the person in recovery was a breadwinner, a carer may step in to take on additional financial responsibility as well as a new role, ensuring medical adherence.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A person in recovery and carer's story is one of strength.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At present, the qualifying criteria is based on someone permanently requiring some assistance with at least three of the six activities of daily living.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such support, particularly for caregivers facing health or ageing challenges of their own would be much appreciated. :   Sir, more than 40% of residents in Ang Mo Kio GRC are aged 60 and above.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our seniors possess invaluable experience and the nation's collective memory, having lived through pandemics and global crises.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I deeply appreciate our seniors for often sharing their advice while their encouragement lifts my spirits.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many seniors have shared with me that they feel the pressures of change, such as declining health and retirement, which disrupt their daily routines.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Additionally, they experience the loss of old friends and family members who, as they grow older, begin to live farther apart.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The resilience they have built over the years has taught them to endure challenges, so feelings of distress are often kept hidden in silence.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some uncles have shared with me their desire to remain active.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, their spirits wane when they are beset by chronic illnesses that require ongoing attention.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Sometimes, fading memory or hearing problems can also lead them to withdraw from others.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am truly inspired, especially with grandmothers who can still work part-time, diligently cook and care for their grandchildren.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For our seniors, I hope it will be easier for them to access mental health care so that it does not feel strange to them and we can mitigate their apprehension towards health screenings.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Seniors must feel that seeing a doctor is akin to working with a personal coach who can improve their quality of life.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As a community, we must go beyond traditional approaches and collaborate with various agencies to reach out to seniors.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Places of worship like the Al-Mutaqqin Mosque have started efforts to engage elderly congregants through sharing on health topics and estate planning.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These sessions are delivered in practical and sensitive ways by weaving together these topics with religious guidance.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For seniors and those who care for them, even as the seasons of life change, this season can be just as beautiful.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Let us bring that same spirit to improve mental health.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have had the joy of serving in youth work for 25 years.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For much of that time, I thought I understood our young friends.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The gap of understanding has widened and I do not like it.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Their world is far more complex, shaped by pressures and influences my generation never had to face.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I do not have children of my own, though I have many godchildren who I love very much, including some entrusted to me in their parents’ wills, which means, if anything happens to their parents, the children come to me.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Their young lives remind me constantly of the responsibility we share for the next generation.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The fight for the health of our youths is not for the fainthearted.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singapore’s Total Defence prepares us for attacks by air, land, sea, cyber and even threats to our social cohesion.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Yet, one dangerous enemy is often overlooked – the battle for our youths’ minds and hearts.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If we fail to recognise this war, we cannot win it.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Today, I will speak on five fronts that demand our urgent attention.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I also appreciate the balanced approach that allows those who step forward to seek help to do so without fear of punishment.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: At the same time, some youth workers have shared that uncertainty remains on whether they will be penalised if they step forward post-1 September, especially for probationers who cannot risk being marked for another offence.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If those guiding our youths have questions, it will naturally be more difficult for our youths themselves to come forward with confidence.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While swift enforcement is both necessary and commendable, we must also engage stakeholders working with youths, so that implementation is smooth and effective.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If our intent is restorative, which I believe it is, then our public communications must clearly reflect this.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have also heard of secondary school students who were involved in selling vapes to classmates before 1 September.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can the Government clarify whether those who voluntarily surrender stock, not just the users, would also be supported if they step forward?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In July this year, I was notified that a primary school boy in Dover was approached by an older youth to buy vapes, a shock to parents.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Before the ban, TikTok videos of youths vaping to music and dance went viral.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It was normalised online, which partly explains its explosion in popularity.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our Internet-savvy youths also find overseas articles and even AI chat responses, portraying vaping as a “safer” alternative to cigarettes.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On social media, it is marketed as stylish and modern, while Singapore’s ban can seem, to them, as odd as our chewing gum prohibition.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
