text: In the words of a 16-year-old, "Social media’s voice is way louder than the school’s.” Meanwhile, predators continue to adapt.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the UK, youths are already moving from vapes to nicotine pouches and snus.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Alarmingly, some websites even advertise direct delivery to Singapore, in open defiance of our laws.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I had raised a PQ this past Monday.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As guardians of our young, we must stay one step ready and ahead of this battle.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If we punish behaviours but ignore distress, we fail our children.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: That is why the battle against vaping cannot be separated from the broader fight for mental health, which I will return to later in my speech.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Bullying in schools, both physical and online, compounds the stresses our youths already face.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some victims may not even recognise they are being bullied, blaming themselves as "not enough".

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is worth noting from the National Institute of Education's survey that many students confide first in parents or friends, rather than teachers.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is not a reflection of our teachers' commitment.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They work tirelessly and often go beyond the classroom to support our students.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Rather, it shows that prevention cannot rest on teachers alone.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Parents and peers must also be equipped, so they know how to respond and whether the student is the bully or the victim.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Several youths have shared that they hold back from reporting bullying, not because they do not care, but because they fear being labelled a "snitch" or a "busybody".

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A larger mindset shift is needed amongst students themselves, to see speaking up not as a betrayal, but as courage for standing for what is right.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, can students report incidents safely and anonymously?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Third, are definitions of bullying versus mischief clear and when must cases be escalated to parents or MOE?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization's (UNESCO's) review shows that the most successful countries do not stop at passing clear laws prohibiting all forms of harm.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They pair those laws with comprehensive interventions: age-appropriate equipping of students; training for every adult in the school environment – teachers, cleaners and canteen staff; strong support systems for victims and active engagement with parents.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It mobilises pro-social classmates to stand with victims and empowers bystanders to intervene.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Closer to home, upper primary students have shared that hearing peers talk about resolved bullying cases is especially powerful.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It shows that they are not alone, that help is possible and that change can happen.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Given the dynamics of school bullying, peer involvement is not optional.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singapore should review our anti-bullying programmes to glean lessons from such models and adopt a more holistic approach.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One that not only addresses bullies but supports victims and reshapes school culture to protect and defend every child.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Social media today is not just a distraction, it has become a powerful force – shaping identity, relationships and the mental and physical well-being of our young.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It influences how they see themselves and how they connect with others, and how they measure their own worth.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Where a child once found refuge at home, bullying now follows them into their bedrooms through their phones.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: France now recommends a ban on social media under 15, and other EU countries are exploring similar steps.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Could the Government update us on its study of Australia's approach?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A teen once told CNA that social media feels like "drugs under the disguise of harmless entertainment".

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If vapes harm physically, unregulated social media harms mentally and emotionally.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Anonymous comments and unrealistic portrayals of life shape how our youths see themselves and others.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Social psychology shows that even witnessing online bullying can cause guilt, anxiety, fear and difficulty in forming a healthy sense of self.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our children live with this daily, even when they are not the direct targets.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In this digital world, families remain the first line of defence.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Conversations, clear limits and healthier alternatives matter, even amid work pressures.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A child told his parents, "I wish I was your phone," reflecting the longing for their time and attention.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It speaks volumes about the need for adults to model well and lead at home.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In Portland, a mother who refused to give her 10-year-old a smartphone revived a household landline.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Children greeted parents before calling friends, memorised numbers and listened attentively instead of scrolling while talking.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It reminded me of my growing-up years, when picking up the phone meant looking forward to an engaging conversation where you can see the smiles and the frowns of the person across the line, and the pause as a friend thought to respond before they spoke.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A 14-year-old girl shared her gratitude for her mom who restricted her use of social media, having witnessed the constant comparison that left many of her peers anxious.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Youths turn to social media for connection, entertainment or relief from school and life pressures.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: That is why our approach to responsible use cannot be separated from supporting their mental health.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Ironically, many youths turn to, as medicine, social media, often deepens the very struggle they try to escape.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Just as Healthier SG takes a preventive approach to physical health, we need a national programme that prepares youths for the mental and emotional impact of digital life, in ways that resonate with them.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When asked about school programmes on responsible social media, a 16-year-old replied, "What your friends say is more effective than what the school says." We must change how we engage.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Australia's Mental Health First Aid often described as "CPR for Emotional Emergencies".

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It equips ordinary people, including youths, to recognise distress and offer immediate support until professional help is available.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singapore could adapt such an approach and enhance peer support.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This requires robust age verification, strict time limits and phone-free zones among other measures we must explore.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Policy may not change the human heart, but it can draw firm boundaries, reinforce social norms and give parents the authority to say, "not yet".

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I first met this autistic boy when he was 16 and I was in my 20s, which is about 100 years ago.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Over the past 25 years, I have been very blessed by this friendship.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: He has taught me what kindness is, what compassion looks like and what it means to have a childlike faith that never grows jaded.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Through him, I learnt to see persons with disabilities with new eyes.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My hope is that you, too, will have the privilege to get to know persons with disabilities, not the "hi-and-bye" kind of knowing, but the kind where you share meals, walk alongside them and do life together.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many retreat online in search of connection, only to encounter comparison, stress, addiction and deeper insecurity.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This leaves them carrying a double stigma: disability and mental health.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Often, depression in youths with disabilities is dismissed as part of the disability.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Autistic youths, for example, may have genuine mental health conditions wrongly attributed solely to autism.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This constant strain directly affects their ward's well-being, deepening the mental health challenges they face.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I was especially encouraged at this year's 60th National Day Parade, witnessing how intentional the entire parade was, including persons with disabilities and with the sign language thoughtfully woven throughout the programme.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This marks the true progress of a nation, one that leaves no one behind.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I see them caring for their families, honouring parents, loving siblings and convinced that family is worth fighting for.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I see young people brave enough to stand up for their friends and rooted in healthy relationships.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I see youths who embrace education as a privilege, ending each day with purpose.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I see young people celebrating the success of others and enjoying wholesome fun in music, sports and nature, without coarse joking or degrading remarks.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I see them whole in school, home and community, skilled and committed to lifelong learning.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I see them recognising that they are part of Singapore's future, thriving in their talents, bold and creative in attempting new things.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I see our young friends resilient and brave in uncertainty, building ideas, products and services that help our communities flourish.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Above all, I see youths who know that blessing the less fortunate is a privilege, and who treat resources and knowledge as a trust, to be used generously in the service of others.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Let us act wisely and decisively, for our youths to lead our Singapore into a stronger future.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Over the last 25 years, ground-up, every house visit, kopitiam conversation and community walkabout has reinforced my belief that Singapore is special because of the resilience and trust of our people.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When I first declined the invitation to enter politics in 1996, I had just become the managing director of an investment firm.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I did not know where my heart truly was.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I counselled those retrenched at a fast food outlet for weeks and to boost morale, I helped the most important person in my firm – our tea lady – secure a new job, which she kept until her retirement.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This painful experience brought me back to the ground.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In 1999, I began volunteering in Aljunied GRC to help those in need, even when I disagreed with some policies.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When a strong PAP team was forsaken in 2011, I stepped forward.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By then, after walking the ground for years, I knew where my heart truly was. 路遥知马力，日久见人心, or "As distance tests a horse's strength, time reveals a person's heart".

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To work the ground, I quit my CEO-level job in 2012.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Later, when I tried to re-enter the workforce, I experienced what some Singaporean PMETs face – rejection, uncertainty and the pain of starting over.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Once, I remember interviewing candidates for a position.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Strangely, they all seemed to come from the same company.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I asked my staff to ensure they were kept separate and seemingly, they were pushed out, quietly displaced.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Together with my early years as a policy-maker in Government, these first-hand, ground experiences help me empathise and understand the real-world challenges faced by our people.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In Aljunied GRC, we worked hard, day-to-day between general elections, outside of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When offered the chance to contest elsewhere, I chose to stay and sent my team mate instead.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Having contested not once, but twice, facing the opposition’s leadership team, I feel like this is my third term.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Leader of the Opposition and his team know how hard we work the ground.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So much so, they coined the term “2-for-the-price-of-1”.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Vote the WP and get the PAP for free.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have had more than my fair share of Aljunied voters who appreciated our groundwork and want the PAP to form the Government, but sheepishly confessed they voted to check on the PAP.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But together, as the Chinese saying goes, 杀鸡取卵.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In other words, killing the goose that lays the golden eggs.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With greater political contestation, we must guard against populist ideas presented by those who do not have to be in the driver's seat.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we can see in many mature democracies, eventually the interests of the country and of its people will be overridden by self-preservation, division and instability.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Taken together, Singapore voters are rational and want an opposition voice.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But I ask Singaporeans to demand from the opposition the same high standards that they expect from the PAP.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also am grateful for the support of Aljunied GRC residents, our activists and volunteers over the years.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To our teams now serving in Aljunied and Sengkang GRCs and in Hougang SMC, I say, jiayou!

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some were still in school when I first met them at community centres or during house visits.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, many of them are young adults, newly married, setting up homes and even raising their toddlers.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: During my walkabouts, quite a few – showing photographs taken with me stored in their phones – tell me they now live in Buangkok-Fernvale South, the newly constituted ward within Ang Mo Kio GRC where I now serve.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It reminds me of our responsibility to ensure that Singapore continues to be a place where families can thrive and where every child can do better than the generation before.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Ultimately, the Singaporean brand of politics must be about making Singaporeans’ lives better.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As a small, resource-scarce, accidental nation, we arose out of adversity.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore is not the result of populist ideas, but of hard, long-term decisions built on trust between our people and our leaders.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, that trust remains the core of our social compact.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must lead with resolve and heart: honouring our seniors, upskilling our people, uplifting the vulnerable, supporting families and inspiring our youths.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With my late parents’ love-language of food and memories of my siblings squabbling over one fried egg, I want food in Singapore to unite and not divide. “Affordable food” means different things to different people.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Left undefined, it can distort the perceptions of the cost of living.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Like many Singaporeans, I am concerned about the rentals, hawker retirements and stall closures.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But we must avoid conflating these arguments and be clearer about the cooked food segments that we are talking about.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, we should ensure fair tenancy practices and discourage speculative investment behaviour.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: More than cost, we should look at revenue.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If we can increase the average length of stay of a tourist just by one day, the multiplier effects on our economy would be significant.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must support also traditional foods which will otherwise disappear in this new economic environment.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In my constituency, I had begun discussing a pilot heritage project to support our merchants and bring more vibrancy to our community with ad hoc work that will inspire our youths and engage our seniors, under my umbrella concept called Community Workfare.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That brings me to the next topic of unlocking our silver dividend.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many still want to contribute – not just in formal jobs, but in mentoring, caregiving and community life.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At a recent community event, I met Abdullah bin Ali, a retiree who teaches gardening at our Home Nursing Foundation Active Ageing Centre in Buangkok Crescent, not because he has to, but because, in his own words, “If I can stay active and share my knowledge, why not?” Or take Mdm Sandy Goh, who despite her own challenges, has rallied seniors to support food rescue programmes, first with me at Bedok Reservoir and Hougang, and now, in my new ward of Buangkok-Fernvale South.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This spirit of staying active, giving back and finding new meaning is the silver dividend we must unlock, where ageing is not a sunset, but a second spring.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To our youths, our education should move from answers to questions.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this AI-era, it is not the answers we give but the questions we must ask.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are our primary classrooms supporting how children's brains actually learn best?

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I recall in my primary school how we were repeatedly drilled for the PSLE.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One classmate was always slower to answer and often punished by being made to stand on his desk.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It was traumatic for him, and painful for us to witness.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: He did not do so well in the PSLE.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yet, in later life, he rose to become a respected editor of a major publication.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That experience reminds us that one exam does not define a child and one-size-fits-all teaching can sometimes wound more than it uplifts.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Brain-based pedagogy is rooted in respect for the learner, that each child’s brain learns through meaning, emotion and connection, not just by rote memory.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many parents will know the helpless feeling, like me, of being unable to solve a math problem alongside their primary school child.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Instead of pushing both parent and child to frustration, imagine a system where adaptive AI helps the child practice at his own pace, while the teacher steps in as a coach in confidence.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our challenge is not to teach more, but to teach differently, supported by adaptive AI tools and teacher-as-coach models.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must invest boldly in every child, because with fewer children, each one matters more.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Unlike the repeated refrain of calling for a smaller class size, we should be advocating how we cater to different learning styles and behaviours.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Class size, the teaching environment and pedagogy are the derivatives.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If we fail to make this shift, the risk is clear.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Affluent parents will move ahead with AI-driven personalised learning outside our school system, while the rest of our children remain in rote-based pathways.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With AI, do we want an education system that hardens inequality, or one that allows each child to learn with confidence?

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For the economic strategy, we should look at GNP instead of GDP.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How Singaporeans can benefit directly from growth, not just from home, but also abroad.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our economic strategy must not only attract activity to Singapore, but also build pathways for Singaporeans, especially our youths, to participate meaningfully in global value chains.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should encourage Singapore firms to internationalise and count their overseas income as part of our national strength.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Look at the region, look at the world with technology.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singaporeans, we are not confined to our own borders.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our companies, our professionals, our entrepreneurs, all should be increasingly international.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By placing more weight on GNP, we shift our focus from the size of the pie on our shores to the larger share that our people can enjoy beyond Singapore.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But as we look to the next 60 years, it is time we look for growth beyond our shores.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: From what is produced in Singapore to what Singaporeans earn globally.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That is the shift from GDP to GNP.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In closing, sir, to keep Singapore special, we must maintain strong trust between our people and our leaders.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And I say across the aisle, Singaporeans must demand the same high standards and accountability as they expect of us.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is not what we say, but what we do.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: More than what we achieve is what we inspire.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this House across both aisles, let us work together to build better lives and livelihoods for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: That unmistakable six-note rhythm, "a mechanical man and his heartbeat", evokes an unstoppable force.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Today, Singapore stands before such a force, the rise of the intelligent robotics.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: In early 2021, I spoke about machine learning, artificial intelligence and the importance of investing for our future growth.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: This was four years ago, two years before the introduction of ChatGPT.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Today, gen AI, Agentic and Predictive AI are prevalent and with some enthusiasm.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: The important question today is where is the return on invesment for AI?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: What are AI’s core revenue drivers and contributions to the economy and society?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Soon, the world will be moving on downstream to intelligent robotics.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: The evolution of the First and the Fifth Industrial Revolution shows the shift from steam-powered mechanisation to intelligent, people-focused industries.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: The First used steam for manufacturing, the Second introduced electricity and mass production, the Third brought computers and automation, the Fourth leveraged AI and smart technologies.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: The emerging Fifth Industrial Revolution integrates advanced technologies like AI, robotics, and Internet of Things in a collaborative human-machine environment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Going forward, intelligent robotics will define our future and our quality of life.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: This double-digit growth, led by manufacturing, healthcare and mobility, is transforming industries.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang predicts that up to a billion human-like robots could help power industries by 2035, collaborating with humans, not just replacing them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: The drivers are clear, ageing populations, shrinking workforces, escalating costs, intense global competition.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Worldwide, leaders are channeling resources like R&D, start-up ecosystems, and forward-thinking policies.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: For governments and businesses, the imperative is simple, invest in intelligent robotics or risk being left behind.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Amazon fields more than 750,000 robots in its warehouses.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Walmart has turned its fulfilment centres fully autonomous.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Tesla’s humanoid Optimus now works inside factories, Starship Technologies and Ocado deploy fleets of service robots, autonomous tractors are tending fields, and this very year, Beijing will open the world’s first humanoid robot dealership.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: How will these technologies impact our day-to-day life and shape the way that we live and work?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Today, Waymo provides 250,000 self-driving rides each week in the US.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Tesla’s pilot robotaxi is now live in Austin.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: And UBTech will soon be selling home-service humanoids for US$20,000.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Because technology costs have fallen off a cliff.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: It is a tipping point, suddenly, advanced robotics are not just possible, they are practical and affordable for every sector.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: For Singapore, intelligent robotics is a necessity and a strategic imperative, against external shocks, labour shortages and global headwinds.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: By adopting intelligent robotics, resource-constrained economies like ours are poised to capture the front wave of development.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: To seize this future, we must secure manufacturing and development capabilities that enable intelligent robotics, such as high-performance processors, sensors, data centers, advanced telecoms, batteries, powering the next generation of solutions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: While we are among the world’s most robotics-dense economies, we cannot afford to be complacent.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We cannot just be a procurer and an implementor of intelligent robotics, we must be at the centre of it.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Our answer must be bold, collective, or risk being left behind.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: With intelligent robotics, how will global and regional economies transform and position themselves?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: What will most likely happen to these economies?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: The most plausible socio-economic model, will have two distinct parts.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: The first part, domestically, one would see a country building a well-paced, progressive adoption of intelligent robotics, where collaboration between humans and robots, enable augmentation and amplification of capabilities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: This enhances quality of life and secures the individuals’ economic value.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: However, when there is an opportunity to reap the maximum economic benefit in pursuit of national interest, especially for trans-national trade and global economic value chain, outwardly, these economies will organise differently.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: It is only advantageous to develop an ultra high-performance intelligent machine economy that deploys autonomous, highly effective, efficient intelligent systems that can deliver high quality goods and services.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: With intelligent robotics, economies can solve, not a dilemma, not a tri-lemma but a quad-lemma of delivering value in terms of quality, cost, speed and creativity.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: This will become their sharp edge of global competitiveness.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: With the combination of these two parts of the model, it will enable a country to excel in inclusive growth and remain globally competitive.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: However, the reality sets in when economies compete on this sharp edge, which is amplified and multiplied by intelligent robotics, limited only by the access to clean and renewable energy, and access to raw materials, the most efficient and effective machine economy will eventually be able to out produce in terms of quality, cost, speed and creativity.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Smaller or less developed economies may experience challenges as their industries struggle to compete with larger-scale, more efficient, or lower cost autonomous production.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: This does not only affect smaller or less developed economies.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: History is replete with the disruption of new manufacturing technology.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We see the transition of the textile industry in the US in the early 2000s.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: The Swiss watch industry which exported 30 million units in Year 2000, but today only exports half the units.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Many more examples such as Solar, Steel, Wind turbines.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Today, we observe how Germany a global car manufacturing and export Juggernaut, ironically, has an increasing trade deficit in the automotive industry, which it used to dominate.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: The world will witness growing protectionism, trade disputes and even political backlash as countries struggle to defend strategic industries and societal interests against relentless machine-driven competition.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: How do we ensure that Singapore and Singaporeans are not left behind?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We must stay ahead of the development curve and pursue it with conviction.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: To secure the future in the machine economy with intelligent robotics, Singapore must act.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: From the days of coolies at Boat Quay to fully automated container operations at Tuas Port, handling over 40 million containers in 2024.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Autonomous vehicles, AI-driven cranes and digital intelligence let us punch above our weight, setting new global standards and future-proofing logistics jobs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: At Changi, intelligent robotics will redefine traveller experiences, security, baggage and aircraft turnaround, making Terminal 5 the benchmark for global aviation efficiency.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Those of my generation will remember Prima Deli, a popular cake shop founded in 1992.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: It is still very popular today and is better known for its aroma of its freshly made waffles.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: It grew from a home-grown bakery to a franchise and now a factory that is constantly improving business automation and introducing intelligent robotics.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: The ability to tweak the recipes, maybe more dark chocolate but less sugar.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: This company is ready to scale and expand its operations domestically and regionally, bringing more jobs and opportunities for all.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Prima Deli has the growth mindset, and it is all about growing the cake and sharing it.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: And We will build closely with our SMEs and our workers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: The road ahead will be fraught with challenges and disruptions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: There will be major shifts and displacement of routine and repetitive jobs, the creation of new roles and the reconfiguration of labor market toward higher-skilled and intelligent robotics.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Workers will need to build entirely new skill sets, combining practical expertise with digital proficiency and adaptability.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We will be together on this journey like we have for the last 60 years.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Just like how Tony Stark in Iron Man was hammering away, together, the first Iron Man suit in a cave with nothing but scraps, Ironman's journey has always symbolised resilience, adaptability and imagination.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: As new threats emerged, so did the need to reinvent.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: He created the Mark V "suitcase" armor, a portable suit designed for rapid deployment, and later, the Mark L nanotech suit, which could materialise weapons and tools on demand, adapting to dynamic threats in real-time.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: At every step, Iron Man did not retreat from complexity, but upgraded in response to it.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: The turning point came when he embedded J.A.R.V.I.S., an intelligent AI co-pilot, into his suits.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: No longer just metal and wires, the suits became an extension of both man and machine, working in seamless collaboration to solve problems faster, smarter and with greater precision.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: This spirit mirrors Singapore's own path from survival in scarcity to building a nation that reinvents itself at every junction, always with the future in mind.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Every one of us knows a family sitting around their dining table, talking about the future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: They see the headlines about global instability, about AI changing the world, and they worry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: They ask the quiet questions we all ask.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: In a world of such turmoil, is my family's future secure?

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: In an age of disruption, is there still a place for me?

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: These are not abstract questions, Mr Deputy Speaker.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: And the reason for that answer is the very anchor of my speech today.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: It is our nation's secret weapon – our unique ability to pull together when the world is pulling apart.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Tripartism, our model of unity, is more than just tradition, it is our answer to the future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: At its core, tripartism is founded on a shared conviction to strive for industrial peace with justice.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: In the early days, our founding leaders stood at a crossroads.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: The world told them that for a union to be effective, it must be adversarial, locked in a perpetual struggle with employers and the government.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: It must at least be seen to be independent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: They saw other nations crippled by this very conflict, caught in a zero-sum game of strikes and standoffs, where for one side to win, the other had to lose.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: In such a game, they knew a small nation like ours could never win.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Mr Lee Kuan Yew said in 1969 that "the unions of Singapore are not here to fight against management.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: They are here to work with management, to ensure that we survive, grow, and prosper together." Tripartism is not a zero-sum game.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: We believe in being partners of progress, not partisans in conflict.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: This philosophy of fair play and gain-sharing remains our compass – pro-worker, pro-business and pro-future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: This partnership is built on more than just economic pragmatism.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: It is built on a shared moral conviction.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: This speaks to the very soul of our Labour Movement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: It is a promise we keep towards our lower-wage workers, from our cleaners to our security officers, like what labour MP Melvin Yong had said too.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: For years, these workers had worked hard but saw their wages stagnate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: They have been trained to be more productive and could take on better jobs – a team supervisor, for example.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: The PWM did not just give them a bigger paycheck, it gave them a new sense of pride, a new set of skills and a new answer to their worries about the future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: We build pathways to it, one worker at a time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: The success of this model hinges on mutual trust and respect fostered through consistent engagement and a shared commitment to national interests.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Our reservoir of trust was not built in times of ease.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: It was forged in the crucible of crisis.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: From the 1985 recession, when unions accepted wage cuts that were later restored, to the 2008 Global Financial Crisis, with its "cut costs to save jobs" philosophy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: During COVID-19, our tripartite partners showed they were willing to make difficult decisions for the greater good.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: This spirit of "we first" is the bedrock that allows us to face today's challenges with unity and confidence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Mr Goh Chok Tong once said, "We can never take tripartism for granted.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: It is a precious asset that has taken years of trust-building." This reservoir of trust is what enables us to face new challenges today – global instability, trade wars and the transformative impact of AI.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: In a turbulent world, Singapore's stability and predictability are rare advantages.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Our unionists are at the core of this effort.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: When they walk into those tough negotiations, they do not just bring charts and figures.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: They bring the stories of our people with them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: They are the ones who can look a CEO in the eye and say, "Let me tell you about the family that is struggling to keep up with their bills." They bring the reality of the coffeeshop into the conference room.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: They mobilise the ground in support of national strategies, thereby increasing our chances of success.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: In difficult conversations like the annual National Wages Council negotiations, our union leaders keep us honest by reflecting workers' anxieties about the cost of living, and by advocating for fair gains-sharing and just transitions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: This insider role allows unionists to shape policy for the better, not just criticise from the sidelines.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Every time a unionist helps a retrenched worker find a new job, they are not just finding a salary, they are restoring a person's dignity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Every time they ensure fair gains-sharing, they are strengthening our social fabric.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: They are the guardians of fairness, the champions of opportunity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: They are the ones on the ground, every single day, building the "we first" society the President spoke about, one worker at a time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: This reflects what Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong once said, "Our unions are not afraid to speak up for workers, but they do so in a constructive spirit, with the long-term interest of workers and the nation at heart." We have seen this in practice.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For Singapore, our people and the ethos of unity and progress for all, regardless of race, language or religion is the cornerstone of the success of our improbable nation these last 60 years.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Our leaders have been intentional in forging our unity while celebrating our diversity through integrated housing policy, education, meritocratic governance, shared values and long-term stewardship.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But Singapore's unity and identity is not static.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is changing, shaped in what is happening in our everyday life in Singapore and globally.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So while vital, forging our unity today is no longer just around integrating and celebrating our diversity of race, language or religion.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Our society is more diverse and younger Singaporeans are voicing new hopes for fairness, autonomy and purpose.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Differences in access can result in who gets access to services, whose voice travels, and what "truths" feel credible.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Hence, people may end up living in different realities even when they are under the same space.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Personalised feeds cluster people into like-minded bubbles, reinforcing beliefs and isolating them from shared facts, where information we consume fragments our shared realities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: They shape how we see ourselves, how we relate to one another across age, income, race, religion, cultures and education.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Some feel secured and heard, others feel left out, or unsure where they fit in.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If we do not respond to these lived realities, unity becomes fragile not because we disagree, but because we stop feeling part of.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This means rethinking the roles we each play.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Government, employers, individuals and building a culture of shared responsibility.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It means designing policies that reflect real lives, not just averages.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Designing for lived experience and not just aggregated outcomes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And it means ensuring that opportunity is not just promised but felt.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We must design systems that are truly inclusive.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Housing, education, work, digital platforms, they must work for everyone across life stages and backgrounds.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We need to support transitions, whether it is a mid-life career shift, a young person finding their voice, a first-time home owner getting a flat or an older adult staying connected.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is not sufficient just to take feedback.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We need platforms where people can speak honestly, listen deeply and shape the future together.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Trust grows when people see that their stories matter and that their feedback leads to change.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What began as a simple idea to activate the under-utilised space under the Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) viaduct to promote residents' well-being has blossomed into a vibrant festival.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: From booths and programmes run by residents, seniors and youths, students and teachers from our schools and tertiary institutions, hospital and healthcare professionals, kopi chat with the Police and movie under the stars, VIASTA! has become a celebration of shared ownership and provides a space that comes alive to benefit the well-being of our residents in Changi Simei.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Although the process required several months to collect residents' feedback and collaboratively utilising AI to visualise the desired VIASTA!, it enabled meaningful participation from both residents and stakeholders.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: They could see their ideas come to life.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Given the volatility as well as the fragmented and fast-moving world we face, we need to continue to have such platforms and I am very heartened to hear Prime Minister Lawrence Wong talk about this deeper engagement, deeper engagement with Singaporeans to be able to co-create policies together.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Some may actually say, "That is too hard, it takes too long." But I think that it is worth the effort and we have seen the policies from Forward Singapore, ideas and feedback from Singaporeans coming to life in our policies already today and I encourage every Singaporean, especially our young, but every Singaporean to really make the effort to come forward and be involved.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Unity in Singapore has never been about sameness.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And that purpose must evolve as we do, grounded in empathy, trust and courage to change together.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If we want growth, we do need to have a strong economy to attract talent and investments.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the current uncertainties and structural shifts that are affecting Singapore, we must support the efforts that Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong has shared about refreshing Singapore's economic blueprint and keeping Singapore's economy strong and resilient by enhancing Singapore's value as a base for leading firms, a key global business hub and a vital connector to the global economy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The strength of our economy lies not in discrete moments of growth, but in sustainable progress.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will then lead to opportunities for businesses and the creation of jobs that are relevant to the new world order.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But more importantly, strong sustainable growth will create quality and meaningful jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is about giving every Singaporean that chance to thrive, to contribute and to shape the future we share.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Technological disruption is accelerating workforce transitions, creating both opportunities and anxieties, affecting opportunities for our young and matured workers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This brings me to the point on what do we do to ensure that businesses contribute to developing an empowered workforce that is ready to seize the opportunities and create jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Supporting companies to create rich career pathways within their organisations, and I repeat this, within the organisation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As they transform, it is important to help retain and stretch our talent, to help them grow and allow them to thrive with these changes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But as we look ahead, we need to take one step back and ask ourselves if we can take a larger view of the whole system and not just specific segments, such as our young graduates, mid-career or matured workers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Is there a better way to achieve our desire of an empowered and future-ready workforce?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How can we bring our learning systems to support our people to be work ready?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I have spoken many times in this House that Singapore must grow and have opportunities to give Singaporeans fulfilling jobs and I believe having meaningful work gives Singaporeans confidence not just to make a living which is very important but also to feel included and to have a sense of purpose, belonging and commitment to the community and to the nation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We must ensure that every Singaporean, regardless of age or background, or where we start, can aspire to seize these opportunities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: That means investing in skills, supporting career transitions, designing workplaces that are inclusive and progressive.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It means refreshing our economic blueprint to stay nimble in a complex world – so that growth uplifts and not divides.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, how can we wholistically rethink our learning systems in an age of rapid change, and disruptions?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Our learning system today is front-loaded and segmented.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Internships help to mitigate with opportunities for industry exposure.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It offers not just skills, but purpose – through real-world experience, mentorship and meaningful contribution.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To unlock its full potential, employers must step up earlier, much earlier in designing pathways with schools, offering industry exposure before graduation and guiding young talent from the start.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This early engagement strengthens the bridge between learning and work, aspiration and opportunity.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Strategically, apprenticeships embed adaptability, deepen knowledge transfer, and foster lifelong learning.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: They have the potential to renew industries, empower individuals, and help Singapore stay agile in a fast-changing world.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: When we build stronger bonds and access to opportunities, we deepen the sense that this country is worth investing in – not only for ourselves, but for one another; a Singapore that we are proud to call home.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Fellow Members, thank you for hearing me out.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I would try to make this worth your while.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I furiously cut out some two paragraphs worth of content but the substantive points remain.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Today, I would like to speak on a hidden social issue in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: It is an issue that many find uncomfortable to speak about but increasingly lurks in the shadows for some: addiction.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: It can affect a person of any age, class, background.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Addictions destroy relationships, break up families, consume lives and we are battling addictions of different forms.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: There are those who are addicted to gadgets and smartphones – gaming, excessive use of social media, doom-scrolling – and others like binge-eating, gambling and alcoholism complete the gamut of addictions afflicting modern life today.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: What I would like to focus on today, however, is the serious and emergent threat or trend of sexually compulsive behaviours, one that is often facilitated by technology.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I look at this through the lenses of two broad archetypes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: First, the invisible, and perhaps more insidious non-offending compulsive behaviour like addiction to pornography.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Such addictions silently chip away at an individual’s productivity and positive relations in his or her life.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: And second, offending behaviours such as voyeurism, upskirt videos, acts which cause significant harm to victims and carry serious legal consequences.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I visited the We Care Community Services recently.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The statistics are worrying, to say the least and two questions come to mind.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: First, are we providing sufficient avenues and options for treatment and early intervention?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Second, what preventive measures can we take before such addictions take root in our society?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: To be sure, Singapore has in place an ecosystem of support for those battling different addictions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The National Addictions Management Service at IMH, the Singapore Anti-Narcotics Association and the National Council on Problem Gambling are familiar go-tos.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: There are also ground-up efforts: We Care Community Services which I have earlier referenced and One Hope Centre, which helps addicts recover from gambling, sex and pornography addiction; and there are also private clinics that provide support for addiction treatment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: First, it does not help that addiction is traditionally viewed as a moral failing or a lack of willpower on the part of the addict.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Due to stigma, addicts would hide their struggles and avoid seeking help, for fear of being judged or for bringing shame to their families.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Often, by the time help is sought, the addict is in crisis as the addiction would have by then already spun out of control.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The staggering level of stigma associated with such deeply personal challenges would also mean that it is extremely difficult to size up just how pervasive this issue is in our community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: For every addict that comes forward to seek help, just how many remain in the shadows?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: But given prevalent societal norms and attitudes, the hyperconnected lives that we lead and the ease of access to explicit materials online, it would only be fair to assume that what we are seeing in reported statistics is but only the tip of a large and deep iceberg.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: There is good scientific evidence that addiction is not as much a personal failing as it is a chronic, progressive and relapse-prone illness that affects an individual both physically and psychologically.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: It is an illness for which there should exist a structured medical treatment plan.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We Care runs a Non-Contact Sexual Offending therapy programme, combining individual counselling with group work to support individuals struggling with compulsive sexual behaviours.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The programme helps participants understand the causes and consequence of their behaviours, address underlying psychological factors, and develop healthier coping skills to break the cycle and prevent re-offending.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Client testimonials and outcomes from this programme show that a structured program is key to helping an addict recover and re-build.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: So, can we as a society accept that addictions of this nature is an illness needing proper treatment?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: And across our healthcare landscape, can an addict receive adequate and affordable treatment from diagnosis to full recovery in a structured manner?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Like other chronic medical conditions, prevention is always better than cure.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: But any course of action begins with the admission, “Yes, we do have a problem.” Steps can be taken to arrest the problems before they even start.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We Care shared that many clients learnt about sex from online sources including pornography at a young age.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Such early experiences shaped undesirable sexual scripts that emphasise availability, instant gratification, objectification.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: As an Asian society where conversations on topics such as the birds and the bees are generally still avoided at home, we are at risk of delegating parenting responsibilities to peer groups, or worse, shady Internet sources.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Addiction expert Gabor Mate theorised, and I quote, “how a lack of healthy adult guidance and unresolved childhood trauma and frustration can lead youths to seek out peer groups for their moral compass, a poor substitute for natural parental guidance.” But I will be one of the first to admit.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: As a dad to a five-year-old boy, I often ask myself, how or where do I even begin?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Our homes must be safe harbours where our young ones feel comfortable enough to talk about anything under the sun.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Families must be the default go-to as our young ones take on adulting and life’s many other challenges.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Parents must meaningfully engage in our children’s lives, debunk myths purported by wayward sources such as pornography, and be their role models, as our young ones seek out the true north when calibrating their impressionable moral compasses.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Like many Members in this Chamber, I run a tight schedule day-to-day.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: What little leisure that remains come in the form of post-midnight Netflix binge watching.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I recently clicked on a title that appeared on my "recommended" list, Adolescence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The series initiated me to the world of incel, manosphere, red pills.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I watched all four riveting episodes in a single sitting.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Quickly realised I made a subpar choice for leisure and relaxation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: But what an educational and eye-opening tour-de-force Adolescence was in framing and illuminating some gripping challenges that youth of this generation faces.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: So, for several sleepless nights after Adolescence, I thought long and hard about how I might broach these issues with my son in a few years to come.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I took heart in practical parenting tips I had received some time ago, which I thought offered good lessons.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Where and when might I talk about sensitive topics with my little one?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The reply was “Consider a long drive!” That way, the setting is relaxed, father and son need not meet eye to eye.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: And when things get too awkward, turn up the stereo; and a few tracks of K-Pop Demon Hunters should help smooth things over.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: It can affect people of any age, social class and background.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Today, I want to focus on “sexually compulsive behaviours” brought about by technology.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Whether it is non-criminal behaviour, such as browsing pornographic websites and becoming addicted as a result; or criminal behaviour, such as voyeurism or upskirt filming, the statistics paint a worrying picture.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Addiction is generally viewed as a moral failing or lack of willpower on the part of the addict.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Feeling shamed, many addicts try to hide their struggles and avoid seeking help.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: They fear being judged or bringing disgrace to their families.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Usually, by the time they actually seek help, addicts are already deeply trapped and their addiction is beyond control.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Regarding this issue, how should Singapore adopt better preventive measures in our communities?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: And how should we help our families mould themselves into a safe haven?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
