text: We have only one ultimate goal: to let the younger generation feel the warmth and love of home, to let them deeply understand that when they encounter problems like addiction or other sensitive issues in life's marathon, their families will never discriminate against them or judge them. : Mr Speaker, Sir, let us do better.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Let us confront the issue of addiction openly.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Let us not shy away from uncomfortable conversations but normalise safe, constructive dialogue, especially with our children.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law, and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Let us work together to strengthen our support ecosystem so individuals suffering in silence feel safe to emerge from the shadows to seek help.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Eric Chua, like you, I also saw Adolescence, very impactful and meaningful movie.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I think, like you, I saw it all at one go.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I rise to support the Motion of Thanks to the President.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In Mandarin): Today, I wish to borrow an old saying from Chinese history to reflect on Singapore's future: "In the land of Shu, there were no great generals, so Liao Hua had to serve as the vanguard." This saying is not just a historical reference – it serves as a stark warning for us today.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This phrase comes from the period of the Three Kingdoms.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In its later years, the Kingdom of Shu faced a severe shortage of talent.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Zhuge Liang had passed away, and Jiang Wei was struggling to hold things together.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Eventually, with limited military strength, Shu had to appoint Liao Hua – an ageing and less capable officer – as its vanguard.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Later generations lamented: when a nation or team lacks capable people, it will have no one to turn to at critical moments.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Although the original saying carries a tone of irony and helplessness, we should treat it today as a wake-up call.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If a country fails to continually nurture talent and establish a robust leadership succession system, it risks being unprepared when crisis strikes.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The current state of the world is deeply concerning – recurring political violence in the United States, severely testing its democratic system; continuous disputes between left and right wings in Europe; frequent changes in leadership in Japan and South Korea, leading to a lack of policy continuity and stability; major electoral recalls and social divisions in Taiwan, severely damaging trust between the government and the people; ongoing political disputes following elections in several Southeast Asian countries; endless conflicts in the Middle East and the Russo-Ukrainian war, with peace nowhere in sight.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Amid global turmoil, Singapore's institutions, culture and mutual trust have forged this hard-won stability.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is our advantage and also our responsibility.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The President emphasised the importance of unity in his address, a point that I believe is crucial.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The political atmosphere is like the air we breathe; fresh air goes unnoticed and unappreciated, but once it lacks harmony and becomes polluted, everyone feels suffocated.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The concept of "harmony" or "hé", as advocated by Confucius, signifies a genuine, principled harmony, and not soulless, superficial conformity.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This "hé" refers to harmonious and dedicated efforts towards the common, supreme goal of national development and the people's welfare.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We must maintain a high degree of consensus on this major objective.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is the foundation upon which we can pool our strengths and accomplish great things.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is the "harmony of the gentleman", a unity stemming from shared ideals and beliefs.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The greatest challenge the world faces today is not economic or military – it is the crisis of social cohesion.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Individualism and a "me first" mindset are eroding the foundations of many societies.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To build a “we first” society, politically, all parties must prioritise the national interest, transcending partisan disputes.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In policy, people should not only ask, "What is in it for me?" but also, "Is this fair for our society?" In daily life, we must care for one another, leaving no one behind.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: MCCY should lead this effort, shifting community building from activity-based projects to building a relational ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We need not merely law-abiding citizens, but community members who actively contribute.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This requires redesigning national education to emphasise that citizens are not only rights-bearers, but also responsibility-takers; developing a grassroots community service framework so that volunteerism becomes a part of life, not just an occasional activity; and creating multicultural competency programmes to equip Singaporeans with the skills to thrive in a diverse society.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Here, I must place special emphasis on the crucial role of the younger generation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The hope and impetus for building a "we first" society lie with our youth.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They are not just future successors; they are a vital force in shaping the social fabric of the present.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Young people are intellectually active, full of ideals, and possess a natural affinity for fairness, justice and sustainable development.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We must create greater space for them, closely integrating their energy and creativity with our shared vision for the future.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We must substantively incorporate their ideas into policy considerations.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When formulating long-term plans, the voices of young people must be heard and their suggestions should have the opportunity to be translated into concrete actions.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: MCCY should support young people in independently launching projects that solve community problems, enabling their transition from being passive recipients of policy to active co-creators.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This hands-on experience in building is the most effective way to foster a sense of ownership and belonging to the nation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A "we first" society requires understanding and continuity between generations.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We should encourage the formation of mentorship groups, pairing youth with experienced seniors to jointly plan community projects.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The combined experience and wisdom of the older generation with the drive and fresh perspectives of the young can create powerful synergies, ensuring both societal stability and vitality.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Develop community archives and digital platforms, allowing every community to preserve and share its history, and enabling youth to become a new force in recording and disseminating these stories.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Create arts and cultural programmes that explore the evolving meaning of being Singaporean, encouraging young artists to interpret and enrich our shared identity from contemporary perspectives.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These efforts, particularly through activating the proactive participation of our youth, will help us build a society that shares not just a common geographical space, but a profound sense of shared destiny.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We must return to the saying with which I began: "In the land of Shu, there were no great generals." It reminds us: to build a "we first" society, we must continuously nurture successors and encourage more young people to enter public service.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We cannot rely only on a small elite – we must build a strong pipeline of talent, ensuring that there are always capable people ready to serve.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It requires the participation and commitment of every Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Let us also cherish our hard-earned political stability and protect this valuable asset.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Let us work together to maintain Singapore's precious political environment, ensure our political atmosphere remains clean, and enable future generations to grow up in a more united and prosperous Singapore.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: (In Malay): It has been an honour for me to serve the Jurong Central constituents over the past five years, and to be given the opportunity to serve the Jurong Central community once again.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Over these five years, there are so many residents who I now consider friends.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: So, to my friends and all residents, I wish to say, the President's speech at the Opening of Parliament reminds us that there is still much more that the Government, together with our people, must do.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And in Singapore, the Government is deeply committed to working together, to do more, and to make life better.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Similarly, we want to provide the best opportunities for our children to develop and reach the peak of their God-given talents and potential.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: To support everyone in raising our children to be honest citizens and people of faith, to celebrate and cultivate our traditional languages and cultural arts, and to develop our society into one that is stronger, more united, more caring and more excellent.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: We will do all this within our meritocracy.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: It may never be perfect, but it remains a vital principle for social harmony and for achieving success as one people.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: For years, in fact, for decades, we have built and developed our meritocracy.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And we must continue to do so, to ensure that our meritocracy continues to work for everyone and makes life better for all our people.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Above all, I wish to remind everyone that in any meritocracy, at any time, there may be some who will be ahead, and some who may be behind.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Everyone must be on this "Escalator of Progress".

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Everyone moves forward together to ensure this meritocracy works.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: The President used the word "escalator" in his speech.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: As we continue to work on our meritocracy to make it work ever better for everyone, we must first put everyone on that same "Escalator of Progress", and we must ensure that this escalator is always moving towards progress.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: The Government must ensure this escalator is always moving towards progress, for everyone.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: It is crucial for us to ensure the success of this meritocracy, and it becomes the fundamental condition for improving our meritocracy.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: (In Mandarin): In 2011, my Parliamentary colleague, Ms Sim Ann, delivered a brilliant speech on Singapore's "haves and have-nots".

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: She used a more relaxed, colloquial approach to discuss, in depth, a very important issue: what strategic advantages and opportunities Singapore possesses, what conditions and trade-offs we lack, and how Singapore should forge a path forward from this position.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: At that time, I had not yet entered politics, she had just entered politics, and Singapore was 46 years old.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Today, on the occasion of Singapore's 60th anniversary, I want to revisit Singapore's "haves and have-nots" and discuss our nation's future path.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: What does Singapore have, and what does it not have?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Singapore's achievements today are all due to the foundation laid by the Pioneer and Merdeka generations.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Without the dedication, sacrifice and contributions of these people, there would be no glorious Singapore today.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: So we have an obligation to give back to them.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Families, communities and the Government must all work together to better care for and support our elderly, to enable them to shine brightly in their golden years.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: I have several suggestions, continue to expand and enhance our healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Ideally, our elderly would not need to see doctors or seek medical care, but when they do need medical care, the elderly must be able to receive timely service without waiting too long.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Therefore, we must continue to expand and enhance our healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: But we must also continue to manage healthcare costs well.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Of course, there is no such thing as a free lunch – healthcare costs ultimately needs to be paid by Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: If we want higher healthcare subsidies, the Government may inevitably have to collect higher taxes, so I hope the Government can continue to govern wisely and maintain the political courage and responsibility to do what must be done.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: The elderly should also have better retirement security.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Currently, when children do not live with the elderly, the elderly can receive many benefits, but when children live with the elderly, they cannot get as much.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Therefore, the entire eligibility criteria framework for Government benefits to the elderly could be more reasonable.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: What else does Singapore have and not have?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: In this era of endless technological innovation, where regional countries are rising and using technology to develop rapidly, standing still means being left behind.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: We have no natural resources, only people, manpower and talent, so everyone must continue to strive and fight. "Those who dare to fight will win." We must work very hard.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Of course, some people say Singapore is under too much pressure and moving too fast.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: I believe we must strive hard, whilst also creating space to take care of ourselves and our loved ones around us.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: We want harmony between the two, not “either/or”.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Pursue what you love, do what you are passionate about.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Our workforce is of high quality, and Singaporeans are capable, so if Singaporeans can have greater space to choose when, where and how to do their work well, we can certainly do good work whilst also achieving better harmony with life.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: I hope the Government can continue to promote flexible work arrangements and work more closely with employers, not only supporting employers in adjusting their operating models, but also helping employers change their mindset.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Furthermore, our entire workforce must better embrace technology, make good use of technology and integrate technology into every position in the economy.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: We have no time to slack off, no room to relax, we must fight, but we absolutely cannot rely on ourselves to fight blindly in the same place.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Instead, we must rely on technology to help us fight, to fight for us.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Let technology be by our side, become our most effective tools and weapons, and fight alongside us to achieve possibilities that, perhaps, even we ourselves cannot yet imagine.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: This is the potential brought by the integration of humans and technology, and it is also one of our nation's greatest opportunities in continued economic transformation.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Besides the pressure being too great and the pace being too fast, more and more Singaporeans are also saying: “it is not that I do not want to fight or work, but I cannot find work, cannot find employers who want to hire me.” Moreover, it is not just middle-aged workers facing this concern – perhaps more and more young graduates entering the workforce are also facing this concern.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Unemployment, career changes, repeated rejections – these challenges faced by our workers deeply affect their daily living, and even their dignity.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And in an era of rapid economic transformation and re-transformation, these challenges will become increasingly frequent.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: We must better empathise with workers and support them with greater effort and more comprehensive systems.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Besides learning how to do things from a young age, what our children need more is to learn how to behave properly from a young age.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: For our education system to successfully achieve this, besides continuing to reform the system, we must also reform everyone's mindset and definition of success.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: What else does Singapore have and not have?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: It also faces greater risks of social division and fragmentation.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: In an information age, truth and falsehood become increasingly difficult to tell.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Hence, in resisting foreign interference and in promoting mutual understanding and trust domestically, we must do better and go deeper.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: What else does Singapore have and not have?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Overall, Singapore has a rapidly ageing population, but also opportunities to better care for the elderly.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: In terms of economic development, Singapore has no time to slack off and no room to relax, but we have opportunities to integrate with technology, and opportunities to deeply reform our labour system and education system.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Singapore has an increasingly diverse society, but also stronger national identity, stronger social cohesion and resilience.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: For 60 years since independence, we have achievements, but we must also have gratitude and humility, and even more importantly, we must not be content with the status quo and must strive for excellence.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: We have challenges, but we should also have confidence.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: We have no reason to feel dejected or discouraged.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Different from the early days of independence, many of our current challenges have no other countries' experiences for reference, no other countries' precedents to rely on.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Many of our current challenges have no answer sheets.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: But we have a good Government with far-sighted vision and strategic planning.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: I firmly believe that as long as the Government, the people, and both ruling and opposition parties work together, there is no battle Singapore cannot win.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: We have strategy, resources, and even more importantly, determination, courage and capability.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: We will certainly be able to build on the past and open up the future, continue writing Singapore's nation-building miracle, and open a new chapter in Singapore's brilliant future!

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We know that each vote was a carefully considered decision and we do not hold that lightly.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We are committed to honouring your trust by working tirelessly to earn your votes again in the coming years.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This message was echoed by the Prime Minister yesterday, who pointed out how other societies have become increasingly stratified, with privilege becoming more entrenched.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If left unchecked, widening inequality can fracture our social compact and undermine the meritocratic system that has been the key to our nation's prosperity.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Meritocracy, in turn, relies on the public's confidence that it can deliver upward social mobility.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: A waning of that confidence could lead to distrust, both between different segments of society and with the Government, making it harder to forge the consensus required to navigate systemic challenges.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Inequality is, therefore, a fundamental faultline in our in our society.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Confronting inequality requires more than just giving everyone the same opportunities in school, as even when public goods are equally available, private advantages remain unequally distributed.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Wealth is frequently passed down from parents to children, not only through inheritances, but a combination of social, informational and financial capital from the time they were born until deep into their adulthood.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This provides children of privilege the best opportunities to thrive at every stage of their lives, and a strong safety net to catch them if they fall.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These translate into a significant and enduring head start in life.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They are subtle and unspoken, but they compound over time.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For a start, well-resource parents cultivate cultural capital by providing a wide range of enriching experiences to their children.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This includes frequent overseas travel and exposure to the arts, which build an understanding of cultural norms in influential circles, and provides a foundation for sophisticated conversations in social and professional settings.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Etiquette lessons and public speaking from a young age equip their children with the confidence highly-valued in the workplace and in leadership roles.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These parents have the resources to send their children for enrichment camps in areas, like artificial intelligence (AI), coding and robotics.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They know that these courses build competence from a young age in science, technology, engineering and maths (STEM), a skillset that generally commands higher salaries in future careers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This hands-on experience beyond what is taught in textbooks can spark interest and give an indirect boost to academic performance.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For parents with resources, hiring top coaches to provide individual training on technique and fitness gives their children a significant head start.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This allows them to become high-performance athletes before their peers, giving them a distinct advantage during school trials.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, if their child does not do well in enough in local exams, their parents have the option of sending them to private schools, locally and overseas.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This additional safety net ensures that a pathway to higher education is always available, a luxury that less-affluent families cannot afford.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As these young adults enter the workforce, their accumulated social capital continues to open doors.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some might lend prized internships at multinational corporations through their parents' professional networks, bypassing traditional hiring procedures.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Likewise, a parent might introduce their child to an influential business contact who can give them their first professional role or provide helpful career tips.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These relationships create an oft hidden job market, leading to opportunities that are not publicly advertised.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This safety net extends into significant housing and financial advantages.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For instance, some well-to-do parents buy property for their children when they are still young to hedge against rising prices, ensuring they would not have to struggle to afford their first home when they get married.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Others hand over their successful businesses to their children after they graduate, removing the need for them to compete with their peers in the in the job market.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To be clear, the actions of these parents are perfectly legal.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They are simply doing their best to help their children in a very competitive economy, but this creates a growing chasm between those with and without these advantages.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This divide will only widen as economic competition intensifies and the nature of entry-level jobs shift to AI, which demands new skills that are more accessible to the privileged.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Our challenge, then, is to bridge this gap, not by suppressing the privileged, but by levelling up everyone else.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To do this, we must bolster our public institutions until they rival the private sphere, ensuring every child has the opportunity to achieve their maximal potential.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I have a few suggestions in this respect.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The SkillsFuture Credit scheme has empowered adults to upskill, but the race for skills and opportunities begins much earlier in life.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This credit could be used for approved enrichment courses in areas, like coding, public speaking, sports and the arts.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: By democratising access to the same hard and soft skills that are often the privilege of the affluent, we can ensure every child has a fair chance to build their confidence and competence from a young age.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I have noted Minister of State Jasmine Lau's earlier response today to Mr David Hoe, who made a similar proposal in his Parliamentary Question (PQ).

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I am glad we are on the same wavelength here.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I acknowledge that schools have many in-school and out-of-school extracurricular opportunities for students, including those from low-income families.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: What I am asking for is a separate credit that gives parents and children the agency to choose enrichment programmes that are not available in their schools.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In today's economy, we cannot precisely predict the skills that will be in demand, or the specific passions and interests that will ignite in our young people.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, by giving parents and children the autonomy and agency to choose enrichment courses, we are empowering them to explore a diverse range of opportunities and build skills in emerging areas, just as well-resourced families can.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This SG Culture Pass, which provides credits for citizens to attend arts and heritage events, is a commendable initiative.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, I am concerned that its take-up rate may be low among households from the lower-income brackets.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Democratising the global exposure that is a key component of cultural capital.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Singapore International Foundation (SIF) would be a natural partner to manage this fund, as its mission already aligns with connecting Singaporeans with global communities.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Through SIF, donations for the fund could be sought from philanthropic foundations, corporate sponsors and individuals who have benefited from such international exposure.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To match up the college preparation provided to higher-income students, education and career guidance services in schools could be enhanced and personalised.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These services could offer comprehensive support to guide students from less-privileged backgrounds through the complex application process for local and foreign universities.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Critically, this service would make them aware of the importance of building up a competitive portfolio early and will help them strategically utilise financial support programmes designed to help them do so.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: At the same time, our local universities should continue to monitor their admissions process to ensure that donations do not impact how students are admitted, a problem which has occurred in other countries.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Existing professional mentorship schemes could be expanded to the National Career Mentorship programme for all young Singaporean professionals, tradespersons and workers seeking career guidance and professional networks.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Crucially, this programme must conduct proactive and targeted outreach to individuals from less-privileged backgrounds who may lack the social and informational capital to access these opportunities.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To attract and retain committed mentors, the programme could offer public recognition and award continuing professional development hours.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These incentives will not only reward their time but also formalise their commitment to guiding young people from all backgrounds, thus helping them to build a more equitable professional landscape.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The programme's recent shift to a one-to-one co-matching ratio presents a financial barrier for first-time entrepreneurs who lack personal savings or family wealth.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This would make crucial seed funding more accessible, ensuring that promising ideas are judged on their merit alone without a founder's financial means becoming an obstacle.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The proposals I have outlined today are not designed to penalise success, but to strengthen our meritocratic system, ensuring that every citizen, regardless of their family's background, has a fair shot at success.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: By giving every Singaporean access to the exclusive advantages that provide a head start in life, we can create a powerful equalising force, offering a clear pathway to upward mobility and a robust safety net for all.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It is their aspirations, struggles and daily lives that form the very foundation of my presence here today, and I believe everyone here today here in this room.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: And I am also grateful to the residents of Jurong East and Bukit Batok GRC for allowing me to represent them in the 15th Parliament.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Allow me to begin by first saying that I am a product of my experiences, from growing up in a dysfunctional family, having gone through the Normal (Technical) stream, fulfilling my dream of becoming an educator, founder to a few social empowerment programmes and today, a husband and a father of two beloved children.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Today, I am very fortunate to be able to represent Clementi residents and people from all walks of life and these experiences will surely influence what I will say, do inside and outside of this House.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But for now, let me to share a few thoughts on being "we first" society.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Underlying the idea of a "we first" society, it is no one gets left behind.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I have some thoughts on what it means to build an inclusive society, which I will continue to develop as I go along in my term and as I grow into my role as a Member of Parliament (MP).

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Most of us have heard this countless number of times, that we should all have our own definition of success.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: And this personal definition matters, because they guide our aspirations in life.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But while having this definition of success is important, today, I want to spotlight on how can ensure that we have the sufficient building blocks to help Singaporeans to not only define but also to realise their own definition of success.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Specifically, I will look into three groups – our young, our families and our seniors.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Exposure to such classes and lessons are important because they help our children to explore their interests beyond a typical school setting.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: From these interests, with time and practice, they grow into strengths and from these strengths, they grow into definition of success.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But these activities are out of reach to children whose families cannot even afford such lessons.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It is to help children to be able to recognise their strengths and interests and perhaps, ignite a spark that could guide them in their lifelong journey.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Think of this similar to SkillsFuture, but SkillsFuture for our young.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Just as SkillsFuture encourages adults to upskill and pursue lifelong learning, curiosity credits would give our children a structured but flexible way to explore, experiment and build confidence in their formative years.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Curiosity credits should and must be means-tested, so that families who need the most support can draw on these credits, because curiosity credits can help close a starting gap in life, by giving children that come from less advantaged background a means to access opportunities that they otherwise cannot have access to.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: To be clear, we already have a wide range of policies and programmes to support our young, but what I am proposing is we can do more.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: A Child Development Account in our early years helps to defray preschool and healthcare expenses.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But it does not allow that very child to explore enrichment classes that are beyond the preschool setting.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Likewise, you cannot tap on your Edusave account to pay for a dance lesson at our Community Centre, or even a robotics class at a private provider.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Curiosity credits can bridge opportunity gaps early, ensuring that every child, regardless of their background, has the foundation to shape his/her own definition of success.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But while curiosity credits can help children discover their passions, this alone is not enough in shaping the outlook of success.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: By moving beyond a single examination as the necessary condition, which is PSLE, we can redefine success more broadly as a society and allow children with different strengths to thrive.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As MOE itself has said in April 2025 in an online primer, they said, I quote: "The future of Singapore’s education system is not just about choosing to keep or eliminate PSLE." I agree. "It is about how we can customise learning pathways to meet diverse abilities, needs, interests and aspirations of future generations.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It is about how we can embrace learning beyond schools and books and help students discover the joy of learning to lay the foundations for self-motivated, lifelong learning." It is in this spirit, broadening entry pathways is not about removing rigour, but it is about right-siting students in environments where they can flourish.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We already see glimpses of this through the DSA, but this remains supplementary to the PSLE rather than a truly parallel route.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I urge MOE to continue to pilot or consider piloting new models.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This could take the form of a through-train programme from primary to secondary school, which we heard before, or alternative entry requirements instead of a single high stake at accumulative examinations that have substantial impact on our child's future.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The truth is, even as I say all these, as a former educator, I know the logistical challenges are real.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But I also know that if we want to embrace a child-centred model of education, we should and we must find ways to make it work.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Examinations and pathways are just one part of the education system.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Because even with the best opportunities, a child cannot pursue his/her own aspirations if their learning environment is not conducive, and bullying has been a pressing concern.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But on this note we should review our existing frameworks on discipline and consequences for bullying.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Current measures today range from warning, counselling and suspension to more serious sanctions.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: These have their place, but we must ask a fundamental question: how effective are they in changing behaviour and preventing repeated harmful acts?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Take suspension, for example, which I mentioned two days ago.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Previously, suspension was painful, painful because you would not have the ability to interact with your friends because you are not in school, and even if you wanted to head out to play basketball in the daytime, there is no one to play with you.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: However, I also said this that if you have access to a mobile phone, because this is what a parent told me, during your suspension, I mentioned you can play Mobile Legend, but you also play Roblox, and suspension is seen as nothing more than just a holiday.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Without a structured approach, the time away from school does not build accountability.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In fact, it risks trivialising the harm caused.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If a child returns without genuine reflection or remorse, the underlying behaviours may continue and the victim remains unprotected.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: So, we must find ways to make disciplinary actions more purposeful.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This could mean compelling bullies to remain in school premises, in a separate room, even if they are suspended from class.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In their suspension, they are to experience a guided reflection session where they have to confront the impact of their actions, reflect why that was not acceptable and arrive at a resolution.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Creating a safe environment for our children goes beyond tackling bullying.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: An equally pressing threat that I want to address today is the access to drugs and youth vaping.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I recognise that tackling both issues require a multi-pronged approach.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: However, I want to highlight, based on what I have heard from different Singaporeans, a key gap in our current reporting mechanisms.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: What this effectively means is that if you are under 15 years old, you cannot make an online report.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Many of these children and students who may witness vaping in schools or even around their town neighbourhoods, are 14 years old and below.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: With the response by Minister Ong Ye Kung, I am heartened to know that our young are able to call at the Tobacco Regulation Branch to report.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But can I also say this: we must understand our target audience.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Today, many youths are less or not comfortable picking up that phone to call and file a report.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But ask them to fill up a form, or anything online?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Also, the hotline operates from 9.00 am to 9.00 pm.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This is why I hope the task force can consider making youth-appropriate channels to make reporting easier.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: On Telegram channel, where you can purchase drugs in Singapore, he asked me, "David, how can I report?" So, David does not know.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: What David did was – I was not sure, so I called the Central Narcotics Bureau (CNB).

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: And follow me; I was told to go to the CNB website, scroll all the way down to e-services, click on feedback and enquiries, and file a report there.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: How is drug reporting the same as general feedback or general enquiries?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: At the end of the day, if we want our children and youths to be able to continue to grow up in a Singapore that is drug-free, then reporting must be accessible and intuitive, beyond just vape or drugs reporting.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Even if you take my recommendation, I wonder whether we can just have a one-stop shop for reporting because today, there are just so many platforms that you can always report things – one service, one form, another form.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: From children, I will move on next to our families.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Every parent wants their child to be born healthy and be healthy.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But let me also say that not every parent will always be so fortunate.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In other words, one in every 10 births is premature in our restructured hospitals.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Many of these preterm babies spend weeks, sometimes months, in hospital.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This translates to significant out-of-pocket costs for parents, even when our subsidies kick in.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We should consider how to help these parents better.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Truth is, parents of preterm babies will likely exhaust their leave before the child even comes home.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: And I know this first-hand because my son was born preterm.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: And yes, this is why I am asking if we could do more for parents of preterm babies because they reached out to me via Instagram after I posted about it before the General Election (GE).

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: One of the ways is whether we can better support them through stronger workplace arrangements at such sudden and overwhelming moments.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Now, supporting parents at the earliest days of a child's life is critical, but you and I know the responsibility does not stop there.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: From ensuring care in their first few fragile months of their life, we must also ensure that our children have healthy opportunities to play, stay active, develop holistically and not being glued to their phones.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This is why I turn, now, to the importance of making sports and recreation more accessible.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: During my house visits, several parents of primary school-going children shared their concerns with me, that in our new Built-To-Order (BTO) estates, and even in my own BTO estate that I live in, we often have playgrounds but know of few sports facilities.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Some even noted that their homes were far away from the nearest basketball court and as a result, the easy option is to keep the child at home and let them use the phone.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Instead, for those who wish to book such sports facilities in schools, they have to pay out of their own pocket with a credit card or PayNow.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Small as this might seem, but these last-mile barriers matter, and I urge a review to ensure that access to sports is affordable, simple and holistic.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If it requires inter-Ministry coordination, then we must do better.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Allow me to move on to the third group, which is seniors, who I have grown to love, about how we can help seniors to thrive in the digital world today.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Hoe, you have a minute and a half left.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: While Clementi is home to many young families, a large part of this community is made out of seniors.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: At a recent community event, I encourage our seniors to embrace technology at their own pace.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: That made me pause and I asked myself, who exactly is our target audience?

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: In fact, this is not just about anti-scam tools.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: It is about the overall direction of our digital Government services.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: ScamShield is just one example, but the principle is broader.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: In closing, for our children and youths to be able to define and realise their aspirations, for our parents to be able to raise their kids well, and for our seniors to be able to thrive in a changing world, this does not happen by chance.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: We need to build the building blocks to make them happen.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: It takes all of us in this House, whether you are a PAP white or a WP blue, whether you are an officeholder or a backbencher, to build and hold these blocks together.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: My hope is simple – that we may join hands, set aside our differences where we can, and focus on what unites us, the aspiration of our people and the Singapore we want to build for them.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I am honoured to have served in Sengkang as a volunteer since 2020 and now, as their elected representative.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I acknowledge the President's call in his address: "Singapore must also remain a home where the vulnerable amongst us are not only cared for with compassion but also empowered to pursue their hopes and dreams." These words remind us of our fundamental duty to ensure that every Singaporean has the opportunity to thrive.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: This year, Singapore celebrates our 60th year of independence.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: This milestone presents us with a crucial opportunity for reﬂection and stocktaking.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: It is a time to assess not only our achievements but also to honestly examine what we can do better.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Most importantly, it compels us to address the emerging cracks in our foundation that threaten to leave some of our fellow Singaporeans behind.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: While I will conﬁne my comments to these areas for now, I look forward to raising other important issues over the course of this term, in particular, the struggles of the sandwiched generation – young parents juggling work, childcare and rising costs of living.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: During Singapore's nation-building period in the 1960s, home ownership was prioritised as a tool for nation-building, allowing Singaporeans to have a stake in our country's development.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: However, we should be concerned that home ownership has become out of reach, especially for lower-income individuals and families who are unable to afford a place of their own.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Many such individuals and families live precariously, in fear of slipping into a situation where they are forced to sell their homes and resort to Government rental ﬂats.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: But in recent years, even securing Government rental ﬂats can be a challenge.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: While we recognise that the Housing and Development Board (HDB) has broadened their criteria for rental ﬂats and do not rely solely on income as the main yardstick, demand often outstrips supply.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Even successful applicants endure an average waiting period of ﬁve months.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Renting from the open market also poses its own challenges.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: As a result, such individuals and families ﬁnd themselves torn between increasing rental prices in the open market and long waiting times for public rental ﬂats, additional stressors on top of the absence of stable housing.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I acknowledge that the Government has continuously worked to improve housing access for Singaporeans, including recent pilot projects, such as Single Room Shared Facilities and Joint Singles Scheme Operator-Run.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: However, more needs to be done to address particular groups disproportionately affected by insufficient housing supply.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I will brieﬂy touch on two groups in my speech today.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: This means that every other single parent – usually young, stressed and limited in options – is denied by the public system, while at their most vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Second, individuals who are unable to stay with their family members.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: HDB has cited availability of housing from family members as grounds for rejecting public rental requests, with a lack of clarity on whether other factors are considered, such as the nature of the relationship with family, particularly where it may be strained or abusive.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: These should not be treated by our public housing system as personal insufficiency.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Instead, we must build a system that empowers individuals and families with equal opportunities for safety, stability and self-sufficiency through basic stable housing.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Increasing supply of rental ﬂats and reassessing barriers to entry will be key tasks I aim to speak up about in this term.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: My proposals include: first, exercising ﬂexibility by always taking applicants' current relationship dynamics with family into consideration before rejecting applications based on availability of housing options with family, and publicly commit to upholding this approach.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Second, expanding the public rental housing market to cater to changing aspirations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: This may include exploring ﬂexible and experimental models, such as introducing a universal buy-back scheme for ageing HDB ﬂats, which can then be rented to Singaporeans at rates between commercial and HDB public rentals, offering larger homes and ﬂexible options for those not ready for long-term leases.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: First, I would like to indicate my support for the overall tough anti-drug stance, coupled with strong education and rigorous enforcement in keeping drug prevalence low.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The prevalence of illicit drug consumption in Singapore was much lower than rates reported in studies from the United States (US), Europe and Australia.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Yet, even with these low overall rates, troubling patterns are emerging, particularly among our youths.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: This rise should not be treated as merely a law enforcement issue; it is a complex social challenge affecting individuals, families and entire communities.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: These trends are undeniably driven by curiosity and peer pressure, but there are also deeper structural and psychological factors that contribute to its increase.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Behind every statistic is a person grappling with trauma and a family striving to rebuild.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Enforcement alone cannot break the cycle of addiction.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Building on existing efforts, we should continue to foster a sustained and rehabilitative approach, one that centres on a community-anchored ecosystem supporting recovery beyond surveillance.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: This includes better access to counselling, community-fostered mentorship and employment support.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Youths who struggle with drug abuse often face significant barriers to successfully reintegrate into society.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Rehabilitation efforts must focus on better reintegration and breaking the revolving door between prison and society.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The Singapore Prison Service's (SPS') Reintegration Hub and CNB's Supervision 2.0 pilot are promising developments.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Hair testing, community supervision sessions, and referrals for housing and employment support are steps in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: However, more must be done to ensure that recovery is not just monitored but meaningfully supported by ensuring that individuals have a strong support network that helps them rebuild their lives, not just to avoid relapse.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: To better tailor interventions, CNB's publicly available data on drug abusers should go beyond race and age to include other data such as education level, socio-economic status, mental health history, employment status and housing type.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: This allows us to grasp the complex patterns driving drug use or design appropriate interventions that truly address individuals' needs.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: As regard to integration of ex-offender, we recognise that Yellow Ribbon Singapore has made significant strides in supporting them, but more can be done to help ex-offenders reintegrate into the society.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: In 2025, The Straits Times reported that while there seems to be more employment opportunities for former offenders after release, other issues, such as, social stigma and personal challenges can affect their retention in those jobs.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The career retention rate among former offenders who got jobs with Yellow Ribbon Singapore's help has dropped over the years.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Therefore, we should examine the outcomes of initiatives like the Digital Literacy Masterplan and the Uplifting Employment Credit, including job retention rates and career progression.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: These metrics will help us understand the effectiveness of our rehabilitation efforts and identify areas for improvement.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: As we move forward, Yellow Ribbon Singapore should be empowered to play a coordinating role across agencies, ensuring that rehabilitation and reintegration of ex-offenders is holistic, sustained and inclusive.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: In 2021, the Centre for Research on Islamic and Malay Affairs (RIMA) published "Dreams Realised, Dreams Deferred: Understanding and Addressing the Racial Gap in Educational Achievement in Singapore." A key point raised was that the Malay students persistently face an education gap.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Then Minister for Education, cited two data points that illustrate this disparity.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: According to recent CNA reporting, fewer than one in 100 students have left secondary school without completing it in the past five years.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: While there has clearly been progress in reducing dropout rates, the broader educational attainment gap remains stark.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: There is therefore a pressing need for more comprehensive research and greater access to disaggregated data.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Only then can we understand the full picture where the Malay community stands, how their challenges compare with other groups and what targeted policies are needed to close the gap meaningfully.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: First, MOE should track university graduation rates annually by ethnicity to better understand educational outcomes across communities.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Second, we need detailed breakdown of data to ascertain the percentage of lower-income Malays reaching university, including release of data on Malay undergraduates applying for MENDAKI Tertiary Tuition Fee Subsidy over the past decade.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: And third, MOE should release data on school dropout rates by income background and ethnicity to identify vulnerable groups requiring additional support.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: (In Malay): Mr Speaker, today I have touched on three areas where we need to continue supporting marginalised segments of society.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Therefore, we call for applicants' relationships with their families to also be taken into consideration before their applications are rejected, and to expand the public rental housing market to meet the evolving aspirations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Second, in drug rehabilitation, we need an approach that is not merely punishment and enforcement alone.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: We need more detailed data to include education levels, socioeconomic status, mental health history, employment status and housing type.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Without these details, we cannot fully understand the complex issues that drive drug use, and will thus face challenges in designing appropriate forms of intervention.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Third, in education, we need broader data sharing to identify community needs more accurately.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Here, I want to emphasise that whilst I focus attention on challenges faced by the Malay community, assistance and support should be given to all who need it, regardless of their background.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: We cannot allow anyone to continue being left behind in the nation's development journey.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Our approach is based on principles of social justice and robust data.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: We want a system that provides equal opportunities to all individuals.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: MPs from the WP will strive and continue to work to be a voice for all Singaporeans, including the Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: We believe that a strongly supported society will benefit Singapore as a whole.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: When we help those who are marginalised amongst us, we will together advance all Singaporeans, regardless of their race or background. : Mr Speaker, I return to the President's address.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: A Singapore that is home to all of us cannot merely be an aspiration, but an imperative for us to achieve together.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The challenges I have outlined today in housing, rehabilitation and education require not just Government action, but a whole-of-society response.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: They demand not just policy changes but a fundamental commitment to seeing the dignity and potential in every Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I assure this House that the problems of those at risk of falling through the cracks, especially but not limited to Malay lower-income households, will be consistently highlighted in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The WP elected representatives will work tirelessly to be the people's voice and to continue working for all Singaporeans, regardless of race or background.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I believe strongly that when we lift the most vulnerable among us, we lift all of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: When we ensure that every family has stable housing, every person struggling with addiction has a meaningful path to recovery and every student has access to quality education regardless of their background, we strengthen the very fabric of our society.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In his Opening address, the President reminded us that the world is entering an era of profound uncertainty, marked by shifting power balances, rapid technological disruptions and new threats to stability.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Unlike other countries, Singapore's survival is based neither on natural resources nor a hinterland, as we have neither.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Rather, our greatest resource has always been, and will always remain, our people.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our forefathers have laid the foundations to transform a largely unskilled workforce into one of the most competitive in the world.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our students are frequently ranked among the very best internationally in mathematics, science and problem-solving; and our universities are ranked among the best in the world.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They are the fruit of deliberate investment in our people.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And as we celebrate 60 years of independence, let us remind ourselves that what we do in this term of Government will lay the foundation for the next 40 years, in the lead up to SG100.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Education must continue to be one of the most powerful instruments to unlock talent, nurture resilience and inspire Singaporeans into our next chapter.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Simply put, you will be replaced and sidelined if you are irrelevant and do not add value in whatever you do.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is true not only for individuals or professionals, but also for nations, as President Tharman reminded us in his Opening address.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore today stands at a pivotal moment of uncertainty and turbulence.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For Singapore to survive and thrive, we must ask ourselves, are we relevant to the rest of the world?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How can we as a nation add value to the broader conversations that are happening elsewhere?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I spent almost 25 years in the education industry and at present, I am the chief executive officer at an international school, so I firmly believe that education, too, must always be seen through this dual lens of relevance and value-adding.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Everything we do for our students, our workers, our people must equip them with the relevant skills so they can plug into the regional and global economy, and education must value-add to their personal and professional growth journey to the day they become better professionals, better individuals, better citizens of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We want to prepare Singaporeans, not just for today, but for tomorrow and, in this regard, I will touch on four areas in my speech: education technology (EdTech) and AI in education; enhancing neurodiverse education; holistic education, incorporating emotional and mental wellness; and more pathways for students and adult learners.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: An area where relevance and value-add intersect is Edtech.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If digital literacy is foundational for the future, then should we not extend this commitment to our primary school students as well?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have spoken on this before in Parliament and I believe that a common tablet-like device preloaded with essential software and learning content that are centrally managed by MOE's Edtech division can be rolled out across primary schools, or we can as a pilot programme, for example.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This initiative is aligned with both our Smart Nation push as well as our National Digital Literacy programme.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would imagine that such a platform could provide every child, every child, regardless of background, with a one stop e-learning gateway.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If done at scale, the cost per device would fall significantly and standardisation would ensure that every student, teacher and even parent is working within a consistent, secure and effective digital ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore is not alone in pursuing such solutions.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Here, I hope that MOE could work closely with the Ministry of Digital Development and Information (MDDI) and even private sector partners to realise this vision.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I said MOE and MDDI, so I am looking at my Ang Mo Kio GRC sister, Minister of State Jasmine Lau, and we should have more conversations over coffee about this.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is evolving even as I am speaking right now, and it is shaping how our students learn and how our teachers teach.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When done right, AI is a legitimate tool and a very effective tool to augment teaching and learning, so we need to figure out how to guide its use so our teachers can benefit from it in a responsible manner.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We want AI to amplify learning, not diminish or detract from it.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One of my biggest concerns in the use of AI in education is how we can ensure that it does not erode critical thinking and original thought.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For instance, assessment can be designed to differentiate between AI-assisted work versus original thought.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Students can use AI for research, data gathering, idea generation with interpretation analysis being in the students' own words.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By redesigning our assessment methods, we can keep education relevant in the AI-age by ensuring that our students reap genuine benefit and not just replicate what machines do.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On to equality and equity in neurodiverse education.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When we first design our education system, we started with ensuring that every child has equal access to opportunities, follows the same school rules and has the same classroom experience.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A child who functions differently may need to stand and pace at the back of the classroom to think clearly.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Another may need to fidget or twirl an object to focus.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Providing these allowances would not necessarily compromise the integrity of a classroom.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On the contrary, these allowances might be the key to create a participative, inclusive learning environment where every child, every child can immerse himself or herself fully in learning.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Equality gives every student a place in the classroom.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Equity gives every student the support they need to flourish within that classroom.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe our goal is to design an education system that is built on the principles of inclusion, not exclusion; and integration, not segregation.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, creating an inclusive classroom requires a mental shift in how we view what participative learning is and how teachers can conduct their lessons.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We, thus, need to find a middle ground by combining equality and equity so that we create classrooms that are not only fair, but also nurturing, where every student, every student, regardless of their learning profile, can develop their strengths, contribute meaningfully and reach their full potential.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe this is how our education system can be relevant to all learners and value-add meaningfully to the learning outcomes of different learners.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Academic competition, performance anxiety, comparison culture on social media, personal challenges and so on.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must, thus, equip them with the emotional and mental resilience to thrive, and this is the third topic in my speech.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Well, because it is typically in the teenage years that many issues and challenges, both mental and emotional, present themselves, and this is where students and parents could use the most help and support.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have a 17-year-old son and a 14-year-old daughter, and I am sure anyone who has teenage children or has been through the experience of teenage children, will probably sympathise with me here.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is not enough to just increase the demand on the number of allied educators or make support available on demand.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is akin to how it is mandatory for students to go for regular school-based dental and medical healthcare screenings.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: After all, let us think about it for a minute.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe there are multiple benefits to this proposal.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It allows students to work on challenges, such as stress, anxiety, anger or social conflicts, before they escalate into bullying and/or emotional outbursts.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We just had a whole session on bullying earlier this week, so my proposal could very well pick up on the anger and the issues that potential students, who might end up bullying others, are struggling with ahead of time.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, it integrates holistic pastoral care into the everyday educational experience in school, reinforcing the idea that emotional and mental wellness are as important as academic achievement.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Thirdly, beyond the students themselves, such a system would create meaningful careers for counsellors, therapists, psychologists and other allied healthcare professionals, thus strengthening Singapore's ecosystem of support by facilitating access to these professionals within the community.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This proposal is not as radical as it sounds, considering that some companies have in place employee support schemes for employees in high-pressure roles to undergo regular counselling.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, why should this not be something we can consider extending to a young adult whose formative years are equally crucial?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
