text: By embedding holistic wellness into education, we are preparing our students not only to succeed academically, but to develop the resilience, empathy and self-awareness they will need to thrive in life.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And my final topic is more pathways for students and adult learners, Mr Speaker.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These schemes have opened doors for students with diverse strengths, offering them alternate routes into the next stage of their education.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The challenge now is to ensure that these pathways remain relevant and responsive to the needs of a changing world.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we look at designing better and more holistic education systems for our young, we must not forget about our adult learners and our workforce.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Only by doing so, we will ensure that our learners, whether they are students, who are just leaving school, or adults seeking mid-career transition can remain relevant in their skills and also add value in the future economy.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For decades, our progress has been built on the capability, skills, the resilience of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This has enabled us to grow from a vulnerable young nation to a successful and respected one, But success brings about its own challenges.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The higher we climb, the more difficult it is for us to keep innovating, evolving and climbing to the next stage.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must, because the world around us is shifting rapidly.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must ensure that our education continues to produce talent that are well sought after because the relevancy of their skills and how they value-add to the work they do.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: MOE is the chief architect, Mr Speaker, that shapes our people and our workforce.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this upcoming term of Government, as Chairman of the Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) for Education, I look forward to working closely with our MOE leaders, our educators, our industry, our parents and other stakeholders, to ensure that we nurture not only resilient and skilled individuals, but also Singaporeans with the compassion, empathy and imagination to take Singapore to the next level and beyond.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: (In Mandarin): Mr Speaker, firstly, I would like to thank my dear residents and voters in Hougang for allowing me to represent them in Parliament again. : Mr Speaker, in his address at the Opening of the 15th Parliament on 5 September 2025, President Tharman Shanmugaratnam spoke on several themes, including enhancing assurance for all Singaporeans, fostering a more compassionate "we first" society, and deepening solidarity, and strengthening our resilience and enhancing sustainable efforts in face of climate challenges.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In my speech, I will be touching on issues relating to these themes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In his National Day Rally in August, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong spoke of the Age Well Neighbourhoods initiative, which would allow for seniors to age in the communities that they are familiar with, and which also aim to deliver assisted living support and services to seniors where they live.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Such services include community health posts, access to wellness and social activities, including new activities for both women and men.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And for those requiring more assistance, there is also help with daily living activities, such as washing, eating and housekeeping.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Such services are currently available in HDB's Community Care Apartments, but in limited estates.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I welcome the provision of such services to our seniors who choose to remain in their own flats in the same neighbourhoods they may have lived in for a long time.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many seniors prefer to continue living in the same neighbourhoods they are familiar with for many years – the familiarity, the neighbourly friendships are important for many seniors.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I do hope that the goals of the Age Well initiative are translated into tangible underground support, including especially through our Active Ageing Centres.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I see that the role of our Active Ageing Centres will become even more important.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In Hougang, we have four Active Ageing Centres within the single member constituency.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: So, while our centres in Hougang and I am sure elsewhere in Singapore are very much in demand and well-appreciated by many residents who use their services, I do note that the size of the centres is often a limitation to the amount of activities they can organise.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many centres need to make use of the common spaces in the vicinity of their centres, requiring access via Town Councils or the local Residents' Networks.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope the Government will make greater efforts to allocate a bigger space to our Active Ageing Centres at the onset, or where ground conditions may allow.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In this connection, I would like to ask: how does MOH determine the number of residents assigned to each centre?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Given the physical limitation of centre spaces, or even manpower shortages, perhaps, it is time to rethink the resident allocation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We may wish to consider reducing the number of residents allocated per centre.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This may allow staff to improve outreach, create more meaningful connections with our seniors and enhance the quality of our seniors' time at the centres.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As indicated earlier, Active Ageing Centres may often need to rely on common spaces in our community for their activities due to space constraints.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I urge the Government to assist centres to make it easier to book these spaces with other agencies, as well as helping to lower, if not, absorb the costs, if any, of using these premises.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Perhaps, MOH can help to coordinate with other agencies and stakeholders in this regard.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I would also like to ask again what is the Government's strategy for reaching residents who are not currently participating in any community activities with the Active Ageing Centres?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I have previously called on MOH to study this issue.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is even more crucial for MOH to dedicate resources to this critical outreach challenge.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: There is now a greater imperative to keep more seniors in touch and engaged.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am keen to understand what percentage of residents the Active Ageing Centres have been unable to engage and how many refuse participation after initial engagement.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Does MOH track the reasons for non-engagement and non-participation, or even those who dropped off after initial contact?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope that MOH will study these issues.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While some seniors may have their own active social networks, better outreach will only help to serve more seniors and better enable the new Age Well initiative and the Healthier SG to achieve their stated goals.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I have previously called for removing Annual Value as a means testing criterion for residents with zero household income.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is also in our WP manifesto, and indeed, MPs across the aisle have raised this issue in the previous Parliament.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We should delink healthcare affordability from property values.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Let us use a more accurate person-centric measures to ensure our social safety net is truly strong and fair, especially for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: He stressed that by strengthening assurance and keeping opportunities open, we can build a more resilient and confident society, even in an uncertain world.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: He also spoke of nurturing a "we first" society, one that is more open and engaged, where citizens are empowered to take initiative and lead ground-up programmes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is about building a society with deepened solidarity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: These aspirations must surely go beyond economic metrics.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: They should allow Singaporeans to pursue their passions and to build a society that is not only prosperous but also rich in culture and spirit.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Former US President John F Kennedy once said, and I quote, "The life of the arts, far from being an interruption, a distraction in the life of a nation, is very close to the centre of a nation's purpose... and is a test of the quality of a nation's civilisation".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This aptly reminds us that while policies have a role to play, it is through art, culture and shared experiences that the people's values are truly shaped.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is paramount that there are spaces for artists to thrive and for our collective spirit to flourish.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It was more than just a cinema; it was a sanctuary for independent artistic expression and a beacon for communities that struggled to find their place.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It follows the permanent closure of The Substation, our first independent art centre.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Among the reasons for The Substation's closure was the changes in the way they were allowed to use the premise, which meant they could no longer operate in the same manner as before.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The impact on our artists and our national soul is indelible, and with every closure of such a space, our country becomes culturally poorer.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: To truly become a world-class arts hub, we must ensure that our own independent and creative voices are not left behind.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A vibrant culture must be nurtured from the ground up, grounded in the authenticity, diversity and the originality of our local artists and the spaces that cultivate them.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: On the occasion of our nation's 60th birthday this year, we must reflect on the society that we are and the society that we hope to become.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Are we content to be a society where homegrown initiatives are almost inevitably replaced by those bigger and better resource?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In his National Day Rally speech, the Prime Minister spoke of the importance of the Singapore Spirit.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This spirit is, of course, more than just economic progress; it must be tempered with a Singaporean soul and I submit that independent public spaces where artists can develop their craft, communities can be nurtured, and hearts and minds can be expanded, can go some way to contribute to this Singaporean soul.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is my hope that we can reimagine the role of the arts in Singapore, not as an indulgence, but as a pillar of who we are.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: First, by creating policies that offer long-term stability for independent art spaces and increasing governmental support where it is most needed for these groups.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Second, and crucially, we must foster a collective mindset that sees the arts as essential to our national fabric.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Together, through more supportive policies and everyday choices, we can ensure the local artists and independent spaces thrive.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: By doing so, we lend our hand to the ground up initiatives of our arts community and, in turn, we can strengthen our society and deepen the solidarity that defines us.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: These climate change targets are important to signal Singapore's commitment to the United Nation (UN) Framework Convention on Climate Change and its Paris Agreement.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: To put into effect these climate targets, Singapore has passed several laws to address climate change, including the Carbon Pricing Act, which puts in place a carbon tax.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: There are several pathways for Singapore to achieve net-zero, but not all of these are entirely clear at the moment, given global uncertainties and rollbacks in climate efforts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In addition to decarbonisation, Singapore is already importing electricity from neighbouring countries and is exploring purchasing carbon credits, carbon captured, utilisation and storage solutions, and even thinking of building small and medium sized nuclear plants to meet our needs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Knowing more details on these pathways will help inspire trust among the Singaporeans in these options.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The question that remains in is whether these laws and measures will be sufficient in its contribution in an era of global boiling, a term coined by former UN Secretary General in July 2023.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The transitory allowance framework provides allowances to ease the financial burden of the carbon tax.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, there is a lack of publicly available information on its implementation and success.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: With greater details, it will be less difficult for Singaporeans to assess whether these allowances are effective in incentivising companies to decarbonise, and to understand how does the Government ensure that businesses do not use carbon offsets to avoid the more challenging and expensive work of transitioning their operations to be more efficient and less carbon intensive.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If so, can the Government share more information on this in this House?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Ultimately, the urgency of the global climate crisis may demand that we prioritise proven, impactful measures.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Are these offsets genuinely leading to a reduction in global emissions?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We must continue to ensure that our commitment to tackling climate change is reflected in a decisive and transparent plan of action that meets the urgency of this crisis.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We must embrace policies that are transparent, fair and grounded in community.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This means providing practical, on-the-ground support for our seniors; ensuring our social safety nets are both just and effective; and fostering a vibrant arts community that strengthens our national soul.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is only by addressing these diverse challenges with unity and a renewed sense of purpose that we can build the caring and confident Singapore we all aspire to be.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: That is what we are as a nation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: That quiet, unwavering tenacity is what brought us from mudflats to metropolis.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: Singapore is safe, stable and secure, but let us be clear that is not our pinnacle.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: For the next phase of Singapore's development, Mr Speaker, I would like us to challenge ourselves to be that swan that paddles strong in order to take flight to set our gaze beyond the waterline, to put the wind beneath our people's wings.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: That is how we will stay stable on the water and soar boldly into an uncertain future.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: To do so, we need to tap into what truly moves us.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: We all know that feeling – that tug at your heartstrings, not because of sadness, but because you care about something so much, it moves you.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: I hope we can build a Singapore where our youths can feel free to pursue what stirs that precise emotion in them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: For us to be a nation that is not just remembered for its order and efficiency but remembered for its soul.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: For the dreams that it ignites, for the passion that it arouses, and for the courage it gives its young people to pursue what matters to them the most.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: But for our youths to dream, we need to recognise the realities that they live in.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: It means little to them when we compare what they have today to our past successes because today is all they know.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: On many accounts, they are in a good position compared to their peers globally.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: Yet many feel unsupported, and some are uncertain about the future.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: While they may have better starting points today, they are unlikely to see as sharp an inflection in our nation's development as their parents did, and that is because we are a maturing economy.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: While they are more connected, they yearn for real connections.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: More importantly, they were more comfortable interacting online than in person.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: While the quality of care is increasing, they will shoulder a greater burden of care.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: So, for our youth to dream, we need to set them on the right path and address three fundamental shifts in their reality, from where they start in life, to how they experience life, and how they care for who they love.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: First, our youth will experience unequal starting points that they have left unchecked will likely widen with intergenerational wealth transfers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: A person is rewarded because of his effort and that remains the best organising principle for a society that is multicultural, multireligious and multiracial like Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: However, we need to recognise its consequences and adapt.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: When everyone started from zero, effort was enough.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: Today, children inherit their parents' advantages, and as such, starting points very greatly right at birth through no effort of the child.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: Let us take a simple example to illustrate.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: He cashes it out, puts it into a fixed deposit of 1.6%.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: He or she then earns $80,000 in interest annually.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: In other words, this person is earning 20% more than your median worker.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: As I said, this is an extremely simplistic example but it is to say that we have to pay attention to returns to capital and returns to labour.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: Those with more wealth tend to have higher investment returns and this is because they have better access to financial literacy and riskier financial products.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: These advantages are then transferred from one generation to the next, widening wealth positions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: This is not a unique problem for Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: Countries around the world recognise this and are trying ways to address wealth inequality.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: For example, Spain has a net wealth tax, France has an inheritance tax.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: Some are prone to loopholes, while others are challenging to administer.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: And that is because wealth is inherently extremely mobile.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: But Singapore must find our own way, one where those with more, must contribute more.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: One that still preserves our values of self-reliance and competitiveness, one where we raise revenues in a way that is fair and progressive.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: To be clear, this is not about culling tall poppies.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: This is about giving greater consideration to one's wealth, in addition to one's income within our tax system.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: This is about channelling accumulated wealth into increasing opportunity and social mobility.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: When we do this well and channel more resources towards youths that are less privileged, they will feel it.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: No youth deserves to start 10 laps behind before the race has even begun.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: In the past few months at Nee Soon, I have seen this myself.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: Students struggling to get back on their two feet because they are from an abusive family.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: One where her dad just passed away and others working part-time to supplement a single parent income.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: These youths need to know that they can break the cycle and chart their own paths.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: That is how we move forward as a nation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: One where every person, every young person has the chance to dream, regardless where they start in life.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: Second, youths today face a rapidly transforming world because of technology especially AI.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: AI has helped to do things faster, better and cheaper that has freed us up from the routine tasks.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: At the same time, there are valid anxieties over how AI impacts our jobs and our sectors.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: Our youths today, wonder whether the skills they pick up will prepare them for the jobs of tomorrow.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: Imagine what that number will be 10 years from now.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: The reality is that no one can predict with certainty how jobs will change, and it is precisely because we cannot predict how jobs will change that we must tap into what makes us human and hone in on that.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: In an everchanging world, I believe that play remains the most important skill to adapt.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: We must ensure that our youths have the opportunities to experiment, construct meaning from experiences and interact in real life.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: Because the messy and imperfect spaces where we interact is where we develop our deepest resilience.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: Now that, is what differentiates human intelligence from artificial.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: As the phrase goes: having an education is one thing, being educated is another.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: Our education system must go beyond teaching people how to do economically productive things to one that teaches them how to be in the world, how to interact with others, how to think.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: Our agencies and other stakeholders have taken steps to address this.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: I saw first-hand how such experiences can be empowering.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: In June this year, I had the chance to attend the National Youth Council's Leaders Course.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: This is an annual three-day two-night programme where they bring students from different backgrounds – ITE, polytechnics and universities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: At the closing event, a few students were invited on stage to share about their experiences.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: One of these experiences and sharing resonated deeply with me.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: He went on stage and he shared that at the start of the programme he initially felt out of place and shy.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: I was surprised by how vulnerable and honest he was in that moment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: Then, he shared that it was through the support of his group mates and the activities over the three days that he too realised that he had something to bring to the table.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: And at the end of it, you could see him standing on stage smiling brightly, presenting confidently and commanding the stage.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: You could tell from his body language how proud he was.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: We need more of such experiences where our youths can move into uncomfortable spaces, tap into what they had all along, and believe in themselves.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: It is by working through our deepest discomfort, engaging with others that we grow.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: It is not by sitting behind a screen alone.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: Third, our youths are growing up in an ageing Singapore that will place immense pressure on them as they enter adulthood.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: Once a nation that cared for babies and children, we are now, a nation that cares for the old.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: Not everyone has children, but everyone has parents.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: Supporting this generation therefore means supporting them and backing them to care for who they love.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: Globally, people spend a staggering 16.4 billion hours every single day on unpaid care.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: As family sizes decrease, the balance between work and caregiving will tip, forcing our youth to choose between family or progression.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: Care is essential to dignity and social cohesion.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: We must create systems where care is shared more fully, recognised more strongly and supported more holistically.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: Progression and family should not be a binary choice.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: In Singapore, we have increased financial support for caregivers and that is a really good start.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: But we all know, it is the visits to the hospital, the unscheduled calls for help that that really, really strains.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: That is something we should evaluate along with similar policies that not only address financial needs, but also time and effort of our caregivers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: So, Mr Speaker, rather than looking in the rear view mirror, our youths must be able to look ahead.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: They must be able to chart their own paths.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: They must be given the room and the ability to dream.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: To our youths, I am committed to meet you at your realities from where you start in life to how you experience life and when you enter adulthood, to how you care for who you love.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: The words of my children's favourite song, and probably some of you as well, it truly describes the future that I hope we can forge for you today: "I am done hiding, now I am shining, like I am born to be.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: We are dreaming hard, we came so far, now, I believe." Mr Speaker, please let me say a few lines in Mandarin.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: (In Mandarin): This year marks the 60th anniversary of Singapore and our society has entered a rapid changing new era.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Goh Hanyan)
text: Although our younger generation does not worry about basic necessities, like every generation of young people, they too have their own anxieties and pressures.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: It seems only yesterday when I delivered my maiden speech in Parliament.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: But five years has since passed and it has certainly been a very eventful and heartwarming five years for me.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I recall my maiden speech, like many in the House, was about kindness and I shared about the childhood days I spent in the 1980s, in the Holland Drive neighbourhood where my father had his clinic.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: It was about the friendships we had with our neighbours, many who I still remember vividly.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Uncle Mohammad and the magazine and stationery store he used to run – it was called PMS – and I remembered 8 Days picked it up as a most noteworthy name.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Aunty Siew Ying, a Malaysian turned Singaporean who ran a snatzy Jantzen hairdressing salon – that wa where I got my first professional haircut after years of grandma's home bowl haircut.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I still remember vividly, ooh, the excitement my sister and I had tasting our first very adult, very grown-up "XO Fishhead Bee Hoon" from Uncle Chang who opened that innovative new stall in the coffeeshop right next to my dad's clinic.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: The fondness I had for the neighbourhood was all about the kindness that the community had for one another.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: My parents trusted our neighbours enough that my sister and I could always run around the neighbourhood unaccompanied.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: We shared news about our lives and families, and most importantly, we counted on each other to seek and give help openly.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I know that these values ring true in many fellow Singaporean's hearts because in the days that followed from that maiden speech, I had Punggol residents and volunteers who came up to me and ask if I was Dr Yeo's daughter, as he used to be their family doctor, and they recall that neighbourhood I grew up in and all its residents there with much fondness.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: One of them recalled me and my sister hanging out in my dad's clinic in our school pinafores, and honestly, that made me feel very warm.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: But I am particularly heart-warmed that one of our Punggol residents who remembered my father well, eventually also had her daughter, Chloe, who is now studying to be a doctor, volunteer with us, and she is now a loved young community leader.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Indeed, kindness begets kindness and that is the true virtuous circle of life.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: It might seem to be a very distant memory, but COVID-19, DORSCON Orange, Circuit-Breaker, contact-tracing, vaccinations, isolation, PETs, swabbings only ended and went into the endemic phase just some 30 months ago.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I remember I spent the first three years of my time as an MP in a mask, dealing with COVID-19 community matters, assuaging fears, comforting distress, dispelling disinformation and getting residents who were new to me to place their trust in me, even in a mask, and to place trust in our Government policies.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: It was only with the kindness and fortitude of our trusty community volunteers and leaders that we were able to do what we did.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: My community leader, Patrick, was with me when we delivered our Care Packs in the middle of the night to residents who had COVID.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Kathryn was with me when we allayed the fears of residents who saw cleaners in full PET kits cleaning up the Punggol Plaza "COVID Cluster".

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Cristine was with me when we identified and set up rest areas in Punggol coffeeshops to allow our delivery riders to rest and eat between their delivery rounds.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Winston and Charles were with me when we set up our first counters to distribute – believe it or not hand-made face masks with care vouchers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: To the Chloes, Patricks, Kathryns, Cristines, Winstons and Charles, and all our brave community leaders, this is a Motion of Thanks, and it is most appropriate that we remember what all of you did.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Indeed, this is the "Secret Lives of Workers", and I believe that should more Singaporeans have a glimpse into this world, they would appreciate the kindness and sacrifices of our workers, and in turn, appreciate why we at the Labour Movement continue to fight for better protection and progress for our Singaporean workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Sometimes, all we need is to take a short pause from our own busyness, take a look around, have a short chat and to unveil these secrets.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I remain appreciative to the dedication and hard work our bus captains put in to ensure a safe and comfortable commute for all of us, and I hope that everyone can encourage our bus captains and public transport workers with an appreciative nod and a nice smile when you next see them.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Articulate, charismatic, nerves of steel, quick on their feet and excellent mediators they are.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: They make for natural leaders, but did you know, that for many of our union leaders, because of the construct of their collective agreements, they choose to forego promotions, to remain in rank-and-file executive positions so that they can continue to represent fellow workers without worries of conflict of interest.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Indeed, it is a calling to be a union leader, and our big brothers and sisters, 大哥大姐们, serve their working lives out in dedicated service to their fellow workers, never seeing their choices as sacrifices, but as choices of care and service.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Building on this vision and our labour values, I call on the Government to continue their good work with tripartite partners to ensure that every worker is recognised and valued for their contributions at work and at home.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: In particular, securing fair pay and a just future for our platform workers; ensuring good jobs for our public transport workers; and supporting our women and caregivers to thrive at home and at work.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I shall speak more on platform workers today.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: For the past decade or so, NTUC and our Platform Work Associations (PWAs) have pushed for the Platform Workers Act to secure better protections for our platform workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: This means that recognition strengthens our PWAs' ability to negotiate with individual platforms to secure better wages, welfare and work prospects for our platform workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Indeed, bilateral negotiations between PWAs and platform operators are an important means for us to secure better outcomes for our platform workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Indeed, our negotiations have already started to yield success for us with Grab and we successfully negotiated for incentive changes after feedback from our drivers, as well as secured priority shift bookings for our food delivery platform workers in high-demand areas.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Most recently, NTUC and our PWAs initiated a senior-level trilateral workgroup to tackle illegal practices that unfairly undercut our platform workers' jobs and earnings.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I am glad that the trilateral workgroup has yielded concrete outcomes that make a difference to our platform workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: While these measures have made a difference, our work is not still far from being done.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Platform workers continue to face challenges, such as unpredictable and unclear earnings, as well as variable incentives that can require them to work excessive hours to unlock targets.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: As a society, we must make progress in recognising and respecting the contributions of our platform workers where it matters most, in how they are paid and treated for work that they have done.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: This is where I am heartened by the progress that our PWAs are making with our platform partners.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Arising from these principles, the platforms have committed to consult drivers and the PWAs on ways to ensure fair and transparent earnings, to proactively engage PWAs prior to major changes to incentive schemes, and to monitor their platform workers' online hours and adjust incentive programmes, where necessary, to ensure that they do not encourage overwork.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: As an update to our platform drivers and riders, do know that our PWAs are in close discussions the platform operators to operationalise these principles in the context of individual platform policies.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Beyond these immediate concerns, we must also work to ensure a just future for our private hire vehicle (PHV), taxi and bus drivers, especially amidst the planned roll-out of autonomous vehicles (AVs), the upcoming Rapid Transit System (RTS) Link and discussions with Malaysia to expand cross-border transport opportunities.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: The Labour Movement recognises the benefits of this technology transition for Singaporeans, especially in augmenting transport networks for travels, including across the border to Malaysia.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: But for our drivers, these announcements can be very concerning.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Will I still be able to make a living?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: It enables us to move faster in deploying technologies while managing disruptions to the workforce and generating new job opportunities." This is why NTUC and PWAs are working very closely with the Ministry of Transport and through committees, such as the Inter-Ministerial Steering Committee on Autonomous Vehicles, to bring our drivers' concerns to the table.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Amidst the roll-out of AVs, the upcoming RTS Link and discussions to expand cross-border transport, our drivers must be assured of a just future, that there will be jobs for them and they will be given the support and time they need to transit to these jobs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: MOM has provided that, as of 2023, close to 90% of full-time employees of working age were provided at least one scheduled flexible work arrangement (FWA) they required.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: We need to understand what the picture is like for FWAs since 2023.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: From the Labour Movement, there have been more reports of employers requiring workers to return to the office fully and to follow standard working hours.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Let us measure our progress on how we have moved as a society to improve the livelihoods of our workers and the lives of the people around us.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Speaking with kindness, acting with kindness, thinking with kindness, I trust these will continue to be the foundations of our treasured Singapore values.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.55 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 3.35 pm until 3.55 pm.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, I would like to declare my interest as the Executive Director of CampusImpact, a charity that serves children from lower-income families.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I stand in this House, knowing that the opportunity to serve is a privilege and a heavy responsibility.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The words spoken in this House are not just words.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They shape the policies and culture of our country and touch the lives of many Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That is why, standing here, making this speech, is terrifying and difficult.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But it is only the second hardest thing I have ever had to do.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For those who are parents among us, do you remember how difficult it was to wake up at 1.00 am, 4.00 am, 7.00 am for night feeds or when your children cannot stop vomiting and you have to rush them to the hospital?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It takes everything you have got to care for a child.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While the responsibility of caring for my fellow citizens as an MP is a weighty one, the responsibility of doing so as a parent to my child is even more so.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But as difficult as it has been, my journey as a mother has also strengthened my belief in strong, thriving families.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This belief drives me, today, to speak up for caregivers, the quiet pillars of our society who hold up our families.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As President Tharman said in his speech, Singapore must remain a home where the vulnerable amongst us are not only cared for with compassion but also empowered to pursue their hopes and dreams.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is our caregivers who made this possible – mothers, fathers, children and spouses who quietly bear the weight of love and responsibility.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the course of the last few months, I have spoken to many residents in Bishan East-Sin Ming and heard their stories.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The first is the sleep-deprived mother, struggling to navigate the complexities of a new family dynamic and the physical demands of ensuring her tiny baby is fed, changed, bathed safely and that every milk bottle is washed and sterilised, all while trying her best to recover and care for herself so that she can function well enough to take better care of her baby.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, caregivers for a loved one with special needs, who have faced stigma and rejection on top of the daily hurdles they have had to overcome just to lead their lives alongside the rest of us.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Third, adult children who are caring for their ageing parents, juggling between work and family, while trying to understand and accept how their parents, who used to be so strong, so dependable, are now losing their mental faculties and their physical abilities.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Yet, after such a major event, a mother may be given only one postnatal check-up.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In contrast, throughout the baby's first and maybe even second year, the child receives multiple milestone checks and vaccinations.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our support systems should look deeper into this imbalance.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mothers' health, physical and mental, is just as crucial as their children's.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We know that postnatal depression is on the rise.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We are relying on a reactive system, waiting for women to seek help.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When mothers bring their babies for check-ups and vaccinations, let us also care for the mothers.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A simple screening, a conversation, can make all the difference between despair and hope.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And yes, fathers too – I see fathers in the Chamber nodding vigorously.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They should be given space to talk about their mental well-being, because our children need both parents.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I would also like to review paternity leave and shared parental leave uptake to normalise caregiving as a joint responsibility, not one carried by mothers alone.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Beyond medical support, mothers also need community support.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Every parent’s journey is different – the single mother juggling work and caregiving, the foreign parent far from family help, the unwed mother or father who faces stigma.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must ensure that parent support groups, community initiatives and counselling are open and welcoming to all.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Consider Safe Place, a ground-up group that walks with women facing unsupported pregnancies.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They found that many married women, not just unwed ones, considered abortion not because of finances alone, but because they felt alone in caregiving.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As its founder, Ms Jennifer Heng, puts it, “We are almost like family members, stepping in where support is missing.” Mr Deputy Speaker, if we want stronger families and more babies in Singapore, we must make sure that every parent has the medical, emotional and community support they need to heal, to recover and to love.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, I would like to explore support for caregivers of those with special needs.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is a phenomenon that many people who have special needs face.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The post-18 cliff usually refers to the sharp drop-off in support and services that happens when a young person with disabilities turns 18, particularly in the context of education, healthcare or disability support.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is called a “cliff” because there is rarely a gradual transition.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is more like stepping off an edge.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Last month, a resident came to me at my meet-the-people session, asking if we could appeal for his daughter to be given a chance to continue the good progress she had been making in her special education school.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is a group of neurological disorders that affect movement and posture, resulting from brain damage or abnormal development.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Rachelle cannot move her body from her neck down.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Imagine not being able to move your body from the neck down.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: She has painted artwork that has been displayed in Alexandra Hospital, and one of her pieces is titled “Holding On, Lifting Up”.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It shows a person carrying a bunch of balloons with sad faces, but only one happy face in the middle.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Explaining her artwork, Rachelle wrote, and I quote, “This piece shows how it feels to carry sadness, like holding a balloon filled with heavy emotions.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Even when the tears come, there’s still a reason to keep holding on.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Among all the frowns is one small smile, reminding us that even a little bit of hope can lift us. ‘Holding On, Lifting Up’ is about strength during hard times, and how something small, like kindness or a happy thought, can help us rise again.” Does Rachelle not have a truly resilient and kind spirit?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Rachelle’s teachers have described her as, “consistently show(ing) a strong passion for illustration and has made significant progress in using her sip-and-puff switch to produce detailed and expressive artwork.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Rachelle also finds it difficult to be fully engaged by the activities at the Day Activity Centre (DAC) because even though she cannot move her body, she has her full mental faculties.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is because there are insufficient DACs and insufficient places offered by DACs.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This problem is essentially the result of insufficient funding to social service agencies operating these services, forcing DACs to limit the scale of their services as they are not able to keep up with the fundraising required to keep these services going.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Then, there is the problem of affordability for parents.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is compounded by the fact that most caregivers of persons with special needs have to pay more for recurring medical appointments and therapy needs, which only worsens if there are medical complications along the way.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: All of these typically start the moment the child is born and continues throughout his or her life.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is also a lack of training and funding for staff in adult disability services, unlike special education, where teachers have a Diploma in Special Education.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Staff in the adult disability services do not have a key milestone training.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As a result, many DAC staff are not equipped to handle the challenges that come with the care of adult persons with disabilities or they may not have enough staff to deliver their services, which lead them to take in clients with less severe needs.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: From her story, it seems that there is a gap in our system.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If so, we need stronger coordination between MOE and the Ministry for Social and Family Development (MSF) to increase support for people like Rachelle.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Who knows how much Rachelle’s artistic potential could contribute to society if we continue to support her?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Let us close the gap for Rachelle and other post-18 persons with disabilities so that they do not step off a cliff but instead, can make the leap into the next exciting chapter of their lives, where there is still so much more to look forward to.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Third, I would like to explore ways to increase respite care options for caregivers.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are over 210,000 caregivers in Singapore supporting an increasing elderly population.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Slightly more than half of care recipients are aged 80 or above; one in seven older adults is a caregiver, with nearly half still working full-time and more than half being women.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What this means is that our caregivers are seniors themselves, they are still trying to work full-time and the caregiving burden tends to fall on women.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many caregivers – one in five – are also taking care of more than one care recipient at a time.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To make the situation even more serious, a significant portion of caregivers are unwell themselves.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: More than one in three caregivers are suffering from two or more chronic health conditions, but often neglect their own health to focus on those they care for.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Two residents I met told me they could not get respite care for just one afternoon to celebrate their daughter’s birthday with their friends because they had to care for a grandparent with dementia.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I replied that I had a contact with Dementia Singapore and could link them up to explore support.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Let us not wait until it is too late.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, with family sizes shrinking and caregiving configurations evolving, policies should adapt to and respond to these changing realities.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, we should dedicate funding not only to care recipients, but also to the caregivers themselves.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Just as we invest in healthcare to prevent illness, we must invest directly in caregivers’ well-being because when caregivers are sustained, those they care for thrive too.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The aspirations I have outlined cannot be achieved by the public service alone.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It requires the partnership of other stakeholders in the care ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Existing ground-up organisations and social service agencies are small, nimble groups that are highly effective in providing the care and support needed.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How can the Government partner better with these organisations?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Beyond simple matters of funding, we should seek to expand access to skills, networks and mentorships for new and emerging initiatives to strengthen capabilities further.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A well-funded and well-equipped social service ecosystem ensures no child, parent or vulnerable person is left without timely care.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Empowering changemakers enables them to reach further, respond faster and lift more lives.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When we provide effective organisations and agencies the tools and resources to thrive through effective policy-making and design, Singapore’s safety nets can be strong, her communities resilient and her compassion as a nation effective.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It has once been said that the sign of a civilised society is a healed femur.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The femur is a long bone that connects the hip to the knee.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the wild, wounded animals who break their legs die because they are unable to run from danger and hunt.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A broken femur that has healed is evidence that someone has taken time to stay with the one who fell, has bound up the wound, has carried the person to safety and has tended the person through recovery.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Helping someone else through difficulty is where civilisation starts.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Again, I say, it is the hardest thing I have ever had to do.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If we stop to care for others, we ourselves may fall behind everyone else who is moving ahead.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Yet, it is a powerful sign that Singapore is truly a civilised society.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A tree longs for stillness, but the wind does not cease; a child longs to care for a parent, but the parent is no longer here.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Caregiving can feel like being surrounded by a howling, relentless wind that never stops.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Like the trees, we bend under the strain, pushed to breaking point.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We wonder, when will we get to rest again?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But this proverb reminds us, caregiving is a responsibility and a privilege.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: From time to time, I will get asked variations of this question, "If you could have a meal with anyone in this world, who would you want to eat with?" My answer: My father.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Watching him fade in hospice care was painful, a man once strong reduced by illness.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: All I could do was hold his hand and sing to him and yet, even that felt hard.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I was preparing for my “O” levels then, and I will be honest, there were afternoons I resented being there.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But what I would not give now to have that one more day with him.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Ms Elysa Chen, you have a minute left.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen
text: And with these efforts, hopefully, caregiving would not be so hard after all.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Yet as our society matures, we face challenges on the road ahead.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: On the social front, we are dealing with ageing and need to guard against inequality and social stratification.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Our demographics are evolving, with smaller families and more singles, and our people have higher and more diverse aspirations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We must grapple with these, even while facing strong external headwinds – geopolitical shifts, economic uncertainty, climate change and disruptions due to technology and AI.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Today, I will talk about two key shifts that we are taking to prepare Singapore for this future.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: First, refreshing our approach to tackling difficult social issues; and second, transforming our education system.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Yesterday, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong spoke about how stratification can occur and gaps in social mobility can widen as our economy grows and develops.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We have seen this happen in other societies where privilege gets entrenched.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, we cannot stand still and must continually work against these forces that can fragment our society.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: That is why, beyond doing more through policies and programmes, we have also been focusing on how we can do better.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This is especially important in our work to help lower-income families who are facing complex challenges and are seeking to break through their circumstances.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: They have consented to us sharing their journey with Members.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: They live in a two-room HDB rental flat and have four children.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Adi is the sole breadwinner and Syaakirah, a homemaker.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The family was struggling financially and faced difficulties meeting their basic needs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Adi and Syaakirah also found it hard to supervise their children's academic progress and were concerned that the children would fall behind in school.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We want to ensure that all families, no matter their circumstances, have the opportunity to thrive.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And that is where Comlink+ and KidSTART come in.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: When the family first joined Comlink+, they needed urgent help with their daily needs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Their family coach, Ken, coordinated with community organisations, such as Willing Hearts, to give them essential groceries and milk powder.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: As Syaakirah wanted to pursue full-time employment, Ken placed her on employment services, too.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: A non-profit organisation, Engineering Good, gave the family a refurbished laptop.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This helped Syaakirah in her job search and allowed the children to do home-based learning.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The older children have also been enrolled in the MENDAKI academic coaching programme, which they enjoy, to keep them on track academically.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Ken also noticed that Akid, the family's youngest son, is passionate about playing football.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: He enrolled Akid in the Comlink+ Community Futsal programme run by SportCares, where he makes friends through sports.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: When Syaakirah was expecting her youngest child, Sofea, Ken linked her up with KidSTART.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The KidSTART practitioner visited the couple at home regularly to guide them through Sofea's infancy.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: KidSTART equipped the family with parenting tips on health, nutrition and child development.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: They also shared knowledge and skills on building positive parent-child interactions and monitored Sofea closely to track her developmental milestones.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: When Syaakirah had difficulties feeding Sofea, KidSTART quickly connected her with a nurse, who provided advice on appropriate feeding practices and milk quantities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: KidSTART also provided books and toys for Sofea and her siblings to cultivate an early interest in reading and strengthen parent-child bonding.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: They journey with the families to develop customised roadmaps that evolve with their changing needs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Our corporate partners provide valuable resources to make lasting change in the lives of families.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We also tap on the strengths of the community to provide Comlink+ with additional resources above and beyond what Government can provide.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Through Gift a Family (GAF), for example, we invite Singaporeans, who have done well, as well as organisations, to partner and support Comlink+ families.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For example, for parents, GAF partners have sponsored courses and upskilling for them, on top of SkillsFuture, so that they can get better jobs and work towards a better future for their families.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For children, GAF partners have also sponsored music and art classes to encourage children to pursue their interests.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This is on top of existing school funds, like Opportunity Funds in our schools, that subsidise co-curricular development opportunities, even overseas learning trips, for students from lower-income households.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This is a much more intense approach compared to just providing more resources.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In 2019, we started piloting Comlink+ at four sites and subsequently scaled it nationwide.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We will also provide dedicated employment and skills assistance that better meets the needs of families.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The shifts in how we, as a nation, tackle difficult social issues, such as inequality and social stratification.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In the early years of nationhood, we focused on survival and economic growth.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For those who were struggling, the Government provided assistance to meet their basic needs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But for this future that we are building, we must, as the Prime Minister said yesterday, continue to tilt the balance to keep opportunities open at every stage of life.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The Government, community, volunteers and corporate partners cannot afford to work on our own but must stand together as close partners.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Over the years we have been moving in this direction.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We formed, for example, the PEERS Network in 2019 as a collaboration among community partners, social service agencies and Government agencies to support rough sleepers and homeless individuals.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: During COVID-19, when the number of people sleeping rough went up and more were seeking shelter, this turned out to be critical.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Today, after six years, the PEERS Network is still growing strong.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It was something we designed after listening to our frontliners, social workers, educators and community workers, who told us that it was not just about doing more or giving more but also about trying to do better.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Earlier this year, the Ministry of National Development (MND) and MSF also formed the New Environment Action Team, a network comprising social service agencies, community groups, trade associations, corporate partners and Government agencies, which seeks to address hoarding issues in people's homes in a more holistic and sustainable manner.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, you can see we are moving away from the models of the past, where the Government and community each worked in silo.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Instead, we wanted to partner Singaporeans and take a whole-of-society approach to solving problems together.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Along the way, we may need to develop new structures, policies, standard operating procedures, data systems that enable greater collaboration and integration.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But more importantly, the key ingredient powering all of this is trust, which enables us to build strong networks and relationships, especially on the ground.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It takes time and effort to build trust and mobilise the community, but it is something that we must do.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: As social issues become increasingly complex and inter-connected, everyone must come on board.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: No one person or organisation, including the Government, has all the solutions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In our "we first" society, we must all come together to lift each person up.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: When we help others thrive, we grow stronger ourselves.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, we will build on this collaborative spirit with more intentionality and heart, to turn our conversations into partnerships; our partnerships into actions; and our actions into lasting meaningful change for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Even as we address the pressing social issues of today, we must also look ahead and prepare the next generation for the challenges of tomorrow.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Yesterday, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong outlined some of the directions that education reform will take in this term of Government to reduce the stakes of single exams, broaden the definition of success and give children the chance to discover and develop their strengths.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In a rapidly changing world, it is no longer enough to equip younger Singaporeans with knowledge alone.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In fact, the knowledge we impart today might well be outdated tomorrow.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: What is more important is for younger Singaporeans to be agile and resilient, think critically, learn continuously, so that they can navigate a more uncertain environment.
