speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And with social issues becoming more complex, we also need to empower Singaporeans who can empathise with others and lead with kindness.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: She was abused by her father for years until she finally summoned the courage to confide about it in her school counsellor, who then alerted the principal and the Police.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Protective Service removed her from her home and she had to move eight times between various temporary accommodations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The instability took a toll on her studies and she had to repeat her Secondary 4 year, but she did not give up.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: She applied for ITE's Early Admission Exercise and managed to secure a place in ITE College East.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: ITE was the first place that she felt safe enough to discover herself and imagine a future beyond survival.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Through her grit and dedication, and with the support of her peers and her teachers, Azalea eventually graduated with a perfect 4.0 GPA.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Today, she is a first-year student pursuing a diploma in media arts and design at Singapore Polytechnic.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This year she was one of 10 recipients of the Lee Kuan Yew Model Student Award and also received the Lee Hsien Loong Award for Outstanding All-round Achievement.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But among her many accomplishments at this young age, what she is proudest of is her work with Owena, the alumni association of the therapeutic group home for children that she was formerly in.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: As a pioneer member and leader, she organises activities and offers emotional support to current residents.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Though still a young adult herself, she is already eager to help build a better world for the generation after hers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Azalea's journey shows us that not everyone takes the same path to success, and success can mean different things to different people.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It is about finding the right path for yourself.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And this is what our education system must continue to uphold: providing pathways for our children to flourish, no matter their starting point, supporting them to pursue their aspirations in their own time and cultivating strong values, so that they give back to society.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We have been moving steadily away from a narrow meritocracy that ties achievement solely to grades and paper qualifications, towards a society that recognises that success comes in many forms.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Whether in the arts, technology, sports or other fields, we want to celebrate the diverse talents of every individual and respect the contribution of every worker.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This shift is not something that can happen overnight.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We are building on an education system that has continuously evolved to stay relevant.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In the past, success was largely measured in grades and paper qualifications.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We focused on those in the early years because we thought they might set our children up for success.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In fact, at times, the system would pit students against one another.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Members would recall that the PSLE used to be graded on a bell curve.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It was not enough to do well; you had to do better than your peers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And this would affect how you were streamed and posted to secondary school.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Over time, we have moved away from this.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We want to ignite our students' curiosity and spark their creativity so that they develop a love for learning that will stay with them even after they complete school.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We introduced multiple pathways to support students with various interests and strengths.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We want to cultivate in our students the right attitudes and dispositions beyond just pursuing academic excellence through our Character and Citizenship Education (CCE) curriculum and co-curricular activities (CCAs), students develop values and 21st Century Competencies.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: They learn to collaborate with one another, build teamwork, develop leadership.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We look out for students who may need more support.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Beyond school, we continue to encourage lifelong learning through SkillsFuture, because in a world that keeps changing ever faster, learning cannot stop once you leave school.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But as Prime Minister said yesterday, the reality is that our society is not entirely moved away from seeing education as an "arms race".

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And while CCAs and CCE are an important part of school life, I am sure many parents and students still do not see them as equally or more important than academic grades.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: That is not entirely surprising, because our traditional theory of success in Singapore is still weighted towards academic achievement.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: While we do want to strive for excellence, an overemphasis on academic grades can create unhealthy levels of competition, pressure and stress, rather than fostering a true love of learning on or focusing on things that matter.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And in an education "arms race", those whose families have more resources are likely to start ahead and then race even further ahead, while those who fall behind may struggle to catch up.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: As we face new and more complex challenges on the horizon, such as AI and social inequality, we must do more to break away from this concept of an education "arms race" and provide opportunities for our students to develop their talents and interests, regardless of starting point.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We will look at many ways to refresh our education system in line with the spirit of the Forward Singapore agenda.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We will study how to reduce the stakes in examinations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Examinations like the PSLE should not remain a high stakes checkpoint for students that is viewed as a determining factor for the trajectory of the rest of their lives.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Instead, we will focus on the more important aspects of our children's experiences in school – developing life skills, interpersonal relationships, good character and values and more.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And in the first half of my speech, I spoke about how, through ComLink+ and other measures, we collaborate more effectively as one.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We also recognise the importance of giving our children the opportunity to interact with peers from different backgrounds from a young age to prevent divisions along lines such as race, religion or socio-economic status.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Our schools and classrooms must continue to be a reflection of society, where people from different walks of life and backgrounds come together, not in cloistered communities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These are not easy changes and they will take time to implement.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Some of them may require us to fundamentally rethink some of our approaches to assessments, curriculum, learning and how we organise our education system, but they are necessary in the long term.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We will work closely with our parents, teachers, researchers, students, and the community, learn from other countries, and keep our focus on what matters most – the future of our children.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: At the core of this is one fundamental question: how do we help our children succeed in life.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Not by sending them to more tuition or enrichment classes, but by developing them holistically and empowering them to learn deeply, helping them to be confident about their strengths and interests, anchoring them in values, and developing them in the adaptability, resilience and determination to thrive in a world of change.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: They are opportunities to grow, to innovate, and to come together to define ourselves as a society.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, let us work together and build a future where every family thrives, every child can reach their fullest potential and every Singaporean has the opportunity to succeed.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: In his words, to put "we" before "me".

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: If "we first" is internalised as a core and innate value that all of us carry deeply as Singaporeans, if we teach "we first" early in our young and in our schools as part of their journey in education, as part of their core values and as part of our collective identity as Singaporeans, and if we echo and remind ourselves of the resonance of "we first" in all that we do, it would be a most powerful enabler for Singapore society on several fronts.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: I will elaborate on these in my speech.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: It informs us that to achieve the optimised collective potential of our society, to realise the full power of a whole that is far greater than the sum of all our parts, sometimes, the unitary parts may require some sub-optimisation and compromise.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: To be clear, in "we first", it is never about a bargaining of our core identity as a people nor the erosion of our diversity, but rather about embracing the process of finding our many points of synergy as a people and nurturing our harmony in concert with one another.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: In putting forward the "we" before "me", we harness the scale and potential capital of the collective and maximise its multiplier effect into our equation of Singapore society.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: First, as alluded to by other hon Members prior, social cohesion is a primary outcome we want to drive in putting the "we" before "me".

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: I have argued before in this House that in wanting to strengthen social cohesion, we must let it be experienced in our everyday and in our common spaces, in our schools, in our neighbourhoods, in our residential estates, in our work and in our play.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: We must enable this by design, in our young through our education curriculum, in our neighbourhoods through how we plan for our public estates and in the gamut of programmes in our workplaces and in our community.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: We must allow for the social interaction across differences to always occur and encourage different opportunities to meet, interface and most importantly, mix.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Like the proverbial melting pot holding the recipe of a brew, Mr Deputy Speaker, it requires a variety of different spices and ingredients to hold, at a constant stir, and it takes a while, for a blended fragrance to emerge.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Stop too early, it never quite works out.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Too few of any one particular ingredient makes the attempt flat.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Too long into the cooking or if we turn up the heat too soon or too late, the recipe eludes us.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Change the pot and the climate for the ingredients, a new approach and recipe would be required.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Each spice and ingredient in the recipe of social cohesion is unique and stands on its own different identity.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: We can taste each and every one of them in the final brew.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: No one tells us how to do our recipe because it is our kitchen.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Through "we first", we allow for a common space to hold us together across differences, whether by language, race, religion or age, to find the recipe for us and our Singapore society.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: We must be broad-based in our approaches, actively reach out to include everyone in our midst and work hard to keep our society close.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: A little tension and some discomfort can be expected.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Where there are emerging weak points to the social equilibrium over time, our natural response must be to honestly examine the issue at hand, to challenge prevailing assumptions and to ask ourselves if the policy remains relevant and what it is about this current recipe that needs tweaking moving forward.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: It does not mean we must agree all the time, but when we must disagree, respectful we remain in our exchanges and with an expressed mutual desire for co-collaboration or solutions that benefit all and for the greater good.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: I know it sounds like a stretched argument but let me explain.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: If we teach our young early in our schools and encourage every Singaporean to really live by the ethos of "we first", and guide them early to be comfortable in working with others different from us to achieve collaborative outcomes, to have the natural willingness and adaptability to together negotiate difficult problems and complex situations, and to recognise the power in working as a team for the greater good, surely, this is a desired trait that works to our advantage as a people.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Singaporeans are known as a competitive and hardworking lot, but through the spirit of "we first", if we are also known for our sense of community, our emotional intellect and our zeal to achieve fair consensus, the value we bring to any table becomes a potent force.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Our value proposition, to the workplace, to prospective employers and to other companies navigating the emerging economic challenges of the day, will rise.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Contrast this against the backdrop of societies today looking inwardly, polarising narratives online that centre around selfish and narrow ideals and a lack of willingness, or sometimes even ability to have deep, thoughtful conversations with nuance and to be comfortable in engaging complexity.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: If "we first" is personified in Singaporeans in finding solutions of tomorrow, we then become the natural team players, the future co-creators and the firm collaborators; the ones whom others can count on to look across the aisle to mediate, to discuss and to engage with comfortably.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: This tells others that Singaporeans make for excellent hires locally and abroad, and that our companies make for trusted and reliable partners in any market for any opportunity.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: When we juxtapose that same mindset to a national level and others recognise that Singapore is a country that is willing to work with others and achieve collective outcomes and that it is in our psyche and persona as a nation to see past ourselves and bring goodness and benefit to the world, Singapore then becomes a trusted partner and facilitator in the room.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: As a country, we never start with a hard-nosed view to negotiations, nor do we willy-nilly or haphazardly take positions.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Taking a "we first" view, we start from the considered and deliberate approach to, first, seeking to understand the different starting positions and others can appreciate that we have a reasonable willingness to negotiate and achieve mutual benefit, so long as it is fair and just.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: From dealings in foreign affairs, to trade and industry, to policy positions in the international stage and fora, this ethos of "we first" will carry us through as a nation, even in the most delicate of dealings and in the most turbulent of disagreements of the world. "We first" puts forth Singapore as a consistent, trusted, amiable and, dare I say, foremost partner and colleague of the international arena, whether in platforms such as the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) or United Nations, or even as a diplomatic arbiter towards consensus and peace between the larger powers of the world.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: In this space, we nurture a caring and values-driven society.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: We will still move with strength and at a keen cadence for our needs and for our future.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Others will know us as a society that is fiercely competitive but always with empathy and concern for the people who walk alongside and especially, towards those of less privilege. "We first" speaks of us a society that does not trample on others for our own gain, that we will not be a racehorse with blinkers and leave others in the dust in order to win at all costs.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: If we must succeed, we only do so with dignity and justice on our side.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: That it is more dignified to lose in fair play than to win dishonourably.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: That at work, a genuine concern for others percolates rather than to consider these traits as blameworthy on the basis of output alone.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: In our neighbourhoods, that we exercise some understanding and flexibility with one another, as well as a give and take in our common spaces.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: That, in our own actions, what we say and how we go about our day to day, we maintain a care and awareness of how others may be impacted by our own actions.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: That when we take the lift and we interface with our neighbours, a good morning greeting or a "how are you" helps break the ice, brings warmth to another and nurtures friendships in our midst.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: And certainly, Mr Deputy Speaker, the shine of our care for situations and people, and the values driven by our ethos of "we first" knows no boundary or border.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: A "we first" society means we are not passive bystanders.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: We bring forth our care and values as part of who we are as a society in service for a better family, a better community, a better country and a better world.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: (In Malay): Mr Deputy Speaker, as we encourage and enable the adoption of "we first", it is actually very much aligned and in sync with the heartbeat of our community.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: The way we care for one another is captured in a Malay saying, "When one part of the body is unwell, other parts feel it too.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: If the right thigh is pinched, the left thigh will also hurt".

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Whenever we come across someone burdened with life's challenges, financial difficulties, isolation and profound hardship, our community's instinct is to act spontaneously to help and show concern.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: This feeling of mutual responsibility, compassion and care towards one another comes naturally to us.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Similarly, we are attuned to the values of solidarity and cooperation to achieve prosperity together.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: While we call upon Singaporeans to embrace the "we first" thinking, our heritage and culture demands that we ensure success and progress should not merely celebrate personal achievements, but we must use them to benefit others.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, our culture which advocates giving back to society is consistent with the phrase "we first".

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: In this regard, "we first" is not solely the Government's responsibility.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: It also involves cooperation with the private sector, businesses and community organisations to collectively strengthen and expand the assistance required to meet the community's needs.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: There are clear examples within our Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Fundraising for madrasahs and mosques, for community organisations, for those in need in Singapore and for the oppressed in Gaza – all of these also embody "we first".

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, the "we first" spirit advocated by the Government has resulted in progress for our community.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: These are community members who feel grateful and who have gone on to have careers, and made it their life's mission and vision to continue contributing to the next generation. "We first" is actually deeply rooted and ingrained in our community.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: It is part of our values and beliefs, a long-standing inclination which ensures that, as a collective, we look after one another and care about what happens around us.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: This is our strength as a community and it is something we must continue to nurture, strengthen and build together in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: We have benefited from the work of those who have come before us and have themselves taken the ethos of "we first" for our benefit today.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: In turning 60, our success as a nation stems from the effort of early Singaporeans from decades ago.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Our past leaders who in their wisdom and acumen put our country first.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Our teachers who sowed the first seeds of knowledge in the generation that came after.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Our parents who toiled time and effort and put their children first.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: And what of our public sector and civil servants who continue to ensure our essential services keep going today?

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Of our uniformed servicemen and servicewomen who keep the peace to give us a strong base from which we can leap forward and achieve more as a country.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: And of the healthcare workers who save lives day in and day out and keep us well.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: All their efforts, Mr Deputy Speaker, embody the spirit of "we first".

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: We should never let arrogance creep in and allow ourselves to assume that our success comes only as a result of our own efforts.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Many have sacrificed for us to be here where we are today as a people and country.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: If we ponder on the term "we first", examples are well and alive around us but, perhaps, as a society, we can do better to enable, to acknowledge, to encourage and to appreciate them.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Philanthropy and volunteering for a community cause is "we first".

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Mentorship to nurture confidence in our young is "we first".

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Saving for a rainy day and ensuring we have sufficient Reserves for generations to come is "we first".

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Addressing climate change for a better tomorrow and environment is "we first".

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: And having tough laws against the scourge of drugs to protect our families is "we first".

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: If there is no "we first", we will, instead, be pulling from multiple polar and opposing ends, and the tension will fray and tear us apart into lonely factions and singular isolated pieces that will not stand against the wind.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Worse still, instead of the beautiful societal tapestry to be admired, we could be left with tattered and torn pieces beyond repair.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: We must continue to passionately mend, to work on, to preserve and to double stitch our social fabric, now more than ever.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is with deep humility and also with deep gratitude, that I deliver my maiden speech in this House.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: When I first knocked on doors in Pasir Ris-Changi, many residents did not just share their problems or feedback; they shared their lives with me.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: A working mom told me how she struggled everyday juggling her job and caring for her toddler and father who now has dementia.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: An elderly couple on Pulau Ubin spoke about their pride in keeping the island's heritage alive, even with inconveniences that come with living on the island.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And a group of youths at Changi Beach showed me the tidal pools with such wonder, reminding me how much they care about the world we live in.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: These conversations left a very deep impression on me.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: They remind me that behind every policy, every statistics, there are real people with genuine struggles and hopes.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And they are the very reason why I stand here today.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: For my maiden speech, I wish to focus on three groups of people who are especially close to my heart.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: First, the sandwiched generation, whose burdens I personally felt as a daughter, a mother and a working professional.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Second, those living at the edge of our country, whom I have come to know very fondly through my time at Pasir Ris-Changi, from the offshore island of Ubin to where the East-West line ends at Pasir Ris Town.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And lastly, the younger generation, whose future depends on how we safeguard the environment we leave behind.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, let me begin with the sandwiched generation.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Singaporeans who are raising children while caring for ageing parents, often while juggling work, housing loans and rising costs.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: They are doing everything "right", working hard, paying taxes, supporting their families.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Yet, many carry a heavy and unseen load and, at times, everything can feel so "wrong" and so overwhelming.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I have experienced a glimpse of this myself.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In the same year that I welcomed my newborn, my father was diagnosed with cancer.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Those days were split between baby care, work and hospital appointments.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Fast forward to just this year, whenever my toddler falls sick, I often catch the same illnesses, from the common flu to hand, foot and mouth disease (HFMD).

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And I know Minister of State Jasmin Lau and her children's book of choice is "Paw Patrol", I think there were many books being introduced in this Chamber.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Mine is "Bizzy Bear" and I must have gone through the entire series more than five times throughout the entire HFMD episode.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: While I am now an expert at reciting Bizzy Bear stories, this had knock-on effects on my work and my community engagements.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But I was able to get through those moments with a supportive family, both at home and at work, and I am very grateful for them.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But I know of many Singaporeans do not have this safety net.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: For many, the load is far heavier: caring for parents with chronic illnesses, raising several children, taking on extra responsibilities at work just to keep the job and to pay the bills, and then receiving news that a loved one has dementia.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Their sacrifices are greater and I feel deeply for them.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: A child's vulnerable years do not end after infancy.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Parents need time, flexibility and support through toddlerhood and early schooling.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And when it comes to caring for ageing parents, many families shoulder equally heavy burdens, from weekly hospital visits for dialysis and chemotherapy, to providing daily supervision for parents with dementia, often while holding full-time jobs.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Caregiving should never ever come at the cost of one's career.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: One should feel no fear of repercussions for choosing a hospital visit with an aged parent over a day at the office.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: One should feel no guilt for staying home to care of a sick child.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Perhaps even a distinct "Sandwich Generation Leave"; for the lack of a better name; separate from childcare or medical leave.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We can also strengthen the national mental health and support services to help families navigate the maze of dual caregiving.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And it requires cultivating workplace cultures that value families as much as productivity.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Because at the heart of it, strong families are the foundation of a strong Singapore.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: They are custodians of our living heritage, yet they face higher electricity tariffs than us on mainland and at times, have difficulty accessing national schemes.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But to this end, I am grateful to have agencies that have actively stepped in to explore how to close these gaps when pointed out – the National Parks Board, the Energy Market Authority, People's Association and the National Environment Agency.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It gives me reassurance that I am working with partners that genuinely care for the people.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Known to many as a leisure spot, but for many residents and business owners, it is their home and livelihood.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: While the rest of Singapore progresses, Changi Village often feels overlooked.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Roadworks have worsened access and businesses are struggling.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Its experience reminds us that progress cannot be measured only by what happens at the centre, while the edges are left behind.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I am often asked, "Why do you care so much for small communities like Ubin and Changi Village?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Why do you turn up there so often?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: There is no "political mileage" in doing that." But as Parliamentarians, our duty extends beyond representing the majority.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is to ensure that those on the margins are seen, are heard and are supported.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: They too feel the pressures of progress; in their case, more than they bargained for.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And these "edges" are not just geographical, like what I described.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In different seasons of life, many of us find ourselves on the margins, living with rare diseases, facing infertility, or struggling quietly in ways that statistics may never capture.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: If we focus solely on numbers, we risk forgetting what matters most – that we are all Singaporeans, with diverse needs, deserving of care, attention and inclusion.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Lastly, let me speak about our shared environment.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But rapid urbanisation has left many feeling we live in a dense, hot, concrete city.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Let us not forget: we aspired to be a City in a Garden – not just a garden in a city.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But this is not a call to halt development, but a call for balance.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Every hectare we reclaim, every tree we fell, comes at a cost.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And this price will be paid for by generations after us.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: On National Day this year, upon their invitation, I joined Julian and Xiao Yun, for an intertidal walk at Changi Beach.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: They were the two young Singaporeans who raised the petition, calling for HDB to scale back its plans for the Changi reclamation project.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Honestly, I was half expecting them to quiz me about my stand on the project but it turns out, all they wanted was to share the magical intertidal pools with me.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: So, together with dozens of youths and families who were miraculously all awake at 4.00 am, we walked through the intertidal pools for two solid hours, spotting stingrays, anemones and starfish, and ended the morning at Changi Village over a breakfast of nasi lemak, "youtiao" and wanton mee.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I learnt much from the group about the unique seagrass meadow that grows along Changi Beach and we exchanged views on how the stakeholder engagement process for development projects like these can be better.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It dawned upon me – that if we want to steer our youths away from despair, or even from vaping, for them to not feel so disconnected, then we must give them causes that matter, not more rules, not more red tape, not more suspensions.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Nature can be that sanctuary, that classroom and that source of resilience where they can find that purpose.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Environmental protection is not a trend, it is an opportunity.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: An opportunity to invest in the wellbeing, identity and future of our youth.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: These are not isolated issues, they are strands of a single fabric that binds us as Singaporeans.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: After all, Singapore was not a nation of choice, but no choice.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Our Pioneers overcame the challenges of the day and built an exceptional multicultural nation – one that we are proud of.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Today, we stand at another important crossroads in history.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: As President and many Members have said, the global order that Singapore has thrived in, is changing.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Geopolitical tensions and tariff wars are raising prices everywhere.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: These difficult economic conditions have led to a rising tide of individualism and "me first" mentalities all around the world.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: The 2025 Edelman Trust Barometer reports that more than six in 10 global respondents feel a deep sense of grievance; that for someone to win, somebody else must lose.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Elsewhere, the 2024 Gallup World Poll reports significant drops in global activities that put others before self; volunteering, donating, helping strangers.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: There are also strong social forces that pull us apart.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Social media ironically, can drive a wedge between us, because algorithms are designed to make us stay online longer by showing us more of what we want to see.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: And we end up being trapped in larger echo chambers and more polarised societies, as many Members have pointed out.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: And we see a loss of social cohesion in many countries, fracturing societies from within.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: As a small, global, hyperconnected city, we will be subjected to the harshest of these pressures.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Our unity will be tested, in a changed world.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: You heard some of these from Prime Minister.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: As the saying goes, amidst order, look for change.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: As we stand at SG60 in a changed world, we are Pioneers once again.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: And we can learn from our Pioneer and Merdeka Generations, as we forge our way forward in the changed world.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Through conversations from when we first started the Pioneer Generation Office, to more recent Project Citizens, our founding generation cited multiculturalism, boldness and service to others before self, as some of the shared values that made us exceptional.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Seniors who lived through the 1964 racial riots recounted how they shared food with neighbours, regardless of race, language or religion – a reminder of the importance of our unity in a moment of darkness in our history.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: And we are one of the very few places in this world where anybody can have a fair chance in life, regardless of where they start.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: We need to do more, to expand our common space, increase social mobility and build a "we first" society to strengthen our unity.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Our pledge begins with a simple word – "we".

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: We build our national identity on top of, not in place of, our individual diverse cultures.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: We are intentional in protecting and expanding this common space that we share as Singaporeans.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Spaces where Singaporeans can come together, interact and bond across socio-economic, ability and cultural divides.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Where we cultivate an inner curiosity to know more about one another.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: And we need to welcome people from all backgrounds, so we know what it feels like to walk a mile in their shoes.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: So, we can make decisions and trade-offs that are better for everyone.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: We must place a special focus on our youths, for they are the architects of a more cohesive Singapore to come.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: While our youths are the most digitally connected generation, they risk becoming the most socially disconnected in real life.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: In other words, where we saw no more than one student in each classroom with no close friends, today, we see two or three.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: We need to tap on the universal language of sports, arts and heritage to build bonds for our youths.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: In 2023, three schools formed one football team – Boon Lay, Methodist Girls' and Westwood Secondary.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: On their own, they did not quite have enough players, but together, they formed the team.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: They trained together three times a week under the School Football Academy Programme.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: And last month, they claimed their first National School Games title.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: And the girls proved that on the football field, with a common goal, school badges faded away.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: They became a "we", and that "we" succeeded in their pursuit of their dream.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: We want to get more students to unite through sports and to play together.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Pin Xiu’s win is a powerful testament to the strength of the human spirit and the importance of building an inclusive society.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: It helps us see diversity not as a barrier but as a source of strength.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: MCCY will deepen our efforts to build an inclusive society across all domains.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: We will also do more to make the arts another platform to unite young Singaporeans, especially in multicultural art forms.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: An example is the recent production of Tempest and Tranquility, by Siong Leng Musical Association, in collaboration with Young Artist Award recipient Nawaz Mirajkar, who is a renowned tabla musician.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: There was a perfect blend of Nanyin and Indian music and dance forms.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: I quote a review by Dr Chang Tou Liang, a prominent music reviewer. "When the two musics coalesced in composer Ng Kang Kee’s sensitive arrangements, it did not matter which was Chinese or which was Indian.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: They simply became one in soul and spirit." And that is what we want our people to be – one in soul and spirit.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: And we stand at almost 100,000 square metres of arts housing to support our vibrant arts groups.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: They, in turn, have doubled our performance activities to almost 13,000.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: It is this outreach that will allow our Singaporeans to understand, appreciate and feel what it means to have the soul of the nation.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: And I also want to thank this House for your continued support for our arts, heritage and cultural groups, for indeed, they play a very strong role in helping us understand what it means to be Singaporean.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Beyond the arts, we also need to bring our understanding of diversity and common space from textbooks into everyday life.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Last month, Minister for Education Desmond Lee and I joined students in Mayflower Secondary School for their CCE class on racial harmony.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Our students told me what was more important than classroom learning, was to take action.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Practise little acts that strengthen racial harmony in their daily lives and create the positive school culture that this House spoke about.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Be the change that we want to see.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Looking ahead, we will create even more of these opportunities for conversations and social mixing amongst our youths to foster mutual understanding.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Second, we must ensure that Singapore remains a place where everyone can succeed, regardless of where we start in life.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: This is not an ideal – this is the story of Singaporeans, many seated in this House, myself included.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: We must do what we can to keep social mobility alive, and help every Singaporean fulfil their fullest potential.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: That includes giving every Singaporean opportunities, uplifting individuals and developing different pathways to success.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: A former Normal (Academic) student, Clarence and his friends felt that barriers – invisible ones, such as a lack of networks and opportunities – held back students from disadvantaged backgrounds.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: With just a handful of university volunteers, he knocked on the doors of schools and companies to initiate programmes such as career guidance and industry attachments.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Because he believes that everyone should have a fair chance in life.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: And Access Singapore grew from a small volunteer group to an organisation with over 150 staff, volunteers and facilitators, uplifting 3,000 students across more than 30 schools.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: MCCY will continue to work with Access Singapore on its mission to improve social mobility.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Be the change that we want to see.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: And we need to broaden our definition of success.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Our youths tell us they want to redefine success and be empowered to chase their dreams whether in the arts, sports, or other fields.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: And we will be there to support them.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: In Tampines, my resident Yazrul and his childhood friends started Sporting Tampines, a community football club with a big dream.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: They want to build a community anchored on a shared love for football.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: And they started in June this year and now have 44 members who participate in both competitive and social games.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: They have made great strides as a new team, having played international friendly matches and also secured corporate sponsors.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: I arranged for the good people behind Unleash The Roar! to meet with Yazrul and his team to see how we can better support their dreams to play on a much larger stage.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Who knows, one day, you will see "Welcome to Tampines" on Netflix.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Ainslee credits her success to the strong team behind her – the high-performance sports fraternity, her coaches, and most importantly her family and friends – and this gives her the confidence to pursue her dreams.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: One question I got from Ainslee and other youths breaking new ground in sports such as diving and Tchoukball, was why they were not recognised in the Singapore Schools Sports Council Colours Award when they represented Singapore, unlike their friends in swimming or track and field.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: It is a question that their parents and coaches, and some of our Members in this House have asked me as well.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Since I am both in MCCY and MOE, I thought we could do better to recognise our youths like Ainslee who are breaking new ground, taking the road less travelled and chasing their dreams.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: So, Ainslee and Team Singapore divers and artistic swimmers who represented us in the recent World Aquatics Championships will all be recognised alongside our swimmers.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: MOE will share more details on this in due course.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: And to Member David Hoe, not to worry, ActiveSG Credits for dual-use facilities is also on my to-do list.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Similarly, in the arts, practitioners like Muhammad Muazzam, or Zam as we call him, are redefining the role of the arts in community building.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Zam believes that the future of Singapore’s arts scene lies in its ability to bring value to other sectors.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: So, to all our young people, be bold, take the road less travelled and chase your dreams.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: And we will be with you every step of the way.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: To be clear, it does not mean that we abandon "me".

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Building a strong "we first" culture means understanding that the "we" and "me" are inextricably linked.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: That when "me" succeeds, it is often because it got a hand up from "we".

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: In turn, "me", must also give back and contribute to "we".

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: At Woodlands Regional Library, I spoke to one of our Project Citizens participants, Mr Dennis Tan, who was in primary school, during the 1964 racial riots.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Dennis recalls there being a lot of misinformation and untruths spread through rumours and gossips, and he did not know what to believe or to expect.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Despite this, people in the kampung put their neighbours first by housing them at night when the curfews kicked in – regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Everyone must play a part in building a "we first" Singapore, whether individuals, community groups, or corporates.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: We want to nurture this mindset amongst our youths.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: At Youth Corps Singapore, we support our youths to take tangible steps to put others before self.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: I met Hannah Batrisyia, one of our youth volunteers.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Her journey started with a three-day leadership camp in 2019, which kindled her passion to put others before self.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Today, while pursuing her Master's degree, she leads multiple projects to benefit the community.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: This December, she is also leading a Youth Expedition Project to go overseas to make a difference to a community in our region.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Like Hannah, many of our youths feel a sense of purpose and they resonate with the call to build a “we first” Singapore.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: We will continue to make it easy for our youths to step up to put "we" before "me", and my Ministry will continue to give our youths a voice, a space, a platform and a space to make a difference.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: To build a Singapore they will be proud to inherit.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: When people are empowered to make a difference, it builds a virtuous cycle of care, trust and collective responsibility.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: And when we all put "we" before "me", we build a better Singapore.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Let us move forward together with a new spirit.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Or a phrase that we are more familiar with: "Marilah kita bersatu,dengan semangat yang baru".

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: As Benjamin Kheng puts it – "If we just look to each other, then this house will feel like home.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: And the more we’re together, the further we’ll go." Let us go further, together.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: (In Mandarin): Facing a world of constant change and an unstable international situation, SG60 is like the juncture during Singapore's founding days – fraught with thorns and obstacles.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Let us learn from the spirit of unity and dedication of our Pioneer and Merdeka generations.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Together with the younger generation, we stride towards a new world.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, I support the Motion.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In a turbulent world, the President's address offers a renewal of faith.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It calls us towards a "we first" society built on the enduring pillars of unity and trust.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is a powerful and essential vision for our nation's next bound, but let us be clear, the fulfilment of that promise does not begin here in this Chamber.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It begins with us in our local communities in the enduring efforts of one Singaporean reaching out to another.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Prior to being a Member of Parliament, I was known as the "Ah Boy" of Geylang.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I grew up there all my life and had a different perspective of the world, one not easily found in textbooks or policy papers.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I saw the complexity of life and met neighbours known to society only by their labels – the nightlife workers, the troubled youths and ex-convicts trying to hold on.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The temptation is to see their lives in black and white, a simple failure of law and order.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But as a neighbour, I saw something else.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I saw human beings resulting to vice, often because they lack options or were escaping a reality much worse.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I learned that we cannot fix what is broken until we recognise the shared humanity in every single individual.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It was with that same understanding that I spent my weekends in 2014, in the back alleys of Geylang, with migrant workers playing badminton, sharing a meal and seeing their sacrifice and commitment to family thousands of miles away.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When my friend, Nurul Bashar from Bangladesh, was counting his every last dollar for his father's urgent surgery, I did what any friend would.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I picked up a pair of scissors, learned from YouTube and offered him a free haircut.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That small act of care grew into a volunteer movement.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I learned the most profound change does not need a massive budget, but sometimes a pepper of courage and a generous serving of human connection.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the lorongs in Geylang, empathy was an emotion I understood long before I ever learnt its name, and it is this fundamental truth that shared human connection that must guide our work today.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Having managed active ageing centres, I have seen the importance of Healthier SG across Singapore and I am grateful for the inter-agency collaboration between MND on the hardware refresh and MOH on the software integration of programming.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is not just our population that is ageing, but our flats too.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Toa Payoh is the first satellite town comprehensively planned and developed in 1965 by HDB.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many of the flats are seniors in age too.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Residents are anxious of their homes and worry about the uncertainty of timing, the future value of their flat and its remaining lease.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many also face the daily realities of defects and look forward to repairs and upgrades through the Home Improvement Programme.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This sentiment is echoed by many seniors I have met, including two pioneers of community building in Toa Payoh Central, Mr Chia Ah Sah, aged 79; and Mr Raman, aged 75.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chia shared, "We are poor, but some people are in even worse situations and so we help." This simple belief of a heart-to-heart service has remained consistent over the past 40 years.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The love and attachment to the community has only grown.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But how do we create more Mr Ramans and Mr Chias?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Like many in the Chamber, I have joined many seniors for workouts, outings and health screenings to discover this answer.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Instead, I have learned extraordinary secrets, what I describe as "non-Google-ables".

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Secrets about the precise herbal ingredients in a 药材汤, or herbal soup, to cure a cold for my pregnant wife; hacks to stretch their dollar, like knowing which store at the wet market, or cai png, economy rice stall offers the best value for money.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They know the latest hack of getting NTUC discounts and the ways to get CDC vouchers from task.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They can also tell you the history behind a street name or the location of a building long gone much faster than ChatGPT can.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And not to mention, advice on a good long-lasting marriage and how I should spend more time with my wife and two children.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is the collective wisdom of a lived experience.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In our communities, seniors rally around one another to celebrate milestones and turn to one another for support in times of grief and sadness, just as friends and family do.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They exist not just as individuals in a neighbourhood, but as a living library of knowledge, and together form a powerful resilient community.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How can the narrative of growing old then be reframed, not as a liability, but as an opportunity to live again.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: After giving their all for decades to work and raising a family, how can we encourage the cultivation and nurturing of new passions, creative talents and entrepreneurship projects through their existing strengths and knowledge?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are experiences that hold our communities together.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Let us ensure our seniors live their final years with dignity, purpose and a good quality of life.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, empathy for the vulnerable must also be at the heart of what we do as Parliamentarians.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I recently journeyed with Toa Payoh residents Ryan and Rae Mok, whose daughter, Rachael, was born with a rare chromosome disorder and had high-care needs.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At the 12th edition this year, I met 31 children with high-care needs and their families, and a village of many helping hands – from extended families to corporate volunteers and medical staff.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As a mother, Rae's journey was one of incredible resilience, and the generosity she received from others spurred her to create a community of support for what would otherwise be an isolating caregiving journey.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As representatives, these are moments of clarity that strengthen our resolve to speak up and I will do so, for caregivers and persons with disabilities, in this House.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The resilience of a society is tested during a pandemic, a crisis, and we are only as strong as the weakest link.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This was evident during the pandemic when the spotlight shone on essential workers and the vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: During the pandemic, I worked as a care staff in a nursing home, assigned to a ward of 16 males.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The daily routine of care was visceral, was intimate and it was intense.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This includes changing their diapers, showering, wound dressing, and managing cognitive conditions and difficult behaviour, on a 24/7 shift-work basis.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It gave me a deeper appreciation for the labour of care, and I admired my colleagues, a largely migrant workforce, but also realised the unaccounted cost of care and trade-offs that family members might make when they choose to undertake caregiving personally.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With love and dedication and devotion which may undergird their decision, many may feel unprepared and helpless too.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must make help visible and accessible and offer it proactively.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must better honour filial piety through stories, and those who choose to personally undertake this responsibility.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must rightfully account for the value these caregivers contribute to our society.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This labour of care does not stop at caregivers to seniors or persons with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must find ways to improve the coordination of our services and close help-seeking time gaps.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This ensures our system can be effective in what is intended to do to deliver compassionate assistance to our people in their moments of need.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The spirit of empathy is the very fabric of our neighbourhoods.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But for our communities to thrive, the systems that support them must be equally compassionate.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Beyond economic calculations, we need to consider the accurate accounting of what truly makes a society strong.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For too long, relational elements like the immense contributions of caregivers and the cultural values of our heritage have been hard to quantify and, thus, undervalued in our balance sheets.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The first being our home; the second being the workplace; and the third, the place which is the anchor of community life, which facilitates and fosters broader and more creative interactions.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They can be in the form of communal social nodes, places like void decks, hawker centres, coffee shops or parks.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As we aspire to improve health-span and the quality of life, we must first ask ourselves what exactly is a life well lived and how do we want to age?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The World Health Organization quality of life measurement assesses a person from the physical, psychological, social relationship and environmental perspectives.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It acknowledges that humans are multidimensional and, therefore, measures various domains of life, not just the absence of illness.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How do we measure the friendships between friends and neighbours?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How do we quantify the psychological pain of a senior who might be leaving a familiar community due to a relocation and the cost to their health?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How do we communicate with one another the sense of loss at the mergers of our schools, or the closure of our favourite youth hangout or even the place where we used to date.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Third places tying closely with the sense of belonging and forms a key part of our identity.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Impact assessments provide some economic measurements towards this, and I am glad that the Government has adopted features of environmental impact assessments in redevelopment works.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am not sure how the age range of our Parliamentarians will be by then, but as the youngest male PAP Member in the 15th Parliament, by then, I will be 60.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What will Singapore be in 2050 when we celebrate SG75?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The country each generation inherits is determined by the actions of the previous one.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am deeply aware that the country my children inherit will be determined by the actions we take now.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The President's address has set a clear direction for our nation and it is up to us to embody that vision.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Let us respond to the needs of our community with purpose and empathy.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Let us build a future where every Singaporean feels seen, heard and valued, a society that truly makes efforts to care for the last, the lost and the least.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And I say with conviction, let our generation respond, in optimism and hope.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I am forever grateful to Prime Minister Wong for reminding us, in his speech yesterday, that a "we first" society is one that values solidarity even as we recognise our differences.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: His words resonate deeply with me, for in my own journey into politics is rooted in a simple belief: when I lift and when we lift others, we all rise together.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I had just left my role as an auditor and was fully occupied with business.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: One day, quite by chance, a business contact around my age invited me to a meet-the-people session over in Fengshan.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Out of curiosity, I accepted the invitation, thinking that it would be just an ordinary evening, a bit of letter writing, perhaps observing how MPs and the volunteers help residents.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I remember my very first case, seated next to the interviewer with my hands on the computer all ready to type.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: An elderly woman walked in, distraught and sad.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: She spoke only in Hokkien and for some reason clutched ever so tightly to my hand, as though I was her last hope.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Her son had failed to enlist into National Service.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: She was struggling to deal with the consequences of that mistake, on top of pressing financial difficulties.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I can still recall the look in her eyes – worry, mixed with shame, a deep sense of desperation and hope that someone might listen and help her, for this burden, she cannot carry alone anymore.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I realised then I had a heart for service which I never knew that existed.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: And so, week after week, I returned to serve.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: The problems were not always easy to solve.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But every story and every one of them mattered to me.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Each resident reminded me that service is not about recognition, but about presence.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: It is not about being served but about serving.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: That elderly woman, in her quiet way, became my first teacher in politics.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: She taught me more in one evening about the dignity of service than any textbook or boardroom ever could.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Along the way, I was truly blessed with mentors who not only shaped my journey but also shaped the person I have become.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: One of them was our former Transport Minister and MP for Fengshan, Mr Raymond Lim.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: He showed me that leadership can be calm, rational and humble.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Despite his position, he always treated the residents and volunteers as equals and never gave the impression that he was above them all.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I remember sitting beside him at Meet the People sessions.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Some came in angry, very angry, some confused, some in tears.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: And he listened, always with patience, always with respect, never raising his voice, never hurry them along.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: From him, I learnt that true leadership is not about titles, but about service.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: It is about lifting others so that they all can stand tall together.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: My parents, in their practical way, told me: "If you choose this path, 'mai kao peh' (in Hokkien).

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Just do it, do not complain."   My mother urged me to sign up for party membership, reminding me that Singapore had given our family much and it was only right to give back when the country asked for it.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: My husband, quietly yet steadfastly, shouldered more of the caregiving duties at home so that I can give my time to serving others.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
