text: (In Mandarin): Mr Speaker, in President Tharman's Address on the Government's policies, he emphasised that our country needs to build a diverse "we first" society.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: I believe that to achieve this goal, we must work hard to take care of Singaporeans' needs at every stage of life.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: In Nee Soon South, my goal is to ensure that seniors remember every day to "move their hands and speak up, move their feet and exercise their minds." We want to encourage the elderly to be more independent and healthier, able to remain active in the community, moving their hands to participate in activities and interacting to make more friends.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: We must also make the community more senior-friendly, allowing the elderly to move their feet to go around with friends and exercise their minds to stay mentally sharp, even initiating activities to engage more elderly friends.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Another group I particularly care about is our "Senior Youths", Singaporeans in their 20s and 30s, of which I am also a part.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Singaporeans of this age suddenly discover one day that we too have become so-called adults, facing real-world challenges.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Some may have just entered the society, others may have just started families, trying to find their footing in this uncertain world.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: We hope to fulfil our responsibilities as children to our parents, or as new parents ourselves, whilst also hoping to advance in our careers and achieve our ideals and aspirations.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Many Senior Youths have told me that the roles of caregiver and working professional often present a difficult choice, but I do not think this is inevitable.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that the Government can provide more support – whether it is more childcare leave or more employers providing better work arrangements – we can do our best to help Singaporeans of this age group balance family and career.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore is moving towards a “we first” society.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: I am very grateful to Nee Soon residents for giving our Nee Soon GRC team this opportunity to be your representatives.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: As a Nee Soon family, it is always residents first.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: They have more computing power in their handphones than many of us have had in our personal computers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Growing up, they are well-educated, well-travelled, healthy and likely to live till their mid to late 80s.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Our reserves and income generated from our investments mean that the majority of Singaporeans do not pay income tax.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We are investing heavily in infrastructure, including in homes and hospitals.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: At the same time, the world is being remade, today is possibly the most uncertain and fragile of times.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Unforeseen, perhaps in nature and direction of change but certainly in speed and in belligerence.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Today can also seem like the worst of times, with rising costs, lower job security and continuing uncertainty.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We are not going back to the golden age of globalisation but Singapore and young Singaporeans can continue to flourish and prosper if we take the right steps now – and we have to do it now.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Today, I would like to speak up for my young residents as well as young jobseekers nationwide.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: They are coming of age in a weak market.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Like all of us, they suffer from the economic uncertainties following the American tariff announcements.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: If the economy goes into recession for a protracted period, it could result in a generation stuck in a cycle of unemployment, career frustration and lost opportunities, or we can turn this crisis into an opportunity for young people by creating new roles in the economy.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Job postings are down 15% or the number of applications has risen by 30%.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In Singapore, the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) released unemployment data.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We are in the calm before the storm ahead during my house visits and walkabouts.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: I spoke with many young undergraduates facing difficulties getting internships.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: University and polytechnic graduates had sent up more than 100 resumes but still they cannot secure a job offer.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: I hear their struggles and concerns especially those from less well-off families who need to contribute to family expenses and pay off their study loans.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Also, from my discussions with human resources (HR) professionals and from recruitment firms feedback many companies are freezing headcounts.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Employers, including government agencies, are offering only one- to two-year contract roles, not permanent roles.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: That is the nature of the market now.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: What more can we do to help the jobseekers?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: I want to talk about a very specific plug-in that will allow young Singaporeans to meet an immediate and tangible need.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: At the recent Institute of Policy Studies and Singapore Business Federation (IPS-SBF) conference, Prime Minister Wong said that "Singapore will have to put more thought into helping businesses, especially smaller ones, harness the use of artificial intelligence in their work processes." Artificial intelligence (AI) is now a general-purpose tool, powerful and highly accessible.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: However, the bottleneck is not in the availability of AI as a resource but in corporate attention.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The problem is that many small and medium enterprises (SMEs) wish to transform their businesses but they are not familiar with AI tools available and they do not have the funds to hire consultants.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: My proposal is for the Government to provide funding, train up young people with AI tools that will help businesses reduce costs, automate work processes and increase their marketing efforts to drive sales.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Today, there are already AI tools that can help businesses achieve these objectives.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: What our SMEs need are young people who are digital natives and adept in this AI tools to reduce repetitive manual work and boost efficiencies in their businesses and operations.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: This AI change agents could undertake a project-based assignment to help companies.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: They can introduce AI tools into their systems and work processes.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: They could customise the AI tools according to the nature of the business and the goals set by the management team.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Upon the completion of the assignment and armed with the implementation experience, they can then move on to another company to help the next company with similar AI driven transition and transformation.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Alternatively, if the companies find the young change agents valuable to their businesses, they may go on to hire them and perhaps as their in-house AI officers together.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The AI change agents and SMEs can create a win-win collaboration and drive an AI powered business transformation in our SMEs.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In fact, there are university and polytechnic graduates who sent more than 100 resumes but were still unable to secure any job offer.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: I hear their struggles and concerns, especially those from less well-off families, who need to contribute to family expenses and pay off their study loans.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: However, this crisis can be seen as an opportunity.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Young people trained in using artificial intelligence (AI) tools can help to digitise and automate many company processes.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: By funding the AI courses and supporting the hiring of young people as AI Change Agents by the SMEs, the Government can catalyse SMEs business transformation and strengthen our country's economic competitiveness. : It has been almost six months since the "Liberation Day" tariff announcement.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We need partners to do this quickly and effectively and so I offer a simple sketch of this scheme which I call which I call "AI traineeship".

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: I should clarify that the AI traineeship is different from the GRaduate Industry Traineeship that was announced by Prime Minister Lawrence Wong at the National Day Rally.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: It is also different from Infocomm Media Development Authority’s (IMDA’s) company-led training, which has included generative AI (gen AI) technical skills and competencies for AI users and practitioners.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The National Trades Union Congress' (NTUC's) Employment and Employability Institute (e2i) can work with AI training companies and run training courses for this 1,000 batches.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: It will typically take two to four weeks to master this AI tools.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Thereafter, e2i will match this trained AI change agents to SMEs who are keen to automate their business processes.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The Government will then fund e2i to run these courses.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: There are more than 200,000 SMEs in Singapore so we should start with the medium enterprises in the manufacturing industry which may be most impacted by the American tariff hikes.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In Sembawang West, I have started a pilot programme working with e2i and AI training companies with the relevant business AI tools.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We plan to start the first run in the next few weeks for young jobseekers, keen to equip themselves with new AI skills.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Meantime, we are also in early discussion with Singapore Manufacturing Federation and food manufacturing companies in the Woodlands Industrial area, situated next to my constituency.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We hope to shortlist these companies and others who are keen to hire these AI change agents as our ground-up initiative.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: After one or two successful pilots, we can consider scaling this up at the national level.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: (In Mandarin):   The world is being disrupted severely by geopolitical tensions, US tariffs and the advent of Artificial Intelligence (AI).

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Many businesses are holding back hiring because of uncertainties.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Hence, young graduates are unable to find jobs in this soft market.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: I propose for the Government to turn this crisis into opportunity.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Young people trained in using AI tools to digitise and automate many administrative processes, can help SMEs improve their business costs, expand marketing and increase their revenue.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: I hope the Government will consider carefully my proposal for this win-win collaboration, that will strengthen our SMEs and equip our young people with practical AI skill sets. : We need to move quickly on this scheme so that young people do not lose more time looking for jobs.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Otherwise, it will become even harder when later cohorts join the workforce.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The last recession was in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Our Government responded swiftly and decisively, using our Reserves to cushion impact on jobs and livelihood with the Job Support Scheme and the Self-Employed Person Income Relief Schemes.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: It is a different world now with the advent of AI and we should make the best use of these opportunities.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: They do the traditional core functions of marketing, administration and corporate planning.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: But now, they are supercharged with the power of AI.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: So, this training scheme is not a way to disguise unemployment or to provide a temporary band aid.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: It is to perform a vital function – to jumpstart a structural transformation of our economy.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In a recent forum with National University of Singapore students, Senior Minister Lee warned young people of the challenges coming their way.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Even as they could take advantage of AI and better education, they had to be, "prepared psychologically for things which human beings do to one another, like great rivalry in power and things which human beings do to the world, such as global warming.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: You did not live through the founding crisis of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: But your challenges will come." Mr Speaker, our challenge has come.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: But in some ways, the best of times.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is a year of uncertainty for workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Over the past few days, my Labour Movement Parliamentary colleagues have shared how global trade tensions and disruptive technologies are transforming the workforce, workplaces and the future of work.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: At NTUC, we have heard the anxieties of young graduates as AI accelerates the shrinking of entry-level jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We have supported the upskilling and career transition aspirations of the mid-career workers and we have championed the platform worker's rights to work injury compensation and even Central Provident Fund (CPF) contributions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As the economy evolves, we must continue to stand in solidarity with our workers and equip them with the skills and protections they need to succeed.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To this end, I will focus my speech on three priorities for the next bound of workforce development, or what I call the three "Ses" – supporting Singaporeans, strengthening the Singaporean Core and a skills-first Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The first "S" in my speech is supporting Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is attributed to drivers, such as the race towards renewable energy and AI, which have already been cited by major companies for mass retrenchment exercises both globally and in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Gen AI especially has the potential to displace entry-level knowledge work by automating mundane or repetitive tasks, which will significantly impact Singapore's knowledge-based workforce, unlike earlier waves of automation that primarily displaced manual work.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The hard truth is that previously secure jobs and valued skills will become obsolete.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Workers cannot remain stagnant and expect to still compete.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In every challenge lies opportunity for those who choose to meet it.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Renewable energy and the generative cognitive AI are generation-defining technologies that can not only create new jobs but make them better and better-paying.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: By supporting workers' learning and upskilling ambitions, businesses and the economy also benefit from more growth and a more skilled workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To ensure no worker is left behind in the adoption of new technologies, we must commit to a Just Transition that prioritises the re-skilling and re-deployment of workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: If you recall the old adage: it is learn, work and retire.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is learn, work; learn, work; learn, work; and maybe retire.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The Labour Movement has persistently advocated for training allowance and subsidies for a second degree or diploma for mid-career and older workers who may be more vulnerable to skills obsolescence, financial support for the involuntarily unemployed to help them bounce back from employment setbacks and, most recently, Government-funded traineeship and apprenticeship opportunities for young graduates to strengthen their employability.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am heartened that the Government has answered our calls with the launch of the SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme, Jobseeker Support Scheme and the GRaduate Industry Traineeships (GRIT) Programme.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: On the ground, I have also heard the anxieties and frustrations of young graduates and involuntarily unemployed jobseekers who have not been able to find jobs after sending out hundreds of applications despite having good diplomas and degrees.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I, therefore, continue to call on the Government to consider three policy moves.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Second, taking stronger action alongside unions against errant employers who do not practice fair and responsible retrenchment practices, as we have seen in the recent spate of retrenchments.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Third, incentivising companies that hire first-time workers for full-time positions, similar to the Jobs Growth Incentive launched during the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Considering the scale and speed of AI's impact on the workforce, I also ask that the Government consider forming a Tripartite Workgroup on Safeguarding Workers in the Age of AI to encourage companies to adopt Just Transition practices, prevent algorithmic discrimination and ensure responsible use of AI-powered human resources (HR) tools.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I opine that the Employment Act should cover more PMEs by raising both the salary caps of workmen and non-workmen, as well as providing more clarity on transfers that impact workers affected by ongoing company restructuring, mergers and acquisitions, and require employers to give explicit reasons for termination or discontinuation of employment initiated by the employer upon the request of the employee.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: During this time of uncertainty, I encourage our workers to adopt a mindset of resilience and adaptability, to find strength in numbers and collective action.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is not the first time new technologies have disrupted the workforce, nor will it be the last.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As with each economic wave and transition, NTUC and our unions stand ready to support our workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The second "S" is strengthening the Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Since my maiden speech in this House in 2011, I have persistently advocated for strengthening the Singaporean Core, especially for our local PMEs, who face increasing competition with foreign PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Over the past decade, I have advocated for a compendium of measures to level the playing field for our local PMEs, including the Workplace Fairness Act, which protects workers against the most common types of workplace discrimination, including age and nationality; a foreign PME dependency ratio; stricter Employment Pass (EP) application conditions and continuous enhancements to the Fair Consideration Framework and many others.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: These protections are important and we should regularly review it.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: A strong Singaporean Core must therefore be a Singaporean-led core.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This means building up our local bench strength through investments in local talent pipelines to set Singaporeans up for senior and leadership positions before turning abroad and facilitating knowledge and skills transfer.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We cannot assume that if we grow the pie, Singaporeans will naturally get their share.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: There must be a concerted effort to encourage companies, especially our multinationals, to groom our local PMEs as part of their leadership identification and developmental process, improve HR standards and practices to ensure compliance with fair employment practices and Tripartite Guidelines, and encourage workers to step-up and step forward for opportunities to relocate for greater international exposure.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I hope the Government will consider extending these opportunities to more Singaporean workers and adopting new levers to improve reciprocity between multinational corporations (MNCs) and our local PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Companies that have a highly disproportionate number of foreign PMEs and weak commitment to nurturing local talent pipelines can also be closely monitored.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: If no improvement is made within a certain time period, the Government can consider even removing preferential tax and other benefits, such as the award of public sector contracts.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Even the US is also mulling over imposing a $100,000 fee on new H-1B visa applications.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is especially critical for MNCs employing foreign HR practitioners who operate within Singapore and help them better understand our tripartite industrial relations framework.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: More widespread certification adoption will be better and will position our HR practitioners to deepen their capabilities and signal a commitment to professional excellence.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To be clear, a Singaporean Core does not mean closing doors to foreign PMEs who can help fill critical skill gaps and support sectors facing labour shortage.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is about building a more competitive economy that is less reliant on external labour and nurturing the next generation of Singaporean leaders.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is about ensuring that Singaporean workers who work hard and can contribute can afford a good life in Singapore, for themselves and their families, in the only home they have.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Third and final "S" is a skills-first Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Today, disruptive technologies, like Gen AI and new work trends, including the rise of gig work, freelancing, remote work and side hustles have transformed how we traditionally define and plan a career.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Instead of a linear progression within a single organisation, more are embracing flexible journeys defined by adaptability, continuous learning and the ability to move across job functions and industries.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Job instability and career transitions are increasingly commonplace, but so are building portfolio careers, pursuing passion-driven pathways and going back to school for reskilling.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This means more voluntary underemployment, but also more involuntary underemployment, an issue NTUC has been studying very, very closely and examining the past decade.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: A two-year research study in collaboration with the Singapore University of Technology and Design on underemployment, especially involuntary skills-jobs mismatch, where workers are unhappily overskilled for their current jobs, will be completing soon, and we will share more in due course.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Against this evolving landscape, diplomas and degrees can no longer act as a proxy for competency.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: According to a Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies study released in 2024, higher levels of education do not always equate to better skills and knowledge.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Earlier data from LinkedIn in 2021 also revealed that employers in Singapore preferred to hire candidates with technical skills and transferable skills over traditional qualifications, such as education and minimum years of experience.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In real-world terms, this means that a student majoring in history, for example, but who has demonstrated coding skills through relevant work experience or winning hackathons should feel confident in applying for an entry-level programmer position.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It also means that two workers who are equally skilled, equally knowledgeable and demonstrate good work performance should receive equal opportunities to advance in their career, regardless of whether one worker holds a diploma and the other has a degree.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: A skills-first economy, therefore, holds powerful potential for the inclusion of non-traditional learners who acquired skills through experience and expanding individuals' career pathways beyond the scope of their formal qualifications.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It supports caregivers, older workers, persons with disabilities, young graduates and freelancers or self-employed persons in asserting the value of their labour, thereby also allowing employers to tap on a wider talent pool.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: For this idea to take flight, however, requires the buy-in of all stakeholders across the workforce development ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The Government will need to create robust and integrated frameworks for credible skills accreditation and transferability across institutions and industries.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Employers will need to adopt progressive practices, such as listing the necessary skills required in job descriptions, on top of formal qualifications and taking skill certifications, testimonials, performance appraisals, awards and leadership experiences outside of work into consideration for progression.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Where relevant and when it does not affect employers' economic interests, employers should not punish the industrious and passionate pursuit of "hobby jobs" and "side hustles" as moonlighting.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Schools and Institutes of Higher Learning will need to adapt their curricula to raise students' curiosity, confidence and creativity in exploring diverse ways of learning and working.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The arts must be as well-funded as the sciences, we need to go beyond STEM to STEAM.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Students must spend as much time in industry and community as they do in classrooms and lecture halls.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: And most importantly, workers will need to be open to learning new skills and exploring new interests, fail and try again.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Unlike other countries, where unions often must lobby for uneven training and upskilling opportunities, Singapore continuously doles out funding.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We undoubtedly have a highly educated workforce, but does that education end when we leave school?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Does a highly educated workforce equate to a highly-skilled and knowledgeable workforce?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The shift towards a skills-led economy, therefore, surfaces starting points for us to boldly reimagine how we learn and work, and also why we learn and work, which lays the groundwork for more flexible and fulfilling careers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To conclude, work is a source of and the pursuit of hope, purpose and dignity.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is the measure of our days, our connections to community.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: By prioritising the three "S" of supporting Singaporeans, strengthening a Singaporean Core, and a skills-first Singapore, we honour workers and commit to helping them earn a better living and live a better life.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: For all to train up to keep up and skill-up to move up.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As we commence this new term of Parliament, I note that there are 31 Members who are entering Parliament for the first time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am privileged to be here for my fifth term.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There are quite a few others who have been here longer, including Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong in his 10th term – more than 40 years.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, I trust I may be permitted to give my personal welcome to the newly-minted Members of Parliament (MPs) from both sides of the House.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One of the themes in the President's address is about trust.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Some Ministers have, in past days, also emphasised the importance of trust in institutions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Today, I wish to say a few words about trust in one of the key institutions we have – this Chamber, Parliament.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: All of us here gained entry through a competitive process, that is, we contested in the recent elections to win the hearts and minds of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Fundamentally, party politics is a competitive process which pits one party against another.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Yes, elections involve a zero-sum game: one vote for you means one less vote for me.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But once the dust of elections has settled, we are entrusted to represent our constituents.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On a broader level, how does one measure the effectiveness of a Parliament?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To answer this question, one needs to return to the purpose of Parliament in the first place.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One respected index that covers this issue is the World Justice Project.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The World Justice Project compiles an index that the Singapore Government frequently cites for its high rankings of Singapore in the area of Order and Security.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To give a bit of background, the World Justice Project declares itself as an independent, multi-disciplinary organisation that seeks to advance the rule of law worldwide.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Project reviews countries around the world to assess each country's laws, institutions, norms and community commitment to the rule of law.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The outcomes it is interested in centre around four principles: accountability, just law, open government and accessible and impartial justice.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I do not think anyone in this House will disagree that these principles apply to us as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In assessing the state of the rule of law, the World Justice Project examines each country on various indicators.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When we look across the different sub-indicators for Singapore, what sticks out is that we have largely healthy scores around six out of eight indicators.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The two indicators where we do not do so well are in the factors called Open Government and Constraints on Government Powers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I believe this has been our consistent scorecard from the World Justice Project for many years.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such a mixed scorecard should also come as no surprise.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In measuring Open Government, the index looks into matters, such as how much information is shared by the government with the public and whether citizens have a right to information.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Open Government also measures public accountability, whether there are effective complaint mechanisms and how far the people are empowered with the tools to hold the government accountable.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As for the factor of Constraints on Government Powers, it is concerned with how far those who govern are bound by law.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One key sub-indicator is whether government powers are effectively limited by the legislature.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On this issue, our score is not respectable.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We should honestly examine why there is an independent, multi-disciplinary opinion that our Parliament is not effective in limiting government powers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is the result of our system design and Singaporeans' votes on Polling Day.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That said, it is a fact that in the House, the Government agenda is set by the leaders of the ruling party and party discipline demands that ruling party MPs vote in support of the Government agenda.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But we should be mindful that, as MPs, our overriding duty is not to our parties, but to Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Regardless of our affiliation, we have a duty to speak for our constituents and ensure that this Chamber works for them.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This means questioning the Government and holding it to account, rigorously, if necessary.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On the Government's part, it should always demonstrate that it is sharing as much information as possible in the House.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And in the long run, it is Singaporeans who need to decide if the balance of power in the House should be changed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On our part as opposition MPs, we are expected to take an independent line, question the Government and vote against proposals when we deem it necessary.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Speaking from experience, this is not easy, especially when one is surrounded and vastly outnumbered.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But that is our obligation and that is what voters expect us to do.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We will play our part to build a Parliament that the people trust.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We are cautiously optimistic that our Parliamentary system has potential to do better.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Many of us would have seen television footage of somewhat rowdy sessions from the UK Parliament and strong exchanges between opposite benches.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But I realise, now, that such scenes do not tell the whole story.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Political competitors, yet able to give each other some credit and credibility.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That is my hope for our Parliament, too.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Politics is competitive, but why are we in this?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In this term of Parliament, I hope we can build trust in the House as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If we can do that, I believe Singaporeans will benefit from a focus on the issues that matter.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Our system of Government expects Parliament to play its role to ensure good governance.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The people have elected us to act on their behalf, to ensure Singapore endures for the long term, to work towards a Singapore built to last.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Victor Lye, do you have a clarification?

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And to the Member's point, I think we are not enemies, and we are friends.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have known each other for a long time.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Ms Lim, you might want to turn on your microphone?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: It came on automatically just now, so I trusted the system, but maybe, I should not.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: And as I mentioned, what was most striking to me was that momentary expression of trust in each other.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: That Singapore is a small island is a matter of geography, but that we can travel swiftly and in comfort across all its corners is a matter of human endeavour.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: It is our transport system that allows us to work, study, exercise, access essential services, socialise, volunteer and live our lives to the fullest.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: These were amongst the topics that hon Members spoke passionately about in this House over the past five days.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: If we do it well, transport becomes an invisible social service, moving from point A to point B is as effortless as stepping through a door.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: This is our urban dream, a 45-minute city and 20-minute town.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: This dream, of freedom and connectivity, is not new.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Although at the time of our Independence 60 years ago, there were immense challenges in ensuring Singapore’s survival, from clean water to housing, such that transport may have seem to be a poorer, lesser cousin.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Once laid down, whether planned or organic, transport lines carve out their place in the history of a place; implacable, immovable and, for better or worse, they shape the fate of cities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We see this now in the gridlocked congested lives of many cities, whose systems had not been built to accommodate growth.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: It is Singapore's good fortune that our early Governments built for the future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: But transport is not just a decision of the past.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: It demands ceaseless attention to keep pace with the needs and lives of the people it serves.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: To neglect investments is to accept time spent in traffic jams, accidents, breakdowns, workdays lost and important occasions missed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Again, we see this in the cities of developed countries, whose transport infrastructure have suffered from decades of under-investment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: These two challenges, greater complexity in needs and financial demands for infrastructure, also apply to Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: As our systems expand and become more complex, the number of potential points of failure increases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: New vulnerabilities will emerge as we digitalise, adopt new technologies and put more of our services online into the cyberspace.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The emerging challenges, coupled with the unprecedented pace of change in our external environment, will mean that we need a new generation of transport professionals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We will enhance our ageing infrastructure, make them robust and flexible so as to meet the needs of our population, which are increasing in volume and complexity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We will seize opportunities from new technologies, while safeguarding against cybersecurity risks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We will continue to build a professional and adaptive transport workforce, the only real piece in the transport landscape that can ensure our systems remains fit for purpose well into the future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Many from my generation remember growing up alongside this journey.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: As a young boy, I took the single-door "bone shaker" public bus to school.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: I would leave home from Sembawang at 5.30 am to catch the 5.45 am bus on a one-hour 30-minute journey to reach school at Newton by 7.15 am, with 15 minutes to spare before morning assembly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: With limited resources then, these "bone shakers" were, in fact, refurbished lorry chassis with suspension systems so poor that they vibrated vigorously.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: But as a young boy, I did not mind it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The same journey today, via Mass Rapid Transit (MRT), would take 30 minutes in air-conditioned comfort, just one-third the time it originally took.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Today, we enjoy a transport system that is admired across the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Changi Airport is our nation’s pride, consistently ranked amongst the world’s best airports.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Our port was recently named the “Best Global Seaport”.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: And our land transport network serves about 10 million journeys each day.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Our transport systems today are extensive and highly complex, with many interconnected elements and moving parts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: As I said at the start of my speech, transport infrastructure incur large sunk costs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Even with long-term planning, we can only build to the best of our knowledge and ability at any given time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We must also make the most prudent choices possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Underneath this, lies years of design, planning, battles over land and billions of dollars in investment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: While 30 years is a short time in the life of a nation, it is long for an MRT line.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Our rail system comprises many mechanical parts, each with specific lifespans, similar to everyday appliances, such as washing machines.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: With different parts of our rail system at different ages, ensuring the smooth operation of all trains in the network becomes increasingly complex and challenging.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We aim to keep our rail network running smoothly, through a combination of maintenance, refurbishments or replacements where needed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We will do so by focusing on the three "Rs": resilience, reliability and recovery.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: First, we will enhance resilience with more alternative routes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Second, we will invest in improving the reliability of our rail assets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: If not for the COVID-19 pandemic which the hon Member, Ms Mariam Jaafar, reminded us in her speech yesterday ended just 30 months ago, the progress on these two "Rs", resilience and reliability, would have been even more significant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Now we are playing catch-up, but catch up we will.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Having regard to the state of affairs now, however, we cannot eliminate rail disruptions entirely.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: But when disruptions occur, we will ensure recovery as quickly and as expeditiously as possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We will communicate with commuters and help them find alternative routes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Failure in service is a justified cause for frustration and disappointment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The Singaporean reputation for reliability and predictability is hard earned.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Nowhere must this be more clearly seen than in our transport system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: So, I accept that we need to work hard to win back the support of frustrated Singaporeans affected by some failures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We will invest to reduce disruptions, but they will not be eliminated.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: I do not take any pleasure in saying this, but this is the hard truth.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: But knowing that disruptions will happen, we have in place systems to help affected people still arrive at their destinations, not on time, unfortunately; not without trouble, regrettably but with all practicable haste.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: I want to assure the House that all my colleagues on the ground, work tirelessly, truly flat out, during disruptions, including the East-West Line disruption in September last year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: I saw that with my own two eyes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Alongside my colleagues were many volunteers to guide and support commuters to use the bridging buses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: These are hardworking transport professionals, including our sisters and brothers of the National Transport Workers Union and fellow Singaporeans who deserve our respect and support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Yet, they have, on occasions, been cathartic vehicles, on the receiving end of abusive language, anger and derision.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: I ask all hon Members in this House for ideas that you may have to improve our transport infrastructure and to build up the resilience of our systems.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: At the same time, I am sure Members will agree that we should forbear from cheap shots and low blows when things go wrong.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Never exploit problems, but by all means, let us work on the problems.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Even as we tackle the challenges of today, we must prepare for the future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We are developing more areas across our island.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We need to move more people who are less mobile across larger tracts of space.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: These are points that hon Members, Ms Valerie Lee and Mr Shawn Loh, admirably made in their respective speeches.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We will engage our members of public on their desires, aspirations and concerns for the future of land transport.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: People remain at the heart of our transport system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: To fellow Singaporeans, I say, preparing for the future is an important journey.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: I hope you will support and join us every step of the way.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Across transport sector, innovative technologies can enhance efficiency and productivity of our systems.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: New technologies are essential for our path to net-zero.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Electrification remains a key strategy to decarbonise Singapore's land transport sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: However, as our system increasingly digitalise and move into the cyberspace, we face unprecedented security challenges.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We are familiar with the cyberattacks on critical infrastructure by UNC3886.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: With so much of our daily lives and economy reliant on our transportation networks, our infrastructure becomes prime targets for malicious actors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Globally, cyberattacks on transport infrastructure have occurred across land, air and sea.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: In July 2023, Nagoya Port, Japan's largest maritime hub, fell victim to a cyberattack that disrupted its container handling operations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: In September 2024, Transport for London reported a cyberattack on their computer systems that lasted for three months.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: And just last week, a cyberattack at a provider of check-in and boarding systems disrupted operations at several major European airports, leading to flight delays and cancellations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: There is no telling when malicious actors may target our systems in similar attacks, these cyberattacks show us that even as we leverage the transforming power of technological advancements, we must put in place appropriate safeguards to address vulnerabilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We must work together, as One Transport Family, with our fellow Singaporeans to secure our critical transport infrastructure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We are only as strong as our weakest link.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Agencies also share critical information with key partners, from public transport operators to aviation partners and maritime companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We are also investing in our people to cultivate their cybersecurity awareness and skills, tailored to the air, land and sea transport sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: This will not only enable them to practise good cyber hygiene, but also uplift them to become the first line of defence to detect anomalies that could signal cyber intrusion attempts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: For example, the Singapore Aviation Academy and the Singapore University of Technology and Design offer a joint course to provide aviation professionals with an understanding of the cybersecurity landscape and specific challenges facing the aviation sector, as well as the key foundations in cybersecurity concepts and controls.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: They will continue to be central to our transport ecosystem as we write the next chapter of this story.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Automation and autonomous innovations have great potential to transform the way we work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: This not only allows our ecosystem to transcend manpower and land constraints, but also creates new good jobs for our people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We are already seeing this transformation on the ground today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Tuas Port is designed to be fully automated, intelligent and sustainable, and will offer new jobs with enhanced career prospects.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: At older port terminals, crane operators work at great heights atop cranes to direct movement of each container from ship to shore, and vice versa.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: With automation, our crane operators are upskilled from doing manual work to directing automated crane operations and troubleshooting exception cases remotely from control centres.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: This is the experience of Mr Muhammad Zulfikar Bin Minhat, from managing manual operations on site at Tanjong Pagar Terminal when he started his career 11 years ago, today, Mr Zulfikar remotely manages automated yard operations from PSA's control centre.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: In fact, when I spoke to him yesterday, he told me that he got promoted and is now in charge of 26 remote operators on his shift.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: He continues to upgrade his skills, enhancing his ability to troubleshoot and navigate operational challenges.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: He is also a proud member of the Singapore Port Workers Union, which supports him in every way possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: What a great example Mr Zulfikar is to his peers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Changi Airport and SATS are also transforming to harness AI automation and robotics to stay competitive and resilient.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Existing jobs, such as airport ground handling services, will change in tandem, and new jobs will be created for a new generation of Singapore workers who are tech savvy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Exciting new mobility options in our public transport network are on the horizon as we plan and start piloting autonomous vehicle (AV) shuttles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: This will better meet the growing and evolving connectivity needs of Singaporeans without running into manpower constraints.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The AV industry will also create good jobs for Singaporeans in roles, such as software developers, engineers and radar designers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: We will continue to collaborate closely with our industry unions and education partners to upscale our workers and ensure their access to these jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: As rightly highlighted by the hon Member Mr Ang Wei Neng, lifelong learning is crucial for our workers as industries are transformed by AI and new technologies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: That is why we are investing in support for training partners and companies to provide upskilling training opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The fund will provide stronger and more targeted support to companies to transform jobs and better support workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Together with our tripartite partners, we are equipping workers with skills that are increasingly sought after in their industries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The transport sector is a rewarding career spent in service of our fellow citizens.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: It is a dynamic sector with good jobs for Singaporeans of all ages and backgrounds.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: The veteran union leader, Sister Mary Liew, General Secretary of the Singapore Maritime Officers' Union, shared with me the heartening story of Miss Valerie Thai, a legal professional turned seafarer, with me recently.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Valerie obtained her law degree from Australia and worked as a paralegal in Singapore but soon found the legal profession a bit too boring for her.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: I met her two days ago, a cadet now, she is eager to blaze the trail for women wanting to be seafarers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: I wish Valerie all the best in her training.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: With the diverse range of career opportunities, whether in traversing our skies, connecting people on land or plying our seas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: I look forward to welcoming all to join our transport family.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: I do hope that fellow Singaporeans, young and old, will consider these options and join our One Transport Family.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: As we write the next chapter of our transport story.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: However, we will also discover new opportunities as our environment changes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong, in a dialogue with young people, said recently, "Being small is a very deep part of our psyche.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law and Transport (Mr Murali Pillai)
text: Some things we cannot change." This is true.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This special constituency reminds us of that moment in 2011 when Singaporeans began to dream of a more plural political system, and I stand here today in service of that dream.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I wish to speak on one of the most important economic questions for our country today: what it will take for Singapore to build inherent capacity.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: By inherent capacity, I mean a rooted high-value local set of companies, local base of companies and industries.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The ultimate defence for our workers is not a certificate from a course.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is being part of a deep industrial ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is tacit knowledge, the unwritten secrets of an industry learned not in a classroom, but in a coffee conversation after work or overheard on a factory floor.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The guarded tricks of building and tuning a foundation model or advance notice of a new industry standard.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is the sticky localised knowledge that gives our workers a genuine defensible edge, justifying their wages and creating the conditions for our best entrepreneurs to thrive.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Of course, we must continue to upskill our people.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But skills-training alone, unmoored from a home industry, is not enough – a skill that can be learned anywhere, can be performed anywhere, often at a lower cost.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We must therefore build the inherent capacity to foster unique knowledge advantages.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Building this inherent capacity requires a resurrected developmental state for our time, a state that actively shapes an ecosystem to benefit our people.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: There are three ways to do this: through research and development (R&D) policy, industrial policy and foreign economic policy.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Today, with only 20 minutes, I will focus on the third pillar: how we engage with the world.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Once, in the 1960s, American giants – Boeing, Lockheed, McDonnell-Douglas – dominated over 80% of the civil aviation market.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Europe’s national champions – like Sud Aviation, Messerschmitt-Bölkow-Blohm and Hawker Siddeley – were confined mainly to national markets and had a bleak future if they stayed alone.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The industry dynamics favoured the American giants due to large economies of scale, enormous R&D commitments rising 20% yearly between 1930 and 1970 and steep learning curves.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In their enlightened self-interest, they turned to a new policy instrument: a transnational industrial consortium.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Airbus, founded in 1970, was designed to preserve the aviation industries of Germany, France and the UK.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is important to note it was not a top-down creation of the European Community.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It was driven from the bottom-up by the firms themselves.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It arose from a group of state-backed enterprises and was founded on commercial principles, learning the lessons from the commercial failure of Anglo-French Concorde.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: State-backing was necessary as the long-duration debt market in Europe was too small to finance this industry alone.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This political decision was made possible by two points of consensus: First, the knowledge that industrial policy was necessary to build inherent capacity – again, a rooted high-value local base of companies.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Second, that national industrial policy would likely prove insufficient.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Transnational projects would be needed to achieve the necessary scale and competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It was sustained by three key points: political will to provide financing until the consortium hit its first financial milestones, demand-assurance for guaranteed orders in the early years and partner lock-in via specialisation and workshare agreements for the different components.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Above all, it was a 50-50 split in equity holding between France and Germany.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Let us turn to our own region, Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The President’s address and its addenda have told us of the multiple platforms we will pursue for economic growth.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We are to deepen engagement in existing trading frameworks, from the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership to our networks of Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) and Digital Economy Agreements.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But we have spent years and decades cultivating these types of platforms without fostering that strong base of locally grown companies.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: For decades, our diplomatic energy has been spent on the idea of "negative integration" – that is to say, integration by way of removal of trade barriers. "Negative integration" has been duly implemented.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In 2009, the ASEAN Trade in Goods Agreement (ATIGA) came into force.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: ASEAN's website states, and I quote, "Through ATIGA, Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, Philippines, Singapore, and Thailand have eliminated intra-ASEAN import duties on 99.65% of their tariff lines.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Cambodia, Lao People's Democratic Republic (PDR), Myanmar and Viet Nam have reduced their import duties to 0%-5% on 98.86% of their tariff lines.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Today, focus is given to addressing non-tariff measures that could have non-tariff barrier effects on the region's trade and business activities"; end quote.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Moreover, for a large fraction of trade, ATIGA offered no real advantage – either "Most-Favored Nation" rates at zero already meant that there were no tariffs to cut, or the special ASEAN discount was so tiny that it made no practical difference.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I am not against negative integration, but it is clearly not a sufficient ideal for Southeast Asian integration.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Against it, I believe Airbus exemplifies an ideal of "positive integration" in the industrial sense.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Our region tried a form of "positive integration" before, with the ASEAN Industrial Projects (AIPs) of the 1970s.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The four non-Singapore projects were geared towards the agricultural industry, a reflection of national development priorities.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: States will only enter enduring cooperation agreements when they do not fear that their partners will gain disproportionately.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The success of Airbus holds a mirror to these past failures and shows us a path forward.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: They will speak of deep-seated political sensitivities, of differing economic priorities and of the cultural gulf that separates our nations.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But I ask: are these differences greater than those that separated France and Germany just two decades after a world war?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: True partnership is not born from the absence of difficulty, but from the shared will to overcome it in the face of a greater common challenge – the squeeze of geoeconomic competition and knowing that going it alone is a losing game.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: First, it requires coalitions of the willing, not committees of the whole.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Some must integrate faster, to demonstrate the benefits of a particular integration model.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This ensures that every nation has an equal stake in shared success, bridging a trust deficit that erects non-tariff barriers.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Defined payoffs and the way they are structured, must be negotiated early on.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: These negotiations reveal the viability or lack thereof regarding long-term cooperation.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And third, today, the industrial bases across Southeast Asia by foreign direct investment give us a foundation that our predecessors never had, that allows us to build complementarity from a higher-base than the agricultural-industrial options available to the previous generation of policy-makers.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I am a believer that foreign investment has been a net positive for this region.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Negative integration in ASEAN, via ATIGA and FTAs, has created a stable potential foundation for increasing regional trade.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But the world is changing and we must now adapt to that changing world.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Positive industrial integration is not the only option available to us.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But it is a necessary diversifier in a portfolio of international strategies.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Above all we should not spend all our diplomatic capital deepening a model that is yielding diminishing returns.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We need to build a future with real, defensible, and shared prosperity.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I read with interest in March 2025, the call in the Malay Mail by the chief executive officer of MIMOS Berhad, Malaysia's national applied R&D centre, calling for strong industrial policy to create a semiconductor chip design ecosystem for Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: To move beyond being a trusted manufacturer for global companies to become innovators.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: When I read this call and others like it, I hear a common developmental language across nations.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But to channel these ambitions through national industrial policy is to face the full cost of global competition alone.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We are in the midst of a global investment cycle in many things.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Budgetary decisions from the Ministry of Finance should begin to inform industrial policy decisions of the Ministry of Trade and Industry.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We should head in broad strokes to what will be the big buckets of spending over the next 20 years – healthcare, the clean energy transition, maritime industrialisation, education.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: To ensure these efforts build our local capacity, Government support, like funding and early contracts, must come with conditions.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Firms must be required to build deep roots here through local engineering teams, apprenticeships, joint-IP and guaranteed work for our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In the 21st century, this need not be a bloated state-owned enterprise.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But rather the principal client and industrial anchor for an entire ecosystem of SMEs, along with the safeguards to make sure that value flows down the value-chain.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Airbus sustains tens of thousands of European SMEs.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Similarly, every successful venture in Southeast Asia could allow an ecosystem of SMEs to thrive.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We do not necessarily need to build the entire metaphorical aircraft at once; we can start by mastering a single critical component – the engine, the avionics, the advanced materials.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This "building block" approach allows each partner to specialise, making us stronger together than apart.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: As we prove the model, we can integrate more partners, even from outside our region, to build more complex systems.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: How might such a cooperation and integration model be replicated?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Once done once, the private sector can increasingly take over.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The same unfolding ladder of ideas from AIPs to ASEAN Industrial Joint Venture (AIJVs) to ATIGA, from positive integration to negative integration.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This requires a change in our Government’s mindset.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The greatest enabler of our local enterprises and not their competitor.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I know that there are many Singaporeans who do not share the views of some who think that Singapore should focus on doing small things and let big countries do big things.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But my message to all is that every ambition has a price.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If a nation wishes to be at the frontier, it needs to be prepared to pay that price to cross that bridge.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And inherent capacity at the frontier, guarded by protectionist sentiment at the best of times, is today a contested ridge-line, with all nations reawakened to the necessity of inherent capacity.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It remains possible, as it always was possible, to cross this bridge, as long as the political will allows.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But it requires no illusions about the limits of different growth models.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It requires both developmental will abroad, and restraint at home.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This generation must decide what our country’s position is in the whole scheme of human progress.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
