text: With over 30 years of service in the Labour Movement, Jiuan is widely respected for her deep institutional knowledge and resourcefulness in extracting and presenting historical data.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Even in her late-60s, instead of resisting the AI tool that might potentially replace her job, Jiuan continues to embrace lifelong learning and took the initiative to upskill herself with the latest tech skills.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Working alongside younger teammates, Jiuan leveraged her experience to identify gaps, accuracy of AI results and propose improvements to the system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Through her quiet resilience and collaborative spirit, she not only contributes valuable insights in the process, but also mentors and inspires her younger colleagues.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Jiuan’s story highlights how multi-generational collaboration efforts fuels innovation and stronger team outcomes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It is a reminder that experience, adaptability and willingness to learn are strategic assets in building a future-ready workforce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Before I conclude, let me leave Members with three calls to action.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: First, to employers, let us invest in older workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Together, they can bring great value to your business.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: To our senior workers, let us be bold to embrace technology and AI, learn and apply ourselves, so that we can be ready for the new AI economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: (In Mandarin): Mr Deputy Speaker, I just mentioned in my English speech that AI represents two key topics, "Artificial Intelligence" and "Ageing Individuals".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Can ageing individuals keep up with artificial intelligence?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The answer is, with AI and with love, we definitely can do it!

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: As long as everyone: has a love for learning, a love for asking questions and a fighting spirit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: By using mobile phones, voice commands and taking photos, we can ask questions and learn.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Language is not a barrier; AI can communicate in most of the world's languages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: With a love for learning, we can make meaningful progress and enhance work efficiency.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It is only fears that you would not ask.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: AI is like an encyclopaedia in your hands, ready to provide answers anytime.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This also proves that technology is making knowledge more accessible, no longer a privilege reserved for a select few.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Technology will help more workers improve both in their work and lives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: AI provides information but critical thinking depends on ourselves, especially the experience and judgement of our senior workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Innovation is not a miracle, but the commitment to doing better tomorrow.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: As long as we are willing to work hard, willing to think and willing to do better, I believe we will thrive in the AI economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Deputy Speaker, fellow Parliamentarians and fellow workers, AI is not the exclusive domain of young people; it is a tool for all of us.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: On this journey of learning and transformation, NTUC will be everyone's steadfast partner, providing practical support and companionship.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The article went on to explain a growing reality that AI can increase productivity by automating administrative processes, research and even content creation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I can imagine the time savings, but I am not sure about the 40%, although I wished it is the case.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The question for us to ponder is if AI can give us X% of time, say 20%, 30% or 40%.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Brother Arvin Tang from the Tech Talent Assembly also asked a similar question last week at the Amazon Web Services Fireside Chat.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: If you think about it, we could reinvest this time to grow our business, to work even harder to pursue our career goals, or we could spend time volunteering doing something meaningful, serving our community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: But deep down, I hope we, and especially our seniors, could live a more balanced life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Cherishing time with family and friends, learning something new and pursuing our passions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This is the true purpose and promise of technology when paired with human intelligence, not just doing more but doing better, together.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The President stated in his address, our first priority is to secure our home and safeguard Singapore's place in the world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: My speech is structured around the theme of security.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Global security, domestic security and, finally, job security.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Over the course of my 14 years in this House, I have spent a decade each in the Government Parliamentary Committees (GPCs) of Defence, Foreign Affairs, Home Affairs and Law, and continue in two GPCs this term.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The foci of these GPCs are Singapore's external and internal security, respectively.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As union advisor, I know job security is a matter close to every worker's heart.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Over the last three decades, the global security situation has fundamentally changed.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Following the end of the Cold War, historian Francis Fukuyama wrote a book on "The End of History" which suggested that liberal democracy had triumphed over communism and the world could continue to look forward to peaceful prosperity.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The inevitable communist revolution that Karl Marx had predicted had not come to pass and hence, the historic dialectic of history had ended.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This did not mean conflict had ended but with the triumph of America in the Cold War, we had a unipolar world and the triumph of a rules-based liberal world order.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Where there were breaches of our fundamental norms of international law, say, in relation to armed conflict, the idea of collective security and international action against the aggressor was real.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Examples of these included the First Gulf War, where Kuwait was liberated following the invasion by Iraq; and the war in Afghanistan following the 9/11 attacks on the World Trade Centre.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Second Gulf War with Iraq, on the basis that it had weapons of mass destruction, was more controversial as there were disagreements on whether Iraq's conduct triggered the requirements for collective response.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If you breach the fundamental norm of international law, collective response was a real possibility.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Actions like this would have had a strong deterrent effect on would-be aggressors.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Many countries cut back on military spending following the end of the Cold War and the reliability of the United States (US) deterrent may have accelerated this process.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Countries that had conscript programs, including in Europe, South Korea and Taiwan, cut back on these and military spending in most of Europe was cut back.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The US had taken up the mantle of global policeman and incurred significant expenses.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: President Obama inherited one of the largest deficits in US history and gradual cut back in US military spending began, which would mean being more careful with foreign interventions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Some analysts believe this gave Russia more confidence that its current attack on Ukraine would go similarly without significant international resistance.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: During the first Trump presidency, there was a view that China was a developing power and security gets particularly dangerous when a rising power threatens the incumbent.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Thucydides, the Greek historian who wrote about the war between Athens and Sparta, was often referred to for the proposition that a confrontation between a rising power and a dominant one could lead in military confrontation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There were several potential flashpoints at the time including over Taiwan and the South China Sea.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If there was a military confrontation between the US and China, the whole world would be impacted by the fallout.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: From the US point of view at the time, the earlier the confrontation, the more likely would it be to triumph, rather than allowing China to catch up with its faster growing economy.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would also suggest that such a confrontation is less likely to happen.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is what seems to be playing out both in Ukraine and in the Middle East.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Allies remain important, though, in the case of Ukraine, it would not have been able to continue this war for so long without financial and weapon support from the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) countries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While none of them are sending boots on the ground, their assistance remains important.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As between allies too, those who have most to lose from your defeat are likely to have a stronger incentive to help you.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the case of Ukraine, it is its European allies who are closer to it that are now playing a more important role in continuing to support its war efforts.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The US remains important in resuming weapon supplies but it has not made significant fresh financial commitments.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The reality is that Singapore is a small country and we never know who our potential aggressor could be.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Sometimes, your closest allies today may turn aggressors tomorrow, as was the case between Russia and Ukraine.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Your aggressors could also come from very far away, as was the case in World War II when we were invaded by Japan.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: An important bulwark against this, in addition to being fully prepared to defend ourselves, is to build a wide set of relationships, both diplomatic and defence-related.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Having a wide range of allies means that there are more potential countries that could be aligned with you and willing to help if the situation calls for it.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In Singapore's case, natural counterparts would be other countries in Southeast Asia and, potentially, Japan and Korea, which are both advanced Asian economies with strong research and development capabilities for potential defence technologies.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think an important priority for this term of Government will be to include our investments in our own defence and our diplomatic and defence relations in the region.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The second aspect I wish to discuss is domestic security.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore prides itself on having one of the lowest crime rates in the world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore is one of the safest cities in the world and our citizens have no fear of walking alone at night or even leaving valuables like mobile phones around to chope dining tables at eateries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Despite this, though, the surge of organised crime lurks beneath the surface.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The same area was also associated with the growing of opium and the trade in heroin.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These stories are horrifying and as the victims of these scams are all over the world, I think stronger transnational cooperation and coordination is needed to deal with these international syndicates, especially where crime originates from areas of states that may be beyond the control of the government of the country involved.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Within Singapore, our war on drugs has generally been successful because of the combination of strong laws, effective enforcement and swift justice.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Drug traffickers know that Singapore is not to be trifled with.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I believe lax penalties for sellers led to the initial spike in sales of both vapes and etomidate.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Interestingly, ketamine, which was also a compound component of Kpod, but classified as a drug, did not see such a large spike, which suggests the classification of the substance as a drug makes a difference for the sellers' behaviour and its proliferation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Around the same time, The Straits Times was running a series of stories on Kpod.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I had met a resident at my meet-the-people session, who shared the story of her son who was struggling with Kpod addiction.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: She wanted her son to get treatment but under the laws as it then stood, the Health Sciences Authority could only confiscate the vapes and issue a fine.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the end, the parent paid the fine and the son got fresh vapes.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The son displayed all the traits of a drug addict, including trying to get high on a daily basis, being unable to concentrate in school and threatening violence or suicide if the vapes were to be taken.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This, coupled with the articles I read at the time, suggested etomidate should be classified as a drug and I made this suggestion.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think it is important for us to set out clearly what will happen once we get to this stage next year.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If there is a public step down in the seriousness with which we treat this, barely months after the crackdown, that may signal to traffickers that it is safe to resume business once again.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I understand, for Minister of Health Ong Ye Kung, that new legislation is contemplated under MOH deal with this matter but if the penalties and measures appear to be a step down from what is available under the Misuse of Drugs Act, this may still send the wrong signal to traffickers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This episode with etomidate also reveals the potent force of our laws and also what happens if a drug-like substance is not captured by them.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think we may need to consider if we need more flexible laws which not only have a list of banned substances but also sets out some general principles of when a hitherto, unclassified substance may be considered a drug, say, if it meets certain objective requirements.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This general provision may help to capture new substances and allow Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) to move more swiftly when new substance comes into circulation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In relation to scams, while the prospect of waging wars in foreign countries with the operators of scam centres may be a stretch too far for Singapore to do alone, I think it is important for us to take all available steps against the arms and legs of scam operators.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This was similar to the approach taken to combat unlicensed money lending more than a decade ago which has almost eradicated the threat from our heartlands.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, many scams are also being done on social media platforms, including Facebook and Telegram.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We are one of the safest countries in the world but in the face of organised transnational crime, we need to remain on our guard and deal with ever-evolving threats.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the last part of my speech, I touch on a deeply personal matter for many Singaporeans, job security.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The President's address sets out the challenges Singapore faces in a changed world, in particular, with a looming trade war sparked by US tariffs and the rise of AI.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One major risk to Singaporeans from these developments is the loss of jobs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore has generally had a very low unemployment rate.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While we were expecting an economic slowdown, this has not materialised yet and the latest labour market report for the second quarter of 2025 shows a resilient labour market.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Government has introduced a slew of well thought through initiatives to address these matters.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This includes the great programme to assist fresh graduates to get work experience if they have difficulty getting jobs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The idea of governments paying private employers to reduce their risk in hiring fresh graduates is a novel support solution.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Likewise, the Mid-career SkillsFuture Grant is there as a support cushion for those who may lose jobs or need to upgrade later in life.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Over my years in this House, I have also spoken up for stronger labour protection in our laws.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I had suggested legislating anti-discrimination laws and retrenchment benefits.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Government has moved forward on these, initially through the tripartite framework, with guidelines on both.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Stronger labour laws change the relationship and negotiating positions as between employers and employees.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Generally, having less legislation creates a freer market with employers having less inhibitions to hire and employees having less incentives to stay at an employer.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This, however, may result in a more transactional relationship between both, resulting in less willingness for employers to invest in employees since they may leave after being trained and less downside for employees for leaving.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On the other hand, if there is legislation that, for example, gives employees legislated redundancy or retirement benefits, employees will have less incentive to leave their employer since these benefits generally kick in only when the employee is made redundant or retired.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These may be linked to their years in service, typically say anywhere from a week to a month worth of pay per year of service.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This creates incentives for employees to stay with their employer and for employers to invest in their employees for a long-term relationship.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Legislated retirement benefits is a suggestion to pay employees at the time they retire, a sum based on their years in service.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Similar to a redundancy benefit in concept, save that it will be paid to all employees at the time of retirement.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This would reduce some of the "cliff" effect that long serving employees currently face in that if they are made redundant before they are 65, they are likely to get a substantial payout pegged to each year of service, based on the current guidelines.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On the other hand, if they are made redundant after 65, say, when they are re-employed, they will not get any redundancy benefits.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On the other hand, if retirement benefits are legislated, every employee knows they will get a good payout at the time they reach retirement age and the cliff effect will not be there.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The upshot of these suggested changes is to gently incentivise longer term relationship between employers and employees by tying financial incentives to long-term employment.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This will also hopefully give employees more security in their employment and some guarantees of payouts in the event they lose their jobs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I support the President’s address and look forward to supporting the work of the Government in overcoming the challenges in the years ahead.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As we look back in our nation’s formation journey, Singapore has indeed been on a "remarkable journey".

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To me, ours is also a never-ending journey because this House can, and will always strive to do better for our Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I pause at this juncture, to register my utmost gratitude towards all who have given me the opportunity and support to continue in this journey as a Member of this 15th Parliament.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With the support of our residents and working hand in hand with our ever-supportive community partners, we turned those missions into reality and built an active, vibrant Woodgrove where residents are proud to call home.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Today, I want to build on this foundation, drawing inspiration from the Draft Master Plan 2025 and the Prime Minister’s recent National Day Rally to transform the northern parts of Singapore, where Marsiling-Yew Tee GRC is situated, into a more family-friendly and senior-friendly, live, work, learn and play hub, while ensuring our residents can realise their Singapore dreams through determination, passion and lifelong learning.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: During the National Day Rally, Prime Minister dispelled the myth that the North is "ulu".

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But I want to take this opportunity to share a few additional ideas and suggestions which I have received from my Woodgrove residents to transform our north even further.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Over the course of this week, many have spoken about how we can become a "we first" society.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many have suggestions on how our Government can do more or better.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On behalf of the Government, I would like to thank everyone for your suggestions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our Public Service will certainly study all these suggestions and especially the new ideas.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As I listened to all the speeches, it struck me that all of us share pretty much the same objectives.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We want a fairer society, we want to give opportunities to everyone regardless of their background.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We want a Singapore that will not only survive, but thrive.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And, most importantly, we want to give our best to the next generation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We may differ here and there on some details and those we can discuss.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Sometimes, our differences are not as large as we make them out to be and certainly, none of us have a monopoly on care, compassion or fairness.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But ultimately, true victory for us is not about winning arguments in this House.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: True victory for us is winning the trust of our people, uplifting lives and delivering a better future for all of us; or in Chinese, we would say: "口舌之争, 胜负一时, 行动耕耘, 造就一世", which means, arguments bring momentary victory; actions forge lifetime success.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It will be up to all of us, as fellow Singaporeans, to encourage each other to step forward and take responsibility for one another.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As mentioned, “we first” does not mean there being no place for individual aspirations or expressions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Instead, it is about mobilising the full spectrum of our society’s capabilities, creativity and commitment to overcome our challenges ahead.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our Government will continue to lead where it must and can.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We will strive to do more and do better.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I always remember this that was taught to me since young.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: No one can do everything, but everyone can do something.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In his speech earlier, Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim spoke about chess and its life lessons for his son and Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It inspired me to think about the game of weiqi, a board game played with white and black pieces.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The aim of the game is to fence off more territory than the opponent.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, unlike chess, weiqi pieces are all the same and are used similarly in the game.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Just like the weiqi pieces, our individual efforts may be insignificant, but together, all of us play a part and any one of us can be that strategic piece in the evolving formation to win the game as the circumstances evolve.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Perhaps, that is the Singapore that we can all aspire to.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Today, I will share my reflections on ways we can deliver with our people and progress towards a "we first" society.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The world will change even more and faster in the years to come.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We must prepare ourselves for a much wider range of scenarios than ever before, including dangerous discontinuities.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should not count on assumptions that have guided us for decades, nor should we expect other countries to respect international laws and norms as in the past.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The question is: how do we anticipate, pre-empt and respond collectively?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I say collectively, because I think all of us can and need to contribute.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And if I may, I can suggest four lines of effort for all of us.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Compared to the past, we all can now access much more information and travel more widely.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, we must not fall into the trap of our own echo chamber to confirm our own biases.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There will also be no shortage of external influences that attempt to shape our views and hopefully our positions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have seen this being played out over the Russian-Ukraine conflict, the situation in the Middle East and even closer to home, in the conflicts and contestations that have happened of late.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Only when we deeply understand ourselves and the world we are operating in, can we come up with propositions that are relevant for our partners so that we can be of value-add in the relationship.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is a discipline to not just view or read what the search engine algorithms throw at us.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I do not need them to write long reports when they come back.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Just come back with a fresh perspective, a new idea that can enrich us.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I learned this when I was younger and I was deployed to Indonesia after the Fall of Suharto, where our greatest fear was what would happen to this big country.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We made it a discipline to travel out of Jakarta at least seven days a month.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We made sure that we covered as many provinces and as many regional commands as we could, making new friends, understanding the diversity of perspective and never kid ourselves that just because we have been to Jakarta and Bali, that therefore we seem to understand Indonesia.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And today, that same principle must apply – just because we have been to Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, it does not mean that we understand China; and just by going to California and New York does not make us an expert in the US.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With my recent trips to both China and the US, we could understand and appreciate the diversity of views and the complex dynamics even within their own country.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If we do not understand or appreciate this deeply, we cannot come up with value propositions that will make us relevant.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, while we adapt our approaches, we must remain a consistent and principled partner where we can continuously strengthen our relevance for others to want to partner us.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am sure we want to partner everybody, but that is different from other people wanting to partner us.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And this applies in the security and economics domains.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We are ultimately responsible for our own destiny.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But we must earn our right to determine that destiny.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Only when we are successful, can we have the right to choose our path and not be held ransom or hostage by others.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Then, we can truly say that we will neither be bribed nor bullied.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: That is something that we have to earn.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Being neutral and principled are two different concepts.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Trying to maintain neutrality and balancing without principles, will only invite contesting larger powers to put more pressure on us to try and shift our "balancing point".

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: You can imagine if two giants are pulling at us and if we are just trying to maintain neutral, when one side squeezes us a bit harder, we move a bit to that side.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It would just encourage them to squeeze us just as hard so that we move back to the balancing position.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And that is why I always encourage all Singaporeans to make a nuanced but important distinction.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How then, can we remain relevant and earn our right to be principled, and be valued on the global stage?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to have our own perspectives and not be a mouthpiece or proxy for others.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to develop capabilities that cannot be easily replicated by others – the ability to think and execute long-term, the ability to build trust internally and externally, and the ability to foster cohesion amidst diversity.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But ultimately, we need real capabilities, in all domains from economics to defence, for others to see value in working with us.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: External parties have asked me what makes the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) strong.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our disciplined investment in equipment and people over the years have certainly helped.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But to me, the biggest advantage the SAF has over many others is that we can draw upon the talent and energies of our entire nation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The best operational and technical ideas do not just come from our regulars, technicians or scientists.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They come from all over, our Full-time National Servicemen (NSFs), NSmen and even pre-enlistees.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Today if you fly the unmanned aerial vehicles in the SAF, you will see them using a console that is exactly like the Playstation console.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This idea came about many years ago from our pre-enlistees.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They helped us to design the systems even before they came into NS.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And when they came into NS, the system was ready for them.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When I was a young officer, the first person to introduce computers into our battle planning process was not a regular.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: He was an NSman working at Apple and he was wondering why we were still using pen and paper.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: That is the power of the SAF, drawn from our people.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is the concept of all of us chipping in, a mindset of delivering with to build defence capabilities ahead of time.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For Ministry of Defence (MINDEF) and the SAF, we will continue to spend wisely and consistently as warfare is redefined, we will make judicious decisions on what to buy, what to build and what to co-develop with partners.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We will also need to evolve our capability development and acquisition processes to deliver at speed.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Timeliness, rather than perfection, matters more very often.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: By strengthening our indigenous capacities and developing unique value propositions, we will position ourself as a partner of choice in the capability development, technological innovation and supply chain resilience.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Today, this is exactly what DSO National Laboratories (DSO), Defence Science and Technology Agency (DSTA), and ST Engineering are doing.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We aim to go beyond a buyer-seller relationship whenever we deal with others.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Together, we must contribute as a whole of nation to safeguard our future.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Every one of us is in some way MINDEF and everyone one of us is also an ambassador, a little ambassador, acting on behalf of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs when we interact with the rest of the world.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We share with the world what we stand for, how we do business and why they should trust in us.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: No one deals with Singapore out of charity or sympathy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many Members in this House will be familiar with our experiences during COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I was then the Minister for Trade and Industry.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: During the crucial moments, very often my team and I have to call up partners to ask for essentials, to ask for people to sell us essentials.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Even if we had or more money than others, we did not always get what we wanted.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Only when we had what our partners needed, could we trade for what we wanted.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is a lesson that is seared in the minds of all the officers of the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) for generations to come.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For our economy to be more resilient, many have talked about the need to diversify.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, we must also be aware that diversification comes with risks, it requires resources and it requires our ability to attract and work with talent beyond our own.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Imagine if Singapore only focused on one or two sectors.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Then surely, we will have enough of our own people to staff all of those positions in that one or two sectors and achieve critical mass.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But when we say that we want to diversify our economy for us to be more resilient, when we say that we want to give more options to our younger generation to chase their dreams in diverse sectors, then we need many more sectors.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have to admit that it will not be easy for us to achieve critical mass in all of these sectors unless we are able to network with the global talent to compliment the best in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is why we must continue our efforts to make sure that we remain an attractive partner for others to want to work with us.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We must continue to grow our homegrown talent so that we can remain an attractive partner.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If we do not have people that can match up to the best in the world, I am not sure many people will want to partner us.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But there is also an opportunity amidst the crisis now.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As the world becomes a more dangerous place, our attractiveness to talent can actually reinforce our competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But we will need to carefully balance our needs of integration with competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is not a binary option of zero or one.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And this will be a topic I am sure we will come back to in this House for many more times to come.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is about balance and never about a binary option.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On the other hand, when long standing platforms or networks no longer work, we will have to set up alternative networks to uphold a more integrated global trading and investment system.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many years ago, we pioneered comprehensive Free Trade Agreements that went beyond traditional tariff reductions to encompass services, investment and regulatory cooperation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As the support for free trade and globalisation fray, we will work with like-minded partners to create new plurilateral and multilateral networks.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is our little contribution to try and uphold the Global Free Trade Order which is in our interest.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As tariffs and retaliatory tariffs reshape trade and investment flows, there is also an opportunity for us if we can position ourselves as a reliable and resilient partner.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many companies are now talking about their "plus one" strategy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We can expect to win some and lose some.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I believe we can still be net positive if we play to our strengths.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have seen this already being played out in various sectors that are visited in the aerospace Maintenance, Repair and Operations (MRO), semi-conductor sector.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We win some, we lose some, but we can be net positive.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To do so, we will double down on our man-made competitive advantages.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is often said that Singapore has no natural resources, but Singapore has many man-made competitive advantages.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: AI is part of this important effort where we have the programme called “AI for Everyone”.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Just as what we have done for the computerisation drive in the late 1980s, early 1990s.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, our ability to uphold the rule of law for investors to have the confidence to mobilise their capital, aggregate their talent and protect their IP here will remain important and more so than ever before.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Third, having a stable Government and forward-looking Public Service, so that investors can be confident that we think and execute long-term.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is especially for investments like pharmaceuticals and semi-conductors that require a long gestation period.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To conclude this section, may I also say that actually, we are all also part of the Economic Development Board (EDB) and MTI.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Whenever we interact with people overseas, we will also need to pitch for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I can understand the concerns that many of us have in the job security front.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But the best strategy for us is to make sure that we continue to attract good quality investments so that our people can continue to have the diverse opportunities that they would aspire towards.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And all of us, at every opportunity, will have to chip in.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And that is why we say we are all part of MTI and EDB.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On the social side, let me say that Singapore's success has never been about economic growth alone.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Ultimately, economic growth needs to translate into growing the overall pie for Singaporeans, creating good jobs and enabling all Singaporeans to improve our lives.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Every one of us aspire to do better.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We also want our next generation to do even better than ourselves.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is only human nature for parents and grandparents to want to give our best that we can do for our children and grandchildren.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, we must not forget that our successes are not just because of our hard work and abilities.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is built upon our society and the help that we receive along the way which enable us to achieve what we have.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And therefore, when we are successful, all of us must remember that we have responsibilities towards those who are further behind.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As societies mature and become more developed, there is always the risk that resources, as well as disadvantages, get passed on from generation to generation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This accentuates inequality and reduces social mobility, and stratification happens.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We see this happening in many countries throughout history.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But I think all of us in this House would be united in saying that we do not want to see this happening in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And therefore, the more successful we are, the greater the dangers we face, and the more we need to double and re-double our efforts to break this inter-generational transfer of disadvantage, which many Members have spoken about.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As Minister Desmond Lee has spoken yesterday, we will do what we can as a Government, we will try to do more and do better.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We are doing this not just only in the early years of a child's life.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We are systematically combing through the entire life cycle of a person to see how we can help everyone who needs the help to break that cycle.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In fact, the more successful we are, the more we need to try.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But we must also see things in context.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our challenge is not so much that the people in our society are left behind, that they are not catching up with the world.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If you look at the statistics, our challenge is slightly different from others.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our challenge is that our gap is not a result of the bottom falling way off the chart.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our gap is the result of the top being even further.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, we must not make our own children feel that just because they are relatively behind, that somehow they have failed themselves or failed us.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our average is way beyond the global average.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Even the students from our so-called neighbourhood schools, as some of you would describe them, are generally above the global average.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We hosted the International Summit of the Teaching Profession last year.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When other people host us, they showed us their best school.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When we hosted them, we showed them 10 schools every day.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Any school that they chose, we would allow them to walk into the school.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many of them asked us, "Are you showing us your best school?" We said, "No, we are just showing you the diversity of our schools.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We will show you schools from Raffles Institution to Northlight, because all of them will have different challenges and we will have different curricula for all of them." In fact, one remarked that he was most impressed, because in Singapore, your zip code does not determine or overwrite your genetic code, as in some other countries.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But having said this, we are not done.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: All these programmes by themselves will not be enough.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Each of us, even those of us who may not feel that we have the most, can and must contribute in our own ways to support those with less and to uplift the less privileged to keep our society mobile.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is why we mobilise the time, talent and treasures of people to complement what the Government and taxation already do.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This reminds all of us that we have agency and responsibility towards one another.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But not all of us will get the same.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am sure Members of the House also agree with me that it also does not make sense for all of us to get the same.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Different strokes for different folks, each according to our needs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I think all of us can agree on this.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, let us not be divided by invidious comparisons when this is actually executed.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am sure Members of the House would have this experience going around in your hawker centres and markets.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Very often, someone would come up and ask, "Minister or MP, why is it this month, I did not get this payout that my neighbour got?" You can try your very best to explain why, but unfortunately, we are all humans and very often, invidious comparisons set in.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If we are true to what we believe, that we should do more to help those with less, then when we execute this, we must also help to explain this to everyone.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In Singapore, we do not have a single yardstick for success.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When I was the Minister for Education, I have seen the diversity of talents among Singaporeans, and this is what makes our country resilient and special.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a society, we must truly respect and reward the diversity of strengths and celebrate excellence in multiple fields.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For many of us, all this have been said very often.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Maybe it is useful for us to start our conversations with our children, not with: "What grades did you get in school?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How did you score compared to your peers?" I have always asked two questions whenever I meet the students when I was Minister for Education.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First question is, "Can you tell me what makes you special?" Because you can score however many "As" that you have, but if throughout the education process, you do not know what are your strengths and weaknesses are, and what makes you special, then I do not think we have succeeded.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And for a child to know that he or she has something special is very important.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When I was in school, I thought my mathematics was so-so.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One day, my teacher told me, "Your mathematics is quite good!" Suddenly, I was like, "Wow, my mathematics is quite good.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I must study harder." Simple words, changed my life.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The other question that I think we can encourage ourselves to ask our children, especially during Chinese New Year, Hari Raya, Deepavali is, not so much, "What have you achieved?", but "Where would you like to make a contribution?" For every Singaporean child growing up to know that, regardless of your station in life, you can make a contribution because you have something special in you, and collectively each of us, just like the weiqi pieces, we will come up with that winning formulation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, let us respect the diversity of talents and let us encourage our children to understand what makes them special, and how each and every one of them can make a special contribution.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Beyond Government policies and institutions, such as the Ethnic Integration Policy, NS and our schools, I think many Members have also highlighted the need for us to enhance our interactions, so that we truly get out of our comfort zone to get to know people who are different from us.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And more importantly, through this process, to try and find common ground, based on mutual respect.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is something that is a work in progress and something that as MPs, we all need to do.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: HDB can build us the most beautiful houses and towns, but it is us, the residents who will build the most heartwarming homes and communities.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, let us not be trapped by this incessant comparison among ourselves.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Yes, look at the right side of the bell curve to try to aspire to do better, but never forget our responsibility to those who are on the left side of the bell curve.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singapore has done reasonably well by most measures, but we must never be complacent.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our accomplishments are not predictions for future successes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And there are many matrices of whether a country, a government has done well.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Sometimes, we get a good ranking – let it not get into our head.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Sometimes, we do not get such a good ranking – it is time for introspection, but also never let it get into our hearts and wear us down.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There will always be room for us to improve.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But what is most important is for us to have the confidence and the conviction to do what we think is right for our people, by our people and to see it through.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In Singapore, we have the privilege of being able to execute this consistently for many years.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: That was what I shared with my overseas counterparts when I was in MOE.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They always thought that Singapore has some brilliant technology or system, but the truth is, whatever MOE can deliver today, we thank our predecessors who have seen it through consistently for us.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Take the example of the adoption of technology, digitalisation and AI.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: An example is the way that the Government is serving citizens and businesses.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Whether it is our ServiceSG centres, Municipal Services Office or the new SME Pro-Enterprise office, these are just ways that we are working across Government to make services simpler, more connected and more helpful to our people and businesses.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Each of these reflect our determination to deliver greater value and to do better things with our finite resources.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On the other hand, we must not copy blindly, but be bold enough to look for our own solutions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We did not copy others, but we found our own way.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Even for something like the CPF, we have continuously evolved it over the years, expanding from retirement savings to meet housing and healthcare needs, while providing stronger safety nets for our elderly and vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Each of these decisions took courage, clarity of vision, a willingness to chart our path and the conviction to see it through.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is not just as simple as just plucking an idea from some other country and copying it.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I come now to the most difficult challenge.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Delivering with our people will require a new approach from our Government and a new understanding with our people.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The first thing he told me was, "Chun Sing, when you become the Minister, you must consult widely.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But remember, after you have consulted 100 people and you have chosen your idea, you must go back to the other 99 to explain to them why their ideas were not chosen.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Each of them must be convinced why their ideas were not chosen after they have given you their feedback".

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: All of us will contribute ideas just like in this House, but not all ideas may be implemented in full or in part.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We will take collective decisions and we hope that we will move forward in the right spirit.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The other thing is this: as we evolve our processes and services at speed to achieve timeliness and relevance, we must also accept that we may not always achieve that perfect or flawless product or policy, if there was ever such a thing.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What matters most is to learn and keep improving fast, rather than to let the pursuit of perfection paralyse us from timely deployment of new solutions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is the spirit that CPF Board and Government Technology Agency (GovTech) have taken.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: No one in CPF Board or GovTech will claim that their product is perfect or flawless.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They all know that they have to keep improving, but they all know that they have to be timely and relevant in their delivery.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As the challenges confronting Singapore are multi-dimensional, we will also need the Public Service to acquire new capabilities.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Public Service will continue to remain open and attract diverse talent, including mid-careerists, and provide opportunities for officers to gain exposure to the private and people sectors.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Now increasingly important, we must also expose our officers to the International Organisations to understand how the world is evolving and we must secure a place at the table where international rules are made.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Otherwise, as the saying goes, we are either at the table or on the menu.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: From the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) in the 1970s to the recent debate on climate change, the biodiversity beyond national jurisdiction and the cyber domains, many new rules are made on the international front.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We will need our people to be au fait with the developments in order to secure our interest.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have been fortunate so far that we have been able to afford what we wanted to, while delivering high quality services, because we run a tight ship.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have been prudent with our spending, saving a little year after year, invested these savings wisely and gradually built up our Reserves; and instituted rigorous safeguards to protect the Reserves, making sure that we only spent the money that we really needed to.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, just as over the course of this week's debate, we have heard many new ideas, many new demands and all of that will ultimately translate into some form of resources needs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hence, in this House, we must be judicious in deciding how to spend our public funds and be honest with ourselves about the trade-offs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Everything we want to do more of, means something less for either current or future needs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should not and cannot pretend that there is somehow, somewhere a free lunch.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I can appreciate the calls for us to spend more, given our challenges.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the 1960s, we had the British withdrawal east of the Suez Canal.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My grandmother and her family lost their job overnight from Sembawang Naval Base.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the 1970s, we had two oil crises.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the 1980s, we had the economic recession.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the 1990s, we had the Asian Financial Crisis.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the 2000s, we had the Global Financial Crisis.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And of course, we had Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS) and COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Did any of our Pioneers say that life was too hard and therefore we would not save for the next generation?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: No matter how tough those times were and arguably there were moments that were even tougher than now, they have made it a point to save up for us.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I think it is only responsible of us to similarly hold on to this spirit.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Of course, the Government will do what we can to spend carefully to take care of this generation but let us not forget that we must also take care of future generations, although they are not here to cast their votes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is what makes Singapore special – that we do not define success by how well we do for ourselves in this generation only.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We define our success by how well we enable the next generation to do even better than us.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the many Committees of Supply debate that I have attended in this House, we have not had to make very difficult decisions on what to cut in order to fund what we want to do more.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But it is not the natural order of things in most countries.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Every grant, expenditure and subsidy has a long tail.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Once committed, they will be hard to remove.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The challenges ahead will be different from those in the past, but the core principles remain: to anticipate change, to be bold, innovative and pragmatic in finding solutions that work for us and keep building a fair, strong, united Singapore for generations to come.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our Pioneer Generation and founding leaders have built a nation upon the foundations of conviction, not convenience.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: From the very beginning we have faced challenges head on, never shirking our responsibility to one another, nor to future generations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Together we have weathered storms, overcome adversity and emerged stronger each time.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Through crises such as the Asian Financial Crisis and COVID-19 pandemic, we stood together – Government, businesses, community, students – supporting one another, overcoming challenges and always promising one another that we will emerge stronger.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These experiences have shown that our strength lies in our unity and our ability to trust and work with one another.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Recently, I gave out scholarships to this year's Public Service Commission (PSC) and MINDEF scholarship recipients.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I shared with them this simple message: "When I was awarded the scholarship, it was SG23.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I told this generation of scholarship holders, "You are taking up the scholarship at SG60.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Your job is to get us to SG100 and beyond".

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I also told them, "If you have a doubt, there is a cooling-off period.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am proud of them, because I did not promise them that if they get a scholarship with the PSC or MINDEF, that life would be a bed of roses.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There is nothing that guarantees that we would get to SG100.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I also told them that, well, if I am so lucky to be able to see the fireworks at the Padang on 9 August 2065, maybe they can spare me a pair of National Day Parade tickets.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Last but not least, we will live by these values that we will put our collective before self, putting the "we" before "me" and taking care of one another, so that we can be truly proud that if you want to have the best opportunities in life, anywhere in the world, you want to be born in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Your insights and ideas will help shape our policies and programmes going forward.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As we chart our path towards SG100 and beyond, let us stand united in purpose in this House.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For there will be no challenge too great, too daunting that we cannot overcome together.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Together, we will write the next chapter of Singapore's history.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This Government will not only deliver for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Before I proceed, may I first convey my gratitude for the privilege of moving the Motion of Thanks to the President for the speech delivered on behalf of the Government at the opening of the First Session of this 15th Parliament.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is a great honour to move this Motion and an equal privilege to round up this debate as we begin the new term.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I also would like to thank all Members of this House.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I have been heartened by the depth of conviction and the clarity of purpose in these speeches and together they reflect our collective resolve to improve the lives of Singaporeans and to advance the progress of our nation as one united people, something that was shared by Minister Chan Chun Sing just now.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: He set out four key challenges and reminded us that our path forward depends on unity, nurturing a "we first" society built on trust, resilience and a shared purpose.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: As I listen to the many thoughtful speeches delivered, similar to what Minister Chan has mentioned earlier, it became clear that certain themes resonated strongly.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And hence, I had to quickly remove quite a lot of my paragraphs – thanks to Minister Chan.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In closing, I will draw out these key themes.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This span geopolitics, the economy, technology and demographics, and they will test us deeply.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Senior Minister of State Sim Ann spoke of great power, contestation, rising protectionism and geopolitical conflicts.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong reminded us that countries are turning inwards while transformative technologies such as AI, coupled with our limits on land, carbon and energy, demand fresh thinking.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling emphasised the need for Singapore to remain relevant.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Ms He Ting Ru cautioned that past performance is no guarantee of future success.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The Leader of Opposition pointed to the weight of international and domestic pressures.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng reminded us that defence and diplomacy are the twin pillars of our survival and Mr Vikram Nair shared the need for allies and self-reliance on defence.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Transformation begins with recognition of the urgency to change.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Not because they are not working, but because we need to prepare for the challenges ahead.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: He spoke of securing footholds in emerging sectors and making Singapore a “home for leading firms.” Ms Jessica Tan and Mr Shawn Huang pointed to intelligent robotics as another exciting frontier.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon spoke of the importance of tripartism in making transformation possible.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In education, Ms Goh Hanyan and Mr Goh Pei Ming urged a relook at how we raise our children and review our exam system, a call echoed by Mr Darryl David and supported by Minister Desmond Lee.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We face huge uncertainty and we must transform to survive.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But as Mr Shawn Loh observed, the President's address over the past two decades have consistently emphasised these same enduring themes: global uncertainty, economic vitality, care for an ageing population, building an inclusive society and then, keeping Singapore united.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The key point is this: as a small nation, we will always face these enduring challenges and emerging trends.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We must be ready to pivot, ready to adapt and ready to transform as circumstances evolve.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Our survival depends on staying agile, nimble and ever ready to renew ourselves.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This acceptance of constant transformation is not optional.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is the very foundation of Singapore’s survival and progress.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The second theme is the diversity of support across society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: While we agree transformation is necessary, Members also recognised that it brings both anxiety and hope.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Above all, there was consensus that growth must never come at the expense of leaving anyone behind.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: For our youths, Miss Rachel Ong, Minister of State Dinesh Vasu Dash and Mr Ng Shi Xuan spoke of creating safe avenues for expression and more community-driven care.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Goh Hanyan and Minister of State Goh Pei Ming highlighted learning through play, while Mr David Hoe suggested “curiosity credits” to spark exploration.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Mr Jackson Lam and Mr Darryl David stressed the need to support marginalised youth and equip them with the skills for the global economy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Together with Ms Jessica Tan, I also called for structured apprenticeships to bridge technical learning with real-world experience.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Ms Lee Hui Ying added that even more "senior youths" in their 20s face the burdens of adulting as they enter the workforce. "Senior youths" is a new term that I learnt yesterday.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Unfortunately, I no longer fall within the group.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Mr Henry Kwek talked about turning technology disruption into opportunities for all.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Ms Yeo Wan Ling and Dr Wan Rizal highlighted the recognition of lower-wage and platform workers, while Ms Gho Sze Kee, Ms Eileen Chong, Ms Poh Li San, myself and others raised support for professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs) and young graduates.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: For our seniors, Mr Alex Yeo, Mr Dennis Tan and Mr Saktiandi Supaat raised concerns on retirement adequacy and dignified living.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Mr Cai Yinzhou proposed the formation of the elder corp to leverage on the skills and wisdom of seniors.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Ms Choo Pei Ling spoke about healthcare and support for those living with illnesses.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Families too were highlighted by Ms Cassandra Lee, Minister of State Jasmin Lau and Ms Valerie Lee, who spoke of the struggles of working parents and the sandwich generation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Ms Elysa Chen and Ms Diana Pang shared the need for stronger support for caregivers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: As Ms Valerie Lee memorably said, we must build a society where “caregiving is supported, not merely tolerated.” Ms Denise Phua shared the need for mandating inclusive designs and deliberately designing in opportunities for the special need individuals, one which I also mentioned in investing in inclusive technology.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Members also raised wider issues: Dr Hamid Razak and Ms Nadia Samdin on mental health, Mr Edward Chia and myself on SME costs of doing business, Mr Shawn Loh on growing our local MNCs, Mr Victor Lye on hawkers, and Mr Gabriel Lam and Senior Parliamentary Secretary Eric Chua on giving second chances.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: On sustainability, Senior Minister of State Zaqy Mohamad, Ms Nadia Samdin and Ms Valerie Lee called for protecting our environment and strengthening food and water resilience.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Even support for animals found a voice through Ms Lee Hui Ying and others.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Every segment of our society – the youths, the workers, our special needs individuals, seniors, families, businesses small and large, and even our natural environment – has found representation in this Chamber.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: That is the strength of our Parliament: no group forgotten, every voice heard.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Inclusiveness and care must guide us as we move forward.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The third theme is that in almost every speech, as Minister Chan Chun Sing has mentioned, MPs spoke about more can be done, and there are three variants of it.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: More can be done, full stop; more can be done with a suggestion; more can be done with a suggestion and something that we do less of.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And more can be done not because nothing is being done, but because Members believe more is required.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
